======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Anti-vaccine activism
======================================================================

{{Short description|None}}
{{Use American English|date=July 2024}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=July 2024}}
[[File:Anti vaccination league postcards.jpg|thumb|upright=1.2|Postcards for the [[National Anti-Vaccination League]]]]
{{Vaccination|expanded=issues}}

'''Anti-vaccine activism''', which collectively constitutes the "'''anti-vax'''" or "'''anti-vaxx'''" '''movement''',<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Benoit |first1=Staci L. |last2=Mauldin |first2=Rachel F. |date=November 17, 2021 |title=The "anti-vax" movement: a quantitative report on vaccine beliefs and knowledge across social media |journal=BMC Public Health |volume=21 |issue=1 |page=2106 |doi=10.1186/s12889-021-12114-8 |doi-access=free |issn=1471-2458 |pmc=8596085 |pmid=34789206}}</ref> is a set of organized activities expressing opposition to [[vaccination]]. These [[Social networking|collaborating networks]] often seek to increase [[vaccine hesitancy]] by disseminating [[vaccine misinformation]] and [[Disinformation attack|disinformation]].<ref name="Carpiano">{{cite journal |last1=Carpiano |first1=Richard M |last2=Callaghan |first2=Timothy |last3=DiResta |first3=Renee |last4=Brewer |first4=Noel T |last5=Clinton |first5=Chelsea |last6=Galvani |first6=Alison P |last7=Lakshmanan |first7=Rekha |last8=Parmet |first8=Wendy E |last9=Omer |first9=Saad B |last10=Buttenheim |first10=Alison M |last11=Benjamin |first11=Regina M |last12=Caplan |first12=Arthur |last13=Elharake |first13=Jad A |last14=Flowers |first14=Lisa C |last15=Maldonado |first15=Yvonne A |display-authors=3 |date=2023 |title=Confronting the evolution and expansion of anti-vaccine activism in the USA in the COVID-19 era |journal=Lancet |volume=401 |issue=10380 |pages=967–970 |doi=10.1016/S0140-6736(23)00136-8 |issn=0140-6736 |pmc=9981160 |pmid=36871571 |last16=Mello |first16=Michelle M |last17=Opel |first17=Douglas J |last18=Salmon |first18=Daniel A |last19=Schwartz |first19=Jason L |last20=Sharfstein |first20=Joshua M |last21=Hotez |first21=Peter J}}</ref> As a [[social movement]], it employs tools ranging from traditional [[news media]] to various forms of [[Internet|online communication]]. Activists have primarily—though not exclusively—focused on opposing childhood vaccination, and have sought to expand their influence from niche subgroups into national [[Politics|political debates]].<ref name="Carpiano" />

Ideas that later coalesced into anti-vaccine activism predate vaccines themselves.<ref name="Tolley"/> The movement, along with [[Fringe science|fringe]] doctors, has propagated various myths and [[Conspiracy theory|conspiracy theories]], alongside misinformation and disinformation. These efforts have significantly increased vaccine hesitancy and influenced [[public policy]] regarding the ethical, legal, and medical aspects of vaccination. In contrast, there is no substantive debate or hesitancy within mainstream [[Medicine|medical]] circles about the benefits of vaccination; the [[scientific consensus]] is "clear and unambiguous" in favor of vaccines.<ref name="Dubé">{{cite journal |last1=Dubé |first1=Ève |last2=Ward |first2=Jeremy K. |last3=Verger |first3=Pierre |last4=MacDonald |first4=Noni E. |title=Vaccine Hesitancy, Acceptance, and Anti-Vaccination: Trends and Future Prospects for Public Health |journal=Annual Review of Public Health |date=April 1, 2021 |volume=42 |issue=1 |pages=175–191 |doi=10.1146/annurev-publhealth-090419-102240 |pmid=33798403 |s2cid=232774243 |language=en |issn=0163-7525 |quote="the scientific and medical consensus on the benefits of vaccination is clear and unambiguous"|doi-access=free }}</ref> Despite this consensus, the anti-vaccine movement has been partially successful in distorting the public understanding of science in [[popular culture]].<ref name="Carpiano"/>

== History ==

=== 18th and 19th century ===
Ideas that would eventually coalesce into anti-vaccine activism have existed for longer than vaccines themselves.<ref name="Tolley">{{cite book |last1=Tolley |first1=Kim |url=https://www.press.jhu.edu/books/title/12694/vaccine-wars |title=Vaccine Wars: The Two-Hundred Year Fight for School Vaccinations |date=2023 |publisher=Johns Hopkins University Press |isbn=978-1-4214-4761-2 |edition=1 |access-date=November 29, 2023 |archive-date=December 8, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231208100224/https://press.jhu.edu/books/title/12694/vaccine-wars |url-status=live }}</ref> Some philosophical approaches (e.g. [[homeopathy]], [[vitalism]]) are incompatible with the microbiological paradigm that explains how the immune system and vaccines work. [[Vaccine hesitancy]] and anti-vaccine activism exist within a broader context that involves cultural tradition, religious belief, approaches to health and disease, and political affiliation.<ref name="Dubé" />

Opposition to [[variolation]] for [[smallpox]] (a predecessor to vaccination) was organized as early as the 1720s around the premise that vaccination was unnatural and an attempt to thwart divine judgment.<ref>{{cite web |date=September 22, 2019 |title=Smallpox |url=https://www.medicalheritage.org/resource-sets/vaccines/smallpox/ |publisher=Medical Heritage Library |access-date=May 8, 2023 |archive-date=May 13, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230513041506/https://www.medicalheritage.org/resource-sets/vaccines/smallpox/ |url-status=live }} Citing Edmund Massey, "A Sermon against the Dangerous and Sinful Practice of Inoculation, preached at St. Andrew's Holborn", July 8, 1722.</ref> [[Vaccination and religion|Religious arguments against inoculation]], the earliest arguments against vaccination, were soon advanced.<ref>{{cite book |author=Andrew Dickson White |url=http://abob.libs.uga.edu/bobk/whitem10.html |title=A History Of The Warfare Of Science With Theology In Christendom |date=1896 |publisher=Appleton & Co |location=New York |chapter=Chapter X. Theological Opposition To Inoculation, Vaccination, And The Use Of Anaesthetics |access-date=September 27, 2023 |archive-date=September 17, 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080917184044/http://abob.libs.uga.edu/bobk/whitem10.html }}</ref> For example, in a 1722 sermon entitled "The Dangerous and Sinful Practice of Inoculation", the English theologian Reverend Edmund Massey argued that diseases are sent by God to punish sin and that any attempt to prevent smallpox via inoculation is a "diabolical operation".<ref name="Early">
Early religious opposition:

* {{cite book |author=White AD |title=A History of the Warfare of Science with Theology in Christendom |publisher=Appleton |year=1896 |location=New York |chapter=Theological opposition to inoculation, vaccination, and the use of anæsthetics |chapter-url=http://defendgaia.org/bobk/whitem10.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230223152248/http://defendgaia.org/bobk/whitem10.html |archive-date=February 23, 2023 }}
* {{cite journal |vauthors=Bazin H |date=September 2001 |title=The ethics of vaccine usage in society: lessons from the past |journal=Endeavour |volume=25 |issue=3 |pages=104–108 |doi=10.1016/S0160-9327(00)01376-4 |pmid=11725304}}
* {{cite journal |vauthors=Noble M |date=December 2005 |title=Ethics in the trenches: a multifaceted analysis of the stem cell debate |journal=Stem Cell Reviews |volume=1 |issue=4 |pages=345–376 |doi=10.1385/SCR:1:4:345 |pmid=17142878 |s2cid=21775014}}</ref> It was customary at the time for popular preachers to publish sermons, which reached a wide audience. This was the case with Massey, whose sermon reached North America, where there was early religious opposition, particularly by [[John Williams (New England minister)|John Williams]]. A greater source of opposition there was [[William Douglass (physician)|William Douglass]], a medical graduate of [[Edinburgh University]] and a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]], who had settled in Boston.<ref name="Williams">{{Cite book |last=Williams |first=Gareth |title=Angel Of Death; the story of smallpox |publisher=Palgrave Macmillan |year=2010 |isbn=978-0-230-27471-6 |location=Basingstoke, UK |pages=87–94 |name-list-style=vanc}}</ref>{{rp |114–22}}
[[File:The cow pock.jpg|thumb|upright=1.4|right|[[James Gillray]]'s 1802 [[caricature]] of [[Edward Jenner]] vaccinating patients who feared it would make them sprout cowlike appendages.]]
Vaccination itself was invented by British physician [[Edward Jenner]], who published his findings on the efficacy of the practice for smallpox in 1798. By 1801, the practice had been widely endorsed in the scientific community and by several world leaders. Philadelphia physician [[John Redman Coxe]], noting that even then false accounts were circulated of negative effects of vaccination, wrote, 
<blockquote>"Such are the falsehoods which impede the progress of the brightest discovery which has ever been made! But the contest is in vain! Time has drawn aside the veil which obstructed our knowledge of this invaluable blessing; and in the examples of the Emperor of Constantinople, of the Dowager Empress of Russia, and the King of Spain, we may date the downfall of further opposition."<ref>[[John Redman Coxe]], ''Practical Observations on Vaccination, Or, Inoculation for the Cow-pock'' (1802), p. 125.</ref></blockquote>
 
Coxe's expectation of an end to opposition to vaccination proved premature, and through much of the nineteenth century, the principles, practices and impact of vaccination were matters of active scientific debate. The principles behind vaccination were not clearly understood until the end of the nineteenth century. The importance of hygiene in the preparation, storage, and administration of vaccines was not always understood or practiced. Reliable statistics on vaccine efficacy and side effects were difficult to obtain before the 1930s.<ref name="Dubé" />

==== Anti-Compulsory Vaccination League ====
In the [[United Kingdom]], the [[Vaccination Act 1853]] ([[16 & 17 Vict.]] c. 100) required that every child be vaccinated within three or four months of birth.<ref name="Tizard">{{cite book |last1=Tizard |first1=Ian R. |title=A History of Vaccines and their Opponents |date=2023 |publisher=Academic Press |isbn=978-0-443-13434-0 |pages=167–179 |chapter=Chapter 12 – The rise of anti-vaccine societies in Britain |chapter-url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/B9780443134340000188}}</ref> It set a precedent for the state regulation of physical bodies, and was fiercely resisted.<ref name="Durbach">{{cite book |last1=Durbach |first1=Nadja |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=TtMDl7n8iq8C |title=Bodily Matters: The Anti-Vaccination Movement in England, 1853–1907 |date=2005 |publisher=Duke University Press |isbn=978-0-8223-3423-1 |pages=41–42 |language=en |access-date=September 29, 2023 |archive-date=October 7, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241007013816/https://books.google.com/books?id=TtMDl7n8iq8C |url-status=live }}</ref>
The following year, in 1854, John Gibbs published the first anti-compulsory-vaccination pamphlet, ''Our Medical Liberties''.<ref name="Cawkwell">{{cite journal |last1=Cawkwell |first1=Philip B. |last2=Oshinsky |first2=David |date=October 2015 |title=Childhood vaccination requirements: Lessons from history, Mississippi, and a path forward |url=http://jamesrobertdeal.org/wp-content/uploads/mississippi-vaccine-history-2015.pdf |journal=Vaccine |volume=33 |issue=43 |pages=5884–5887 |doi=10.1016/j.vaccine.2015.08.087 |pmid=26409142 |access-date=September 29, 2023 |archive-date=October 2, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231002171748/http://jamesrobertdeal.org/wp-content/uploads/mississippi-vaccine-history-2015.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref>
By the 1860s, anti-vaccinationism in Britain was active in the working class, labor aristocracy, and lower middle class. It had become associated with alternative medicine and was part of a larger culture of social and political dissent that included both labor unions and religious dissenters.<ref name="Durbach" /><ref name="Fitzpatrick">{{cite journal |last1=Fitzpatrick |first1=Michael |date=2005 |title=Review: The Anti-Vaccination Movement in England, 1853–1907. Nadja Durbach |journal=Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine |publisher=Duke University Press |volume=98 |issue=8 |pages=384–385 |issn=0141-0768 |pmc=1181850 |isbn=0-8223-3423-2}}</ref>

In June 1867, the publication "Human Nature" campaigned in the United Kingdom against "The Vaccination Humbug",<ref name="vac">{{Cite web |date=April 20, 2003 |title=Philip Hoare: When you play virtual war games, spare a thought for the real veterans |url=http://www.independent.co.uk/voices/commentators/philip-hoare-when-you-play-virtual-war-games-spare-a-thought-for-the-real-veterans-115851.html |url-access=subscription |url-status=live |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220618/http://www.independent.co.uk/voices/commentators/philip-hoare-when-you-play-virtual-war-games-spare-a-thought-for-the-real-veterans-115851.html |archive-date=June 18, 2022 |access-date=September 13, 2020 |website=The Independent |language=en}}</ref> reporting that many petitions had been presented to Parliament against Compulsory Vaccination for [[smallpox]], including from parents who alleged that their children had died through the procedure, and complaining that these petitions had not been made public. The journal reported the formation of the Anti-Compulsory Vaccination League "To overthrow this huge piece of physiological absurdity and medical tyranny", and quoted Richard Gibbs (a cousin of John Gibbs), who ran the Free Hospital at the same address, as stating "I believe we have hundreds of cases here, from being poisoned with vaccination, I deem incurable. One member of a family dating syphilitic symptoms from the time of vaccination, when all the other members of the family have been clear. We strongly advise parents to go to prison, rather than submit to have their helpless offspring inoculated with scrofula, syphilis, and mania".<ref name="vac" />

Notable members of the Anti-Compulsory Vaccination League included [[James Burns (Spiritualist)|James Burns]], [[George Dornbusch]] and [[Charles Thomas Pearce]].<ref>Barrow, Logie. (2016). ''Independent Spirits Spiritualism and English Plebeians, 1850–1910''. Routledge. pp. 186–187. {{ISBN|978-1-138-66565-1}}</ref> After the death of Richard B. Gibbs in 1871, the Anti-Compulsory Vaccination League "languished"<ref name="Tizard" /> until 1876 when it was revived under the leadership of [[Mary Hume-Rothery]] and the Rev. W. Hume-Rothery.<ref name="mary">{{Cite ODNB|title=Rothery, Mary Catherine Hume (1824–1885), campaigner for medical reform and author|url=https://www.oxforddnb.com/view/10.1093/ref:odnb/9780198614128.001.0001/odnb-9780198614128-e-49483|year=2004|language=en|doi=10.1093/ref:odnb/49483|isbn=978-0-19-861412-8|access-date=May 28, 2020}}</ref> The Anti-Compulsory Vaccination League published the ''Occasional Circular'' which later merged into the ''National Anti-Compulsory Vaccination Reporter''.<ref name="Porter 1988">{{cite journal |last1=Porter |first1=Dorothy |last2=Porter |first2=Roy |year=1988 |title=The Politics of Prevention: Anti-Vaccinationism and Public Health in Nineteenth-Century England |journal=[[Medical History (journal)|Medical History]] |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=231–252 |doi=10.1017/s0025727300048225 |pmc=1139881 |pmid=3063903}}</ref>

==== Anti-Vaccination Society of America ====
In the United States, many states and local school boards established immunization requirements, beginning with a compulsory school vaccination law in [[Massachusetts]] in 1855.<ref name="Cawkwell" /> 
The [[Anti-Vaccination Society of America]] was founded in 1879, after a visit to the United States by British anti-vaccine activist [[William Tebb]],<ref name="history">{{cite news |date=March 8, 2012 |title=History of Anti-vaccination Movements |url=http://www.historyofvaccines.org/content/articles/history-anti-vaccination-movements |access-date=February 11, 2015 |publisher=[[College of Physicians of Philadelphia]] |archive-date=July 10, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180710235227/https://www.historyofvaccines.org/content/articles/history-anti-vaccination-movements |url-status=live }}</ref> and opposed compulsory [[smallpox vaccination]] for smallpox from the final decades of the 19th century through the 1910s.<ref name="cpp">{{cite news |author=Karie Youngdahl |date=March 8, 2012 |title=The Anti-Vaccination Society of America |url=http://www.historyofvaccines.org/content/blog/anti-vaccination-society-america-correspondence |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150302065350/http://www.historyofvaccines.org/content/blog/anti-vaccination-society-america-correspondence |archive-date=March 2, 2015 |access-date=February 11, 2015 |publisher=[[College of Physicians of Philadelphia]]}}</ref> During this period, smallpox vaccination was the only form of vaccination that was widely practiced, and the society published a periodical opposing it, called ''Vaccination''.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Anti-Vaccination Society of America: Correspondence &#124; History of Vaccines |url=https://www.historyofvaccines.org/content/blog/anti-vaccination-society-america-correspondence |access-date=August 10, 2023 |archive-date=January 23, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190123171725/https://www.historyofvaccines.org/content/blog/anti-vaccination-society-america-correspondence }}</ref>

A series of American legal cases, beginning in various states and culminating with that of Henning Jacobson of Massachusetts in 1905, upheld the mandating of compulsory smallpox vaccination for the good of the public. The court ruled in ''[[Jacobson v. Massachusetts]]'' that "the liberty secured by the Constitution of the United States to every person within its jurisdiction does not import an absolute right in each person to be, at all times and in all circumstances, wholly freed from restraint. There are manifold restraints to which every person is necessarily subject for the common good".<ref name="Cawkwell" />

==== London Society for the Abolition of Compulsory Vaccination ====
[[File:London Society for the Abolition of Compulsory 1880s.png|thumb|"Death the Vaccinator", published by the London Society for the Abolition of Compulsory Vaccination in the late 1800s]]
In 1880, William Tebb enlarged and reorganized the Anti-Compulsory Vaccination League in the UK with the formation of the London Society for the Abolition of Compulsory Vaccination, with William Young as secretary.<ref name="Porter 1988" /> The ''Vaccination Inquirer'', established by Tebb in 1879, was adopted as the official organ of the Society.<ref name="Porter 1988" /> A series of fourteen "Vaccination Tracts" was begun by Young in 1877 and completed by [[James John Garth Wilkinson|Garth Wilkinson]] in 1879. William White was the first editor of the ''Vaccination Inquirer'' and after his death in 1885, he was succeeded by Alfred Milnes.<ref name="Porter 1988" /> [[Frances Hoggan]] and her husband authored an article for the ''Vaccination Inquirer'' in September 1883 which argued against compulsory vaccination.<ref>[https://www.blfhs.co.uk/index.php/newsletters/send/2-newsletters/164-newsletter-70 "Frances Hoggan MD 1843–1927"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231008111954/https://www.blfhs.co.uk/index.php/newsletters/send/2-newsletters/164-newsletter-70 |date=October 8, 2023 }}. Breconshire Local & Family History Society (BLFHS) Cymdeithas Hanes Lleol a Theuluoedd Brycheiniog Newsletter 70 – October 2017.</ref> The London Society focused on lobbying parliamentary support in the 1880s and early 1890s.<ref name="Porter 1988" /> They gained support from several members of the [[House of Commons of the United Kingdom|House of Commons]] of which the most prominent was [[Peter Alfred Taylor]], the member for [[Leicester (UK Parliament constituency)|Leicester]], which was described as the "Mecca of antivaccination".<ref>{{cite journal |year=1902 |title=Antivaccination Propaganda: The Bane And Its Antidote |url=https://archive.org/details/britishmedicaljo1902unse/page/n95/mode/2up |journal=[[The BMJ|The British Medical Journal]] |volume=2 |issue=2166 |pages=50–52 |doi=10.1136/bmj.2.2166.50 |pmc=2401264 |pmid=20760356 |s2cid=32125316}}</ref>

==== The National Anti-Vaccination League ====
The UK movement grew, and as the influence of the London Society overshadowed the Hume-Rotherys and it took the national lead,<ref name="mary" /> it was decided in February 1896 to re-form the Society as [[The National Anti-Vaccination League]].<ref name="Porter 1988" /> [[Arthur Phelps (anti-vaccinationist)|Arthur Phelps]] was elected as president.<ref name="Porter 1988" /> In 1898, the league took on a school leaver named [[Lily Loat]], who was elected as the league's Secretary by 1909.<ref name="loat">{{Cite ODNB|title=Loat, Lily (1879/80–1958), anti-vaccination activist|url=https://www.oxforddnb.com/view/10.1093/ref:odnb/9780198614128.001.0001/odnb-9780198614128-e-50749|access-date=September 13, 2020|year=2004|language=en|doi=10.1093/ref:odnb/50749|isbn=978-0-19-861412-8|last1=Kramer|first1=Molly Baer}}</ref> In 1906, [[George Bernard Shaw]] wrote a supportive letter to the National Anti-Vaccination League, equating methods of vaccination with "rubbing the contents of the dustpan into the wound".<ref>Yang, Jennifer. (2014). [https://sites.utexas.edu/ransomcentermagazine/2014/10/16/vaccination-policies/ "Contemporary debates on vaccination policies have historical parallels in Ransom Center's collections"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211030210347/https://sites.utexas.edu/ransomcentermagazine/2014/10/16/vaccination-policies/ |date=October 30, 2021 }}. Ransom Center Magazine. Retrieved June 20, 2021.</ref>

==== Anti-Vaccination League of America ====
In 1908, the Anti-Vaccination League of America was created by [[Charles M. Higgins]] and industrialist [[John Pitcairn Jr.]],<ref name="Wallach 2015">Walloch, Karen L. (2015). ''The Antivaccine Heresy: Jacobson v. Massachusetts and the Troubled History of Compulsory Vaccination in the United States''. University of Rochester Press. pp. 4–5. {{ISBN|978-1-58046-537-3}}</ref> with anti-vaccination campaigns focused on New York and [[Pennsylvania]].<ref name="Wallach 2015" /> Members were opposed to compulsory vaccination laws.<ref name="Colgrove 2006">Colgrove, James. (2006). ''State of Immunity: The Politics of Vaccination in Twentieth-Century America''. University of California Press. pp. 52–54. {{ISBN|978-0-520-24749-9}}</ref> Higgins was the League's chief spokesman and pamphleteer.<ref>Altenbaugh, Richard J. (2018). ''Vaccination in America: Medical Science and Children's Welfare''. Palgrave. p. 51. {{ISBN|978-3-319-96348-8}}</ref> Historian James Colgrove noted that Higgins "attempted to overturn the New York State's law mandating vaccination of students in public schools".<ref name="Colgrove 2006" /> The League should not be confused with the [[Anti-Vaccination Society of America]], which was formed in 1879.<ref name="Wallach 2015" /> Higgins was criticized by medical experts for spreading misinformation and ignoring facts as to the efficacy of vaccination.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Tolley |first1=Kim |date=May 2019 |title=School Vaccination Wars: The Rise of Anti-Science in the American Anti-Vaccination Societies |journal=History of Education Quarterly |volume=59 |issue=2 |pages=161–194 |doi=10.1017/heq.2019.3 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |date=February 6, 1915 |title=Antivaccinationists in Albany |url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=hvd.32044103075685;view=1up;seq=526 |journal=Journal of the American Medical Association |volume=64 |issue=6 |page=520 |access-date=September 27, 2023 |archive-date=September 6, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230906142051/https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=hvd.32044103075685;view=1up;seq=526 |url-status=live }}</ref> The League dissolved after the death of Higgins in 1929.<ref>Colgrove, James. (2006). ''State of Immunity: The Politics of Vaccination in Twentieth-Century America''. University of California Press. p. 74. {{ISBN|978-0-520-24749-9}}</ref>

=== 20th century ===
[[File:Rally of the Anti-Vaccination League of Canada.jpg|thumb|Rally of the Anti-Vaccination League of Canada in 1919]]
Anti-vaccine activism ebbed for much of the twentieth century, but never completely vanished. In the UK, the National Anti-Vaccination League continued to publish new issues of its journal until 1972,<ref name="loat" /> by which time the global campaign for [[smallpox eradication]] through vaccination had made the disease so uncommon that compulsory vaccination for smallpox was no longer required in the United Kingdom.<ref name="Millward">{{cite book |last1=Millward |first1=Gareth |url=https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK545998/ |title=Vaccinating Britain: Mass vaccination and the public since the Second World War [Internet] |date=2019 |publisher=Manchester University Press |language=en |chapter=Chapter 2: Smallpox |access-date=October 2, 2023 |archive-date=October 7, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241007013817/https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK545998/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

New vaccines were developed and used against diseases such as [[diphtheria]] and [[whooping cough]]. In the UK, these were often introduced on a voluntary basis, without arousing the same kind of anti-vaccination response that had accompanied compulsory smallpox vaccination.<ref name="Millward" />

In the United States, numerous measles outbreaks occurred in the 1960s and 1970s and were more frequent in states that lacked mandatory vaccination requirements. This led to calls in the 1970s for a national-level vaccination requirement for children entering schools.
[[Joseph A. Califano Jr.]] appealed to state governors, and by 1980, all 50 states legally required vaccination for school entrance. Many of these laws allowed exemptions in response to lobbyists. In New York State, a 1967 law allowed exemptions from receiving [[polio vaccine]] for members of religious organizations such as [[Christian Scientists]].<ref name="Cawkwell" />

=== 21st century ===

==== Lancet MMR autism fraud ====
{{main|Lancet MMR autism fraud}}
Anti-vaccine activism in the 2000s regained prominence through exploratory research by [[Andrew Wakefield]] based on 12 selected cases. He then made claims about a link between the [[MMR vaccine and autism]].<ref name="Wang" /> These claims were subsequently extensively investigated and found to be false, and the original study turned out to be based on faked data. The [[scientific consensus]] is that there is no link between the MMR vaccine and [[autism]], and that the MMR vaccine's benefits in preventing [[measles]], [[mumps]], and [[rubella]] greatly outweigh its potential risks.<ref name="Cochrane2020">{{cite journal |last1=Di Pietrantonj |first1=C |last2=Rivetti |first2=A |last3=Marchione |first3=P |last4=Debalini |first4=MG |last5=Demicheli |first5=V |date=November 22, 2021 |title=Vaccines for measles, mumps, rubella, and varicella in children. |journal=Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews |volume=2021 |issue=11 |article-number=CD004407 |doi=10.1002/14651858.CD004407.pub5 |pmc=8607336 |pmid=34806766}}</ref>

The idea of an autism link was first suggested in the early 1990s and came to public notice largely as a result of the 1998 ''Lancet'' MMR autism fraud, which Dennis K Flaherty at the University of Charleston characterized as "perhaps the most damaging medical hoax of the last 100 years".<ref>{{cite journal |last=Flaherty |first=Dennis K. |date=October 2011 |title=The vaccine-autism connection: a public health crisis caused by unethical medical practices and fraudulent science |journal=The Annals of Pharmacotherapy |volume=45 |issue=10 |pages=1302–1304 |doi=10.1345/aph.1Q318 |issn=1542-6270 |pmid=21917556 |s2cid=39479569}}</ref> The fraudulent research paper authored by Wakefield and published in ''[[The Lancet]]'' falsely claimed the vaccine was linked to [[colitis]] and [[autism spectrum]] disorders. The paper was retracted by ''Lancet'' in 2010<ref>{{cite journal |last=Dyer |first=Clare |date=February 2, 2010 |title=''Lancet'' retracts Wakefield's MMR paper |url=https://www.bmj.com/content/340/bmj.c696 |journal=BMJ |volume=340 |article-number=c696 |doi=10.1136/bmj.c696 |issn=0959-8138 |pmid=20124366 |s2cid=43465004 |access-date=September 28, 2023 |archive-date=March 25, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190325210816/https://www.bmj.com/content/340/bmj.c696 |url-status=live |url-access=subscription }}</ref> but is still cited by anti-vaccine activists.<ref>{{cite web |title=Public Health Education |url=https://sites.psu.edu/kyraschwartztechwriting/2015/10/15/public-health-education/ |access-date=February 3, 2019 |publisher=Kyra Schwartz Technical Writing Samples |archive-date=May 13, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210513052350/https://sites.psu.edu/kyraschwartztechwriting/2015/10/15/public-health-education/ }}</ref>

The claims in the paper were widely reported,<ref name="Goldacre-2008">{{cite news |last=Goldacre |first=B. |date=August 30, 2008 |title=The MMR hoax |url=https://www.theguardian.com/society/2008/aug/30/mmr.health.media |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150206073230/http://www.theguardian.com/society/2008/aug/30/mmr.health.media |archive-date=February 6, 2015 |access-date=August 30, 2008 |work=The Guardian |location=London }} [http://www.badscience.net/2008/08/the-medias-mmr-hoax/ Alt URL] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100416141256/http://www.badscience.net/2008/08/the-medias-mmr-hoax/ |date=April 16, 2010 }}</ref> leading to a sharp drop in vaccination rates in the UK and Ireland. Promotion of the claimed link, which continued in anti-vaccination propaganda for the next three decades despite being refuted,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hussain |first1=Azhar |last2=Ali |first2=Syed |last3=Ahmed |first3=Madiha |last4=Hussain |first4=Sheharyar |year=2018 |title=The Anti-vaccination Movement: A Regression in Modern Medicine |journal=Cureus |volume=10 |issue=7 |article-number=e2919 |doi=10.7759/cureus.2919 |issn=2168-8184 |pmc=6122668 |pmid=30186724 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=Gross |first=Liza |date=May 26, 2009 |title=A Broken Trust: Lessons from the Vaccine–Autism Wars |journal=PLOS Biology |volume=7 |issue=5 |article-number=e1000114 |doi=10.1371/journal.pbio.1000114 |issn=1544-9173 |pmc=2682483 |pmid=19478850 |doi-access=free}}</ref> was estimated to have led to an increase in the incidence of [[measles]] and [[mumps]], resulting in deaths and serious permanent injuries.<ref name="McIntyre">{{cite journal |last1=McIntyre |first1=P |last2=Leask |first2=J |year=2008 |title=Improving uptake of MMR vaccine |journal=The BMJ |volume=336 |issue=7647 |pages=729–730 |doi=10.1136/bmj.39503.508484.80 |pmc=2287215 |pmid=18309963}}</ref><ref name="Pepys">{{Cite journal |vauthors=Pepys MB |date=December 2007 |title=Science and serendipity |journal=Clinical Medicine |volume=7 |issue=6 |pages=562–578 |doi=10.7861/clinmedicine.7-6-562 |pmc=4954362 |pmid=18193704}}</ref> Following the initial claims in 1998, multiple large [[epidemiologic]]al studies were undertaken. Reviews of the evidence by the [[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]],<ref name="CDC-MMR-autism">{{cite web |date=August 22, 2008 |title=Measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine |url=http://cdc.gov/vaccinesafety/concerns/mmr_autism_factsheet.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080407015528/http://www.cdc.gov/vaccinesafety/concerns/mmr_autism_factsheet.htm |archive-date=April 7, 2008 |access-date=December 21, 2008 |publisher=Centers for Disease Control and Prevention}}</ref> the [[American Academy of Pediatrics]], the [[Institute of Medicine]] of the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|US National Academy of Sciences]],<ref name="IOM">{{cite book |last=Institute of Medicine (US) Immunization Safety Review Committee |url=http://www.iom.edu/Reports/2004/Immunization-Safety-Review-Vaccines-and-Autism.aspx |title=Immunization Safety Review: Vaccines and Autism |date=May 17, 2004 |publisher=[[Institute of Medicine]] of the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]] |isbn=978-0-309-09237-1 |doi=10.17226/10997 |pmid=20669467 |bibcode=2004nap..book10997I |access-date=June 13, 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091026043205/http://www.iom.edu/reports/2004/immunization-safety-review-vaccines-and-autism.aspx |archive-date=October 26, 2009 }}</ref> the UK [[National Health Service]],<ref name="MMRthefacts">{{cite web |year=2004 |title=MMR The facts |url=http://www.dh.gov.uk/en/Publicationsandstatistics/Publications/PublicationsPolicyAndGuidance/DH_4002972 |archive-url=http://webarchive.nationalarchives.gov.uk/20130107105354/http://www.dh.gov.uk/en/Publicationsandstatistics/Publications/PublicationsPolicyAndGuidance/DH_4002972 |archive-date=January 7, 2013 |access-date=September 19, 2007 |publisher=[[National Health Service|NHS]] Immunisation Information}}</ref> and the [[Cochrane Library]]<ref name="Cochrane2020" /><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Di Pietrantonj |first1=Carlo |last2=Rivetti |first2=Alessandro |last3=Marchione |first3=Pasquale |last4=Debalini |first4=Maria Grazia |last5=Demicheli |first5=Vittorio |date=April 20, 2020 |title=Vaccines for measles, mumps, rubella, and varicella in children |journal=The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews |volume=4 |issue=4 |article-number=CD004407 |doi=10.1002/14651858.CD004407.pub4 |issn=1469-493X |pmc=7169657 |pmid=32309885}}</ref> all found no link between the MMR vaccine and autism.<ref name="Klaherty">{{cite journal |last1=Flaherty |first1=Dennis K |date=October 2011 |title=The vaccine-autism connection: a public health crisis caused by unethical medical practices and fraudulent science |journal=Annals of Pharmacotherapy An investigation by journalist [[Brian Deer]] found that Wakefield, the author of the original research paper linking the vaccine to autism, had multiple undeclared [[conflicts of interest]],<ref name="Deer04a">''The Sunday Times'' 2004:

* {{cite news |last1=Deer |first1=Brian |date=February 22, 2004 |title=Revealed: MMR research scandal |url=https://www.thetimes.com/article/revealed-mmr-research-scandal-7ncfntn8mjq |access-date=January 31, 2025 |work=The Times |location=London}}
* {{cite web |last1=Deer |first1=Brian |year=2007 |title=The Lancet scandal |url=http://briandeer.com/mmr-lancet.htm |access-date=September 23, 2007 |archive-date=September 27, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110927000055/http://briandeer.com/mmr-lancet.htm |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="Patent-and-test-results">2004 BBC documentary:
* {{cite web |last1=Deer |first1=Brian |year=2007 |title=The Wakefield factor |url=http://briandeer.com/wakefield-deer.htm |access-date=September 23, 2007 |archive-date=September 26, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110926235810/http://briandeer.com/wakefield-deer.htm |url-status=live }}
* {{cite journal |last1=Deer |first1=Brian |year=2004 |title=Dispatches. MMR: What They Didn't Tell You |journal=The BMJ |volume=329 |issue=7477 |page=1293 |doi=10.1136/bmj.329.7477.1293 |pmc=534460}}</ref> had manipulated evidence,<ref name="Deer2009">{{cite news |last1=Deer |first1=Brian |date=February 8, 2009 |title=MMR doctor Andrew Wakefield fixed data on autism |url=http://www.thesundaytimes.co.uk/sto/public/news/article148992.ece |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140227222152/http://www.thesundaytimes.co.uk/sto/public/news/article148992.ece |archive-date=February 27, 2014 |access-date=February 9, 2009 |work=The Sunday Times |location=London}}</ref> and had broken other ethical codes. After a subsequent 2.5-year investigation, the [[General Medical Council]] ruled that Wakefield had acted "dishonestly and irresponsibly" in doing his research, carrying out unauthorized procedures for which he was not qualified, and acting with "callous disregard" for the children involved.<ref name="BBC GMC result">{{cite news |last=Triggle |first=Nick |date=January 28, 2010 |title=MMR scare doctor 'acted unethically', panel finds |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/health/8483865.stm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100128033313/http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/health/8483865.stm |archive-date=January 28, 2010 |access-date=January 28, 2010 |work=BBC News}}</ref> 
Wakefield was found guilty by the General Medical Council of serious professional misconduct in May 2010, and was struck off the [[General Medical Council#Registering doctors to practise in the UK|Medical Register]], meaning he could no longer practise as a physician in the UK.<ref name="Triggle, Nick">{{cite news |last1=Triggle |first1=Nick |date=May 24, 2010 |title=MMR doctor struck off register |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/health/8695267.stm |access-date=May 24, 2010 |work=[[BBC News]] |archive-date=April 11, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170411105047/http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/health/8695267.stm |url-status=live }}</ref>

The ''Lancet'' paper was partially retracted in 2004 and fully retracted in 2010, when ''Lancet''{{'}}s editor-in-chief [[Richard Horton (editor)|Richard Horton]] described it as "utterly false" and said that the journal had been deceived.<ref name="Boseley, Sarah">{{cite news |last1=Boseley |first1=Sarah |date=February 2, 2010 |title=Lancet retracts 'utterly false' MMR paper reports in the ''[[British Medical Journal]]'',<ref name="Deer fixed">{{cite journal |author=Deer B |year=2011 |title=How the case against the MMR vaccine was fixed Wakefield continues to promote anti-vaccine beliefs and conspiracy theories in the United States.<ref name="Boseley">{{cite news |last1=Boseley |first1=Sarah |date=July 18, 2018 |title=How disgraced anti-vaxxer Andrew Wakefield was embraced by Trump's America |url=https://www.theguardian.com/society/2018/jul/18/how-disgraced-anti-vaxxer-andrew-wakefield-was-embraced-by-trumps-america |work=The Guardian |access-date=September 29, 2023 |archive-date=December 16, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201216084528/https://www.theguardian.com/society/2018/jul/18/how-disgraced-anti-vaxxer-andrew-wakefield-was-embraced-by-trumps-america |url-status=live }}</ref> 
In February 2015, Wakefield denied that he bore any responsibility for the [[Measles outbreaks in the 21st century#United States|measles epidemic]] that started at [[Disneyland]] among unvaccinated children that year. He also reaffirmed his discredited belief that "MMR contributes to the current autism epidemic".<ref name="Ziv">{{cite news |last=Ziv |first=Stav |date=February 10, 2015 |title=Andrew Wakefield, Father of the Anti-Vaccine Movement, Responds to the Current Measles Outbreak for the First Time |url=http://www.newsweek.com/2015/02/20/andrew-wakefield-father-anti-vaccine-movement-sticks-his-story-305836.html |access-date=February 17, 2015 |work=[[Newsweek]] |archive-date=July 31, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170731161218/http://www.newsweek.com/2015/02/20/andrew-wakefield-father-anti-vaccine-movement-sticks-his-story-305836.html |url-status=live }}</ref> By that time, at least 166 measles cases had been reported. [[Paul Offit]] disagreed, saying that the outbreak was "directly related to Dr. Wakefield's theory".<ref name="Axelrod">{{Cite news |last=Axelrod |first=Jim |date=February 10, 2015 |title=Doctor blames discredited autism research for measles outbreak |url=http://www.cbsnews.com/news/doctor-blames-discredited-autism-vaccine-link-research-for-measles-outbreak/ |access-date=February 16, 2015 |work=[[CBS News]] |archive-date=May 22, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190522035346/https://www.cbsnews.com/news/doctor-blames-discredited-autism-vaccine-link-research-for-measles-outbreak/ |url-status=live }}</ref> 
Wakefield and other anti-vaccine activists were active in the American-Somali community in Minnesota, where a drop in vaccination rates was followed by the largest measles outbreak in the state in nearly 30 years in 2017.<ref name="Dyer">{{cite journal |last1=Dyer |first1=Owen |date=May 16, 2017 |title=Measles outbreak in Somali American community follows anti-vaccine talks |journal=BMJ |language=en |volume=357 |article-number=j2378 |doi=10.1136/bmj.j2378 |issn=1756-1833 |pmid=28512183 |s2cid=27124692 }}</ref><ref name="Sohn">{{cite news |last1=Sohn |first1=Emily |date=May 3, 2017 |title=Understanding The History Behind Communities' Vaccine Fears |url=https://www.npr.org/sections/health-shots/2017/05/03/526595475/understanding-the-history-behind-communities-vaccine-fears |work=NPR |access-date=September 29, 2023 |archive-date=February 21, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180221072444/https://www.npr.org/sections/health-shots/2017/05/03/526595475/understanding-the-history-behind-communities-vaccine-fears |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="Lena">{{cite news |last1=Sun |first1=Lena H. |date=April 9, 2023 |title=Anti-vaccine activists spark a state's worst measles outbreak in decades |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/national/health-science/anti-vaccine-activists-spark-a-states-worst-measles-outbreak-in-decades/2017/05/04/a1fac952-2f39-11e7-9dec-764dc781686f_story.html |newspaper=Washington Post |access-date=September 29, 2023 |archive-date=December 21, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201221020322/https://www.washingtonpost.com/national/health-science/anti-vaccine-activists-spark-a-states-worst-measles-outbreak-in-decades/2017/05/04/a1fac952-2f39-11e7-9dec-764dc781686f_story.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

The anti-vaccination movement was historically apolitical, but in the 2010s and 2020s, the movement in the United States has increasingly targeted conservatives.<ref name="Carpiano" /> As measles outbreaks increased, so did calls to eliminate exemptions from vaccine administration. As of 2015, 19 American states had suggested legislation to eliminate or increase the difficulty of exemptions.<ref name="Cawkwell" /> Concurrently, American anti-vaccine activists reached out to libertarian and right-leaning groups such as the [[Tea Party movement]] to broaden their base. While earlier anti-vaccination activists focused on health impacts and safety of vaccines, recent themes increasingly involve philosophical arguments about liberty, medical freedom and parental rights.<ref name="Carpiano" />

With the growing anti-vaccine movement from the 2010s onwards, the United States has seen a resurgence of certain [[vaccine-preventable diseases]]. The measles virus lost its elimination status in the US as the number of cases continued to rise in the late 2010s, with 17 outbreaks in 2018 and 465 in 2019 (as of April 4, 2019).<ref>{{Cite web |date=March 24, 2019 |title=Measles {{!}} Cases and Outbreaks {{!}} CDC |url=https://www.cdc.gov/measles/cases-outbreaks.html |access-date=March 28, 2019 |website=www.cdc.gov |archive-date=February 13, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150213145736/http://www.cdc.gov/measles/cases-outbreaks.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

==== 2019 and 2025 measles outbreaks ====
Vaccine hesitancy led to declining rates of vaccination for measles, culminating in the [[2019–2020 measles outbreaks]]. The most significant of these, in proportion to the national population, was the [[2019 Samoa measles outbreak]].<ref name="Samoa Ministry">{{Cite web |date=November 16, 2019 |title=Ministry of Health Press Release 1 – Measles Epidemic – Samoa |url=https://reliefweb.int/report/samoa/ministry-health-press-release-1-measles-epidemic |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191201145254/https://reliefweb.int/report/samoa/ministry-health-press-release-1-measles-epidemic |archive-date=December 1, 2019 |website=ReliefWeb |publisher=Government of Samoa |language=en}}</ref>

In July 2018, two 12-month-old children died in Samoa after receiving incorrectly prepared MMR vaccinations.<ref name="Samoa Telegraph">{{Cite news |last=Deer |first=Brian |date=December 20, 2019 ==== COVID-19 pandemic activism ====

During the [[COVID-19 pandemic]], anti-vaccine activists undertook various efforts to hinder people who wanted to receive the vaccines, with such activities occurring in countries including Australia,<ref>{{cite web |last1=Cassidy |first1=Caitlin |date=October 4, 2021 |title=Anti-vaxxers trying to disrupt Australian rollout by making fake vaccine bookings |url=https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/2021/oct/05/anti-vaxxers-trying-to-disrupt-australian-rollout-by-making-fake-vaccine-bookings |work=[[The Guardian]] |access-date=May 5, 2023 |url-status=live }}</ref> Israel,<ref>{{cite web |date=February 8, 2021 |title=Facebook removes anti-vaxxer group encouraging public to make fake appointments |url=https://www.timesofisrael.com/facebook-removes-anti-vaxxer-group-encouraging-public-to-fake-appointments/ |work=[[The Times of Israel]]}}</ref> the United Kingdom,<ref>{{cite web |last1=Roberts |first1=Lizzie |date=December 19, 2021 |title=Anti-vaxxers block-book appointments to stop people getting In some instances, anti-vaccine rhetoric has been traced to [[State-sponsored terrorism|state-sponsored]] [[internet troll]] activities designed to create social dissension.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Howard |first1=Jacqueline |date=August 24, 2018 |title=Why Russian trolls stoked US vaccine debates |url=https://www.cnn.com/2018/08/23/health/russia-trolls-vaccine-debate-study/index.html |work=[[CNN]] |access-date=May 5, 2023 |archive-date=May 5, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230505225456/https://www.cnn.com/2018/08/23/health/russia-trolls-vaccine-debate-study/index.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Dettmer |first1=Jamie |date=November 18, 2021 |title=Russian Anti-Vaccine Disinformation Campaign Backfires |url=https://www.voanews.com/a/russian-anti-vaccine-disinformation-campaign-backfires/6318536.html |work=[[Voice of America]] |access-date=May 5, 2023 |archive-date=May 5, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230505225458/https://www.voanews.com/a/russian-anti-vaccine-disinformation-campaign-backfires/6318536.html |url-status=live }}</ref> Worldwide, foreign disinformation campaigns have been associated with declining vaccination rates in target countries.<ref name="Wilson">{{cite journal |last1=Wilson |first1=Steven Lloyd |last2=Wiysonge |first2=Charles |date=October 1, 2020 |title=Social media and vaccine hesitancy |url=https://gh.bmj.com/content/5/10/e004206 |journal=BMJ Global Health |language=en |volume=5 |issue=10 |article-number=e004206 |doi=10.1136/bmjgh-2020-004206 |issn=2059-7908 |pmc=7590343 |pmid=33097547 |access-date=October 2, 2023 |archive-date=February 7, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210207170033/https://gh.bmj.com/content/5/10/e004206 |url-status=live }}</ref>
Anti-vaccine activism online, both before and during the pandemic, has been linked to extreme levels of falsehoods, rumors, hoaxes, and conspiracy theories.<ref name="Carpiano" /><ref name="Grimes">{{cite journal |last1=Grimes |first1=David Robert |date=March 12, 2021 |title=Medical disinformation and the unviable nature of COVID-19 conspiracy theories |journal=PLOS ONE |language=en |volume=16 |issue=3 |article-number=e0245900 |bibcode=2021PLoSO..1645900G |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0245900 |issn=1932-6203 |pmc=7954317 |pmid=33711025 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="Kata" />

Anti-vaccine activists have falsely claimed in social media posts that numerous deaths or injuries had to do with reactions to vaccines. In one highly publicized instance in early 2023, after Buffalo Bills football player [[Damar Hamlin]] experienced an in-game episode of [[commotio cordis]], there was an increase in rhetoric and disinformation from figures such as [[Charlie Kirk]] and [[Drew Pinsky]] making [[COVID-19 vaccine misinformation and hesitancy|unfounded claims]] about Hamlin's cardiac arrest and [[COVID-19 vaccine]]s.<ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Ecarma |first=Caleb |date=January 3, 2023 |title=Right-Wingers Are Exploiting Damar Hamlin's Medical Emergency to Push Anti-Vax Conspiracies |magazine=Vanity Fair |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Payton |first=L'oreal Thompson |date=January 3, 2023 |title=Blaming Damar Hamlin's cardiac arrest on the COVID vaccine is "wildly and |website=Fortune |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Loka |first=Gayathri |date=January 9, 2023 |title=False: Damar Hamlin collapsed due to COVID-19 vaccine poisoning. |language=en-gb |archive-date=February 4, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240204032041/https://www.logicallyfacts.com/en/fact-check/false-damar-hamlin-collapsed-due-to-covid-19-vaccine-poisoning |url-status=live }}</ref> In another 2023 incident, college basketball player [[Bronny James]] experienced cardiac arrest at the [[Galen Center]] at the [[University of Southern California]], leading to assertions that this was a result of receiving a COVID-19 vaccine; it was later revealed that the episode had been caused by a [[congenital heart defect]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Polacek |first=Scott |title=Bronny James' Collapse Caused
