}}</ref> Also, anti-vaccine activists believed [[Foo Fighters]] drummer [[Taylor Hawkins]] died in 2022 from the COVID-19 vaccine, while in actuality it was a drug overdose.<ref>{{cite web |last1=O'Rourke |first1=Ciara |date=March 29, 2022 |title=Social media post claims without evidence Foo Fighters drummer Taylor Hawkins died from COVID-19 |url=https://www.politifact.com/factchecks/2022/mar/29/facebook-posts/social-media-post-claims-without-evidence-foo-figh/ |website=PolitiFact}}</ref> In December 2023, ''The New York Times'' published a detailed investigation of the distortion and misrepresentation of the circumstances surrounding the death of 24-year-old George Watts Jr. by [[Robert F. Kennedy Jr.]] and other anti-vaccine activists.<ref>{{cite web |last=Thompson |first=Stuart A. |date=December 13, 2023 |title=Behind the birth of an anti-vaccine story |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2023/12/13/technology/covid-anti-vaccine.html |url-access=subscription |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231215122344/https://www.nytimes.com/2023/12/13/technology/covid-anti-vaccine.html |archive-date=December 15, 2023 |access-date=December 18, 2023 |work=The New York Times}}</ref> Some unvaccinated persons opposed to COVID-19 vaccination began referring to themselves in social media groups as "purebloods", a term historically connoting racial purity.<ref>{{Cite web |date=January 25, 2023 |title=Vaccine misinformation spawns 'pure blood' movement |url=https://www.france24.com/en/live-news/20230125-vaccine-misinformation-spawns-pure-blood-movement |website=France 24 |access-date=June 3, 2024 |archive-date=June 2, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240602234032/https://www.france24.com/en/live-news/20230125-vaccine-misinformation-spawns-pure-blood-movement |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Owen |first=Tess |date=September 15, 2021 |title=Unvaccinated TikTokers Are Calling Themselves 'Purebloods' |url=https://www.vice.com/en/article/unvaccinated-tiktok-purebloods-covid/ |access-date=June 3, 2024 |archive-date=June 2, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240602234031/https://www.vice.com/en/article/7kvywd/unvaccinated-tiktok-purebloods-covid |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Spitzer |first=Jennifer |date=August 3, 2022 |title=Purebloods: The Anti-Semitism and White Supremacy of the Anti-Vax Movement |url=https://www.theedgemedia.org/purebloods-anti-semitism-white-supremacy-anti-vax/ |website=The EDGE |access-date=June 3, 2024 |archive-date=June 2, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240602234031/https://www.theedgemedia.org/purebloods-anti-semitism-white-supremacy-anti-vax/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

Prominent biomedical researcher [[Peter Hotez]] asserted that he and other American scientists who publicly defend vaccines have been attacked on social media, harassed with threatening emails, intimidated, and confronted physically by opponents of vaccination. He further attributes the increase in aggressiveness of the anti-vaccination movement to the influence of the extreme wing of the Republican Party. Hotez estimates that roughly 200,000 preventable deaths from COVID-19, mainly among Republicans, occurred in the US because of refusal to be vaccinated.<ref name="Hotez 2023">{{cite book |last=Hotez |first=Peter J. |title=The Deadly Rise of Anti-science: A Scientist's Warning |date=2023 |publisher=Johns Hopkins University Press |isbn=978-1-4214-4722-3}}</ref> A 2023 study published in ''[[The Journal of the American Medical Association]]'' found "evidence of higher excess mortality for Republican voters compared with Democratic voters in Florida and Ohio after, but not before, COVID-19 vaccines were available to all adults in the US".<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wallace |first1=Jacob |last2=Goldsmith-Pinkham |first2=Paul |last3=Schwartz |first3=Jason L. |title=Excess Death Rates for Republican and Democratic Registered Voters in Florida and Ohio During the COVID-19 Pandemic |journal=[[JAMA Internal Medicine]]|date=2023 |volume=183 |issue=9 |pages=916–923 |doi=10.1001/jamainternmed.2023.1154 |pmid=37486680 |pmc=10366951 }}</ref>

==Strategies and tactics==
=== Arguments used === 
In a 2002 paper in the ''[[British Medical Journal]]'', two medical historians suggested that the arguments made against the safety and effectiveness of vaccines in the late 20th century are similar to those of the early anti-vaccinationists. Both the 19th and 20th century arguments included "vaccine safety issues, vaccine failures, infringement of personal liberty, and an unholy alliance between the medical establishment and the government to reap huge profits for the medical establishment at the expense of the public."<ref name="wolfesharp"/> However, the authors only considered the use of "newspaper articles and letters, books, journals, and pamphlets to warn against the dangers of vaccination", and did not address the impact of the internet.<ref name="wolfesharp">{{cite journal |last1=Wolfe |first1=Robert M |last2=Sharp |first2=Lisa K |title=Anti-vaccinationists past and present |journal=BMJ: British Medical Journal |date=August 24, 2002 |volume=325 |issue=7361 |pages=430–432 |doi=10.1136/bmj.325.7361.430 |pmid=12193361 |pmc=1123944 |issn=0959-8138}}</ref> Comments on YouTube videos during the COVID-19 pandemic clustered similarly around "concerns about side-effects, effectiveness, and lack of trust in corporations and government".<ref name="Teng"/>

=== Misrepresentation===
In some instances, anti-vaccine organizations have used names intended to sound non-partisan on the issue: e.g. [[National Vaccine Information Center]] (USA), Vaccination Risk Awareness Network (Canada), Australian Vaccination Network.<ref name="Kata">{{cite journal |last1=Kata |first1=Anna |date=May 28, 2012 |title=Anti-vaccine activists, Web 2.0, and the postmodern paradigm – An overview of tactics and tropes used online by the anti-vaccination movement |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0264410X11019086 |journal=Vaccine |volume=30 |issue=25 |pages=3778–3789 |doi=10.1016/j.vaccine.2011.11.112 |issn=0264-410X |pmid=22172504 |s2cid=38720733 |access-date=October 2, 2023 |archive-date=November 12, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201112000301/https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0264410X11019086 |url-status=live |url-access=subscription }}</ref> In November 2013 the Australian Vaccination Network was ordered by the New South Wales Administrative Decisions Tribunal to change their name so that consumers are aware of the anti-vaccination nature of the group. ''[[Lateline]]'' reported that former AVN president Meryl Dorey "claimed she was a victim of hate groups and vested interests" in response to the ruling.<ref name="lateline">{{cite web | url=http://www.abc.net.au/lateline/content/2013/s3898842.htm | title=Australian Vaccination Network told to change its name | publisher=[[Australian Broadcasting Corporation]] | work=Lateline | date=November 25, 2013 | access-date=January 30, 2014 | archive-date=July 31, 2016 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160731061513/http://www.abc.net.au/lateline/content/2013/s3898842.htm | url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Information quality ===
{{Alternative medicine sidebar|expanded=conspiracy}}
Although physicians and nurses are still rated as the most trusted source for vaccine information, some vaccine-hesitant individuals report being more comfortable discussing vaccines with providers of complementary and alternative medical (CAM) treatments.<ref name="Dubé"/> With the rise of the internet, many people have turned online for medical information.<ref name="Rainie">{{cite news |last1=Rainie |first1=Lee |title=The Online Health Care Revolution |url=https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2000/11/26/the-online-health-care-revolution/ |work=Pew Research Center: Internet, Science & Tech |date=November 26, 2000}}</ref> In some instances, anti-vaccine activists seek to steer people away from vaccination and health-care providers and towards [[alternative medicine]]s sold by certain activists.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.npr.org/sections/health-shots/2021/05/12/993615185/for-some-anti-vaccine-advocates-misinformation-is-part-of-a-business|title=For Some Anti-Vaccine Advocates, Misinformation Is Part Of A Business|first1=Geoff|last1=Brumfiel|work=NPR|date=May 12, 2021|access-date=August 6, 2023|archive-date=May 5, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230505043950/https://www.npr.org/sections/health-shots/2021/05/12/993615185/for-some-anti-vaccine-advocates-misinformation-is-part-of-a-business|url-status=live}}</ref>

Anti-vaccination writings on the internet have been argued to be characterized by a number of differences from medical and scientific literature. These include:
*Promiscuous copying and reduplication.<ref name="Wolfe2000">{{cite journal | last1=Wolfe |first1=R |last2=Sharp |first2=L |last3=Lipsky |first3=M | title = Content and design attributes of antivaccination web sites. | journal = JAMA | volume = 287 | issue = 24 | pages = 3245–8 | date = June 26, 2002 | doi = 10.1001/jama.287.24.3245 | pmid = 12076221 | url=http://members.tripod.com/vaccinesupport-ivil/antivaxsites/design.html | format=Reprint| url-access=subscription }}</ref>
*Ignoring corrections, even when an initial report or data point is shown to be false.<ref name="Kata"/><ref name="Zollo">{{cite journal |display-authors=3 |last1=Zollo |first1=Fabiana |last2=Bessi |first2=Alessandro |last3=Vicario |first3=Michela Del |last4=Scala |first4=Antonio |last5=Caldarelli |first5=Guido |last6=Shekhtman |first6=Louis |last7=Havlin |first7=Shlomo |last8=Quattrociocchi |first8=Walter |title=Debunking in a world of tribes |journal=PLOS ONE |date=July 24, 2017 |volume=12 |issue=7 |article-number=e0181821 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0181821 |pmid=28742163 |pmc=5524392 |bibcode=2017PLoSO..1281821Z |language=en |issn=1932-6203 |doi-access=free }}</ref>
*Lack of [[Citation|references]], difficulty in checking sources and claims.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Davies |first1=P |last2=Chapman |first2=S |last3=Leask |first3=J | title = Antivaccination activists on the world wide web. | journal = Arch Dis Child | volume = 87 | issue = 1 | pages = 22–5 | year = 2002 | doi = 10.1136/adc.87.1.22 | pmid = 12089115 | pmc = 1751143 | url=http://adc.bmjjournals.com/cgi/content/full/87/1/22}}</ref>
*[[Ad hominem|Personal attacks]] on individual doctors.<ref name="Pendergrast Royan"/><ref name="Carpiano"/><ref name="Kata"/> <!--{{fact}} White on Jenner, Whale on everyone, and the BMJ paper referred to. -->
*A high degree of interlinkage between sites.<ref name="Wolfe2000"/><ref name="Johnson">{{cite journal |display-authors=3 |last1=Johnson |first1=Neil F. |last2=Velásquez |first2=Nicolas |last3=Restrepo |first3=Nicholas Johnson |last4=Leahy |first4=Rhys |last5=Gabriel |first5=Nicholas |last6=El Oud |first6=Sara |last7=Zheng |first7=Minzhang |last8=Manrique |first8=Pedro |last9=Wuchty |first9=Stefan |last10=Lupu |first10=Yonatan |title=The online competition between pro- and anti-vaccination views |journal=Nature |date=June 2020 |volume=582 |issue=7811 |pages=230–233 |doi=10.1038/s41586-020-2281-1 |pmid=32499650 |bibcode=2020Natur.582..230J |s2cid=218625185 |issn=1476-4687|doi-access=free }}</ref>
*Dishonest or fallacious arguments.<ref>{{cite web | author=Ed Friedlander | title=The Anti-Immunization Activists: A Pattern of Deception | url=http://www.pathguy.com/antiimmu.htm | access-date=November 2, 2006 | archive-date=March 19, 2018 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180319101705/http://www.pathguy.com/antiimmu.htm }}</ref><ref name="Kata"/>

For example, a 2020 study examined Instagram posts related to the [[HPV vaccine]], which can prevent some types of cancer. Anti-vaccine posts were more likely than pro-vaccine posts to be sent by non-healthcare individuals, to include personal narratives, and to reference other Instagram users, links, or reposts. Anti-vaccine posts were also more likely to involve concealment or distortion, particularly conspiracy theories and unsubstantiated claims. In total, 72.3% of antivaccine posts made inaccurate claims, including exaggerating the risks of vaccines and minimizing risks of disease.<ref name="Massey">{{cite journal |display-authors=3 |last1=Massey |first1=PM |last2=Kearney |first2=MD |last3=Hauer |first3=MK |last4=Selvan |first4=P |last5=Koku |first5=E |last6=Leader |first6=AE |title=Dimensions of Misinformation About the HPV Vaccine on Instagram: Content and Network Analysis of Social Media Characteristics. |journal=Journal of Medical Internet Research |date=December 3, 2020 |volume=22 |issue=12 |article-number=e21451 |doi=10.2196/21451 |pmid=33270038 |pmc=7746500 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

=== Disinformation tactics ===
A number of specific disinformation tactics have been noted in anti-vaccination messaging, including:<ref name="Kata"/><ref name="MacDonald">{{cite journal |last1=MacDonald |first1=Noni E |title=Fake news and science denier attacks on vaccines. What can you do? |journal=Canada Communicable Disease Report |date=November 5, 2020 |volume=46 |issue=1112 |pages=432–435 |doi=10.14745/ccdr.v46i1112a11 |pmid=33447164 |pmc=7799877 |s2cid=230647269 |url=https://www.canada.ca/content/dam/phac-aspc/documents/services/reports-publications/canada-communicable-disease-report-ccdr/monthly-issue/2020-46/issue-11-12-nov-5-2020/ccdrv46i1112a11-eng.pdf|access-date=October 10, 2023 |archive-date=October 10, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231010165926/https://www.canada.ca/content/dam/phac-aspc/documents/services/reports-publications/canada-communicable-disease-report-ccdr/monthly-issue/2020-46/issue-11-12-nov-5-2020/ccdrv46i1112a11-eng.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref>
* Conspiracy theories alleging lies, trickery, cover-ups, and secret knowledge<ref name="MacDonald"/>
* Messages crafted for psychological appeal rather than truthfulness<ref name="Ecker"/>
* Appeals to purported authorities falsely represented as being experts in their field<ref name="MacDonald"/>
* Impossible expectations:<ref name="MacDonald"/> claiming that anything less than 100% certainty in a scientific claim implies doubt and that the existence of doubt disproves the existence of consensus<ref name="Cranor">{{cite journal |author-first=Carl F. |author-last=Cranor  |title=Public Health: The Tobacco Strategy Entrenched |journal=[[Science (journal)|Science]] |volume=321 |issue=5894 |pages=1296–1297 |date=September 5, 2008 |doi= 10.1126/science.1162339|s2cid=153706560 |url=http://www.sciencemag.org/cgi/content/summary/321/5894/1296|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
* Selective use and interpretation of evidence ("[[cherry-picking]]"): using obscure or debunked sources while ignoring counter-evidence and scientific consensus<ref name="Kata"/><ref name="MacDonald"/>
* Result-oriented revision of claims' content: Continually introducing new claims alleging vaccines to be harmful; moving to new claims in support of a preconceived conclusion when existing claims in support of that conclusion are shown to be false<ref name="Kata"/>
* Misrepresentation, appeals to [[Logical fallacy|logical fallacies]], and appeals to improper analogy (''i.e.'', to analogy between cases that do not in fact share the parameter[s] on which the claimed analogy is based)<ref name="Kata"/><ref name="MacDonald"/>
* Personal attacks on critics, ranging from online criticism, [[Doxing|public revelation of personal details]], and threats to offline activities such as legal actions, targeting of employers, and violence<ref name="Carpiano"/><ref name="Kata"/><ref name="Pendergrast Royan"/>
* Targeting of the vaccine produced by the People's Republic of China: During the pandemic, as retaliation for the PRC's attempts to blame the United States for the pandemic, [[The Pentagon]] [[ChinaAngVirus disinformation campaign|targeted]] the PRC's [[CoronaVac|Sinovac COVID-19 vaccine]] by spreading anti-vaccine misinformation in the Philippines.<ref name="Bing_Schectman_6/14/2024">{{cite web | last1=Bing | first1=Chris | last2=Schectman | first2=Joel | title=Pentagon ran secret anti-vax campaign to incite fear of China vaccines | website=[[Reuters]] | date=June 14, 2024 | url=https://www.reuters.com/investigates/special-report/usa-covid-propaganda/ | access-date=June 18, 2024 | archive-date=July 20, 2024 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240720114242/https://www.reuters.com/investigates/special-report/usa-covid-propaganda/ | url-status=live }}</ref>
* Assertions that the existence of the [[National Childhood Vaccine Injury Act|1986 National Childhood Vaccine Injury Act]] implies that the [[Risk–benefit ratio|risk of injury by vaccines]] is high rather than very low<ref name="auto12">{{Cite web|author=Washington post|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/10/31/us/politics/trump-rfk-jr-vaccine-skepticism.html|title=Trump's Transition Team Head Says R.F.K. Jr. Converted Him to Vaccine Skeptic |website=[[The New York Times]] |date=October 31, 2024 }}</ref>

=== Economics of vaccine disinformation ===
Information is more likely to be believed after repeated exposure. Disinformers use this [[illusory truth effect]] as a tactic, repeating false information to make it feel familiar and influence belief.<ref name="Linden"/> Anti-vaccine activists have leveraged social media to develop interconnected networks of influencers that shape people's opinion, recruit allies, impact policy<ref name="Carpiano"/> and monetize vaccine-related disinformation.<ref name="Herasimenka"/> 
In 2022, the ''[[Journal of Communication]]'' published a study of the [[political economy]] underlying vaccine disinformation. Researchers identified 59 English-language "actors" that provided "almost exclusively anti-vaccination publications". Their websites [[monetization|monetized]] disinformation through appeals for donations, sales of content-based media and other merchandise, third-party advertising, and membership fees. Some maintained a group of linked websites, attracting visitors with one site and appealing for money and selling merchandise on others. Their activities to gain attention and obtain funding displayed a "hybrid monetization strategy". They attracted attention by combining eye-catching aspects of "junk news" and online celebrity promotion. At the same time, they developed campaign-specific communities to publicize and legitimize their position, similar to radical social movements.<ref name="Herasimenka">{{cite journal |display-authors=3 |last1=Herasimenka |first1=Aliaksandr |last2=Au |first2=Yung |last3=George |first3=Anna |last4=Joynes-Burgess |first4=Kate |last5=Knuutila |first5=Aleksi |last6=Bright |first6=Jonathan |last7=Howard |first7=Philip N |title=The political economy of digital profiteering: communication resource mobilization by anti-vaccination actors |journal=Journal of Communication |date=December 24, 2022 |volume=73 |issue=2 |pages=126–137 |doi=10.1093/joc/jqac043 |pmid=37016634 |pmc=10066223 }}</ref>

===Misrepresentation of the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System===
In the United States, the [[Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System]] (VAERS) is used to gather information on potential vaccine adverse reactions, but is susceptible to unverified reports, misattribution, [[underreporting]], and inconsistent [[data quality]].<ref name="Shimabukuro2015">{{cite journal |last1=Shimabukuro |first1=TT |last2=Nguyen |first2=M |last3=Martin |first3=D |last4=DeStefano |first4=F |title=Safety monitoring in the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS). |journal=Vaccine |date=August 2015 |volume=33 |issue=36 |pages=4398–4405 |doi=10.1016/j.vaccine.2015.07.035 |pmid=26209838 |pmc=4632204 }}</ref> Raw, unverified data from VAERS has often been used by the anti-vaccine community to justify misinformation regarding the safety of vaccines; it is generally not possible to find out from VAERS data if a vaccine caused an adverse event, or how common the event might be.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.cdc.gov/vaccinesafety/ensuringsafety/monitoring/vaers/index.html |title=Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS) |date=February 27, 2019 |website=www.cdc.gov |language=en-us |access-date=December 6, 2019}}</ref>

=== Use of misinformation in Philippine anti-vaccine activism ===
Anti-vaccine activism in the Philippines has been amplified through social media platforms such as Facebook, where misinformation spreads widely among low-income users with "free Facebook" access.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Soriano |first=Jake |title=Anti-vaxxer misinformation goes viral in Philippines |url=https://www.philstar.com/headlines/2020/10/07/2047832/anti-vaxxer-misinformation-goes-viral-philippines |access-date=2025-11-16 |website=Philstar.com}}</ref>Online groups like No to Vaccine - Philippine propagate messages about vaccine harms<ref>{{Cite web |last=Jake Soriano, Agence France-Presse |title=Anti-vaxxer misinformation goes viral in the Philippines {{!}} ABS-CBN |url=https://www.abs-cbn.com/spotlight/10/07/20/anti-vaxxer-misinformation-goes-viral-in-the-philippines |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251125180428/https://www.abs-cbn.com/spotlight/10/07/20/anti-vaxxer-misinformation-goes-viral-in-the-philippines |archive-date=2025-11-25 |access-date=2026-09-15 |website=ABS-CBN |language=en-US}}</ref>, while emotionally charged narratives rooted in the 2017 [[Dengvaxia controversy|''Dengvaxia'' controversy]] continue to undermine public trust in immunization programs.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Miras |first1=Alejandro Perez |last2=Regencia |first2=Zypher Jude G. |last3=Baja |first3=Emmanuel S. |date=2023-11-29 |title='I was terrified for my child': understanding the link between the Dengvaxia® controversy and the measles vaccine hesitancy in Pasay City, Philippines |journal=Journal of Public Health |volume=45 |issue=4 |pages=912–918 |doi=10.1093/pubmed/fdad091 |issn=1741-3850 |pmid=37340460}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Yu |first1=Vincen Gregory |last2=Lasco |first2=Gideon |last3=David |first3=Clarissa C. |date=2021-08-16 |title=Fear, mistrust, and vaccine hesitancy: Narratives of the dengue vaccine controversy in the Philippines |journal=Vaccine |volume=39 |issue=35 |pages=4964–4972 |doi=10.1016/j.vaccine.2021.07.051 |issn=1873-2518 |pmid=34330555}}</ref>

Health activists and pro-vaccine groups have pushed back: for instance, the Vaccine Solidarity Movement called on media outlets to stop amplifying unscientific anti-vax views and to rely on qualified experts.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Vaccine Solidarity Movement calls out 'anti-vaxxers', vows to address hesitancy |url=https://www.philstar.com/headlines/2021/08/23/2122074/vaccine-solidarity-movement-calls-out-anti-vaxxers-vows-address-hesitancy |access-date=2025-11-16 |website=Philstar.com}}</ref> Misinformation about vaccine brands (such as ''[[Sinovac Biotech|Sinovac]]'') and perceived regulatory failures contributes to hesitancy, a tactic leveraged by anti-vaxxers to sow doubt.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Amit |first1=Arianna Maever L. |last2=Pepito |first2=Veincent Christian F. |last3=Sumpaico-Tanchanco |first3=Lourdes |last4=Dayrit |first4=Manuel M. |date=2022 |title=COVID-19 vaccine brand hesitancy and other challenges to vaccination in the Philippines |journal=PLOS Global Public Health |volume=2 |issue=1 |article-number=e0000165 |doi=10.1371/journal.pgph.0000165 |doi-access=free |issn=2767-3375 |pmc=10021706 |pmid=36962166}}</ref>

In addition, some disinformation campaigns have geopolitical dimensions: a covert campaign reportedly run by the U.S. military in the Philippines spread fears that Chinese-made COVID-19 vaccines were unsafe.<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Bing |first1=Chris |last2=Schectman |first2=Joel |date=June 14, 2024 |title=Pentagon ran secret anti-vax campaign to incite fear of China vaccines |url=https://www.reuters.com/investigates/special-report/usa-covid-propaganda/ |access-date=November 16, 2025 |website=Reuters}}</ref>

Community-level mistrust is also fueled by moral panic and institutional distrust. Ethnographic studies among Filipino parents document how fear from past vaccine controversies, such as ''Dengvaxia'', continues to resonate in discussions about routine immunization.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Yu |first1=Vincen Gregory |last2=Lasco |first2=Gideon |last3=David |first3=Clarissa C. |date=2021-08-16 |title=Fear, mistrust, and vaccine hesitancy: Narratives of the dengue vaccine controversy in the Philippines |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0264410X21009294 |journal=Vaccine |volume=39 |issue=35 |pages=4964–4972 |doi=10.1016/j.vaccine.2021.07.051 |pmid=34330555 |issn=0264-410X|url-access=subscription }}</ref> At the same time, negative vaccine narratives garner strong engagement: a content analysis of YouTube comments on national TV vaccination campaigns found that 80% of comments expressed vaccine-hesitant discourse, and these often received more engagement than pro-vaccine responses.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Silvallana |first1=Daniel Fritz |last2=Elias |first2=Carlos |last3=Catalan-Matamoros |first3=Daniel |date=2025-05-22 |title=Exploring Vaccine Hesitancy in the Philippines: A Content Analysis of Comments on National TV Channel YouTube Videos |journal=International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health |volume=22 |issue=6 |page=819 |doi=10.3390/ijerph22060819 |doi-access=free |issn=1660-4601 |pmc=12193359 |pmid=40566247}}</ref>

=== Legal action ===

After Republicans gained a majority in the U.S. House of Representatives in January 2023, the House Judiciary Committee used legal action to oppose both disinformation research and government involvement in fighting disinformation. One of the projects targeted was the Virality Project, which has examined the spread of false claims about vaccines. The House Judiciary Committee sent letters, subpoenas, and threats of legal action to researchers, demanding notes, emails and other records from researchers and even student interns, dating back to 2015. Institutions subjected to such inquiries included the [[Stanford Internet Observatory]] at [[Stanford University]], the [[University of Washington]], the [[Atlantic Council]]'s Digital Forensic Research Lab and the social media analytics firm Graphika. Researchers emphasized that they have [[academic freedom]] to study disinformation as well as [[freedom of speech]] to report their results.<ref name="Myers"/><ref name="Starks">{{cite news |last1=Starks |first1=Tim |title=Analysis {{!}} GOP legal attacks create a chilling effect on misinformation research |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2023/09/25/gop-legal-attacks-create-chilling-effect-misinformation-research/ |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |date=September 25, 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Misinformation research is buckling under GOP legal attacks |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/2023/09/23/online-misinformation-jim-jordan/ |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |date=September 23, 2023 |language=en |access-date=October 13, 2023 |archive-date=September 23, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230923115829/https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/2023/09/23/online-misinformation-jim-jordan/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

Despite conservative claims that the government acted to censor speech online, "no evidence has emerged that government officials coerced the companies to take action against accounts".<ref name="Myers"/> The actions of the House Judiciary Committee have been described as an "attempt to chill research,"<ref name="Myers">{{cite news |last1=Myers |first1=Steven Lee |last2=Frenkel |first2=Sheera |title=G.O.P. Targets Researchers Who Study Disinformation Ahead of 2024 Election |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2023/06/19/technology/gop-disinformation-researchers-2024-election.html |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=June 19, 2023}}</ref> creating a "chilling effect"<ref name="Starks"/> through increased time demands, legal costs and online harassment of researchers.<ref name="Starks"/><ref name="Myers"/>

A 2025 [[Associated Press]] investigation reported the filing in state legislatures of more than 420 bills that undermined established longstanding public health protections, on matters including [[vaccines]], [[milk pasteurization]], and [[water fluoridation]]. Many of these efforts were reported to have been connected to groups linked with Health and Human Services Secretary [[Robert F. Kennedy Jr]]. and his "[[Make America Healthy Again]]" movement, which critics and professionals say disguises conspiracy theory-driven, anti-science ideas under the label of "health freedom". At the time of the report around 30 measures had already become laws in 12 states.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Smith |first=Michelle |date=2025-10-21 |title=Anti-science bills hit statehouses, stripping away public health protections built over a century |url=https://www.twincities.com/2025/10/21/anti-science-movement/ |access-date=2025-11-13 |website=San Diego Union-Tribune |language=en-US}}</ref>

=== Harassment=== 
Persons undertaking efforts to counter vaccine misinformation, including public health experts who use social media, have been targeted for harassment by anti-vaccine activists.<ref name="Carpiano"/><ref name="Pendergrast Royan">{{Cite web |last1=Pendergrast |first1=Tricia |last2=Royan |first2=Regina |last3=Arora |first3=Vineet |date=June 23, 2023 |title=Peter Hotez is not alone: Online harassment of doctors is a public health issue |url=https://www.statnews.com/2023/06/23/peter-hotez-joe-rogan-rfk-jr-harassment-doctors-scientists/ |access-date=June 23, 2023 |website=STAT |archive-date=October 7, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241007012811/https://www.statnews.com/2023/06/23/peter-hotez-joe-rogan-rfk-jr-harassment-doctors-scientists/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Baker |first1=Russ |title=But Wait, Folks, There's More: Anti-Vaxxers and Snake Oilers Are a Team | url=https://whowhatwhy.org/science/health-medicine/but-wait-folks-theres-more-anti-vaxxers-and-snake-oilers-are-a-team/ |work=WhoWhatWhy |date=April 16, 2024}}</ref>

For example, Slovak medical doctor [[Vladimír Krčméry]] was a prominent member of the government advisory team during the [[COVID-19 pandemic in Slovakia]], and was the first person in that country to receive a [[COVID-19 vaccine]]. Due to his prominent role in the vaccination campaign, Krčméry and his family became a target of anti-vaccine activists, who physically threatened him and his family.<ref name="Krempaský">{{Cite web |last=Krempaský |first=Ján |title=Zachránil tisícky životov, antivaxeri sa mu vyhrážali smrťou. Zomrel Vladimír Krčméry |url=https://domov.sme.sk/c/23099357/vladimir-krcmery-umrtie.html |access-date=December 21, 2022 |website=domov.sme.sk |language=sk |archive-date=December 21, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221221051328/https://domov.sme.sk/c/23099357/vladimir-krcmery-umrtie.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

In June 2023, Texas-based physician and researcher [[Peter Hotez]] tweeted his concerns about Robert F. Kennedy Jr. sharing misinformation about vaccines on [[Joe Rogan]]'s podcast. Rogan, Kennedy, and Twitter owner [[Elon Musk]] asked Hotez to participate in a debate on the podcast. Upon declining the invitation, Hotez was harassed by their fans, with anti-vaccine activist [[Alex Rosen]] confronting him at his home.<ref name="Pendergrast Royan" /><ref name="Munce">{{Cite news |last=Munce |first=Megan Fan |date=June 19, 2023 |title=COVID-19 expert Peter Hotez harassed outside his home by anti-vaccine advocates |url=https://www.houstonchronicle.com/news/houston-texas/article/peter-hotez-joe-rogan-stalked-anti-vaccine-18158864.php |access-date=September 19, 2023 |website=Houston Chronicle |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Maruf |first=Ramishah |date=June 19, 2023 |title=A prominent vaccine scientist says he was 'stalked' in front of home after Joe Rogan Twitter exchange {{!}} CNN Business |url=https://www.cnn.com/2023/06/19/business/hotez-joe-rogan-elon-musk-spotify-rfk-vaccine/index.html |access-date=September 19, 2023 |website=CNN |language=en |archive-date=October 7, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241007012851/https://www.cnn.com/2023/06/19/business/hotez-joe-rogan-elon-musk-spotify-rfk-vaccine/index.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

In his book ''The Deadly Rise of Anti-science: A Scientist's Warning'', Hotez describes how he and other scientists who publicly defend vaccines have been attacked on social media, harassed with threatening emails, intimidated, and confronted physically by opponents of vaccination. He attributes the increase in aggressiveness of the anti-vaccination movement to the influence of the extreme wing of the Republican Party.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Nowogrodzki |first1=Julian |title=Vaccine specialist Peter Hotez: scientists are 'under attack for someone else's political gain' |journal=Nature |date=September 21, 2023 |volume=621 |issue=7980 |pages=681–682 |doi=10.1038/d41586-023-02981-z |pmid=37735191 |bibcode=2023Natur.621..681N |s2cid=262073883 |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-023-02981-z |language=en|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=In 'Deadly Rise of Anti-Science,' vaccine researcher Peter Hotez sounds the alarm on science denial |url=https://www.wbur.org/hereandnow/2023/09/19/deadly-rise-anti-science-book |work=WBUR / Here & Now |date=September 19, 2023 |language=en |access-date=September 29, 2023 |archive-date=September 28, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230928185907/https://www.wbur.org/hereandnow/2023/09/19/deadly-rise-anti-science-book |url-status=live }}</ref> Hotez estimates that roughly 200,000 preventable deaths from COVID-19, mainly among Republicans, occurred in the US because of refusal to be vaccinated.<ref name="Bostwick">{{cite news |last1=Bostwick |first1=Will |title=Anti-Science Views Are Literally Killing Us, Peter Hotez Warns |url=https://www.texasmonthly.com/news-politics/peter-hotez-book-antiscience-deadly/ |work=Texas Monthly |date=September 19, 2023 |language=en |access-date=September 29, 2023 |archive-date=September 27, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230927142852/https://www.texasmonthly.com/news-politics/peter-hotez-book-antiscience-deadly/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last=Hotez|first=Peter J.|title=The Deadly Rise of Anti-science: A Scientist's Warning|publisher=Johns Hopkins University Press|year=2023|isbn=978-1-4214-4722-3}}</ref>

At the extreme end, opposition to vaccination has resulted in substantial violence against vaccinators. In Pakistan, "more than 200 polio team workers have lost their lives" (team members include not only vaccinators but police and security personnel) from "targeted killing and terrorism" while working on polio vaccination campaigns.<ref name="History-APJPH-2023">{{cite journal |last1=Wahid |first1=Braira |last2=Kumari |first2=Babita |last3=Saifullah |first3=Khaled Mohammed |last4=Idrees |first4=Muhammad |title=The History and Current Killings of Polio Vaccinators in Pakistan: A Need for Targeted Surveillance Strategy |journal= Asia Pacific Journal of Public Health|date=March 2023 |volume=35 |issue=2–3 |pages=183–188 |doi=10.1177/10105395231158866|pmid=36856226 |pmc=10185917 |s2cid=257257554 }}</ref>

==Countering anti-vaccine activism==
Various efforts have been suggested and undertaken to address [[vaccine hesitancy|concerns about vaccines]] and counter anti-vaccine disinformation. Efforts include social media advertising campaigns, by public health organizations, in support of public health goals.<ref name="Athey">{{cite journal |last1=Athey |first1=Susan |last2=Grabarz |first2=Kristen |last3=Luca |first3=Michael |last4=Wernerfelt |first4=Nils |title=Digital public health interventions at scale: The impact of social media advertising on beliefs and outcomes related to COVID vaccines |journal=PNAS |date=January 26, 2023 |volume=120 |issue=5 |article-number=e2208110120 |doi=10.1073/pnas.2208110120 |doi-access=free |pmid=36701366 |pmc=9945974 |bibcode=2023PNAS..12008110A }}</ref><ref name="Teng">{{cite journal |last1=Teng |first1=Shasha |last2=Jiang |first2=Nan |last3=Khong |first3=Kok Wei |title=Using big data to understand the online ecology of COVID-19 vaccination hesitancy |journal=Humanities and Social Sciences Communications |date=May 6, 2022 |volume=9 |issue=1 |pages=1–15 |article-number=158 |doi=10.1057/s41599-022-01185-6 |s2cid=257095447 |language=en |issn=2662-9992|doi-access=free }}</ref>

Best practices for combating vaccine mis- and disinformation include addressing issues openly, clearly identifying areas of scientific consensus and areas of uncertainty, and being sensitive to the cultural and religious values of communities.<ref>{{cite web |title=How to Address COVID-19 Vaccine Misinformation |url=https://www.cdc.gov/vaccines/covid-19/health-departments/addressing-vaccine-misinformation.html |website=Centers for Disease Control and Prevention |language=en-us |date=November 3, 2021 |access-date=October 3, 2023 |archive-date=October 4, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231004154322/https://www.cdc.gov/vaccines/covid-19/health-departments/addressing-vaccine-misinformation.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="OECD">{{cite news |title=Transparency, communication and trust: The role of public communication in responding to the wave of disinformation about the new Coronavirus |url=https://www.oecd.org/coronavirus/policy-responses/transparency-communication-and-trust-the-role-of-public-communication-in-responding-to-the-wave-of-disinformation-about-the-new-coronavirus-bef7ad6e/ |access-date=January 25, 2023 |work=OECD Policy Responses to Coronavirus (COVID-19) |agency=Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development |date=July 3, 2020 |language=en |archive-date=January 25, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230125132619/https://www.oecd.org/coronavirus/policy-responses/transparency-communication-and-trust-the-role-of-public-communication-in-responding-to-the-wave-of-disinformation-about-the-new-coronavirus-bef7ad6e/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="Wang"/> In countering anti-vaccine disinformation, both factual and emotional aspects need to be addressed.<ref name="Stolle">{{cite journal |display-authors=3 |last1=Stolle |first1=Lucas B. |last2=Nalamasu |first2=Rohit |last3=Pergolizzi |first3=Joseph V. |last4=Varrassi |first4=Giustino |last5=Magnusson |first5=Peter |last6=LeQuang |first6=JoAnn |last7=Breve |first7=Frank |title=Fact vs Fallacy: The Anti-Vaccine Discussion Reloaded |journal=Advances in Therapy |date=November 2020 |volume=37 |issue=11 |pages=4481–4490 |doi=10.1007/s12325-020-01502-y |pmid=32965654 |pmc=7509825 |issn=1865-8652}}</ref>

Whether people will update a mistaken belief is complicated and involves psychological factors and social goals as well as accuracy of information.<ref name="Lewandowsky">{{cite journal |last1=Lewandowsky |first1=Stephan |last2=Ecker |first2=Ullrich K. H. |last3=Seifert |first3=Colleen M. |last4=Schwarz |first4=Norbert |last5=Cook |first5=John |title=Misinformation and Its Correction: Continued Influence and Successful Debiasing |journal=Psychological Science in the Public Interest |date=December 2012 |volume=13 |issue=3 |pages=106–131 |doi=10.1177/1529100612451018 |pmid=26173286 |s2cid=261453468 |language=en |issn=1529-1006|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Linden"/><ref name="Ecker"/> There is some evidence that both debunking and "[[Inoculation theory|pre-bunking]]" of disinformation can be effective, at least in the short term.<ref name="Linden">{{cite journal |last1=van der Linden |first1=Sander |title=Misinformation: susceptibility, spread, and interventions to immunize the public |journal=Nature Medicine |date=March 2022 |volume=28 |issue=3 |pages=460–467 |doi=10.1038/s41591-022-01713-6 |pmid=35273402 |s2cid=247384353 |language=en |issn=1546-170X|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Ecker">{{cite journal |display-authors=3 |last1=Ecker |first1=Ullrich K. H. |last2=Lewandowsky |first2=Stephan |last3=Cook |first3=John |last4=Schmid |first4=Philipp |last5=Fazio |first5=Lisa K. |last6=Brashier |first6=Nadia |last7=Kendeou |first7=Panayiota |last8=Vraga |first8=Emily K. |last9=Amazeen |first9=Michelle A. |title=The psychological drivers of misinformation belief and its resistance to correction |journal=Nature Reviews Psychology |date=January 2022 |volume=1 |issue=1 |pages=13–29 |doi=10.1038/s44159-021-00006-y |s2cid=245916820 |language=en |issn=2731-0574|doi-access=free |hdl=1983/889ddb0f-0d44-44f4-a54f-57c260ae4917 |hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Zhao">{{cite journal |display-authors=3 |last1=Zhao |first1=Sihong |last2=Hu |first2=Simeng |last3=Zhou |first3=Xiaoyu |last4=Song |first4=Suhang |last5=Wang |first5=Qian |last6=Zheng |first6=Hongqiu |last7=Zhang |first7=Ying |last8=Hou |first8=Zhiyuan |title=The Prevalence, Features, Influencing Factors, and Solutions for COVID-19 Vaccine Misinformation: Systematic Review |journal=JMIR Public Health and Surveillance |date=January 11, 2023 |volume=9 |article-number=e40201 |doi=10.2196/40201 |pmid=36469911 |pmc=9838721 |issn=2369-2960 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Walter">{{cite journal |last1=Walter |first1=Nathan |last2=Brooks |first2=John J. |last3=Saucier |first3=Camille J. |last4=Suresh |first4=Sapna |title=Evaluating the Impact of Attempts to Correct Health Misinformation on Social Media: A Meta-Analysis |journal=Health Communication |date=November 10, 2021 |volume=36 |issue=13 |pages=1776–1784 |doi=10.1080/10410236.2020.1794553 |pmid=32762260 |s2cid=221076451 |language=en |issn=1041-0236 }}</ref> Elements that may help to correct inaccurate information include: warning people before they are exposed to misinformation; high perceived credibility of message sources, affirmations of identity and social norms; graphical presentation; and focusing attention on clear core messages.<ref name="Paynter">{{cite journal |display-authors=3 |last1=Paynter |first1=Jessica |last2=Luskin-Saxby |first2=Sarah |last3=Keen |first3=Deb |last4=Fordyce |first4=Kathryn |last5=Frost |first5=Grace |last6=Imms |first6=Christine |last7=Miller |first7=Scott |last8=Trembath |first8=David |last9=Tucker |first9=Madonna |last10=Ecker |first10=Ullrich |title=Evaluation of a template for countering misinformation—Real-world Autism treatment myth debunking |journal=PLOS ONE |date=January 30, 2019 |volume=14 |issue=1 |article-number=e0210746 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0210746 |pmid=30699155 |pmc=6353548 |bibcode=2019PLoSO..1410746P |issn=1932-6203 |doi-access=free }}</ref>
Alternative explanations of a situation need to fit plausibly into the original scenario and ideally indicate why the incorrect explanation was previously thought to be correct.<ref name="Lewandowsky"/>

The cultivation of critical thinking, health and science awareness, and media literacy skills are recommended to help people critically assess information credibility.<ref name="Wang"/> People who seek out multiple reputable news sources at local and national levels are more likely to detect disinformation than those who rely on few sources from a particular viewpoint.<ref name="Atske">{{cite news |last1=Atske |first1=Sara |title=3. Misinformation and competing views of reality abounded throughout 2020 |url=https://www.pewresearch.org/journalism/2021/02/22/misinformation-and-competing-views-of-reality-abounded-throughout-2020/ |access-date=January 19, 2023 |work=Pew Research Center's Journalism Project |date=February 22, 2021 |archive-date=October 7, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241007012744/https://www.pewresearch.org/journalism/2021/02/22/misinformation-and-competing-views-of-reality-abounded-throughout-2020/ |url-status=live }}</ref> 

===Operation of social media===
Other suggestions for countering anti-vaccine activism focus on changing the operation of social media platforms. Interventions such as accuracy nudges and source labeling change the context in which information is presented.<ref name="Tay">{{cite journal |last1=Tay |first1=Li Qian |last2=Lewandowsky |first2=Stephan |last3=Hurlstone |first3=Mark J. |last4=Kurz |first4=Tim |last5=Ecker |first5=Ullrich K. H. |title=A focus shift in the evaluation of misinformation interventions |journal=Harvard Kennedy School Misinformation Review |date=October 5, 2023 |volume=4 |issue=5 |pages=mr-2020–124 |doi=10.37016/mr-2020-124 |pmid=39301480 |s2cid=263715886 |doi-access=free |pmc=7616579 }}</ref> For example, correct information can be directly presented to counter disinformation.<ref name="Bode">{{cite journal |last1=Bode |first1=Leticia |last2=Vraga |first2=Emily K. |title=In Related News, That Was Wrong: The Correction of Misinformation Through Related Stories Functionality in Social Media: In Related News |journal=Journal of Communication |date=August 2015 |volume=65 |issue=4 |pages=619–638 |doi=10.1111/jcom.12166 |s2cid=142769329 |url=https://academic.oup.com/joc/article-abstract/65/4/619/4082315?redirectedFrom=fulltext |access-date=October 3, 2023 |archive-date=October 7, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241007012744/https://academic.oup.com/joc/article-abstract/65/4/619/4082315?redirectedFrom=fulltext |url-status=live |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="Ozturk">{{cite book |last1=Ozturk |first1=Pinar |last2=Li |first2=Huaye |last3=Sakamoto |first3=Yasuaki |title=2015 48th Hawaii International Conference on System Sciences |chapter=Combating Rumor Spread on Social Media: The Effectiveness of Refutation and Warning |date=January 2015 |pages=2406–2414 |doi=10.1109/HICSS.2015.288|isbn=978-1-4799-7367-5 |s2cid=1822644 }}</ref> Other possibilities include flagging or removing misleading information on social media platforms.<ref name="Lanius">{{cite journal |last1=Lanius |first1=Candice |last2=Weber |first2=Ryan |last3=MacKenzie |first3=William I. |title=Use of bot and content flags to limit the spread of misinformation among social networks: a behavior and attitude survey |journal=Social Network Analysis and Mining |date=March 12, 2021 |volume=11 |issue=1 |page=32 |doi=10.1007/s13278-021-00739-x |pmid=33747252 |pmc=7954364 |language=en |issn=1869-5469 }}</ref><ref name="Yaraghi">{{cite news |last1=Yaraghi |first1=Niam |title=How should social media platforms combat misinformation and hate speech? |url=https://www.brookings.edu/articles/how-should-social-media-platforms-combat-misinformation-and-hate-speech/ |work=Brookings |date=April 9, 2019 |access-date=September 29, 2023 |archive-date=September 30, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230930122523/https://www.brookings.edu/articles/how-should-social-media-platforms-combat-misinformation-and-hate-speech/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="Desai">{{cite journal |last1=Desai |first1=Angel N |last2=Ruidera |first2=Diandra |last3=Steinbrink |first3=Julie M |last4=Granwehr |first4=Bruno |last5=Lee |first5=Dong Heun |title=Misinformation and Disinformation: The Potential Disadvantages of Social Media in Infectious Disease and How to Combat Them |journal=Clinical Infectious Diseases|date=May 15, 2022 |volume=74 |issue=Suppl 3 |pages=e34–e39 |doi=10.1093/cid/ciac109 |pmid=35568471 |pmc=9384020 |issn=1058-4838}}</ref> Research suggests that a majority of individuals in the United States would support the removal of harmful misinformation posts and the suspension of accounts. This position is less popular with Republicans than Democrats.<ref name="Kozyreva">{{cite journal |display-authors=3 |last1=Kozyreva |first1=Anastasia |last2=Herzog |first2=Stefan M. |last3=Lewandowsky |first3=Stephan |last4=Hertwig |first4=Ralph |last5=Lorenz-Spreen |first5=Philipp |last6=Leiser |first6=Mark |last7=Reifler |first7=Jason |title=Resolving content moderation dilemmas between free speech and harmful misinformation |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America |date=February 14, 2023 |volume=120 |issue=7 |article-number=e2210666120 |doi=10.1073/pnas.2210666120 |doi-access=free |pmid=36749721 |pmc=9963596 |bibcode=2023PNAS..12010666K |issn=1091-6490}}</ref>

While private entities like Facebook, Twitter and Telegram could legally establish guidelines for moderation of information and disinformation on their platforms (subject to local and international laws)<ref name="ALA">{{cite web |title=First Amendment and Censorship |url=https://www.ala.org/advocacy/intfreedom/censorship |website=Advocacy, Legislation & Issues |access-date=January 25, 2023 |language=en |date=June 13, 2008 |archive-date=January 30, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230130051751/https://www.ala.org/advocacy/intfreedom/censorship |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="Fellmeth">{{cite news |last1=Fellmeth |first1=Robert C. |title=Social media must balance 'right of free speech' with audience 'right to know' |url=https://thehill.com/opinion/technology/3814620-social-media-must-balance-right-of-free-speech-with-audience-right-to-know/ |access-date=January 24, 2023 |work=The Hill |date=January 20, 2023}}</ref><ref name="Nossel">{{cite news |last1=Nossel |first1=Suzanne |title=Social Media, Free Speech, and the Scourge of Misinformation |url=https://www.aft.org/hc/fall2020/nossel |access-date=January 24, 2023 |work=American Federation of Teachers |date=April 29, 2021 |language=en |archive-date=January 24, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230124224623/https://www.aft.org/hc/fall2020/nossel |url-status=live }}</ref> such companies do not have strong incentives to control disinformation or to self-regulate. Algorithms that are used to maximize user engagement and profits can lead to unbalanced, poorly sourced, and actively misleading information.<ref name="Liedtke">{{cite news |last1=Bauder |first1=David |last2=Liedtke |first2=Michael |title=Whistleblower says Facebook routinely chose 'profit over safety' when it came to misinformation |url=https://fortune.com/2021/10/04/facebook-whistleblower-social-media-misinformation-hate-algorithm/ |access-date=January 26, 2023 |work=Fortune |date=October 4, 2021 |archive-date=October 7, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241007013340/https://fortune.com/2021/10/04/facebook-whistleblower-social-media-misinformation-hate-algorithm/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="Doomscrolling">{{cite news |title=Doomscrolling and negativity bias: The way we consume news may be detrimental to our health |url=https://whatsnewinpublishing.com/doomscrolling-and-negativity-bias-the-way-we-consume-news-may-be-detrimental-to-our-health/ |access-date=January 27, 2023 |work=What's New in Publishing {{!}} Digital Publishing News |date=October 26, 2020 |archive-date=January 27, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230127025418/https://whatsnewinpublishing.com/doomscrolling-and-negativity-bias-the-way-we-consume-news-may-be-detrimental-to-our-health/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="Sutcliffe">{{cite news |last1=Sutcliffe |first1=Chris |title='Disinformation is a business': media execs explore how to demonetize falsehoods |url=https://www.thedrum.com/news/2021/10/01/disinformation-business-media-execs-explore-how-demonetize-falsehoods |access-date=January 26, 2023 |work=The Drum |date=October 1, 2021 |archive-date=January 26, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230126150813/https://www.thedrum.com/news/2021/10/01/disinformation-business-media-execs-explore-how-demonetize-falsehoods |url-status=live }}</ref>

Criticized for its role in vaccine hesitancy, Facebook announced in March 2019 that it would provide users with "authoritative information" on the topic of vaccines.<ref>{{cite news|title=Facebook announces anti-vaxx crackdown, will block ads with vaccine misinformation|author=Graham, Jefferson|date=March 7, 2019|access-date=March 8, 2019|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/tech/talkingtech/2019/03/07/facebook-looks-tackle-vaccine-misinformation/3092719002/|newspaper=[[USA Today]]|archive-date=December 12, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201212215603/https://www.usatoday.com/story/tech/talkingtech/2019/03/07/facebook-looks-tackle-vaccine-misinformation/3092719002/|url-status=live}}</ref> Facebook introduced several policies chosen to reduce the impact of anti-vaccine content, without actually removing it. These included reducing the ranking of anti-vaccine sources in searches and not recommending them; rejecting ads and targeted advertising that contained vaccine misinformation; and using banners to present vaccine information from authoritative sources. A study examined the six months before and after the policy changes. It found a moderate but significant decrease in the number of likes for anti-vaccine posts following the policy changes. Likes of pro-vaccine posts were unchanged.<ref name="Gu">{{cite journal |display-authors=3 |last1=Gu |first1=Jiayan |last2=Dor |first2=Avi |last3=Li |first3=Kun |last4=Broniatowski |first4=David A. |last5=Hatheway |first5=Megan |last6=Fritz |first6=Lailah |last7=Abroms |first7=Lorien C. |title=The impact of Facebook's vaccine misinformation policy on user endorsements of vaccine content: An interrupted time series analysis |journal=Vaccine |date=March 25, 2022 |volume=40 |issue=14 |pages=2209–2214 |doi=10.1016/j.vaccine.2022.02.062 |pmid=35246311 |s2cid=247206495 |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0264410X22002092 |issn=0264-410X |access-date=October 9, 2023 |archive-date=October 10, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231010165925/https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0264410X22002092 |url-status=live |url-access=subscription }}</ref> Facebook has been criticized for not being more aggressive in countering disinformation.<ref name="Beckett">{{cite news |last1=Beckett |first1=Lois |title=Misinformation 'superspreaders': Covid vaccine falsehoods still thriving on Facebook and Instagram |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2021/jan/06/facebook-instagram-urged-fight-deluge-anti-covid-vaccine-falsehoods |work=The Guardian |date=January 6, 2021 |access-date=October 9, 2023 |archive-date=October 7, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241007013300/https://www.theguardian.com/world/2021/jan/06/facebook-instagram-urged-fight-deluge-anti-covid-vaccine-falsehoods |url-status=live }}</ref> In response to efforts to police misinformation, anti-vaccine communities on social media have adopted coded language to refer to vaccinated persons and the vaccines themselves.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://theweek.com/news/1002899/how-anti-vaccine-groups-are-camouflaging-themselves-on-facebook|title=How anti-vaccine groups are camouflaging themselves on Facebook|first1=Brigid|last1=Kennedy|work=The Week|date=July 22, 2021|access-date=October 24, 2023|archive-date=October 7, 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241007013310/https://theweek.com/news/1002899/how-anti-vaccine-groups-are-camouflaging-themselves-on-facebook|url-status=live}}</ref>

Supply-side interventions reduce circulation of misinformation directly at their sources through actions such as application of social media policies, regulation, and legislation.<ref name="Tay"/>
A study published in the journal ''[[Vaccine (journal)|Vaccine]]'' examined advertisements posted in the three months prior to the Facebook's 2019 policy changes. It found that 54% of the anti-vaccine advertisements on Facebook were placed by just two organizations, funded by well-known anti-vaccination activists.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Vaccine-related advertising in the Facebook Ad Archive|journal=Vaccine|year=2020|doi=10.1016/j.vaccine.2019.10.066 |display-authors=3 |last1=Jamison|first1=Amelia M.|last2=Broniatowski|first2=David A.|last3=Dredze|first3=Mark|last4=Wood-Doughty|first4=Zach|last5=Khan|first5=Dureaden|last6=Quinn|first6=Sandra Crouse|volume=38|issue=3|pages=512–520|pmid=31732327|pmc=6954281}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2019/nov/13/majority-antivaxx-vaccine-ads-facebook-funded-by-two-organizations-study|title=Majority of anti-vaxx ads on Facebook are funded by just two organizations|date=November 14, 2019|website=[[The Guardian]]|access-date=November 14, 2019|archive-date=February 21, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210221010843/https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2019/nov/13/majority-antivaxx-vaccine-ads-facebook-funded-by-two-organizations-study|url-status=live}}</ref> The [[Children's Health Defense]] / World Mercury Project chaired by [[Robert F. Kennedy Jr.]] and [[Stop Mandatory Vaccination]], run by campaigner Larry Cook, posted 54% of the advertisements. The ads often linked to commercial products, such as natural remedies and books.<ref name="Sun">{{cite news |last1=Sun |first1=Lena H. |title=Majority of anti-vaccine ads on Facebook were funded by two groups |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/health/2019/11/15/majority-anti-vaccine-ads-facebook-were-funded-by-two-groups/ |newspaper=Washington Post |date=November 16, 2019 |access-date=September 29, 2023 |archive-date=November 17, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191117003403/https://www.washingtonpost.com/health/2019/11/15/majority-anti-vaccine-ads-facebook-were-funded-by-two-groups/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Kennedy was suspended from Facebook in August 2022,<ref>{{cite news |title=Facebook and Instagram ban US anti-vaccine group |url=https://www.lemonde.fr/en/international/article/2022/08/19/facebook-instagram-ban-major-us-anti-vaccine-group_5994026_4.html |work=Le Monde |date=August 19, 2022 |language=en |access-date=October 3, 2023 |archive-date=October 7, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241007013813/https://www.lemonde.fr/en/international/article/2022/08/19/facebook-instagram-ban-major-us-anti-vaccine-group_5994026_4.html |url-status=live }}</ref> but reinstated in June 2023.<ref name="Lima">{{cite news |last1=Lima |first1=Cristiano |title=Instagram reinstates Robert Kennedy Jr. after launch of presidential bid |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/2023/06/04/robert-kennedy-instagram/ |newspaper=Washington Post |date=June 5, 2023 |access-date=October 3, 2023 |archive-date=June 5, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230605034220/https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/2023/06/04/robert-kennedy-instagram/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

In 2023, however, state governments that were politically aligned with anti-vaccine activists successfully sought a [[preliminary injunction]] to prevent the [[Biden Administration]] from seeking to pressure social media companies into fighting misinformation. The order issued by [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit]] "severely limits the ability of the White House, the surgeon general, [and] the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention... to communicate with social media companies about content related to Covid-19... that the government views as misinformation".<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.cnn.com/2023/10/03/tech/cybersecurity-and-infrastructure-security-agency-social-media-lawsuit-injunction/index.html|title=Federal appeals court extends limits on Biden administration communications with social media companies to top US cybersecurity agency|first=Devan|last=Cole|date=October 3, 2023|website=CNN|access-date=October 10, 2023|archive-date=October 7, 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241007013815/https://www.cnn.com/2023/10/03/tech/cybersecurity-and-infrastructure-security-agency-social-media-lawsuit-injunction/index.html|url-status=live}}</ref> In October 2023, this injunction was paused by the [[Supreme Court of the United States]], pending further litigation.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.cnn.com/2023/10/20/politics/supreme-court-social-media/index.html|title=Supreme Court lifts restrictions on Biden administration communications with social media companies|first1=Devan|last1=Cole|work=[[CNN]]|date=October 20, 2023|access-date=October 21, 2023|archive-date=October 21, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231021021054/https://www.cnn.com/2023/10/20/politics/supreme-court-social-media/index.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

===Use of algorithms and data===
Algorithms and user data can be used to identify selected subgroups who can then be provided with specialized content. This type of approach has been used both by anti-vaccine activists<ref name="Wang">{{cite journal |last1=Wang |first1=Yuxi |last2=McKee |first2=Martin |last3=Torbica |first3=Aleksandra |last4=Stuckler |first4=David |title=Systematic Literature Review on the Spread of Health-related Misinformation on Social Media |journal=Social Science & Medicine |date=November 1, 2019 |volume=240 |article-number=112552 |doi=10.1016/j.socscimed.2019.112552 |pmid=31561111 |pmc=7117034 |issn=0277-9536}}</ref><ref name="Carpiano"/> 
and by health providers who hope to counter vaccine-related disinformation.<ref name="Bicher">{{cite journal |display-authors=3 |last1=Bicher |first1=Martin |last2=Rippinger |first2=Claire |last3=Zechmeister |first3=Melanie |last4=Jahn |first4=Beate |last5=Sroczynski |first5=Gaby |last6=Mühlberger |first6=Nikolai |last7=Santamaria-Navarro |first7=Julia |last8=Urach |first8=Christoph |last9=Brunmeir |first9=Dominik |last10=Siebert |first10=Uwe |last11=Popper |first11=Niki |title=An iterative algorithm for optimizing COVID-19 vaccination strategies considering unknown supply |journal=PLOS ONE |date=May 2, 2022 |volume=17 |issue=5 |article-number=e0265957 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0265957 |pmid=35499997 |pmc=9060336 |bibcode=2022PLoSO..1765957B |language=en |issn=1932-6203 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Fressin"/><ref name="Schmitzberger"/> 
For example, in the United States, the CDC's [[Social Vulnerability Index]] (SVI) has been used to identify communities that have traditionally been under-served or are at elevated risk for infection, morbidity, and mortality.<ref name="Bicher"/> Programs have been developed in such communities to address disinformation and vaccine hesitancy.<ref name="Dada"/>

===Community engagement===
Steps have been taken to counter anti-vaccine messaging by directly engaging with communities. Outreach efforts include call centers and texting campaigns, partnering with local community leaders, and holding community-based vaccine clinics.<ref name="Dada">{{cite journal |last1=Dada |display-authors=3 |first1=Debbie |last2=Djiometio |first2=Joseph Nguemo |last3=McFadden |first3=SarahAnn M. |last4=Demeke |first4=Jemal |last5=Vlahov |first5=David |last6=Wilton |first6=Leo |last7=Wang |first7=Mengzu |last8=Nelson |first8=LaRon E. |title=Strategies That Promote Equity in COVID-19 Vaccine Uptake for Black Communities: a Review |journal=Journal of Urban Health journal |last1=Fressin |first1=Francois |last2=Wen |first2=Amy |last3=Shukla |first3=Samta |last4=Mok |first4=Kelly |last5=Chaguturu |first5=Sreekanth |title=How We Achieved More Equitable Vaccine |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241007013815/https://www.healthaffairs.org/content/forefront/we-achieved-more-equitable-vaccine-distribution-social-vulnerability-analytics |url-status=live |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lacy |first1=Leandra |last2=Solosi |first2=Izabela |title=Addressing the Social Determinants of Health May Help Increase COVID-19 Vaccine Uptake {{!}} Urban Institute |url=https://www.urban.org/urban-wire/addressing-social-determinants-health-may-help-increase-covid-19-vaccine-uptake |website=Urban Institute |date=May 27, 2022 |language=en}}</ref> Creating digital and science literacy resources and distributing them via schools, libraries, municipal offices, churches and other community groups can help to counter misinformation in under-resourced communities.<ref name="AuYoung">{{cite journal |display-authors=3 |last1=AuYoung |first1=Mona |last2=Rodriguez Espinosa |first2=Patricia |last3=Chen |first3=Wei-ting |last4=Juturu |first4=Preeti |last5=Young |first5=Maria-Elena De Trinidad |last6=Casillas |first6=Alejandra |last7=Adkins-Jackson |first7=Paris |last8=Hopfer |first8=Suellen |last9=Kissam |first9=Ed |last10=Alo |first10=Audrey Kawaiopua |last11=Vargas |first11=Roberto A. |last12=Brown |first12=Arleen F. |title=Addressing racial/ethnic inequities in vaccine hesitancy and uptake: lessons learned from the California alliance against COVID-19 |journal=Journal of Behavioral Medicine |date=April 2023 |volume=46 |issue=1–2 |pages=153–166 |doi=10.1007/s10865-022-00284-8 |pmid=35066696 |pmc=8783654 |s2cid=246166545 }}</ref>

The Black Doctors COVID-19 Consortium in Philadelphia is one example of a successful direct outreach initiative.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Lopez-Lloreda |first1=Claudia |title=Meet the Black Physicians Bringing Covid Vaccines to Hard-Hit Philadelphia Communities |url=https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/meet-group-black-physicians-working-increase-vaccinations-hard-hit-communities-philadelphia-180977564/ |work=[[Smithsonian Magazine]] |access-date=December 25, 2021 |date=April 23, 2021 |archive-date=December 25, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211225053136/https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/meet-group-black-physicians-working-increase-vaccinations-hard-hit-communities-philadelphia-180977564/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Another is the New York State Vaccine Equity Task Force.<ref name="Dada"/>
In line with the [[Strategic Advisory Group of Experts]] (SAGE)'s 3C's model, outreach to communities has focused on addressing mistrust and increasing Confidence, providing information to improve risk assessment (Complacency), and improving access to COVID-19 vaccines (Convenience). It has been necessary to counter disinformation in all three areas.<ref name="Schmitzberger">{{cite journal  |display-authors=3 |last1=Schmitzberger |first1=Florian F. |last2=Scott |first2=Kirstin W. |last3=Nham |first3=Wilson |last4=Mathews |first4=Kusum |last5=Schulson |first5=Lucy |last6=Fouche |first6=Sydney |last7=Berri |first7=Nasma |last8=Shehab |first8=Alex |last9=Gupta |first9=Ashwin |last10=Salhi |first10=Rama A. |last11=Kamdar |first11=Neil |last12=Bouey |first12=Jennifer |last13=Abir |first13=Mahshid |title=Identifying Strategies to Boost COVID-19 Vaccine Acceptance in the United States |journal=Rand Health Quarterly |date=June 30, 2022 |volume=9 |issue=3 |page=12 |pmid=35837516 |pmc=9242559 |issn=2162-8254}}</ref><ref name="Dada"/>

In the Philippines, countermeasures include nationwide information campaigns led by the Department of Health, collaborations with UNICEF to address circulating misinformation, and initiatives by medical and scientific groups such as the Vaccine Solidarity Movement,<ref>{{Cite web |last=sunnexdesk@gmail.com |date=2021-08-23 |title=Group fights Covid-19 vaccine disinformation, misinformation |url=https://www.sunstar.com.ph/manila/local-news/new-group-fights-covid-19-vaccine-disinformation-misinformation |access-date=2026-09-15 |website=SunStar Publishing Inc. |language=en}}</ref> which urges media outlets to prioritize expert guidance and avoid amplifying unverified claims. Local health workers and barangay officials are trained to respond to vaccine concerns at the household level, while fact-checking organizations regularly debunk viral social-media posts linking unrelated deaths or illnesses to vaccination.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-08-27 |title=FACT CHECK: 'Newscast' of possible diseases caused by COVID-19 vaccine is AI-generated |url=https://www.rappler.com/newsbreak/fact-check/newscast-possible-diseases-causedco-covid-19-vaccine-ai-generated/ |access-date=2025-11-16 |website=RAPPLER |language=en-US}}</ref> Researchers also highlight the effectiveness of "prebunking" strategies like educating the public about common misinformation techniques before they encounter them, which can reduce susceptibility to anti-vaccine narratives and improve understanding of scientific evidence.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wang |first1=Ke |last2=Goldenberg |first2=Amit |last3=Dorison |first3=Charles A. |last4=Miller |first4=Jeremy K. |last5=Uusberg |first5=Andero |last6=Lerner |first6=Jennifer S. |last7=Gross |first7=James J. |last8=Agesin |first8=Bamikole Bamikole |last9=Bernardo |first9=Márcia |last10=Campos |first10=Olatz |last11=Eudave |first11=Luis |last12=Grzech |first12=Karolina |last13=Ozery |first13=Daphna Hausman |last14=Jackson |first14=Emily A. |last15=Garcia |first15=Elkin Oswaldo Luis |date=August 2021 |title=A multi-country test of brief reappraisal interventions on emotions during the COVID-19 pandemic |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s41562-021-01173-x |journal=Nature Human Behaviour |language=en |volume=5 |issue=8 |pages=1089–1110 |doi=10.1038/s41562-021-01173-x |pmid=34341554 |issn=2397-3374|hdl=11336/148368 |hdl-access=free |pmc=8742248 }}</ref>

Recommendations for combating vaccine disinformation include increasing the presence of trusted health agencies and credible information on social media, partnering with social media platforms to promote evidence-based public health information, and identifying and responding to emerging concerns and disinformation campaigns.<ref name="Schmitzberger" /> 
Networked communities of public health officials and other stakeholders, connecting with the public through a variety of credible and trusted messengers, are recommended. Sharing of messages through such networks could help to debunk and counter highly networked and coordinated disinformation attacks.<ref name="Carpiano" />

A networked community approach would differ from the current model of US public health communication, which tends to rely on a single credible messenger (e.g. [[Anthony Fauci]]) and is susceptible to disinformation attacks. To deal with disinformation, community networks would need to address issues of liberty and human rights as well as vaccine safety, effectiveness and access. Networks could also help to show support for those attacked by anti-vaccine activists.<ref name="Carpiano"/>

=== Strategic messaging and narrative framing ===
Communications strategies often combine factual information with emotionally resonant narratives to enhance vaccine acceptance. Storytelling, testimonials, and culturally relevant examples help convey the benefits of vaccination and counter fear-based narratives. In the Philippines, campaigns have used community stories and real-life experiences to contextualize scientific data and improve public understanding.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Steffens |first1=Maryke S. |last2=Dunn |first2=Adam G. |last3=Wiley |first3=Kerrie E. |last4=Leask |first4=Julie |date=2019-10-23 |title=How organisations promoting vaccination respond to misinformation on social media: a qualitative investigation |journal=BMC Public Health |volume=19 |issue=1 |page=1348 |doi=10.1186/s12889-019-7659-3 |pmid=31640660 |pmc=6806569 |doi-access=free |issn=1471-2458}}</ref>

Narrative framing also involves tailoring messages to specific audiences by aligning content with their values, beliefs, and cultural context. By framing vaccination as a protective measure for families, communities, or national health, public health authorities can more effectively reach hesitant populations. Strategic messaging is particularly effective when combined with factual evidence, local engagement, and repeated reinforcement across multiple communication channels.

=== Policy, regulation, and institutional measures ===
Governments implement policy interventions to regulate the dissemination of vaccine-related information. Expert advisory committees, regulations, and penalties for spreading false health claims help maintain the integrity of public health messaging. In the Philippines, transparency initiatives ensure that adverse event data and vaccine information are publicly available and accessible.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Lawmaker seeks probe into Pentagon's 'secret' anti-Covid vax drive |url=https://www.pna.gov.ph/articles/1227064 |access-date=2025-11-16 |website=www.pna.gov.ph |language=en}}</ref>

Institutional measures also include collaboration between health agencies, media regulators, and digital platforms. These partnerships enable rapid responses to misinformation, reinforce accurate reporting, and ensure that public trust is maintained. Policy interventions complement community and digital strategies by providing legal and structural support for evidence-based health communication.
