===== Cancer =====
The website ''[[Natural News]]'' has published claims that mRNA vaccines for COVID-19 can cause [[cancer]] by inactivating [[tumor-suppressing protein]]s. This claim was based on a misrepresentation of a 2018 study at [[Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center]] (MSKCC), which did not involve the mRNA used in vaccines.{{r|Gregory}} The study found that [[Transcription (biology)|transcription]] errors in certain mRNA molecules could disrupt production of tumor-suppressing proteins. However, mRNA used in vaccines is made artificially, and poses no risk of transcription errors once made.<ref>{{cite news |title=Study did not find link between Covid-19 mRNA vaccines and cancer |url=https://factcheck.afp.com/study-did-not-find-link-between-covid-19-mrna-vaccines-and-cancer |work=AFP Fact Check |agency=Agence France-Presse |date=18 March 2021 |language=en}}</ref>

A retracted Japanese study titled "''Increased Age-Adjusted Cancer Mortality After the Third mRNA-Lipid Nanoparticle Vaccine Dose During the COVID-19 Pandemic in Japan''" was used to claim that [[COVID-19 vaccine|COVID-19 vaccine recipients]] were more likely to develop various [[cancer]]s, although the authors themselves admitted that their results were not clinically verified. The study does not present data breaking down [[cancer]] deaths by vaccination status, nor does it show that it increases after vaccination, or that it is higher in vaccinated compared to unvaccinated individuals of the same age or comorbidity status, nor does it provide any epidemiological evidence that vaccines increased the risk of [[cancer]].<ref>{{Cite news |date=2024-05-07 |title=Fact Check: No evidence of mRNA cancer 'explosion' in Japan, no national emergency declared |url=https://www.reuters.com/fact-check/no-evidence-mrna-cancer-explosion-japan-no-national-emergency-declared-2024-05-07/ |access-date=2025-07-05 |work=Reuters |language=en}}</ref>

In 2025, American cardiologist [[Peter A. McCullough]] co-authored a [[Retraction in academic publishing|withdrawn]] [[preprint]] titled "''Synthetic mRNA Vaccines and Transcriptomic Dysregulation: Evidence from New-Onset Adverse Events and Cancers Post-Vaccination''", in which he argued for an unsubstantiated connection between COVID-19 vaccination and cancer, and that was also heavily criticized for its methodological errors.<ref>{{Cite web |last=|first=|date=2025-07-26|title=Preprint claiming that COVID-19 mRNA vaccines cause transcriptomic dysregulation is deeply flawed|url=https://scienceintegritydigest.com/2025/07/25/preprint-claiming-that-covid-19-mrna-vaccines-cause-transcriptomic-dysregulation-is-deeply-flawed/|access-date=2026-07-13|website=Science Integrity Digest|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-07-28|title=No, mRNA vaccines do not cause “transcriptomic chaos”|url=https://reeserichardson.blog/2025/07/28/no-mrna-vaccines-do-not-cause-transcriptomic-chaos/|access-date=2026-07-13|website=Reese Richardson|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-07-28|title=Now It’s “Gaslight” Preprints|url=https://www.the-geyser.com/now-its-gaslight-preprints/|access-date=2026-07-13|website=The Geyser|language=en}}</ref> A similar South Korean study titled “''1-year risks of cancers associated with COVID-19 vaccination: a large population-based cohort study in South Korea''" was also used to claim that [[COVID-19 vaccine|COVID-19 vaccine recipients]] were more likely to develop various [[cancer]]s, although researchers themselves emphasised that their conclusions only showed an "epidemiological association", [[Correlation does not imply causation|not a causal relationship]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Agency |first=Sanad Verification |title=Did a South Korean study really claim that COVID-19 vaccines cause cancer? |url=https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2025/10/11/did-a-south-korean-study-really-claim-that-covid-19-vaccines-cause-cancer |access-date=2025-11-11 |website=Al Jazeera |language=en}}</ref> Several hypothesis have been proposed to explain the increase of early-onset cancers worldwide, such as [[obesity]], an [[Microplastics and human health|overabundance of microplastics in human bodies]], certain bacterial infections or just improved diagnostic methods.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-05-14 |title=Why Is Early-Onset Cancer On the Rise? - NCI |url=https://www.cancer.gov/news-events/cancer-currents-blog/2025/early-onset-cancer-research-environment-genetics-support |access-date=2026-05-17 |website=www.cancer.gov |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Albert |first=Helen |date=2025-09-29 |title=Rise in Early Onset Cancer in U.S. Linked to Increased Diagnosis |url=https://www.insideprecisionmedicine.com/topics/oncology/rise-in-early-onset-cancer-in-u-s-linked-to-increased-diagnosis/ |access-date=2026-05-17 |website=Inside Precision Medicine |language=en-US}}</ref>

===== Prion disease =====
A widely reposted 2021 Facebook post claiming that the mRNA vaccines against [[COVID-19]] could cause [[prion]] diseases was based on a paper by [[J. Bart Classen]].{{r|Gregory}} The paper was published in ''Microbiology and Infectious Diseases'', whose publisher, Scivision Publishers, is included in [[Beall's list]] of publishers of [[predatory journal]]s.{{r|Himmelman}} Classen's only published evidence for his claim was a brief summary of an "unspecified analysis of the Pfizer/BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine", according to [[NewsGuard]].{{r|Gregory}} [[Vincent Racaniello]], professor of microbiology and immunology at Columbia University, described the claim as "completely wrong".<ref name="Himmelman">{{cite news |vauthors=Himmelman K |title=Could the mRNA Vaccines Lead to an Increase in Neurodegenerative Disorders? |url=https://factcheck.thedispatch.com/p/could-the-mrna-vaccines-lead-to-an |access-date=8 April 2021 |agency=[[The Dispatch]] |date=8 April 2021 |archive-date=8 April 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210408194745/https://factcheck.thedispatch.com/p/could-the-mrna-vaccines-lead-to-an |url-status=live}}</ref>
Previous mRNA vaccines have been tested in humans, and were not found to cause prion disease.{{r|Gregory}} The mRNA contained in the vaccine is degraded within a few days of entering the cells of a person receiving it and does not accumulate in the brain.<ref>{{cite web |title=How long do mRNA and spike proteins last in the body? |url=https://www.nebraskamed.com/COVID/where-mrna-vaccines-and-spike-proteins-go |publisher=Nebraska Medicine |language=en |date=2 July 2021}}</ref> The U.S. Alzheimer's Association has stated that currently available COVID-19 vaccines are safe for persons with Alzheimer's disease and other forms of [[dementia]].<ref>{{cite news |author1=<!--Staff writer, no byline--> |title=Fact Check-No evidence that Pfizer's COVID-19 vaccine causes Alzheimer's disease |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/fact-check-no-evidence-that-pfizers-covi/fact-check-no-evidence-that-pfizers-covid-19-vaccine-causes-alzheimers-disease-idUSL1N2MZ382 |work=Reuters |date=12 May 2021}}</ref>

====Polio vaccine as a claimed COVID-19 carrier====
Social media posts in [[Cameroon]] pushed a conspiracy theory that [[polio vaccine]]s contained COVID-19, further complicating [[polio eradication]] beyond the logistical and funding difficulties created by the COVID-19 pandemic.<ref name="Rauhala">{{Cite news |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/polio-was-almost-eradicated-then-came-the-coronavirus-then-came-a-threat-from-president-trump/2020/05/15/ed9d26fe-831c-11ea-81a3-9690c9881111_story.html |title=Polio was almost eradicated. Then came the coronavirus. Then came a threat from President Trump. |vauthors=Rauhala E, Paquette D, George S |date=15 May 2020 |newspaper=The Washington Post |url-access=limited |access-date=13 September 2021 |archive-date=1 July 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200701014250/https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/polio-was-almost-eradicated-then-came-the-coronavirus-then-came-a-threat-from-president-trump/2020/05/15/ed9d26fe-831c-11ea-81a3-9690c9881111_story.html |url-status=live}}</ref>

==== Antibody-dependent enhancement ====
[[Antibody-dependent enhancement]] (ADE) is the phenomenon in which a person with antibodies against one virus (i.e. from infection or vaccination) can develop worse disease when infected by a second closely related virus, due to a unique and rare reaction with proteins on the surface of the second virus.<ref name="NaturePerspectiveADECOVID">{{cite journal | vauthors = Arvin AM, Fink K, Schmid MA, Cathcart A, Spreafico R, Havenar-Daughton C, Lanzavecchia A, Corti D, Virgin HW | display-authors = 6 | title = A perspective on potential antibody-dependent enhancement of SARS-CoV-2 | journal = Nature | volume = 584 | issue = 7821 | pages = 353–363 | date = August 2020 | pmid = 32659783 | doi = 10.1038/s41586-020-2538-8 | s2cid = 220509274 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Huisman W, Martina BE, Rimmelzwaan GF, Gruters RA, Osterhaus AD | title = Vaccine-induced enhancement of viral infections | journal = Vaccine | volume = 27 | issue = 4 | pages = 505–512 | date = January 2009 | pmid = 19022319 | pmc = 7131326 | doi = 10.1016/j.vaccine.2008.10.087 }}</ref> ADE has been observed ''[[in vitro]]'' and in animal studies with many different viruses that do not display ADE in humans.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Duehr J, Lee S, Singh G, Foster GA, Krysztof D, Stramer SL, Bermúdez González MC, Menichetti E, Geretschläger R, Gabriel C, Simon V, Lim JK, Krammer F | display-authors = 6 | title = Tick-Borne Encephalitis Virus Vaccine-Induced Human Antibodies Mediate Negligible Enhancement of Zika Virus Infection ''In Vitro'' and in a Mouse Model | journal = mSphere | volume = 3 | issue = 1 | article-number = e00011-18 | date = 7 February 2018 | pmid = 29435494 | pmc = 5806211 | doi = 10.1128/mSphereDirect.00011-18  | doi-access = free}}</ref><ref name="NaturePerspectiveADECOVID" /> Researchers acknowledge that "Fundamentally, this question should be asked of all vaccine candidates under development, despite the rarity of the phenomenon."<ref name="Haynes"/>

Prior to the pandemic, ADE was observed in animal studies of laboratory rodents with vaccines for [[SARS-CoV]], the virus that causes severe acute respiratory syndrome ([[SARS]]). However, {{as of|lc=yes|2022|01|27}} there have been no observed incidents with vaccines for COVID-19 in trials with nonhuman primates, in clinical trials with humans, or following the widespread use of approved vaccines.<ref name="Hotez">{{cite journal |last1=Hotez |first1=Peter J. |last2=Bottazzi |first2=Maria Elena |title=Whole Inactivated Virus and Protein-Based COVID-19 Vaccines |journal=Annual Review of Medicine |date=27 January 2022 |volume=73 |issue=1 |pages=55–64 |doi=10.1146/annurev-med-042420-113212 |pmid=34637324 |s2cid=238747462 |issn=0066-4219|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |vauthors=Hackethal V |title=Why ADE Hasn't Been a Problem With COVID Vaccines |url=https://www.medpagetoday.com/special-reports/exclusives/91648 |access-date=1 July 2021 |work=www.medpagetoday.com |date=16 March 2021 |archive-date=25 June 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210625153011/https://www.medpagetoday.com/special-reports/exclusives/91648 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Haynes">{{cite journal |last1=Haynes |first1=Barton F. |last2=Corey |first2=Lawrence |last3=Fernandes |first3=Prabhavathi |last4=Gilbert |first4=Peter B. |last5=Hotez |first5=Peter J. |last6=Rao |first6=Srinivas |last7=Santos |first7=Michael R. |last8=Schuitemaker |first8=Hanneke |last9=Watson |first9=Michael |last10=Arvin |first10=Ann |title=Prospects for a safe COVID-19 vaccine |journal=Science Translational Medicine |date=4 November 2020 |volume=12 |issue=568 |article-number=eabe0948 |doi=10.1126/scitranslmed.abe0948 |pmid=33077678 |s2cid=224809822 |issn=1946-6242|doi-access=free }}</ref> Molecular simulations indicate that ADE might play a role in new strains such as delta, but none in the strains that the vaccines were originally designed for.<ref>{{cite journal | pmc=8351274 | year=2021 | last1=Yahi | first1=N. | last2=Chahinian | first2=H. | last3=Fantini | first3=J. | title=Infection-enhancing anti-SARS-CoV-2 antibodies recognize both the original Wuhan/D614G strain and Delta variants. A potential risk for mass vaccination? | journal=The Journal of Infection | volume=83 | issue=5 | pages=607–635 | doi=10.1016/j.jinf.2021.08.010 | pmid=34384810 }}</ref> [[Anti-vaccination]] activists cited ADE as a reason to avoid vaccination against COVID-19.<ref name="Gorski infertile">{{cite web |website=Science-Based Medicine |vauthors=Gorski DH |title=It was inevitable that antivaxxers would claim that COVID-19 vaccines make females infertile |url=https://sciencebasedmedicine.org/it-was-inevitable-that-antivaxxers-would-claim-that-covid-19-vaccines-make-females-infertile/ |date=14 December 2020 |access-date=13 September 2021 |archive-date=9 February 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210209003222/https://sciencebasedmedicine.org/it-was-inevitable-that-antivaxxers-would-claim-that-covid-19-vaccines-make-females-infertile/ |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |publisher=[[Climate Feedback|Health Feedback]] |url=https://science.feedback.org/review/no-evidence-that-covid-19-vaccines-cause-more-severe-disease-antibody-dependent-enhancement-has-not-been-observed-in-clinical-trials/ |date=27 November 2020 |type=Fact check |title=No evidence that COVID-19 vaccines cause more severe disease; antibody-dependent enhancement has not been observed in clinical trials |veditors=Teoh F |access-date=15 March 2026 }}</ref>

==== Vaccines contain aborted fetal tissue ====
{{further|Use of fetal tissue in vaccine development}}

In November 2020, claims circulated on the web that the [[Oxford–AstraZeneca COVID-19 vaccine]] contained tissue from aborted fetuses. While it is true that [[cell line]]s derived from a fetus aborted in 1970 plays a role in the vaccine development process, the molecules for the vaccine are separated from the resulting cell debris.<ref name="fetus">{{cite web |date=2 December 2020 |title=Does AstraZeneca's COVID-19 Vaccine Contain Aborted Fetal Cells? |url=https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/astrazeneca-covid-vaccine-fetal/ |website=[[Snopes]] |vauthors=Kasprak A |access-date=13 September 2021 |archive-date=16 February 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210216032441/https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/astrazeneca-covid-vaccine-fetal/ |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |date=November 2020 |title=Innovating Production and Manufacture to meet the Challenge of COVID-19 |url=https://www.astrazeneca.com/what-science-can-do/topics/technologies/innovating-production-and-manufacture-to-meet-the-challenge-of-covid-19.html |publisher=AstraZeneca |access-date=13 September 2021 |archive-date=16 February 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210216032534/https://www.astrazeneca.com/what-science-can-do/topics/technologies/innovating-production-and-manufacture-to-meet-the-challenge-of-covid-19.html |url-status=live}}</ref>
Several other COVID-19 vaccine candidates use fetal cell lines descended from fetuses aborted between 1972 and 1985. No fetal tissue is present in these vaccines.{{r|Gregory}}

==== Spike protein cytotoxicity ====
In 2021, anti-vaccination misinformation circulated on social media saying that [[SARS-CoV-2 spike protein]]s were "very dangerous" and "[[Cytotoxicity|cytotoxic]]". At that time, all COVID-19 vaccines approved for emergency use either contained mRNA or mRNA precursors for the production of the spike protein. This mRNA consists of instructions which, when processed in cells, cause production of spike proteins, which trigger an adaptive immune response in a safe and effective manner.<ref name="Gorski cytotoxic">{{cite web |date=18 June 2021 |title=COVID-19 vaccines are not 'cytotoxic' |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/factcheck-vaccine-cytotoxic-idUSL2N2O01XP |publisher=Reuters |type=Fact check |access-date=13 September 2021 |archive-date=27 June 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210627224723/https://www.reuters.com/article/factcheck-vaccine-cytotoxic-idUSL2N2O01XP |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |date=24 May 2021 |title=The 'deadly' coronavirus spike protein (according to antivaxxers) |url=https://sciencebasedmedicine.org/the-deadly-coronavirus-spike-protein/ |website=Science-Based Medicine |vauthors=Gorski DH |access-date=13 September 2021 |archive-date=2 July 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210702230700/https://sciencebasedmedicine.org/the-deadly-coronavirus-spike-protein/ |url-status=live}}</ref>

==== Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome ====
In October 2021, the website ''[[The Exposé]]'' used data published by the [[UK Health Security Agency]] (UKHSA), which misleadingly indicated that COVID-19 infection rates were higher among fully-vaccinated than unvaccinated people, to falsely claim that the COVID-19 vaccines were not only ineffective but were also causing vaccinated people to develop [[AIDS]] "much faster than anticipated". The website's claims were cited in a speech by Brazilian president [[Jair Bolsonaro]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Benedictus |first=Leo |date=2021-11-05 |title=How the UK Health Security Agency's misleading data fuelled a global vaccine myth |url=https://fullfact.org/health/phe-ukhsa-bolsonaro/ |access-date=2022-10-17 |website=[[Full Fact]] |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |first=Flora |last=Teoh |date=5 November 2021 |title=Article by The Exposé failed to account for caveats listed in U.K. vaccine surveillance reports; falsely claims fully vaccinated people have weakened immunity |url=https://science.feedback.org/review/article-by-the-expose-failed-to-account-for-caveats-listed-in-u-k-vaccine-surveillance-reports-falsely-claims-fully-vaccinated-people-have-weakened-immunity/ |access-date=15 March 2026 |website=Health Feedback |language=en-US}}</ref> The video of Bolsonaro's speech was removed from [[Facebook]], [[Instagram]] and [[YouTube]] for violating their policies regarding COVID-19 vaccines.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Biller |first=David |date=2021-10-25 |title=Facebook yanks Bolsonaro video claiming vaccines cause AIDS |url=https://apnews.com/article/coronavirus-pandemic-technology-health-caribbean-brazil-9abd4832762e9ed405858248547955c3 |access-date=2022-10-22 |website=[[Associated Press]] |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=26 October 2021 |title=Facebook, YouTube remove Bolsonaro video over vaccine claims |url=https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2021/10/26/facebook-youtube-remove-bolsonaro-video-over-vaccine-claims |access-date=2022-10-22 |website=[[Al Jazeera Media Network|Al Jazeera]] |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=26 October 2021 |title=Facebook yanks Bolsonaro video claiming vaccines cause AIDS |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/news/latino/facebook-yanks-bolsonaro-video-claiming-vaccines-cause-aids-rcna3771 |access-date=2022-10-22 |website=[[NBC News]] |language=en |agency=[[Reuters]]}}</ref>

In January 2022, ''The Exposé'' promoted a conspiracy theory claiming that Germans fully-vaccinated against COVID-19 "[would] have full blown Covid-19 vaccine induced acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) by the end of [the month]."<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-01-10 |title=Vaccinated Germans won't have AIDS by the end of January 2022 |url=https://fullfact.org/health/germany-covid-omicron-aids-expose-false/ |access-date=2022-09-04 |website=Full Fact |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Zhang |first1=Legu |last2=Echols |first2=William |date=2022-04-01 |title=Made by Moderna? China Spreads Yet Another Debunked COVID-19 Conspiracy Theory |url=https://www.polygraph.info/a/fact-check-moderna-vaccine-covid-conspiracy/31781624.html |access-date=10 August 2022 |website=[[Polygraph.info]]}}</ref>

====<span class="anchor" id="Vaccines as a cause of death"></span>Vaccines as a cause of death====
===== United States =====

A 2021 transparency report from [[Facebook]] found that the most popular shared link in the United States from January to March was an article from the ''[[South Florida Sun-Sentinel]]'' about a doctor's death two weeks after getting a COVID-19 vaccine. The medical examiner later found no evidence of a link to the vaccine, but the article was promoted and twisted by anti-vaccine groups to raise doubt about vaccine safety.<ref name="Dwoskin">{{Cite web |vauthors=Dwoskin E |url=https://www.bostonglobe.com/2021/08/21/nation/facebook-says-post-that-cast-doubt-coronavirus-vaccine-among-most-popular-platform-this-year/ |title=Facebook says post that cast doubt on coronavirus vaccine among the most popular on the platform this year |work=The Boston Globe |agency=The Washington Post |date=21 August 2021 |archive-date=15 September 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210915091545/https://www.bostonglobe.com/2021/08/21/nation/facebook-says-post-that-cast-doubt-coronavirus-vaccine-among-most-popular-platform-this-year/ |url-status=live |url-access=limited}}</ref> Anti-vaccine activists [[Robert F. Kennedy Jr.]] and [[Del Bigtree]] have suggested without evidence that the death of Baseball Hall of Fame member [[Hank Aaron]] was caused by receiving the COVID-19 vaccine. Aaron's death was reported as being due to natural causes, and medical officials did not believe the COVID-19 vaccine had any adverse effect on his health.{{r|Gregory}}

On 7 October 2022, [[Florida]] [[Surgeon General]] Dr. [[Joseph Ladapo]] issued a press release discouraging men aged 18 to 39 from taking the COVID-19 vaccine since a study by the [[Florida Department of Health]] concluded vaccinated men of the age group had an 84% increased likelihood of dying from [[heart problems]]. The study was neither [[peer-reviewed]], nor published in a [[scientific journal]], while its authors, source of funding, and methods of analysis were not disclosed. The study faced ample criticism, contending misrepresentation of data, that the time frame for examining deaths was too long, a lack of transparency, and that the efficacy and safety of the vaccines were ignored. [[Steve Kirsch]], an [[entrepreneur]] who promotes COVID-19 vaccine misinformation, cited the study as proof that [[mRNA vaccines]] are fatal to children.<ref name="pf-fl">{{Cite web|last=Settles|first=Gabrielle|date=2022-10-13|title=Why an analysis of COVID-19 vaccines from Florida's surgeon general is flawed|url=https://www.politifact.com/article/2022/oct/13/why-analysis-covid-19-vaccines-floridas-surgeon-ge/|website=[[PolitiFact]]|access-date=2022-11-25|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=Gorski|first=David|date=2022-10-10|title=The State of Florida spreads antivaccine disinformation disguised as an epidemiological 'study'|url=https://sciencebasedmedicine.org/the-state-of-florida-spreads-antivaccine-disinformation-disguised-as-an-epidemiological-study/|website=[[Science-Based Medicine]]|access-date=2022-11-25|language=en}}</ref> A study published in ''[[JAMA]]'' showed an increased risk for [[myocarditis]] within seven days of vaccination. The  group with most recorded cases (males aged 16 to 17) had 106 per million doses, though the actual incidence is likely higher due to overall underreporting. 96% of patients were hospitalized, but most cases were mild and patients typically experienced symptomatic recovery by discharge.<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Oster M, Shady D, Su J, Gee J, Creech C, Broder K, Edwards K, Soslow J, Dendey J, Schlaudecker E, lang S, Barnett E, Ruberg F, Smith M, Campbell M, Lopes R, Sperling L, Baumblatt J, Thompson D, Marquez P, Strid P, Woo J, Pugsley R, Reagen-Steiner S, DeStefano F, Shimanukuro T |date=2022-01-25 |title=Myocarditis Cases Reported After mRNA-Based COVID-19 Vaccination in the US From December 2020 to August 2021 |journal=[[JAMA]] |language=en |volume=327 |issue=4 |pages=331–340 |doi=10.1001/jama.2021.24110 |pmc=8790664 |pmid=35076665 |quote="[A]s a passive system, VAERS data are subject to reporting biases in that both underreporting and overreporting are possible.38 Given the high verification rate of reports of myocarditis to VAERS after mRNA-based COVID-19 vaccination, underreporting is more likely. Therefore, the actual rates of myocarditis per million doses of vaccine are likely higher than estimated."}}</ref><ref name="pf-fl"/>

On 17 September 2023, a flawed analysis co-authored by [[Denis Rancourt]] and published by the Correlation Research in the Public Interest organization claimed that all-cause mortality data didn’t indicate any benefit from COVID-19 vaccination in 17 examined countries, estimating that the COVID-19 vaccinations had killed around 17 million people instead.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Funke |first=Daniel |date=October 5, 2023 |title=Report falsely claims Covid vaccines killed 17 million worldwide |url=https://factcheck.afp.com/doc.afp.com.33XF3CN |website=[[Agence France-Presse]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Yandell |first=Kate |date=2024-01-13 |title=Tucker Carlson Video Spreads Falsehoods on COVID-19 Vaccines, WHO Accord |url=https://www.factcheck.org/2024/01/scicheck-tucker-carlson-video-spreads-falsehoods-on-covid-19-vaccines-who-accord/ |access-date=2026-07-14 |website=FactCheck.org |language=en-US}}</ref> The report faultily correlates vaccine rollout with increases in mortality, ignoring the role of [[SARS-CoV-2]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Jacob |first=Manon |date=December 8, 2022 |title=Covid-19 vaccination not responsible for excess deaths in US |url=https://factcheck.afp.com/doc.afp.com.32ZT4XW |website=[[Agence France-Presse]]}}</ref>
The authors also didn’t establish whether the people who died had been vaccinated, since their all-cause mortality data was population-level data, not individual-level data.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-10-11 |title=Analysis claiming to find COVID-19 vaccines killed 17 million people is highly flawed, doesn't account for COVID-19 mortality surges - Science Feedback |url=https://science.feedback.org/review/analysis-claiming-covid-19-vaccines-killed-17-million-people-flawed/ |access-date=2026-07-14 |website=[[Science Feedback]] |language=en-GB}}</ref>

In 2024, American [[cardiologist]] [[Peter A. McCullough]] co-authored a narrative review titled: "''COVID-19 mRNA Vaccines: Lessons Learned from the Registrational Trials and Global Vaccination Campaign''", which claims that COVID-19 vaccines have killed nearly 14 times as many people as they saved. The article, which uncritically cites erroneous previous analysis as evidence, was [[Retraction in academic publishing|retracted]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Jaramillo|first=Catalina|date=2024-02-16|title=Review Article By Misinformation Spreaders Misleads About mRNA COVID-19 Vaccines|url=https://www.factcheck.org/2024/02/scicheck-review-article-by-misinformation-spreaders-misleads-about-mrna-covid-19-vaccines/|access-date=2026-07-13|website=FactCheck.org|language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-03-12|title=Retracted study provides 'greatest hits' of vaccine misinfo|url=https://aapnews.aap.com.au/news/retracted-study-provides-greatest-hits-of-vaccine-misinfo|access-date=2026-07-13|website=AAP News|language=en}}</ref> In May 2025, he testified before the [[United States Senate]] claiming that 73.9% of all deaths during the COVID-19 pandemic were caused by the adverse effects of COVID-19 vaccines. He based his claim on a discredited and [[Retracted paper|retracted]] scientific study: "''A systematic review of autopsy findings in deaths after COVID-19 vaccination''", which was heavily criticized for its methodological errors.<ref>{{Cite web |last=McDonald |first=Jessica |date=2024-07-05 |title=Flawed Autopsy 'Review' Revives Unsupported Claims of COVID-19 Vaccine Harm, Censorship |url=https://www.factcheck.org/2024/07/flawed-autopsy-review-revives-unsupported-claims-of-covid-19-vaccine-harm-censorship/ |access-date=2025-06-14 |website=FactCheck.org |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |first=Iria |last=Carballo-Carbajal |date=31 July 2023 |title=Flawed preprint based on autopsies inadequate to demonstrate that COVID-19 vaccines caused 74% of those deaths |url=https://science.feedback.org/review/flawed-preprint-autopsies-inadequate-demonstrate-covid19-vaccines-caused-74-percent-deaths/ |access-date=15 March 2026 |website=Health Feedback |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-05-27 |title='How much money have you made?': Blumenthal vs Dr McCullough at COVID vaccine side effects hearing |url=https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/news/international/world-news/how-much-money-have-you-made-blumenthal-vs-dr-mccullough-at-covid-vaccine-side-effects-hearing/videoshow/121439161.cms |access-date=2025-06-14 |website=The Economic Times |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Opening Statement of Dr. Peter A. ====Vaccine contains tracking agent====
In November 2021, a White House correspondent for the conservative outlet [[Newsmax]] falsely tweeted that the [[Moderna]] vaccine contained [[luciferase]] "so that you can be tracked."<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/luciferase-covid-19-vaccines/ |title='Luciferase' Is Not an Ingredient in COVID-19 Vaccines |date=2 November 2021 |author=Dan Evon |website=Snopes.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/factcheck-moderna-luciferin-idUSL1N2MT265 |title=Fact Check-Moderna's COVID-19 vaccine does not contain luciferin or luciferase |newspaper=Reuters |date=6 May 2021 |via=www.reuters.com}}</ref>

A [[Misinformation|false claim]] asserting that [[Graphite oxide|graphene oxide]] was a vaccine ingredient spread on [[social media]] in 2023.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-04-07 |title=No, Pfizer doc doesn't say graphene oxide is vaccine ingredient |url=https://apnews.com/article/fact-check-fda-pfizer-document-vaccine-graphene-oxide-988165173107 |access-date=2025-06-15 |website=AP News |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-11-30 |title=No graphene oxide in Pfizer's Covid-19 vaccine – Full Fact |url=https://fullfact.org/health/pfizer-graphene-oxide-mesh/ |access-date=2025-06-15 |website=fullfact.org |language=en}}</ref>

==== Vaccine 'reversal' and detox ====
In November 2021, erroneous claims arose that a "detox bath" of [[Magnesium sulfate|epsom salt]], [[borax]] and [[Bentonite|bentonite clay]] can remove the effects of the vaccine.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Vaccine holdouts are caving to mandates — then scrambling to 'undo' it |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/tech/tech-news/covid-vaccine-mandates-push-holdouts-get-shot-detox-rcna4859 |access-date=2021-11-14 |website=NBC News |language=en}}</ref> In fact, a rapid review of literature shows that no known mechanism exists for removing a vaccine from a vaccinated person.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-11-14 |title=Can you reverse COVID-19 vaccination? |url=https://chrisvoncsefalvay.com/2021/11/13/reverse-covid-19-vaccination/ |access-date=2021-11-14 |website=Chris von Csefalvay: Bits and Bugs |language=en-US |archive-date=14 November 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211114042654/https://chrisvoncsefalvay.com/2021/11/13/reverse-covid-19-vaccination/ }}</ref>

==== Approved vaccines "not available" in the United States ====
Under U.S. FDA regulations, a product approved under an [[Emergency Use Authorization]] (EUA) is considered "legally distinct" from a product that has received full approval by the FDA. Besides differences in naming and labeling to account for its approval, and increased FDA oversight over its production, there are no formulaic differences between the EUA and approved versions of a vaccine, and the two are considered interchangeable once approved. For example, the [[Pfizer vaccine]] has been labeled as "Pfizer–BioNTech COVID-19 Vaccine" since distribution began, but was assigned the [[United States Adopted Name]] "Comirnaty" upon its approval.<ref name="PolitiFact" /><ref name="Washington Post-2021" /> 

Some anti-vaccine advocates have made claims surrounding scenarios where this distinction is allegedly applicable; claims have been made that no FDA-approved vaccine is "available" in the United States because doses labeled as "Pfizer–BioNTech COVID-19 Vaccine" were still being distributed, and not "Comirnaty".<ref>{{Cite web | vauthors = Funke D |title=Fact check: Pfizer's FDA-approved vaccine is available in US |url= https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/factcheck/2021/10/20/fact-check-comirnaty-pfizers-fda-approved-vaccine-available-us/8538861002/ |access-date=2022-01-08 |website=USA TODAY |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name="PolitiFact" /> This claim was cited by a group of Louisiana Republican lawmakers,<ref name="PolitiFact" /> Senator [[Ron Johnson]],<ref>{{cite news |last=Blake |first=Aaron |date=5 October 2021 |title=Ron Johnson takes 2 covid conspiracy theories from fever swamps to Fox News prime time |newspaper=Washington Post |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2021/10/05/ron-johnson-takes-2-covid-conspiracy-theories-fever-swamps-fox-news-primetime/ |access-date=5 October 2021}}</ref> and in a lawsuit filed by the [[First Liberty Institute]] against a COVID-19 vaccine mandate implemented by the U.S. military. In the case of the latter, the plaintiffs claimed that the mandate applied specifically to Comirnaty only, and not the "experimental" Pfizer–BioNTech COVID-19 Vaccine.<ref>{{Cite web |vauthors=Shomaker C |title=New River Marine, N.C. Marine officer plaintiffs in military vaccine mandate lawsuits |url=https://www.jdnews.com/story/news/2021/11/26/multiple-lawsuits-pending-that-challenge-militarys-vaccine-mandate-as-deadlines-near/8673596002/ |access-date=2022-01-08 |website=The Daily News |language=en-US |archive-date=8 January 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220108210259/https://www.jdnews.com/story/news/2021/11/26/multiple-lawsuits-pending-that-challenge-militarys-vaccine-mandate-as-deadlines-near/8673596002/ }}</ref>

Another claim was that the approved version does not share the same liability protection as the version produced under an EUA. Under the [[Public Readiness and Emergency Preparedness Act|Public Readiness and Emergency Preparedness (PREP) Act]], individuals are eligible for compensation via the [[Countermeasures Injury Compensation Program]] (CICP) for severe outcomes or death caused by COVID-19 countermeasures such as vaccines.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Mandavilli |first=Apoorva |date=2024-05-03 |title=Thousands Believe Covid Vaccines Harmed Them. Is Anyone Listening? |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/05/03/health/covid-vaccines-side-effects.html |access-date=2024-05-03 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> This applies generally to all COVID-19 vaccines, including those not yet given formal approval.<ref name="PolitiFact">{{Cite web |title=What's in a name? Louisiana lawmakers wrongly say name change scuttles FDA COVID-19 vaccine approval |url=https://www.politifact.com/factchecks/2021/oct/07/10-louisiana-lawmakers/whats-name-louisiana-lawmakers-wrongly-say-name-ch/ |access-date=2022-01-08 |website=PolitiFact |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name="Washington Post-2021">{{Cite news |date=2021-08-30 |title=The false claim that the fully-approved Pfizer vaccine lacks liability protection |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2021/08/30/false-claim-that-fully-approved-pfizer-vaccine-lacks-liability-protection/ |access-date=2022-01-08 |newspaper=Washington Post}}</ref>

==== Vaccines as an "operating system" ====
A statement on the Moderna website which likens mRNA vaccines to operating systems as an analogy, but does not literally state that the vaccines were operating systems.<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.reuters.com/article/uk-factcheck-operating-system-idUSKBN2A913W | title=Fact check: The COVID-19 vaccine is not an operating system designed to program humans | newspaper=Reuters | date=9 February 2021 }}</ref>

==== Department of Defense disinformation campaign ====
{{main|ChinaAngVirus disinformation campaign}}

A [[Reuters]] investigation found that the [[United States Department of Defense]] (DoD), as retaliation for China's attempts to blame the United States for the pandemic, undertook a [[disinformation]] campaign in the Philippines, later expanded to Central Asia and the Middle East, which sought to discredit China, in particular its [[Sinovac Biotech|Sinovac]] vaccine.<ref name="Bing_Schectman_6/14/2024">{{cite web | last1=Bing | first1=Chris | last2=Schectman | first2=Joel | title=Pentagon ran secret anti-vax campaign to incite fear of China vaccines | website=[[Reuters]] | date=June 14, 2024 | url=https://www.reuters.com/investigates/special-report/usa-covid-propaganda/ | access-date=June 18, 2024}}</ref> The campaign was described as "payback" for [[COVID-19 misinformation by China|COVID-19 disinformation by China]] directed against the U.S. and an effort to counter China's [[vaccine diplomacy]].<ref name="Toropin-2024">{{Cite web |last=Toropin |first=Konstantin |date=2024-06-14 |title=Pentagon Stands by Secret Anti-Vaccination Disinformation Campaign in Philippines After Reuters Report |url=https://www.military.com/daily-news/2024/06/14/pentagon-stands-secret-anti-vaccination-disinformation-campaign-philippines-after-reuters-report.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240614223757/https://www.military.com/daily-news/2024/06/14/pentagon-stands-secret-anti-vaccination-disinformation-campaign-philippines-after-reuters-report.html |archive-date=2024-06-14 |access-date=2024-06-19 |website=[[Military.com]] |language=en}}</ref> The campaign ran from 2020 to 2021 and was overseen by [[Special Operations Command Pacific]] as well as the [[United States Central Command]].<ref name="Bing_Schectman_6/14/2024" /> Military personnel at [[MacDill Air Force Base]] in Florida operated phony social media accounts, some of which were more than five years old according to Reuters. During the COVID-19 pandemic, they disseminated hashtags of #ChinaIsTheVirus and posts claiming that the Sinovac vaccine contained gelatin from pork and therefore was ''[[haram]]'' or forbidden for purposes of Islamic law. US diplomats aware of the campaign were against the idea, but they were overruled by the military, which also asked tech companies not to take down the content after it was discovered by Facebook and X. A retrospective review by the DoD subsequently uncovered other social and political messaging that was "many leagues away" from acceptable military objective. The primary [[Arms industry|defence contractor]] on the project was [[General Dynamics|General Dynamics IT]], which received $493 million for its role.<ref name="Bing_Schectman_6/14/2024"/>

=== Socially based claims ===
{{see also|Protests over responses to the COVID-19 pandemic}}

==== Claims about a vaccine before one existed ====
Multiple social media posts promoted a conspiracy theory claiming that in the early stages of the pandemic, the virus was known and that a vaccine was already available. [[PolitiFact]] and [[FactCheck.org]] noted that no vaccine existed for COVID-19 at that point. The patents cited by various social media posts reference existing patents for genetic sequences and vaccines for other strains of coronavirus such as the [[Severe acute respiratory syndrome–related coronavirus|SARS coronavirus]].<ref name=20200123politifact>{{cite web |url=https://www.politifact.com/factchecks/2020/jan/23/facebook-posts/there-outbreak-china-wuhan-coronavirus-there-not-v/ |title=No, there is no vaccine for the Wuhan coronavirus |vauthors=Kertscher T |website=Politifact |date=23 January 2020 |access-date=7 February 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200207133056/https://www.politifact.com/factchecks/2020/jan/23/facebook-posts/there-outbreak-china-wuhan-coronavirus-there-not-v/ |archive-date=7 February 2020 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="20200124factcheckA">{{cite web |vauthors=McDonald J |date=24 January 2020 |title=Social Media Posts Spread Bogus Coronavirus Conspiracy Theory |url=https://www.factcheck.org/2020/01/social-media-posts-spread-bogus-coronavirus-conspiracy-theory/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200206102802/https://www.factcheck.org/2020/01/social-media-posts-spread-bogus-coronavirus-conspiracy-theory/ |archive-date=6 February 2020 |access-date=10 February 2020 |work=Factcheck.org}}</ref> The WHO reported that as of 5 February 2020, despite news reports of "breakthrough drugs" being discovered, there were no treatments known to be effective;<ref name="WHO no known">{{Cite news |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-china-health-treatments-who-idUSKBN1ZZ1M6 |title=WHO: 'no known effective' treatments for new coronavirus |date=5 February 2020 |work=Reuters |access-date=6 February 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200205155653/https://www.reuters.com/article/us-china-health-treatments-who-idUSKBN1ZZ1M6 |archive-date=5 February 2020 |url-status=live}}</ref> this included antibiotics and herbal remedies not being useful.<ref name=aljazeera2002020934>{{cite news |title=Dispelling the myths around the new coronavirus outbreak |url=https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2020/2/2/dispelling-the-myths-around-the-new-coronavirus-outbreak |access-date=8 February 2020 |publisher=Al Jazeera |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200206033735/https://www.aljazeera.com/amp/news/2020/02/dispelling-myths-coronavirus-outbreak-200202093426388.html |archive-date=6 February 2020 }}</ref>

On Facebook, a widely shared post claimed in April 2020 that seven Senegalese children had died because they had received a COVID-19 vaccine. No such vaccine existed, although some were in clinical trials at that time.<ref name=20200408afp>{{cite web |vauthors=Faivre Le Cadre AS |url=https://factcheck.afp.com/senegalese-children-did-not-die-coronavirus-vaccine-which-does-not-yet-exist |title=Senegalese children did not die from a coronavirus vaccine (which does not yet exist) |date=8 April 2020 |website=AFP Fact Check |access-date=13 September 2021 |archive-date=8 March 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210308134151/https://factcheck.afp.com/senegalese-children-did-not-die-coronavirus-vaccine-which-does-not-yet-exist |url-status=live}}</ref>

====Magnetization====
Some social media users have falsely asserted COVID-19 vaccines cause people to [[Human magnetism|become magnetized]] such that metal objects stick to their bodies, which afterwards could also be sensible to [[Bluetooth]].<ref>{{cite news |vauthors=Camero K |title=No, COVID vaccines don't make you magnetic. Experts debunk social media videos |url=https://www.miamiherald.com/news/coronavirus/article251955083.html |work=Miami Herald |date=7 June 2021 |access-date=13 September 2021 |archive-date=15 June 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210615023357/https://www.miamiherald.com/news/coronavirus/article251955083.html |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-12-17 |title=Las vacunas contra la covid-19 no hacen que las personas sean detectables por Bluetooth - Verificat |url=https://www.verificat.cat/es/las-vacunas-contra-la-covid-19-no-hacen-que-las-personas-sean-detectables-por-bluetooth/ |access-date=2026-05-20 |language=es-ES}}</ref> Video clips of people showing magnets sticking to the injection site have been spread on social media platforms such as [[Instagram]], [[Facebook]], [[Twitter]], [[YouTube]], and [[TikTok]], claiming that vaccination implants a [[microchip]] in people's arms.<ref name="AFP microchips">{{cite news |vauthors=Wade N |title=Covid-19 vaccines do not contain magnetic microchips |url=https://factcheck.afp.com/covid-19-vaccines-do-not-contain-magnetic-microchips |work=AFP Fact Check |agency=Agence France-Presse |date=13 May 2021}}</ref><ref name="Fichera">{{cite news |vauthors=Fichera A |title=Magnet Videos Refuel Bogus Claim of Vaccine Microchips |url=https://www.factcheck.org/2021/05/scicheck-magnet-videos-refuel-bogus-claim-of-vaccine-microchips/ |work=FactCheck.org |date=14 May 2021}}</ref> Called by Republicans as an expert witness before a June 2021 hearing of the Ohio House Health Committee, anti-vaccine activist [[Sherri Tenpenny]] promoted the false claim, adding, "There's been people who have long suspected that there's been some sort of an interface, yet to be defined interface, between what's being injected in these shots and all of the 5G towers."<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.dispatch.com/story/news/2021/06/09/doctor-sherri-tenpenny-testimony-ohio-lawmakers-vaccines-magnetized-5-g/7616027002/ |title=GOP-invited Ohio doctor Sherri Tenpenny falsely tells Ohio lawmakers COVID-19 shots 'magnetize' people, create 5G 'interfaces' |vauthors=Bischoff LA |website=The Columbus Dispatch |access-date=13 September 2021 |archive-date=14 June 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210614222249/https://www.dispatch.com/story/news/2021/06/09/doctor-sherri-tenpenny-testimony-ohio-lawmakers-vaccines-magnetized-5-g/7616027002/ |url-status=live}}</ref>

[[5G]]-compatible chips are about 13 times too large to fit through the needles used to administer COVID-19 vaccines, whose internal diameter is between 0.26 and 0.41 millimeters.<ref>{{cite news |vauthors=Black E, Schoolov K |title=Why the Covid vaccines can't contain a tracking microchip or make you magnetic |url=https://www.cnbc.com/video/2021/10/01/why-theres-no-5g-tracking-microchip-in-the-covid-vaccine.html |work=CNBC |date=1 October 2021}}</ref> Most microchips do not contain [[ferromagnetic]] components, being made mostly of [[silicon]].{{r|Fichera}} It is possible for smooth objects such as magnets to stick to one's skin if the skin is slightly oily.{{r|AFP microchips}} No COVID-19 vaccines authorized for use in the U.S. or Europe contain magnetic or metal ingredients or microchips. Instead the vaccines contain proteins, lipids, water, salts, and [[pH buffer]]s.{{r|Gregory|Fichera|AFP microchips}}

====Disappearing needles====
Twitter and YouTube users circulated video clips purporting to show that vaccine injections given to health care workers were staged for the press using syringes with "disappearing needles". The syringes used were actually [[safety syringe]]s, which automatically retract the needle once the vaccine is injected in order to reduce accidental [[needlestick]] injuries to nurses and lab workers.{{r|Gregory}}<ref>{{cite news |title=Millions move into tier 3 of virus rules in England |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/live/world-55345020 |work=BBC News |date=17 December 2020}}</ref>

==== Political divides and distrust in government ====

vaccines.<ref>{{cite news |author1=Andrew Russell |author2=Stewart Bell  |title=Self-declared 'Queen of Canada' detained by RCMP after alleged threats to health-care workers |url=https://globalnews.ca/news/8417379/queen-of-canada-covid-online-threats/ |access-date=3 February 2022 |work=Global News |date=1 December 2021 |location=Toronto ON}}</ref>

[[Anti-statism|Anti-government]] groups such as [[Sovereign citizen movement|sovereign citizens]] and [[Freeman on the land|freemen on the land]] also took part in the anti-vaccine movement.<ref>{{citation|title= Anti-vaxxers, anti-maskers and the sovereign citizen movement|work= New York Daily News|date= 14 August 2021|url= https://www.tribpub.com/gdpr/nydailynews.com/|access-date= 2022-01-13|archive-date= 13 August 2020|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20200813153626/https://www.tribpub.com/gdpr/nydailynews.com/}}</ref><ref>{{citation |title= Anti-vax protests: 'Sovereign citizens' fight UK Covid vaccine rollout|work=   |publisher = BBC|date=18 January 2022 |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/59870550 |access-date= 2022-01-18}}</ref><ref name="UKonnotice">{{citation |title=Putting the UK on notice: How US legal fiction inspired aggressive action from UK anti-vaxxers|work = The Independent|date=31 October 2021 |url= https://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/home-news/sovereign-citizens-uk-antivaxxers-b1947186.html |access-date= 2022-01-24}}</ref><ref>{{citation |title=Republic of Kanata convener says its sheriffs will stop distribution of COVID-19 vaccines in Vancouver   |work= |publisher=The Georgia Straight |url= https://www.straight.com/news/republic-of-kanata-convener-says-its-sheriffs-will-stop-distribution-of-covid-19-vaccines-in |date= 10 December 2020|access-date= 5 February 2022 }}</ref> 

During lockdowns in Bulgaria, many Roma neighborhoods claimed that they were subject to lockdowns without proper explanations even though the level of infections to other parts of the country were higher than their neighborhoods. The communities already held a distrust of institutions and the government, and helped create an even more strained relationship and lack of trust.<ref name="Kottasová-2021">{{Cite web | vauthors = Kottasová I |title=They have all the vaccines they need, yet these EU nations are still miles behind their neighbors |url=https://www.cnn.com/2021/10/01/europe/eastern-europe-vaccine-takeup-bulgaria-romania-intl-cmd/index.html |access-date=2021-10-01 |website=CNN |date=October 2021 |archive-date=1 October 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211001153611/https://www.cnn.com/2021/10/01/europe/eastern-europe-vaccine-takeup-bulgaria-romania-intl-cmd/index.html |url-status=live}}</ref>

In France, [[Florian Philippot]] and [[Nicolas Dupont-Aignan]], right-wing candidates to the [[2022 French presidential election|2022 presidential election]], have both cast doubts about the vaccine's effectiveness and safety.<ref name="BFM">{{Cite news | vauthors =Roussey E |title="Non je ne suis pas vacciné": l'échange houleux entre Florian Philippot et le médecin Ludovic Toro|url=https://www.bfmtv.com/sante/non-je-ne-suis-pas-vaccine-l-echange-houleux-entre-florian-philippot-et-ludovic-toro_AV-202108050429.html |access-date=2022-02-14 |date= 8 August 2021|work=BFM TV}}</ref><ref name="RTL">{{Cite news | vauthors = Garin V  |title=FACT CHECKING - 63% des morts du Covid étaient-ils vaccinés, comme l'affirme Dupont-Aignan ?|url=https://www.rtl.fr/actu/politique/fact-checking-63-des-morts-du-covid-etaient-ils-vaccines-comme-l-affirme-dupont-aignan-7900108030 |access-date=2022-02-14 |date= 22 December 2021|work=RTL}}</ref>

=== Government investigations ===

In December 2022, vaccine-skeptical Florida Governor [[Ron DeSantis]] requested the impaneling of a [[grand jury]] to "investigate criminal or wrongful activity in Florida relating to the development, promotion, and distribution of vaccines purported to prevent COVID-19 infection, symptoms, and transmission", specifically mentioning statements made by drug manufacturers and federal officials.<ref>{{cite news |title=Florida Supreme Court impanels grand jury on COVID-19 vaccines |url=https://wusfnews.wusf.usf.edu/health-news-florida/2022-12-23/florida-supreme-court-impanels-grand-jury-on-covid-19-vaccines |publisher=[[WUSF (FM)|WUSF]] |author=Jim Saunders |agency=[[News Service of Florida]]
|date=23 December 2022}}</ref>

==Vaccine hesitancy==
{{Further|Vaccine hesitancy|Vaccine misinformation}}

=== Concerns about menstrual irregularities ===
Concerns about menstrual irregularities caused by COVID-19 have led to vaccine hesitancy. A meta-analysis from 2023 indicated that COVID-19 vaccination can lead to menstrual irregularities but that more studies are required to establish a causal relationship.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Al Kadri |first1=Hanan M. |last2=Al Sudairy |first2=Atika A. |last3=Alangari |first3=Abdulaziz S. |last4=Al Khateeb |first4=Badr F. |last5=El-Metwally |first5=Ashraf A. |date=May 2023 |title=COVID-19 vaccination and menstrual disorders among women: Findings from a meta-analysis study |journal=Journal of Infection and Public Health |volume=16 |issue=5 |pages=697–704 |doi=10.1016/j.jiph.2023.02.019 |issn=1876-0341 |pmc=9979695 |pmid=36934644}}</ref>

=== Pregnancy and vaccine hesitancy ===
A 2022 meta-analysis on COVID-19 vaccines and pregnancy found that pregnant people were less likely to get vaccinations compared with non-pregnant cohorts. Factors associated with lower takeup of vaccination during pregnancy included younger age, lower education, lower [[socioeconomic status]], and lack of adherence to [[Influenza vaccine|influenza vaccination]] recommendations.<ref name="Badell-2022">{{Cite journal |last1=Badell |first1=Martina L. |last2=Dude |first2=Carolynn M. |last3=Rasmussen |first3=Sonja A. |last4=Jamieson |first4=Denise J. |date=2022-08-10 |title=Covid-19 vaccination in pregnancy |url=https://www.bmj.com/content/378/bmj-2021-069741 |journal=BMJ |language=en |volume=378 |article-number=e069741 |doi=10.1136/bmj-2021-069741 |issn=1756-1833 |pmid=35948352|pmc=9363819 }}</ref> 

One study in the analysis found varying influence of education and influenza vaccination history depending on race, suggesting that lived experiences with [[Institutional racism|systemic racism]] may have an effect on vaccine hesitancy in pregnancy.<ref name="Badell-2022" />[[File:Facts about COVID-19 vaccines (English).pdf|thumb|A [[Centers for Disease Control|CDC]] Fact sheet about COVID-19 vaccines]]

===Hong Kong===
In Hong Kong, the lower perceived risk of catching COVID-19 when it was under control, misinformation about the vaccines' side effects and efficacy, as well as political events and distrust of the HKSAR government, contributed to a low rate of vaccination.<ref name=nature2022>{{cite news |last1=Silver |first1=Andrew |title='COVID zero' regions struggle with vaccine complacency |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-022-00554-0 |journal=Nature |date=4 March 2022 |language=en |doi=10.1038/d41586-022-00554-0}}</ref><ref name=nyt2022-Stevenson>{{cite news |last1=Stevenson |first1=Alexandra |last2=Ramzy |first2=Austin |title='I Don't Dare Get the Shot': Virus Ravages Unvaccinated Older Hong Kongers |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/02/25/business/hong-kong-unvaccinated-elderly.html |work=The New York Times |date=25 February 2022}}</ref> To some extent, similar complacency occurred in Taiwan, Macau, and mainland China. Many Hongkongers felt that the government was actively pushing the SinoVac vaccine despite its lower efficacy compared with BioNTech and AstraZeneca. Older residents might believe the BioNTech vaccine lead to severe side effects. Officials also stated that people with "uncontrolled severe chronic diseases" should not receive the SinoVac vaccine and urged those who weren't sure to consult with their doctors first. Conspiracy theories about the government spread as well due to a packaging issue with the BioNTech vaccine.<ref name=theatlantic_618469>{{Cite web|url=https://www.theatlantic.com/international/archive/2021/04/hong-kong-trust-vaccine/618469/|title=The Place With Surprisingly High Vaccine Hesitancy|first=Timothy|last=McLaughlin|date=1 April 2021|website=The Atlantic|access-date=9 April 2021|archive-date=8 April 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210408054242/https://www.theatlantic.com/international/archive/2021/04/hong-kong-trust-vaccine/618469/|url-status=live}}</ref> Skepticism of Western and preventive medicine further contributed to the hesitancy.<ref name="apnews_20210617">{{cite web|url=https://apnews.com/article/hong-kong-lifestyle-travel-coronavirus-vaccine-coronavirus-pandemic-28c1947c8576453ac08ecacf614b7dea|title=Get a jab, win a condo: Hong Kong tries vaccine incentives|first=Zen|last=Soo|work=[[AP News]]|date=17 June 2021|access-date=12 July 2021}}</ref><ref name=nyt2022-Stevenson />

Towards the end of May 2021, about 19% of Hongkongers had received their first dose and 13.8% their second.<ref name="theguardian_20210525_covid">{{Cite web|url=http://www.theguardian.com/world/2021/may/25/covid-vaccine-hesitancy-could-see-hong-kong-throw-away-millions-of-doses|title=Covid vaccine hesitancy could see Hong Kong throw away doses|date=25 May 2021|website=The Guardian|access-date=1 June 2021|archive-date=2 June 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210602081539/https://www.theguardian.com/world/2021/may/25/covid-vaccine-hesitancy-could-see-hong-kong-throw-away-millions-of-doses|url-status=live}}</ref> By 1 January 2022, 62% of the population was fully vaccinated, but as of 7 February, only 33% of those aged 80 or older had received one dose.<ref name=nature2022 /> As Omicron subvariants spread across the city, a study showed that 15% of those aged 80 or older who weren't immunized at all died after contracting the disease, compared with 3% of those who got two SinoVac shots and 1.5% of those who received two BioNTech doses.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Cortez |first1=Michelle Fay |last2=Lew |first2=Linda |title=Sinovac's Low Efficacy in Hong Kong Is a Worrying Sign for China |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2022-03-20/hk-s-immunized-who-died-of-covid-mainly-got-sinovac-ming-pao |work=Bloomberg.com |date=20 March 2022 |language=en}}</ref>

===United States===
[[File:202003- Cumulative county COVID-19 death rates - by share of votes for Donald Trump.svg |thumb|After the December 2020 introduction of COVID vaccines, a partisan gap in death rates developed, indicating the effects of vaccine skepticism.<ref name=NYTimes_20240311/> As of March 2024, more than 30 percent of Republicans had not received a Covid vaccine, compared with less than 10 percent of Democrats.<ref name=NYTimes_20240311>{{cite news |last1=Leonhardt |first1=David |title=The Fourth Anniversary of the Covid Pandemic |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/03/11/briefing/covid-pandemic-anniversary.html |newspaper=The New York Times |date=11 March 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251029005241/https://www.nytimes.com/2024/03/11/briefing/covid-pandemic-anniversary.html |archive-date= 2025-10-29|url-status=live }} "Data excludes Alaska. Sources: C.D.C. Wonder; Edison Research. (Chart) By The New York Times. Source credits chart to Ashley Wu.</ref>]]
[[File:Covid misinformation mobile.jpg|thumb|Vehicle with vaccine conspiracy theories written on it]]

[[COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy in the United States|In the United States, COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy]] varies largely by region; however, regardless of region, medical professionals are vaccinated at higher rates than the general public.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-08-08 |title=Vaccination rates among hospital staffs in Alabama likely '50-60%' |url=https://www.al.com/news/2021/08/vaccination-rates-among-hospital-staffs-in-alabama-likely-50-60.html |access-date=2021-09-04 |website=al |language=en |archive-date=4 September 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210904145613/https://www.al.com/news/2021/08/vaccination-rates-among-hospital-staffs-in-alabama-likely-50-60.html |url-status=live}}</ref> Estimates from two surveys were that 67% or 80% of people in the U.S. would accept a new vaccination against COVID-19, with wide disparity by education level, employment status, ethnicity, and geography.<ref name="malik">{{cite journal | vauthors = Malik AA, McFadden SM, Elharake J, Omer SB | title = Determinants of COVID-19 vaccine acceptance in the US | journal = eClinicalMedicine | volume = 26 | article-number = 100495 | date = September 2020 | pmid = 32838242 | pmc = 7423333 | doi = 10.1016/j.eclinm.2020.100495 | title-link = doi | doi-access = free }}</ref> A US study conducted in January 2021 found that trust in science and scientists was strongly correlated with likelihood to get vaccinated for COVID-19 among those who had not already gotten vaccinated.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Agley J, Xiao Y, Thompson EE, Golzarri-Arroyo L | title = Factors associated with reported likelihood to get vaccinated for COVID-19 in a nationally representative US survey | journal = Public Health | volume = 196 | pages = 91–94 | date = July 2021 | pmid = 34171616 | pmc = 8157318 | doi = 10.1016/j.puhe.2021.05.009 }}</ref> In March 2021, 19% of US adults claimed to have been vaccinated while 50% announced plans to get vaccinated.<ref>{{cite news |date=5 March 2021 |title=More in U.S. Embrace Covid Vaccines, Pew Poll Shows |work=[[The New York Times]] |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/03/05/world/americans-vaccinations-survey.html |access-date=8 March 2021 |archive-date=6 March 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210306080550/https://www.nytimes.com/2021/03/05/world/americans-vaccinations-survey.html |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |vauthors=Funk C |title=Growing Share of Americans Say They Plan To Get a COVID-19 Vaccine – or Already Have |website=Pew Research Center Science & Society |date=5 March 2021 |url=https://www.pewresearch.org/science/wp-content/uploads/sites/16/2021/03/PS_2021.03.05_covid-19-vaccines_REPORT.pdf |archive-date=6 March 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210306185703/https://www.pewresearch.org/science/wp-content/uploads/sites/16/2021/03/PS_2021.03.05_covid-19-vaccines_REPORT.pdf |url-status=live |access-date=8 March 2021}} * {{Lay source | url=https://www.pewresearch.org/science/2021/03/05/growing-share-of-americans-say-they-plan-to-get-a-covid-19-vaccine-or-already-have/ | title = Growing Share of Americans Say They Plan To Get a COVID-19 Vaccine – or Already Have | work = Pew Research Center }}</ref>

A 2022 study found a link between online COVID-19 misinformation and early vaccine hesitancy and refusal.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Pierri |first1=Francesco |last2=Perry |first2=Brea |last3=DeVerna |first3=Matthew |last4=Yang |first4=Kai-Cheng |last5=Flammini |first5=Alessandro |last6=Menczer |first6=Filippo |last7=Bryden |first7=John |title=Online misinformation is linked to early COVID-19 vaccination hesitancy and refusal |journal=Scientific Reports |date=2022 |volume=12 |issue=1 |page=5966 |doi=10.1038/s41598-022-10070-w  |doi-access=free|pmid=35474313 |pmc=9043199 |arxiv=2104.10635 |bibcode=2022NatSR..12.5966P }}</ref> Despite a strong association between vaccine hesitancy and Republican vote share at the US county and state levels, the authors found that the associations between vaccine outcomes and misinformation remained significant when accounting for political, demographic, and socioeconomic factors.

In the United States, vaccine hesitancy could be seen in certain social groups due to lack of trusted medical sources, traumatic past experiences with medical care and widespread theories.<ref>{{Cite web | vauthors = Wazir Z |date=30 September 2021 |title=Vaccine Hesitancy Higher in Wealthy Nations, Survey Shows |url=https://www.usnews.com/news/best-countries/articles/2021-09-30/vaccine-hesitancy-isnt-unique-to-the-us-survey-shows |url-status=live |access-date=1 October 2021 |website=US News |archive-date=25 October 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211025173751/https://www.usnews.com/news/best-countries/articles/2021-09-30/vaccine-hesitancy-isnt-unique-to-the-us-survey-shows}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web | vauthors = Choi HA |date=7 September 2021 |title=Why some US Blacks and Latinos remain COVID-19 'vaccine deliberate' |url=https://abcnews.go.com/Health/us-blacks-latinos-remain-covid-19-vaccine-deliberate/story?id=79830353 |url-status=live |access-date=2021-10-01 |website=ABC News |language=en |archive-date=1 October 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211001155507/https://abcnews.go.com/Health/us-blacks-latinos-remain-covid-19-vaccine-deliberate/story?id=79830353}}</ref>  Distrust can be seen in the African American population where many see the history in the United States of using African Americans as experiments, such as the [[Tuskegee Syphilis Study|Tuskegee experiments]] and the work of [[J. Marion Sims]], as basis to refuse the vaccine.<ref>{{Cite web | vauthors = Jeter J |date=3 September 2021 |title=Vaccination hesitancy among Blacks based on mistrust of an unjust system |url=https://spokesman-recorder.com/2021/09/03/vaccination-hesitancy-among-blacks-based-on-mistrust-of-an-unjust-system/ |url-status=live |access-date=2021-10-01 |website=spokesman-recorder.com |language=en-US |archive-date=1 October 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211001155513/https://spokesman-recorder.com/2021/09/03/vaccination-hesitancy-among-blacks-based-on-mistrust-of-an-unjust-system/}}</ref>

According to ''[[The New York Times]]'', only 28 percent of Black New Yorkers ages 18 to 44 years were fully vaccinated {{As of|2021|August|lc=yes}}, compared with 48 percent of Latino residents and 52 percent of White residents in that age group. Interviewees cited mistrust of the government, personal experiences of [[medical racism]], and historical medical experimentation on Black people such as the [[Tuskegee Syphilis Study]] as reasons for their reluctance to be vaccinated.<ref name="Goldstein Aug 2021">{{Cite news | vauthors = Goldstein J, Sedacca M |date=2021-08-12 |title=Why Only 28 Percent of Young Black New Yorkers Are Vaccinated |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/08/12/nyregion/covid-vaccine-black-young-new-yorkers.html |url-access=limited |issn=0362-4331 |access-date=9 October 2021 |archive-date=25 October 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211025173742/https://www.nytimes.com/2021/08/12/nyregion/covid-vaccine-black-young-new-yorkers.html |url-status=live}}</ref> A professor from the [[University of Warsaw]] in Poland, claimed that her research found that medical mistrust was higher in nations that had experienced [[Soviet Union|Soviet]]-style [[communism]] in the past, and vaccine hesitancy could be seen if the countries introduced compulsory vaccination regulations.<ref name="Kottasová-2021" /> Medical mistrust is also seen in Russia where one person described a lack of understanding what the vaccine is and claimed that if there was more statistics and research about the [[Sputnik V COVID-19 vaccine|Sputnik V]] and other Russian made vaccines they would be more "loyal". She also stated that there was also mistrust over the lack of consistent medical information about the vaccine coming from many sources including the authorities of the region.<ref>{{Cite news | vauthors = Galpin R |date=2021-10-21 |title=Russia's Covid nightmare driven by vaccine rejection |language=en-GB |work=BBC News |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-europe-58998366 |access-date=2021-10-22 |archive-date=22 October 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211022130349/https://www.bbc.com/news/world-europe-58998366 |url-status=live}}</ref>

According to prominent biomedical researcher [[Peter Hotez]], he and other scientists who publicly defend vaccines have been attacked on social media, harassed with threatening emails, intimidated, and confronted physically by opponents of vaccination. He further attributes the increase in aggressiveness of the anti-vaccination movement to the influence of the extreme wing of the Republican Party. Hotez estimates that roughly 200,000 preventable deaths from COVID-19, mainly among Republicans, occurred in the US because of refusal to be vaccinated.<ref name="Hotez 2023"/> A 2023 study published in the ''[[Journal of the American Medical Association]]'' found "evidence of higher excess mortality for Republican voters compared with Democratic voters in Florida and Ohio after, but not before, COVID-19 vaccines were available to all adults in the US".<ref>{{cite journal|title=Excess Death Rates for Republican and Democratic Registered Voters in Florida and Ohio During the COVID-19 Pandemic|first1=Jacob|last1=Wallace|journal=[[JAMA Internal Medicine]]|first2=Paul|last2=Goldsmith-Pinkham|first3=Jason L.|last3=Schwartz|date=2023 |volume=183 |issue=9 |pages=916–923 |doi=10.1001/jamainternmed.2023.1154 |pmid=37486680 |pmc=10366951}}</ref>

==Countermeasures==
=== COVID-19 passes ===
Some countries are using vaccination tracking systems, apps, or [[Vaccine passports during the COVID-19 pandemic|passports]] that are labeled as passes to allow individuals certain freedoms. In France, every adult must present a "pass sanitaire" before entering specific locations such as restaurants, cafes, museums, and sports stadiums after a new law was passed in July 2021.<ref name="WLFI News">{{Cite web |title=A Covid pass takes France by storm |url=https://www.wlfi.com/content/national/575351212.html |access-date=2021-09-20 |website=WLFI News |language=en |archive-date=20 September 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210920212523/https://www.wlfi.com/content/national/575351212.html |url-status=live}}</ref> Italy reported a 40% increase in the number of people who received the first dose of the vaccine after a governmental decree in September 2021 requiring a health pass for all workers either in the public or private sectors starting in October 2021. Similar passes have been put into effect in countries such as Slovenia and Greece.<ref>{{Cite web |date=18 September 2021 |title=Coronavirus: What's happening in Canada and around the world on Saturday |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/world/coronavirus-covid19-canada-world-sept18-2021-1.6181116 |url-status=live |access-date=20 September 2021 |website=CBC |archive-date=20 September 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210920024633/https://www.cbc.ca/news/world/coronavirus-covid19-canada-world-sept18-2021-1.6181116}}</ref> Lithuania introduced vaccination certificates that citizens 12-years and older must show to enter most public indoor spaces.<ref name="Mackintosh_2021">{{Cite web | vauthors = Mackintosh E |date=3 December 2021 |title=Making Covid-19 vaccines mandatory was once unthinkable. But European countries are showing it can work |url=https://www.cnn.com/2021/11/30/europe/covid-vaccine-mandates-austria-europe-cmd-intl/index.html |access-date=2021-12-28 |website=CNN}}</ref>

===Encouragement by public figures and celebrities===
Many public figures and celebrities have publicly declared that they have been vaccinated against COVID-19, and encouraged people to get vaccinated. Many have made video recordings or otherwise documented their vaccination. They do this partly to counteract [[vaccine hesitancy]] and [[COVID-19 misinformation#Vaccines|COVID-19 vaccine conspiracy theories]].<ref name="Sky News" /><ref>{{cite news |date=21 December 2020 |title='I'm ready': Joe Biden receives coronavirus vaccine live on TV |work=[[The Guardian]] |url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2020/dec/21/joe-biden-coronavirus-vaccine-covid-public |access-date=26 December 2020 |vauthors=Bekiempis V}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |date=18 December 2020 |title=Mike Pence receives Covid-19 vaccine on live TV: 'I didn't feel a thing' |work=[[The Guardian]] |url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2020/dec/18/mike-pence-receives-covid-19-vaccine-live-tv |access-date=26 December 2020 |vauthors=Aratani L}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |date=3 December 2020 |title=Obama, Clinton and Bush pledge to take Covid vaccine on TV to show its safety |work=[[The Guardian]] |url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2020/dec/03/obama-clinton-bush-covid-vaccine-safety |access-date=26 December 2020 |vauthors=Gabbatt A |archive-date=28 December 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201228213932/https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2020/dec/03/obama-clinton-bush-covid-vaccine-safety |url-status=live}}</ref>

====Politicians====
Many current and former heads of state and government ministers have released photographs of their vaccinations, encouraging others to be vaccinated, including [[Kyriakos Mitsotakis]], [[Zdravko Marić]], [[Olivier Véran]], [[Mike Pence]], [[Joe Biden]], [[Barack Obama]], [[George W. Bush]], [[Bill Clinton]], the [[Dalai Lama]], [[Narendra Modi]], [[Justin Trudeau]], [[Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez]], [[Nancy Pelosi]] and [[Kamala Harris]].<ref name="People">{{cite web |title=See Amy Schumer, Oprah Winfrey and More Celebs and Politicians Who've Gotten Their COVID-19 Vaccines |url=https://people.com/health/celebrities-and-politicians-get-covid-19-vaccine-photos/ |access-date=31 March 2021 |website=People |archive-date=29 March 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210329030136/https://people.com/health/celebrities-and-politicians-get-covid-19-vaccine-photos/ |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |vauthors=Elan P |date=12 March 2021 |title=Why are male politicians in love with topless vaccine selfies? |work=[[The Guardian]] |url=http://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2021/mar/12/male-politicians-vaccine-selfies-vaxxie |access-date=31 March 2021 |archive-date=31 March 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210331042759/https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2021/mar/12/male-politicians-vaccine-selfies-vaxxie |url-status=live}}</ref>

[[Elizabeth II]] and [[Prince Philip, Duke of Edinburgh|Prince Philip]] announced they had the vaccine, breaking from protocol of keeping the [[British royal family]]'s health private.<ref name="Sky News">{{cite web |title=COVID-19: Celebrities who have had the coronavirus vaccination |url=https://news.sky.com/story/covid-19-celebrities-who-have-had-the-coronavirus-vaccination-12165332 |access-date=31 March 2021 |website=Sky News |archive-date=25 April 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210425174547/https://news.sky.com/story/covid-19-celebrities-who-have-had-the-coronavirus-vaccination-12165332 |url-status=live}}</ref> [[Pope Francis]] and [[Pope Benedict XVI|Pope Emeritus Benedict]] both announced they had been vaccinated.<ref name="Sky News" /> In a call-in-television special President [[Vladimir Putin]] told listeners that he had received the [[Sputnik V COVID-19 vaccine|Sputnik V vaccine]] and stressed that all the vaccines were safe.<ref name="Burakovsky-2021">{{Cite web | vauthors = Burakovsky A |date=2021-08-28 |title=Russia's COVID-19 response slowed by population reluctant to take domestic vaccine |url=https://www.krqe.com/health/coronavirus/russias-covid-19-response-slowed-by-population-reluctant-to-take-domestic-vaccine/ |url-status=live |access-date=2021-09-20 |website=KRQE NEWS 13 - Breaking News, Albuquerque News, New Mexico News, Weather, and Videos |language=en-US |archive-date=21 September 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210921011759/https://www.krqe.com/health/coronavirus/russias-covid-19-response-slowed-by-population-reluctant-to-take-domestic-vaccine/}}</ref>
