The [[Emergency Medical Treatment and Active Labor Act]] of 1986, an [[unfunded mandate]], mandates that no person may ever be denied emergency services regardless of ability to pay, citizenship, or immigration status.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cms.gov/priorities/your-patient-rights/emergency-room-rights|title=Overview|date=March 26, 2012|website=cms.hhs.gov}}</ref> The Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act has been criticized by the [[American College of Emergency Physicians]] as an unfunded mandate.<ref>[http://www.acep.org/patients.aspx?id=25936 American College of Emergency Physicians Fact Sheet: EMTALA] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080527040835/http://www.acep.org/patients.aspx?id=25936 |date=May 27, 2008 }}. Retrieved November 1, 2007.</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Rowes |first=Jeffrey |s2cid=39874605 |year=2000 |title=EMTALA: OIG/HCFA Special Advisory Bulletin Clarifies EMTALA, American College of Emergency Physicians Criticizes It
 |journal=Journal of Law, Medicine & Ethics |volume=28 |issue=1 |pages=90–2 |url=http://www.aslme.org/news/jlme/28.1e.html |access-date= January 2, 2008 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080129005052/http://www.aslme.org/news/jlme/28.1e.html <!-- Bot retrieved archive --> |archive-date = January 29, 2008 |doi=10.1111/j.1748-720x.2000.tb00324.x|pmid=11067641 |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

46.6 million residents, or 15.9 percent, were without [[health insurance coverage in the United States|health insurance coverage]] in 2005.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.cbpp.org/8-29-06health.htm|title=The number of uninsured Americans is at an all-time high|publisher=[[Center on Budget and Policy Priorities|CBPP]]|date=August 29, 2006|access-date=May 28, 2007}}</ref> This number includes about 10 million non-citizens, millions more who are eligible for Medicaid but never applied, and 18 million with annual household incomes above $50,000.<ref>{{Cite news|author=[[N. Gregory Mankiw]] |title=Beyond Those Health Care Numbers |work=The New York Times|date=November 4, 2007 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2007/11/04/business/04view.html }}</ref> According to a study led by the Johns Hopkins Children's Center, uninsured children who are hospitalized are 60% more likely to die than children who are covered by health insurance.<ref>{{cite web| url=http://www.hopkinschildrens.org/Lack-of-Insurance-May-Have-Figured-In-Nearly-17000-Childhood-Deaths.aspx| title=Lack of Insurance May Have Figured In Nearly 17,000 Childhood Deaths, Study Shows| publisher=Johns Hopkins Children's Center| date=October 29, 2009}}</ref>

==Justice system==
The [[Fourth Amendment to the United States Constitution|Fourth]], [[Fifth Amendment to the United States Constitution|Fifth]], [[Sixth Amendment to the United States Constitution|Sixth]], and [[Eighth Amendment to the United States Constitution|Eighth]] amendments to the [[United States Constitution]] (each part of the [[US Bill of Rights|Bill of Rights]]), as well as the [[Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution|Fourteenth amendment]], ensure that [[criminal defendant]]s have significant [[United States criminal procedure|procedural rights]].<ref name="Lieberman382">{{cite book |last=Lieberman |first=Jethro Koller |title=A practical companion to the Constitution: how the Supreme Court has ruled on issues from abortion to zoning |publisher=University of California Press |page=[https://archive.org/details/practicalcompani00lieb/page/382 382] |isbn=0-520-21280-0 |year=1999 |url=https://archive.org/details/practicalcompani00lieb/page/382}}</ref> The [[incorporation of the Bill of Rights]] has extended these constitutional protections to the state and local levels of law enforcement.<ref name="Lieberman382"/> The United States also possesses a system of [[Judicial review in the United States|judicial review]] over government action.<ref name="Lieberman6">Lieberman, Jethro Koller, ''A practical companion to the Constitution: how the Supreme Court has ruled on issues from abortion to zoning'', University of California Press, 1999, {{ISBN|0-520-21280-0}}, page 6</ref>

===Punishment===
====Death penalty====
{{Further|Capital punishment in the United States|Capital punishment debate in the United States}}
[[File:Death penalty in the United States with hiatuses.svg|thumb|upright=1.2|{{legend|#4daf4a|Capital punishment repealed or struck down as unconstitutional}}{{legend|#377eb8|Capital punishment in statute, but executions formally suspended}}{{legend|#ffff33|Capital punishment in statute, but no recent executions}} {{legend|#984ea3|Capital punishment in statute, other unique circumstances apply}}{{legend|#e41a1c|Executions recently carried out}}]]
[[Capital punishment]] is a legal penalty in the [[United States]], currently used by 23 states, the federal government, and the military.<ref>{{cite news|title=States and capital punishment|publisher=National Conference of State Legislatures|url=http://www.ncsl.org/research/civil-and-criminal-justice/death-penalty.aspx|access-date=June 23, 2017}}</ref> {{as of|2020|3|5}}, there have been 1,517 executions in the United States since 1976 (when the death penalty was reinstated after it had been effectively invalidated as a punishment by [[Furman v. Georgia|a 1972 Supreme Court ruling]]).<ref name = "Death Penalty Info">{{cite web|url=http://deathpenaltyinfo.org/executions/executions-overview|title=Executions Overview|website=deathpenaltyinfo.org|access-date=April 12, 2020}}</ref> The United States is one of [[Capital punishment by country|55 countries worldwide]] that uses the death penalty, and was the first to develop [[lethal injection]] as a method of execution.<ref>{{cite web|title=Lethal injection.|url=http://www.capitalpunishmentuk.org/injection.html|access-date=March 16, 2016|publisher=capitalpunishmentuk.org|quote=China...Guatemala, Philippines, Thailand...Vietnam}}</ref> Among the 56 countries categorized as 'Very high' on the [[Human Development Index]], it is one of only 12 that retain the death penalty (the others being [[Capital punishment in Singapore|Singapore]], [[Capital punishment in Japan|Japan]], the [[Capital punishment in the United Arab Emirates|United Arab Emirates]], [[Capital punishment in Saudi Arabia|Saudi Arabia]], [[Bahrain]], [[Oman]], [[Capital punishment in Belarus|Belarus]], [[Kuwait]], [[Qatar]], [[Capital punishment in Malaysia|Malaysia]], and [[Capital punishment in Taiwan|Taiwan]]). Among the world's most economically and politically powerful countries, it is one of the few who utilize capital punishment. In 2011, for instance, it was the only country in the [[G8]] that carried out executions, and was among only three countries in the [[G20]] (along with [[Human rights in China|China]] and [[Human rights in Saudi Arabia|Saudi Arabia]]) that carried out executions. Of the 56 members states of the [[Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe]], the United States and [[Human rights in Belarus|Belarus]] were the only two that carried out executions in 2011.<ref>[https://www.amnesty.org/en/documents/act50/001/2012/en/ Death sentences and executions in 2011] Amnesty International March 2012</ref>

The vast majority of executions are carried out by state governments,<ref>{{cite web|author1=Torsten Ove|author2=Chris Huffaker|title=Death penalty cases rare in federal court; executions more rare|work=Pittsburgh Post-Gazette |url=https://www.post-gazette.com/news/crime-courts/2018/10/31/Death-penalty-cases-rare-in-federal-court-executions-more-rare/stories/201810300164|access-date=November 14, 2019|publisher=post-gazette.com}}</ref> largely as a result of the [[federal republic|federal]] political structure of the United States, in which most crimes are prosecuted by state governments rather than the federal government.<ref>{{cite web|title=State and Federal Responsibilities for Criminal Justice|url=https://www.fcnl.org/updates/state-and-federal-responsibilities-for-criminal-justice-117|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200420143729/https://www.fcnl.org/updates/state-and-federal-responsibilities-for-criminal-justice-117|archive-date=20 April 2020|access-date=15 July 2020|website=Friends Committee on National Legislation|date=September 28, 2016 }}</ref> Capital punishment is heavily concentrated among several states,<ref>{{cite news|last=Ford|first=Matt|date=21 April 2015|title=The Death Penalty Becomes Rare|work=The Atlantic|url=https://www.theatlantic.com/politics/archive/2015/04/the-death-penalty-becomes-unusual/390867/|url-status=live|access-date=16 July 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200622163638/https://www.theatlantic.com/politics/archive/2015/04/the-death-penalty-becomes-unusual/390867/|archive-date=22 June 2020}}</ref> with Texas overwhelmingly leading in number of executions at 569 between 1976 and 2020, followed by Virginia with 113 executions, and Oklahoma with 112.<ref name = "Death Penalty Info"/> The disparity is particularly stark when broken down by county: since 1976, only 2% of counties have been responsible for more than half of all executions.<ref>{{cite news|date=4 July 2020|title=Cruel, unusual, and costly: American conservatives are pushing for the repeal of the death penalty|newspaper=The Economist|url=https://www.economist.com/united-states/2020/07/04/american-conservatives-are-pushing-for-the-repeal-of-the-death-penalty|url-status=live|access-date=16 July 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200714054743/https://www.economist.com/united-states/2020/07/04/american-conservatives-are-pushing-for-the-repeal-of-the-death-penalty|archive-date=14 July 2020}}</ref> As of 2024, the death penalty has been abolished in the [[Washington, D.C.|District of Columbia]] and twenty-three [[U.S. state|states]], mainly in the [[Northeastern United States|Northeast]] and [[Midwestern United States|Midwest]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=State by State |url=https://deathpenaltyinfo.org/states-landing |access-date=2025-01-02 |website=Death Penalty Information Center |language=en-US}}</ref>

The death penalty has a complex legal history. While modern critics have challenged capital punishment on grounds that it violates the [[Eighth Amendment to the United States Constitution|Eighth Amendment's]] ban on the use of "cruel and unusual punishment",<ref name="ACLU-Death-Penalty">{{cite web|title=The Case Against the Death Penalty|url=https://www.aclu.org/other/case-against-death-penalty|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200605013128/https://www.aclu.org/other/case-against-death-penalty|archive-date=5 June 2020|access-date=15 July 2020|website=American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU)}}</ref> the [[United States Supreme Court]] has held that it does not.<ref>{{cite web|title=Death Penalty|url=https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/death_penalty|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200610082408/https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/death_penalty|archive-date=10 June 2020|access-date=15 July 2020|website=Legal Information Institute}}</ref> At the time of the ratification of the [[United States Bill of Rights|Bill of Rights]], societal moral standards did not hold the death penalty was "cruel and unusual", so it was used throughout early American history. However, the death penalty was temporarily halted by the Supreme Court on Eighth Amendment grounds from 1972 to 1976. In 1958, the [[United States Supreme Court]] ruled in ''[[Trop v. Dulles]]'' that the Eighth Amendment "must draw its meaning from the evolving standards of decency".<ref>{{cite web|title=William Henry FURMAN, Petitioner, v. State of GEORGIA. Lucious JACKSON, Jr., Petitioner, v. State of GEORGIA. Elmer BRANCH, Petitioner, v. State of TEXAS.|url=https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/408/238|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200713044122/https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/408/238|archive-date=13 July 2020|access-date=15 July 2020|website=Legal Information Institute|publisher=Cornell Law School}}</ref> This opened the way to the 1972 US Supreme Court case ''[[Furman v. Georgia]]'' {{ussc|408|238|1972}}, which found that the imposition of the death penalty at the states' discretion constituted [[cruel and unusual punishment]] in violation of the [[Eighth Amendment to the United States Constitution]], with the Court stating that the death penalty had been applied in a "harsh, freakish, and arbitrary" manner.<ref name="ACLU-Death-Penalty"/> This ruling was preceded by the [[Supreme Court of California]]'s ruling in ''[[California v. Anderson]]'' 64 Cal.2d 633, 414 P.2d 366 (Cal. 1972), which classified capital punishment as [[Cruel and unusual punishment|cruel and unusual]] and outlawed the use of capital punishment in California (however, this was reversed the same year through a [[ballot initiative]], [[California Proposition 17 (1972)|Proposition 17]]). However, the death penalty was ultimately reinstated nationally in 1976 after the US Supreme Court rulings ''[[Gregg v. Georgia]]'', {{ussc|428|153|1976}}, ''[[Jurek v. Texas]]'', {{ussc|428|262|1976}}, and ''[[Proffitt v. Florida]]'', {{ussc|428|242|1976}}.<ref name="alaska-law">{{cite web|url=http://justice.uaa.alaska.edu/death/history.html|title=History of the Death Penalty & Recent Developments|date=May 2005|access-date=January 25, 2008|author=Melissa S. Green|publisher=Justice Center, University of Alaska Anchorage|archive-date=July 24, 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100724120224/http://justice.uaa.alaska.edu/death/history.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> Further refinements have been made to the death penalty since then, with a ruling on March 1, 2005, by the Supreme Court in ''[[Roper v. Simmons]]'' prohibiting the execution of people who committed their crimes when they were under the age of 18<ref>{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/world/americas/4308881.stm|title=S court bans juvenile executions|work=BBC News|date=March 1, 2005|access-date=June 3, 2007}}</ref> (between 1990 and 2005, [[Amnesty International]] recorded 19 executions in the United States for crimes committed by juveniles<ref>{{cite web|url=http://web.amnesty.org/pages/deathpenalty-children-stats-eng|title=Executions of child offenders since 1990|publisher=[[Amnesty International]]|access-date=June 3, 2007|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070617034429/http://web.amnesty.org/pages/deathpenalty-children-stats-eng|archive-date=June 17, 2007|df=mdy-all}}</ref>). In [[international law]], it has been argued that the United States may be in violation of international human rights treaties in its use of the death penalty. In 1998, the UN special [[rapporteur]] recommended to a committee of the UN General Assembly that the United States be found to be in violation of Article 6 of the [[International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights]] with regards to the death penalty, and called for an immediate capital punishment moratorium.<ref>{{cite magazine|author=Rights Watch|url=https://www.un.org/Pubs/chronicle/1998/issue2/0298p72.html|title=Death Penalty Issue Addressed by Special Rapporteur|magazine=UN Chronicle|volume=XXXV|issue=2|year=1998|access-date=June 28, 2017|archive-date=August 7, 2007|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070807202217/http://www.un.org/Pubs/chronicle/1998/issue2/0298p72.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> The recommendation of the special [[rapporteur]], however, is not legally binding under international law and in this case the UN did not act upon the lawyer's recommendation.

Capital punishment within the United States is controversial. Death penalty opponents consider it "inhumane",<ref name="amnesty-ill">{{cite web|title=Cruel and Unusual: Executing the mentally ill|url=http://www.amnestyusa.org/page.do?id=1105184In|author=Dan Malone|publisher=Amnesty International Magazine|date=Fall 2005|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090116081317/http://www.amnestyusa.org/page.do?id=1105184In|archive-date=January 16, 2009|df=mdy-all}}</ref> criticize it for its irreversibility,<ref name="amnesty-irreversible">{{Cite web|url=http://www.amnestyusa.org/Our_Issues/Death_Penalty/page.do?id=1011005&n1=3&n2=28|title=Abolish the death penalty|publisher=Amnesty International|access-date=January 25, 2008|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080119233113/http://www.amnestyusa.org/Our_Issues/Death_Penalty/page.do?id=1011005&n1=3&n2=28|archive-date=January 19, 2008|df=mdy-all}}</ref> and assert that it is ineffective as a deterrent against crime,<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.amnestyusa.org/death-penalty-facts/the-death-penalty-and-deterrence/page.do?id=1101085&n1=3&n2=28&n3=99 |title=The Death Penalty and Deterrence |publisher=Amnestyusa.org |date=February 22, 2008 |access-date=May 23, 2009}} {{dead link|date=November 2017 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes}}</ref> pointing to several studies which show it has little deterring effect on crime<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.math.dartmouth.edu/~lamperti/capitalpunishment.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20010813164705/http://www.math.dartmouth.edu/~lamperti/capitalpunishment.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=August 13, 2001 |title=John W. Lamperti &#124; Capital Punishment |publisher=Math.dartmouth.edu |date=March 10, 1973 |access-date=May 23, 2009 }}</ref> (though this point is controversial as studies have conflicted in their conclusions on the effectiveness of the death penalty as a deterrent<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.deathpenaltyinfo.org/article.php?&did=2374 |title=Discussion of Recent Deterrence Studies &#124; Death Penalty Information Center |publisher=Deathpenaltyinfo.org |access-date=May 23, 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080501140145/http://www.deathpenaltyinfo.org/article.php?&did=2374 |archive-date=May 1, 2008 |df=mdy-all }}</ref>). Human rights organizations have been particularly critical of it, with [[Amnesty International]], for example, stating that "the death penalty is the ultimate, irreversible denial of human rights."<ref name="amnesty-irreversible" /> Notably, the [[European Union]], in accordance with its official policy of attempting to achieve global abolition of the death penalty, has been vocal in its criticism of the death penalty in the US and has submitted ''[[amicus curiae]]'' briefs in a number of important US court cases related to capital punishment.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Abolition of the Death Penalty|publisher=The EU's Human rights & Democratisation Policy|url=http://ec.europa.eu/external_relations/human_rights/adp/index.htm|access-date=June 2, 2007|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070519200016/http://ec.europa.eu/external_relations/human_rights/adp/index.htm|archive-date=May 19, 2007|df=mdy-all}}</ref> The [[American Bar Association]] also sponsors a project aimed at abolishing the death penalty in the United States,<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.abanet.org/moratorium/|title=Death Penalty Moratorium Implementation Project|publisher=The American Bar Association|access-date=January 25, 2008|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080724133322/http://www.abanet.org/moratorium|archive-date=July 24, 2008|df=mdy-all}}</ref> criticizing the US's execution of minors and the mentally disabled and arguing that the US fails to adequately protect the rights of the innocent.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Why a moratorium?|publisher=American Bar Association (Death Penalty Moratorium Implementation Project)|url=http://www.abanet.org/moratorium/why.html|access-date=January 25, 2008|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080516212303/http://www.abanet.org/moratorium/why.html|archive-date=May 16, 2008|df=mdy-all}}</ref>

Some opponents criticize the over-representation of [[black people]] on death row as evidence of the [[Race and capital punishment in the United States|unequal racial application]] of the death penalty. In ''[[McCleskey v. Kemp]]'', for example, it was alleged the capital sentencing process was administered in a racially discriminatory manner in violation of the [[Equal Protection Clause]] of the [[Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution|Fourteenth Amendment]]. This over-representation is not limited to capital offenses—in 1992, at a time when black people accounted for 12% of the US population, about 34% of prison inmates were from this group.<ref name=Free1997>{{Cite journal|title=The Impact of Federal Sentencing Reforms on African Americans|author=Free, Marvin D. Jr.|s2cid=147206362|journal=Journal of Black Studies|volume=28 |issue=2| pages=268–286 |issn=0021-9347|date=November 1997|jstor=2784855|doi=10.1177/002193479702800208|doi-access=free}}</ref> Furthermore, in 2003 [[Amnesty International]] reported those who kill whites are more likely to be executed than those who kill blacks, citing that of the 845 people executed since 1977 eighty percent were put to death for killing whites and 13 percent were executed for killing blacks, even though blacks and whites are murdered in almost equal numbers.<ref name="autogenerated5">{{Cite news|title=Death Penalty Discrimination: Those Who Murder Whites Are More Likely To Be Executed | date=April 24, 2003|publisher=Associated Press ([[CBS News]])|url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/death-penalty-discrimination/|access-date=June 3, 2007}}</ref>

====Solitary confinement====
{{main|Solitary confinement in the United States}}
The [[United Nations]] estimates that as of 2013, there were 80,000 prisoners in solitary confinement in the U.S., 12,000 of whom are in California.<ref>{{cite web| url=http://www.ohchr.org/EN/NewsEvents/Pages/DisplayNews.aspx?NewsID=13655&LangID=E| title=California jails: "Solitary confinement can amount to cruel punishment, even torture" – UN rights expert| publisher=UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights| date=August 23, 2013}}</ref> The use of [[solitary confinement]] has drawn criticism and is increasingly viewed as a form of torture because of the psychological harm it causes.<ref>{{Cite magazine|last=Gawande|first=Atul|date=23 March 2009|title=Hellhole: The United States holds tens of thousands of inmates in long-term solitary confinement. Is it torture?|magazine=The New Yorker|url=https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2009/03/30/hellhole|url-status=live|access-date=14 July 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200628173357/https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2009/03/30/hellhole|archive-date=28 June 2020}}</ref> The United Nations Special Rapporteur on torture, Juan E. Méndez, has requested that the United States stop holding prisoners in solitary confinement, as "it often causes mental and physical suffering or humiliation, amounting to cruel, [[inhuman or degrading treatment]] or punishment, and if the resulting pain or sufferings are severe, solitary confinement even amounts to torture." In a severe example, [[Angola Three|Herman Wallace]] and [[Angola Three|Albert Woodfox]], two prisoners at the [[Angola prison]] in Louisiana, have each spent more than 40 years in solitary confinement.<ref>{{cite news| url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2012/apr/16/angola-prison-forty-years-solitary-confinement| author=Ed Pilkington| title=Forty years in solitary: two men mark sombre anniversary in Louisiana prison| newspaper=The Guardian| date=April 16, 2012}}</ref>

====Sex offender registries====
{{main|Sex offender registries in the United States}}
The NGO [[Human Rights Watch]] has stated that there are human rights issues created by the current [[Sex offender registries in the United States|sex offender registration]] laws, and that they believe that the burden of being publicly listed as a [[sex offender]], combined with the restrictions placed on former offenders and their family members, are human rights violations. They have criticized the breadth of the registration requirements, which often treats all offenders the same regardless of the nature of the offense and without accounting the risk of future re-offending, as well as the application of such laws to [[juvenile offender]]s, and to crimes such as [[prostitution]] and [[Exhibitionism|exposing oneself as prank]].<ref>{{cite book|last1=Pittman|first1=Nicole|last2=Parker|first2=Alison|title=Raised on the registry : the irreparable harm of placing children on sex offender registries in the US|date=2013|publisher=Human Rights Watch|location=New York|isbn=978-1-62313-0084|url=https://www.hrw.org/reports/2013/05/01/raised-registry-0}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=No Easy Answers - Sex Offender Laws in the US|url=https://www.hrw.org/reports/2007/09/11/no-easy-answers-0|publisher=Human Rights Watch|date=September 12, 2007}}</ref> The ACLU<ref name="aclu">{{cite news|last1=Hegeman|first1=Roxana|title=ACLU says offender registry unconstitutional Registry includes sex offenders, people convicted of certain violent crimes|url=http://cjonline.com/news/2014-08-12/aclu-says-offender-registry-unconstitutional|work=The Topeka Capital- Journal|date=August 12, 2014}}</ref> and advocacy group [[RSOL]]<ref>{{cite news|last1=Long|first1=Matt|title=Group calls for moratorium on sex offender registry after killings|url=http://www.southcarolinaradionetwork.com/2013/07/29/group-calls-for-moratorium-on-sex-offender-registry-after-killings/|work=South Carolina Radio Network|date=July 29, 2013|access-date=February 24, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141216224148/http://www.southcarolinaradionetwork.com/2013/07/29/group-calls-for-moratorium-on-sex-offender-registry-after-killings/|archive-date=December 16, 2014|url-status=dead|df=mdy-all}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last1=Zakalik|first1=Lauren|title=National conference aims to soften, reform sex offender laws|url=http://www.koat.com/news/new-mexico/albuquerque/National-conference-aims-to-soften-reform-sex-offender-laws/16402040|access-date=November 14, 2014|work=KOAT|date=August 29, 2012}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last1=Lovett|first1=Ian|title=Restricted Group Speaks Up, Saying Sex Crime Measures Go Too Far|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2013/10/02/us/restricted-group-speaks-up-saying-sex-crime-measures-go-too-far.html|access-date=November 14, 2014|work=The New York Times|date=October 1, 2013}}</ref> also believe that measures against sex offenders are inhumane and that current legislation violates the constitutional rights of those with a legal obligation to register. Both organizations have challenged elements of the registration laws in court.<ref name="aclu" /><ref>{{cite news|last1=Belluci|first1=Janice|title=CA RSOL Challenges El Dorado County Sex Offender Ordinance|url=http://www.inedc.com/1-5380|access-date=November 14, 2014|work=In Eldorado County News|date=July 21, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141129023539/http://www.inedc.com/1-5380|archive-date=November 29, 2014|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last1=Howes|first1=Rebecca|title=Attorney files sex offender lawsuit against Lompoc|url=http://lompocrecord.com/news/local/crime-and-courts/attorney-files-sex-offender-lawsuit-against-lompoc/article_e7818850-cb71-11e3-bfd8-001a4bcf887a.html|access-date=November 14, 2014|work=Lompoc Record|date=April 24, 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last1=Case|first1=Stephanie|title=City of Orange Sued Over Sex Offender Halloween Restrictions|url=http://ktla.com/2013/09/19/city-of-orange-sued-over-sex-offender-halloween-restrictions/|access-date=November 14, 2014|work=KTLA 5|date=September 19, 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last1=Johnson|first1=Shea|title=County sued over sex offender ordinance|url=http://www.vvdailypress.com/article/20141021/News/141029976|access-date=November 14, 2014|work=Daily Press|date=October 21, 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last1=Nelson|first1=Joe|title=SPECIAL REPORT: Pair seeks repeal of sex-offender laws in California|url=http://www.dailybreeze.com/general-news/20141011/special-report-pair-seeks-repeal-of-sex-offender-laws-in-california|access-date=November 14, 2014|work=Daily Breeze|date=November 10, 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://fairregistry.org|title=FAIR|publisher=Fairegistry.org|access-date=December 16, 2014}}</ref> By comparison, the [[European Court of Human Rights]] has found that indefinite placement on the United Kingdom sex offender registry, which is not available to the general public, is incompatible with an offender's right to privacy if the person has no right to judicial review.<ref>{{cite news|title=Sex offenders to get right of appeal against lifetime registration|url=https://www.theguardian.com/law/2011/feb/16/sex-offenders-right-of-appeal-lifetime-registration|work=The Guardian|date=February 16, 2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Sex offenders will be able to challenge inclusion on register for life|url=https://www.theguardian.com/society/2011/jun/14/sex-offenders-register-right-to-challenge|work=The Guardian|date=June 14, 2011}}</ref>

===Prison system===
{{further|Incarceration in the United States|Prisoner rights in the United States|Prison–industrial complex|Cutter v. Wilkinson}}
[[Human rights]] groups, [[civil rights]] organizations, and social critics have criticized the United States for violating fundamental human rights through the use of disproportionately heavy penalties compared to many other countries, overly long prison sentences, over-reliance on police control, excessive control of individual behavior, and societal control of [[Racial inequality in the United States|disadvantaged groups]].<ref>[https://www.amnesty.org/en/region/usa Amnesty International, Human Rights in United States of America] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150220152337/http://www.amnesty.org/en/region/usa |date=February 20, 2015 }}, Amnesty International</ref> [[Human Rights Watch]], for instance, has argued that "the extraordinary rate of incarceration in the United States wreaks havoc on individuals, families and communities, and saps the strength of the nation as a whole."<ref name="hrw20061201">{{Cite web|author=Fellner, Jamie|title=US Addiction to Incarceration Puts 2.3 Million in Prison|date=November 30, 2006 |url=http://hrw.org/english/docs/2006/12/01/usdom14728.htm|access-date=June 2, 2007|publisher=Human Rights Watch}}</ref> Political scientist [[Marie Gottschalk]] of the [[University of Pennsylvania]] writes that a country's expansive carceral state and incarceration rate are major barometers of the level of [[state violence]] and control in a society, and that this violence in the United States is being directed at the poor and [[Working class in the United States|working classes]] while there has simultaneously been a mass [[deregulation]] and decriminalization of  corporate and [[white collar crime]] despite "a tsunami of elite-level criminal activities by leading banks, accounting firms and major corporations" throughout the [[neoliberal]] era.<ref>{{cite book |last= Gottschalk|first=Marie|date=2025 |title=Crime and No Punishment: Wealth, Power, and Violence in America|publisher=[[Princeton University Press]]|location= |isbn=978-0691275253|pages=3-15, 33 |url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/Crime_and_No_Punishment/bF1OEQAAQBAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=crime%20and%20no%20punishment&pg=PA3&printsec=frontcover|access-date=}}</ref>

The United States has been criticized for its [[Incarceration in the United States|large prison population]],<ref>{{Cite news|last=Tuhus-Dubrow|first=Rebecca|date=December 19, 2003|title=Prison Reform Talking Points|work=[[The Nation]]|url=http://www.thenation.com/doc/20040105/tuhusdubrow|access-date=May 27, 2007}}</ref> which as of 2023 is the largest in the world at 1,767,200.<ref name="WPB">[http://www.prisonstudies.org/country/united-states-america United States of America]. [[World Prison Brief]].</ref> While having the [[List of countries by incarceration rate|sixth highest per-capita incarceration rate]] globally,<ref name="WPB"/> it has the highest incarceration rate among liberal democracies,  and disproportionately imprisons [[minority groups in the united states|racial minorities]] and those from the lowest [[social class in the United States|socioeconomic backgrounds]];<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|date=December 2006|title=Facts about Prisons and Prisoners|url=http://www.sentencingproject.org/pdfs/1035.pdf|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061229161850/http://www.sentencingproject.org/pdfs/1035.pdf|archive-date=December 29, 2006|access-date=May 27, 2007|publisher=[[Sentencing Project|The Sentencing Project]]|df=mdy-all}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.pewcenteronthestates.org/uploadedFiles/8015PCTS_Prison08_FINAL_2-1-1_FORWEB.pdf|title=One in 100: Behind Bars in America 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090327182002/http://www.pewcenteronthestates.org/uploadedFiles/8015PCTS_Prison08_FINAL_2-1-1_FORWEB.pdf |archive-date=March 27, 2009 |publisher=[[Pew Research Center]]}}</ref><ref>[http://www.pewcenteronthestates.org/report_detail.aspx?id=49382 "One in 31: The Long Reach of American Corrections"] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090513010402/http://www.pewcenteronthestates.org/report_detail.aspx?id=49382 |date=May 13, 2009}}, Pew Research Center, released March 2, 2009</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Desmond|first=Matthew |author-link=Matthew Desmond|date=2023 |title=[[Poverty, by America]]|location= |publisher=Crown Publishing Group|pages=22–23 |isbn=9780593239919}}</ref> according to some scholars including [[Loïc Wacquant]], [[Elizabeth S. Anderson]] and Reuben J. Miller, the "explosive growth" of the incarcerated poor can be seen as part of the "punitive regulation" of [[Poverty in the United States|poverty]] in the [[Neoliberalism|post-Keynesian]] era in order to mitigate the social fallout from economic [[deregulation]], increasing inequality, and [[Precarity|precarious employment]], with corporations exploiting "carceral labor" for pennies an hour.<ref>{{cite book |last = Wacquant |first = Loïc |date = 2009 |title = Punishing the Poor: The Neoliberal Government of Social Insecurity|chapter=America as Living Laboratory of the Neoliberal Future|url =https://read.dukeupress.edu/books/book/1399/Punishing-the-PoorThe-Neoliberal-Government-of|chapter-url=https://read.dukeupress.edu/books/book/1399/chapter/167554/PrologueAmerica-as-Living-Laboratory-of-the|publisher = [[Duke University Press]] |pages = xi-xxiii |isbn = 978-0822344223 |author-link = Loïc Wacquant }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|title=The Routledge Handbook of Poverty in the United States|publisher=[[Routledge]]|year=2015|isbn=978-0-41-567344-0|editor-last=Haymes|editor-first=Stephen N.|location=London and New York|pages=[https://books.google.com/books?id=qnHfBQAAQBAJ&pg=PA2 2-4], [https://books.google.com/books?id=qnHfBQAAQBAJ&pg=PA346 346]|editor-last2=de Haymes|editor-first2=María V.|editor-last3=Miller|editor-first3=Reuben J.|url=https://www.routledge.com/The-Routledge-Handbook-of-Poverty-in-the-United-States/Haymes-Vidal-de-Haymes-Miller/p/book/9780415673440}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last= Anderson|first=Elizabeth|author-link=Elizabeth S. Anderson|date=2023 |title=Hijacked: How Neoliberalism Turned the Work Ethic against Workers and How Workers Can Take It Back|location= |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]]|pages=267–271 |isbn= 978-1009275439|quote=''The Criminalization of Poverty and the Corporate Exploitation of Carceral Labor.'' In Bentham's vision, the poor should be treated like criminals, forced to labor in prison for the private profit of capitalist entrepreneurs. Such a totalitarian idea might seem remote from purportedly enlightened twenty-first-century practices in liberal democracies. Yet both the criminalization of poverty, and the subjection of the criminalized poor to unpaid labor for corporate profit, exist in the United States today.}}</ref> It also incarcerates a large number of non-violent and [[victim-less offender]]s.<ref name="hrw20061201" /><ref>{{Cite book|last=Abramsky|first=Sasha|title=Hard Time Blues: How Politics Built a Prison Nation|date=January 22, 2002|publisher=Thomas Dunne Books}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last=Hardaway|first=Robert|title=No Price Too High: Victimless Crimes and the Ninth Amendment|date=October 30, 2003|publisher=Praeger Publishers|isbn=0-275-95056-5}}</ref> Half of all persons incarcerated under State jurisdiction were convicted of non-violent offenses and 20 percent for drug offenses, mostly the possession of [[cannabis (drug)|cannabis]].<ref>{{Cite web|date=November 2006|title=Prisoners in 2005|url=http://www.ojp.usdoj.gov/bjs/pub/pdf/p05.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070409064857/http://www.ojp.usdoj.gov/bjs/pub/pdf/p05.pdf <!-- Bot retrieved archive -->|archive-date=April 9, 2007|access-date=June 3, 2007|publisher=[[United States Department of Justice]]: [[Office of Justice Programs]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=America's One-Million Nonviolent Prisoners|url=http://www.cjcj.org/pubs/one_million/onemillionexec.html|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070606172630/http://www.cjcj.org/pubs/one_million/onemillionexec.html|archive-date=June 6, 2007|access-date=June 3, 2007|publisher=Center on Juvenile and Criminal Justice|df=mdy-all}}</ref> Marijuana legalization and decriminalization is seen as a step of progress in decreasing the prison population.

The United States also has a high rate of youth imprisonment, with many held in the same prisons as adults. According to The National Council on Crime and Delinquency, since 1990 the incarceration of [[Minor (law)|youth]] in adult jails has increased 208%.<ref>[The Consequences Aren't Minor, The Impact of Trying Youth as Adults and Strategies for Reform - A [[Campaign for Youth Justice]] Report March 2007 pg 7.]</ref> They found that some juveniles had been incarcerated awaiting trial for a long time - up to two years, subjected to the same treatment as adult inmates, and were at greater risk of assault, abuse, or death.

The US also has a large number of [[foreign national]]s in US prisons, with 21% of all federal inmates in 2017 being non-citizens or non-nationals.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Ramón|first=Cristobal|date=6 March 2018|title=Data on Foreign-Born in Federal Prisons Says Little About Overall Immigrant Criminality|url=https://bipartisanpolicy.org/blog/data-on-foreign-born-in-federal-prisons-says-little-about-overall-immigrant-criminality/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200509125808/https://bipartisanpolicy.org/blog/data-on-foreign-born-in-federal-prisons-says-little-about-overall-immigrant-criminality/|archive-date=9 May 2020|access-date=14 July 2020|website=Bipartisan Policy Center}}</ref> Additionally, the US Justice Department rarely approves extraditions of foreign prisoners to their home countries, and most are deported after serving their sentences rather than before their trials. This is seen as a contributor to [[Prison overcrowding in the United States|prison overcrowding]], especially in California, Arizona, and Texas. This goes hand-in-hand with the US immigration policies, which have also been criticized by human rights groups.

Tolerance of [[sexual abuse]] and [[Prison rape in the United States|rape in United States prisons]] is also an area of concern to human rights watchers. [[Human Rights Watch]], for instance, raised concerns with [[prisoner rape]] and [[Prison#Health care|medical care for inmates]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://hrw.org/english/docs/2005/02/28/usdom10223.htm |title=Inhumane Prison Conditions Still Threaten Life, Health of Alabama Inmates Living with HIV/AIDS, According to Court Filings |date=February 27, 2005 |publisher=Human Rights Watch |access-date=June 13, 2006}}</ref> In a survey of 1,788 male inmates in Midwestern prisons by [[Prison Journal]], about 21% claimed they had been coerced or pressured into sexual activity during their incarceration and 7% claimed that they had been raped in their current facility.<ref>{{Cite web| title=Sexual Coercion Rates in Seven Midwestern Prisons for Men| author=[[Cindy Struckman-Johnson]] & David Struckman-Johnson| work=The Prison Journal| year=2000| url=http://www.spr.org/pdf/struckman.pdf| access-date=May 28, 2007| archive-date=February 17, 2012| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120217180113/http://www.spr.org/pdf/struckman.pdf| url-status=dead}}</ref> The [[Prison Rape Elimination Act|Prison Rape Elimination Act of 2003]] unanimously passed in the House and Senate, to wide acclaim from human rights advocates.

===Police brutality===
{{main|Police brutality in the United States}}
In a 1999 report, [[Amnesty International]] said it had "documented patterns of ill-treatment across the U.S., including police beatings, unjustified shootings and the use of dangerous restraint techniques."<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.amnestyusa.org/document.php?id=133746465C2D34CA8025690000692D98 |title=Race, Rights and Police Brutality |year=1999 |publisher=[[Amnesty International]] USA |access-date=December 22, 2007}} {{dead link|date=November 2017 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes}}</ref>
According to a 1998 Human Rights Watch report, incidents of police use of excessive force had occurred in cities throughout the U.S., and this behavior goes largely unchecked.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://hrw.org/english/docs/1998/07/07/usdom1224.htm |title=Report Charges Police Abuse in U.S. Goes Unchecked |date=July 7, 1998 |publisher=[[Human Rights Watch]]
 |access-date=December 22, 2007}}</ref> An article in ''USA Today'' reports that in 2006, 96% of cases referred to the U.S. Justice Department for prosecution by investigative agencies were declined. In 2005, 98% were declined.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.usatoday.com/news/nation/2007-12-17-Copmisconduct_N.htm |title=Police brutality cases on rise since 9/11 |work=USA Today |date=December 17, 2007 |access-date=December 22, 2007 |first=Kevin |last=Johnson}}</ref> In 2001, ''[[The New York Times]]'' reported that the U.S. government is unable or unwilling to collect statistics showing the precise number of people killed by the police or the prevalence of the use of excessive force.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9505E6DD1139F93AA15757C0A9679C8B63 |title=When the Police Shoot, Who's Counting? |work=The New York Times |date=April 29, 2001 |access-date=December 22, 2007 | first=Fox | last=Butterfield}}</ref>
From 1999 to 2005, at least 148 people have died in the United States and Canada after being shocked with Tasers by police officers, according to a 2005 ACLU report.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.aclu.org/police/abuse/19977prs20051006.html |title=Unregulated Use of Taser Stun Guns Threatens Lives, ACLU of Northern California Study Finds |publisher=[[ACLU]] |date=October 6, 2005 |access-date=December 22, 2007}}</ref>

On June 2, 2020, [[George Floyd]]'s official post-mortem report declared the cause of death as [[asphyxia]] (lack of oxygen) due to a compression on his neck and back. It also found that the death was a homicide, a statement from the family's legal team said.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-us-canada-52886593|title=George Floyd death homicide, official post-mortem declares|work=BBC News |date=June 2, 2020 |access-date=2 June 2020}}</ref> According to a 2021 article published in ''[[The Lancet]]'', more than 30,000 people have died by police violence in the United States from 1980 to 2018.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sharara |first1=Fablina |last2=Wool |first2=Eve E |display-authors=etal. |date=October 2, 2021 |title=Fatal police violence by race and state in the USA, 1980–2019: a network meta-regression |journal=The Lancet |volume=398 |issue=10307 |pages= 1239–1255|doi=10.1016/S0140-6736(21)01609-3 |pmid=34600625 |pmc=8485022 |quote=Across all races and states in the USA, we estimate 30 800 deaths (95% uncertainty interval [UI] 30 300–31 300) from police violence between 1980 and 2018; this represents 17 100 more deaths (16 600–17 600) than reported by the NVSS.}}</ref> In June 2020, a report from the [[University of Chicago Law School]] stated that law enforcement policies in the police departments of 20 largest cities in the [[United States]] failed to meet basic standards under international [[human rights]] guidelines. According to the report, law enforcement forces are authorized to commit ‘state-sanctioned violence’ without significant reform.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/americas/police-racism-us-cities-human-rights-cops-george-floyd-breonna-taylor-a9580251.html|title=Not a single police department in 20 largest US cities compliant with international rights laws, report finds|access-date=23 June 2020|website=Independent|date=June 22, 2020 }}</ref>

The use of [[strip search]]es and [[cavity search]]es by law enforcement agencies and in the prison system has raised human rights concerns.<ref>{{cite web|title=Prison Strip Search is Sexually Abusive|work=American Civil Liberties Union |url=https://www.aclu.org/prisoners-rights-womens-rights/prison-strip-search-sexually-abusive|publisher=ACLU|access-date=December 24, 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Strip Searching Americans Without Cause: A Blow to Personal Privacy|url=http://www.huffingtonpost.com/arjun-sethi/strip-search-supreme-court-decision-_b_1571935.html|access-date=December 24, 2013|newspaper=Huffington Post|date=June 6, 2012}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=In U.S. justice system, the strip-search is common practice|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-india-usa-stripsearches-idUSBRE9BJ04M20131220|access-date=December 24, 2013|newspaper=Reuters|date=December 19, 2013|archive-date=December 24, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131224110529/http://www.reuters.com/article/2013/12/20/us-india-usa-stripsearches-idUSBRE9BJ04M20131220|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Strip Searches|url=http://www.huffingtonpost.com/news/strip-searches|work=Huffington Post|access-date=December 24, 2013}}</ref>

The practice of taking an arrested person on a [[perp walk]], often handcuffed, through a public place at some point after the arrest, creating an opportunity for the media to take photographs and video of the event has raised civil and human rights concerns.<ref>{{cite news|title=Case Study: DSK Fallout: Time for the Perp Walk to Take a Hike?|url=http://content.time.com/time/nation/article/0,8599,2082329,00.html|access-date=May 26, 2014|newspaper=Time|date=July 11, 2011}}</ref>

===Racial discrimination===
[[Human rights organization]]s, [[civil rights]] groups, academics, journalists, and other critics have argued that the US justice system [[Race in the United States criminal justice system|exhibits racial biases]] that harm minority groups, particularly [[African American]]s.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Balko|first=Radley|date=10 June 2020|title=There's overwhelming evidence that the criminal justice system is racist. Here's the proof.|newspaper=The Washington Post|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/graphics/2020/opinions/systemic-racism-police-evidence-criminal-justice-system/|url-status=live|access-date=14 July 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200712154031/https://www.washingtonpost.com/graphics/2020/opinions/systemic-racism-police-evidence-criminal-justice-system/|archive-date=12 July 2020}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Criminal Justice Fact Sheet|url=https://www.naacp.org/criminal-justice-fact-sheet/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200712041609/https://www.naacp.org/criminal-justice-fact-sheet/|archive-date=12 July 2020|access-date=14 July 2020|website=National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP)}}</ref> There are significant racial disparities within the prison population of the United States, with black individuals making up 38.2% of the federal prison population in 2020, despite the fact that African Americans only comprise 13.4% of the nation's entire population.<ref>{{Cite web|date=4 July 2020|title=Inmate Race|url=https://www.bop.gov/about/statistics/statistics_inmate_race.jsp|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200706084618/https://www.bop.gov/about/statistics/statistics_inmate_race.jsp|archive-date=6 July 2020|access-date=14 July 2020|website=Federal Bureau of Prisons}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Quick Facts|url=https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/fact/table/US/PST045219|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200713175224/https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/fact/table/US/PST045219|archive-date=13 July 2020|access-date=14 July 2020|website=United States Census Bureau}}</ref> Studies have also found that black people, as well as other minority groups, are shot and killed by the police at higher rates than white people,<ref>{{Cite news|date=13 July 2020|title=Fatal Force|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/graphics/investigations/police-shootings-database/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200713045858/https://www.washingtonpost.com/graphics/investigations/police-shootings-database/|archive-date=13 July 2020|access-date=14 July 2020|newspaper=The Washington Post}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|date=2016|title=The Counted: People killed by police in the US|url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-interactive/2015/jun/01/the-counted-police-killings-us-database|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200710034206/https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-interactive/2015/jun/01/the-counted-police-killings-us-database|archive-date=10 July 2020|access-date=14 July 2020|website=The Guardian}}</ref> tend to receive harsher punishments than white people,<ref>{{Cite web|title=Demographic Differences in Sentencing|url=https://www.ussc.gov/research/research-reports/demographic-differences-sentencing|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200707091745/https://www.ussc.gov/research/research-reports/demographic-differences-sentencing|archive-date=7 July 2020|access-date=14 July 2020|website=United States Sentencing Commission|date=November 13, 2017 |publisher=United States Federal Judiciary|quote=[T]he commission found: 1. Black male offenders continued to receive longer sentences than similarly situated White male offenders.}}</ref> are more likely to be charged for [[drug crime]]s despite consuming drugs at similar rates as white people,<ref>{{Cite web|title=Decades of Disparity: Drug Arrests and Race in the United States|url=https://www.hrw.org/report/2009/03/02/decades-disparity/drug-arrests-and-race-united-states|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200707221109/https://www.hrw.org/report/2009/03/02/decades-disparity/drug-arrests-and-race-united-states|archive-date=7 July 2020|access-date=14 July 2020|website=Human Rights Watch|date=March 2, 2009 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|date=21 October 2016|title=Rates of Drug Use and Sales, by Race; Rates of Drug Related Criminal Justice Measures, by Race|url=https://www.hamiltonproject.org/charts/rates_of_drug_use_and_sales_by_race_rates_of_drug_related_criminal_justice|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200702122534/https://www.hamiltonproject.org/charts/rates_of_drug_use_and_sales_by_race_rates_of_drug_related_criminal_justice|archive-date=2 July 2020|access-date=14 July 2020|website=The Hamilton Project|publisher=The Brookings Institution}}</ref> are at higher lifetime risk of being killed by police than white people,<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Edwards|first=Frank|date=3 July 2019|title=Risk of being killed by police use of force in the United States by age, race–ethnicity, and sex|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|volume=116 |issue=34 |pages=16793–16798 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1821204116 |doi-access=free |pmid=31383756 |pmc=6708348 |bibcode=2019PNAS..11616793E }}</ref> are more likely to be stopped by police while driving,<ref>{{Cite web|title=Findings|url=https://openpolicing.stanford.edu/findings/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200713080955/https://openpolicing.stanford.edu/findings/|archive-date=13 July 2020|access-date=14 July 2020|website=Stanford Open Policing Project|quote=The data show that officers generally stop black drivers at higher rates than white drivers, and stop Hispanic drivers at similar or lower rates than white drivers.}}</ref> and are more likely to be arrested during a police stop.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Kochel|first1=Tammy Rhineheart|last2=Wilson|first2=David B.|last3=Mastrofski|first3=Steven D.|date=25 May 2011|title=Effects of Suspect Race on Officers' Arrest Decisions|journal=Criminology|volume=49|issue=2|pages=473–512|doi=10.1111/j.1745-9125.2011.00230.x}}</ref> As the [[Sentencing Project]] said in their report to the [[United Nations]]:<ref>{{Cite web|date=19 April 2018|title=Report to the United Nations on Racial Disparities in the U.S. Criminal Justice System|url=https://www.sentencingproject.org/publications/un-report-on-racial-disparities/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200630151510/https://www.sentencingproject.org/publications/un-report-on-racial-disparities/|archive-date=30 June 2020|access-date=14 July 2020|website=The Sentencing Project}}</ref>
<blockquote>
[[African American]]s are more likely than white Americans to be arrested; once arrested, they are more likely to be convicted; and once convicted, they are more likely to experience lengthy prison sentences.
</blockquote>

The cause of this is disputed. There is a widespread belief among the American public that racial discrimination by the police is a persistent problem,<ref>{{Cite web|last1=Best|first1=Ryan|last2=Rogers|first2=Kaleigh|date=10 June 2020|title=Do You Know How Divided White And Black Americans Are On Racism?|url=https://projects.fivethirtyeight.com/racism-polls/|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200705070956/https://projects.fivethirtyeight.com/racism-polls/|archive-date=5 July 2020|access-date=14 July 2020|website=FiveThirtyEight|quote=[A] majority of black and white respondents agree that police don’t treat black and white people equally.}}</ref> and many academics and journalists assert that [[systemic racism]], as well as a number of factors like [[concentrated poverty]] and higher rates of substandard housing (which has also led to greater rates of [[lead poisoning]] among African Americans) that they argue arise out of past [[Racial segregation in the United States|racial segregation]] or other forms of historical oppression,<ref name="Economist-July2020">{{Cite news|date=9 July 2020|title=How black lives can get better: Segregation still blights the lives of African-Americans|newspaper=The Economist|url=https://www.economist.com/briefing/2020/07/09/segregation-still-blights-the-lives-of-african-americans|url-status=live|access-date=14 July 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200713042130/https://www.economist.com/briefing/2020/07/09/segregation-still-blights-the-lives-of-african-americans|archive-date=13 July 2020}}</ref> contribute to the racial disparities.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Collins|first=Sean|date=17 June 2020|title=The systemic racism black Americans face, explained in 9 charts|work=Vox|url=https://www.vox.com/2020/6/17/21284527/systemic-racism-black-americans-9-charts-explained|url-status=live|access-date=14 July 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200712225940/https://www.vox.com/2020/6/17/21284527/systemic-racism-black-americans-9-charts-explained|archive-date=12 July 2020}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|last=Pierson|first=Emma|date=20 June 2020|title=Barr says there's no systemic racism in policing. Our data says the attorney general is wrong.|newspaper=The Washington Post|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2020/06/20/barr-says-theres-no-systemic-racism-policing-our-data-say-attorney-general-is-wrong/|url-status=live|access-date=14 July 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200712071320/https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2020/06/20/barr-says-theres-no-systemic-racism-policing-our-data-say-attorney-general-is-wrong/|archive-date=12 July 2020}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|last=Lopez|first=German|date=15 August 2016|title=How systemic racism entangles all police officers — even black cops|work=Vox|url=https://www.vox.com/2015/5/7/8562077/police-racism-implicit-bias|url-status=live|access-date=14 July 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200702162724/https://www.vox.com/2015/5/7/8562077/police-racism-implicit-bias|archive-date=2 July 2020}}</ref>

===Procedural concerns===
The [[National Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers]] and [[Human Rights Watch]] have argued that there exists a "[[trial penalty]]"—a penalty for electing to go to trial that arises from the discrepancy between the punishment a defendant would receive by waiving the right to trial and accepting a [[plea bargain]] compared to the punishment they might receive at trial—which they argue abridges the right to trial guaranteed by the [[Sixth Amendment to the United States Constitution]].<ref name="NACDL-web">{{cite web |title=The Trial Penalty: The Sixth Amendment Right to Trial on the Verge of Extinction and How to Save It |url=https://www.nacdl.org/Document/TrialPenaltySixthAmendmentRighttoTrialNearExtinct |publisher=National Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers |date=10 July 2018}}</ref><ref name="HRW">{{cite web |title=An Offer You Can't Refuse: How US Federal Prosecutors Force Drug Defendants to Plead Guilty |url=https://www.hrw.org/report/2013/12/05/offer-you-cant-refuse/how-us-federal-prosecutors-force-drug-defendants-plead |publisher=Human Rights Watch |date=5 December 2013}}</ref>

There has also been criticism over [[qualified immunity]], a [[Precedent|judicial precedent]] that grants government officials—including police officers— certain immunity from [[civil suit]]s.<ref>Harlow v. Fitzgerald, 457 U.S. 800, 818 (1982).</ref> Critics have argued that qualified immunity makes it unnecessarily difficult to sue public officials for misconduct, including civil rights violations;<ref>{{cite web |title=Frequently Asked Questions About Qualified Immunity |url=https://www.unlawfulshield.com/frequently-asked-questions-about-qualified-immunity/ |website=Unlawful Shield |publisher=The Cato Institute |access-date=4 June 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200604231400/https://www.unlawfulshield.com/frequently-asked-questions-about-qualified-immunity/ |archive-date=June 4, 2020 |url-status=live }}</ref> this has been implicated in particular for enabling [[police brutality]].<ref name="cops who kill">{{cite news |last1=Chung |first1=Andrew |last2=Hurley |first2=Lawrence |last3=Botts |first3=Jackie |last4=Januta |first4=Andrea |last5=Gomez |first5=Guillermo |title=For cops who kill, special Supreme Court protection |url=https://www.reuters.com/investigates/special-report/usa-police-immunity-scotus/ |publisher=Reuters |date=8 May 2020 |access-date=June 5, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200601022624/https://www.reuters.com/investigates/special-report/usa-police-immunity-scotus/ |archive-date=June 1, 2020 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Jaicomo |first1=Patrick |last2=Bidwell |first2=Anya |title=Police act like laws don't apply to them because of 'qualified immunity.' They're right. |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/opinion/2020/05/30/police-george-floyd-qualified-immunity-supreme-court-column/5283349002/ |work=USA Today |date=20 May 2020 |access-date=June 4, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200603233143/https://www.usatoday.com/story/opinion/2020/05/30/police-george-floyd-qualified-immunity-supreme-court-column/5283349002/ |archive-date=June 3, 2020 |url-status=live }}</ref> Despite safeguards in place around recruitment, some police departments have hired officers who had histories of poor performance or misconduct in other departments, an issue known as hiring [[gypsy cop|"gypsy cops"]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Cast-Out Police Officers Are Often Hired in Other Cities|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/09/11/us/whereabouts-of-cast-out-police-officers-other-cities-often-hire-them.html|access-date=1 October 2017|work=The New York Times|date=September 10, 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Fired/Rehired: Police chiefs are often forced to put officers fired for misconduct back on the streets|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/graphics/2017/investigations/police-fired-rehired/|access-date=1 October 2017|newspaper=Washington Post|date=August 3, 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=How Police Unions and Arbitrators Keep Abusive Cops on the Street|url=https://www.theatlantic.com/politics/archive/2014/12/how-police-unions-keep-abusive-cops-on-the-street/383258/|access-date=1 October 2017|work=The Atlantic|date=December 2, 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Barker|first1=Tom|title=Police ethics: crisis in law enforcement|date=2011|publisher=Chares C. Thomas|isbn=978-0398086152|page=134|edition=3rd|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=H3ZlS6ff520C&pg=PA134}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Push to keep "gypsy cops" with questionable pasts off the streets|url=http://www.cbsnews.com/news/gypsy-cops-with-questionable-pasts-hired-by-different-departments-lack-of-oversight-police/|access-date=9 February 2017|work=CBS News|date=27 September 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Shielded from Justice: Police Brutality and Accountability in the United States|url=https://www.hrw.org/legacy/reports98/police/uspo12.htm|publisher=Human Rights Watch|access-date=1 October 2017}}</ref>

==Human rights and foreign policy==
The [[U.S. Department of State]] publishes a yearly report "Supporting Human Rights and Democracy: The U.S. Record" in compliance with a 2002 law that requires the department to report on actions taken by the U.S. Government to encourage respect for human rights.<ref name=StateDeptUSRecord>{{Cite web|url=https://2001-2009.state.gov/g/drl/rls/shrd/|access-date=June 22, 2007|title=Supporting Human Rights and Democracy: The U.S. Record|date=April 20, 2004 |publisher=[[United States Department of State]]: [[Bureau of Democracy, Human Rights, and Labor]]}}</ref> It also publishes yearly "[[Country Reports on Human Rights Practices]]."<ref name=StateDept>{{Cite web|url=https://2001-2009.state.gov/g/drl/rls/hrrpt|access-date=May 28, 2007|title=Human Rights|date=March 6, 2007 |publisher=[[United States Department of State]]: Bureau of Democracy, Human Rights, and Labor}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Xypolia |first=Ilia |url=https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-030-99815-8 |title=Human Rights, Imperialism, and Corruption in US Foreign Policy |publisher=Palgrave Macmillan |year=2022 |isbn=978-3-030-99814-1 |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-030-99815-8|s2cid=248384134 }}</ref>

According to the Canadian historian [[Michael Ignatieff]], both during and after the [[Cold War]], the US emphasized human rights more than other nations emphasized it as a part of its [[Foreign policy of the United States|foreign policy]], awarded foreign aid to facilitate progress on human rights, and annually assessed the human rights records of other national governments.<ref name="Ignatieff1"/>

The US has also faced criticism over its human rights foreign policy. For example, numerous academics and journalists, among them [[J. Patrice McSherry]] and [[Vincent Bevins]], have documented significant [[Foreign policy of the United States#Support for authoritarian governments|US support for right-wing dictatorships]], [[State terrorism#United States|state terrorism]], and [[Anti-communist mass killings|mass killings during the Cold War]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Blakeley|first=Ruth|date=2009 |title=State Terrorism and Neoliberalism: The North in the South|url=http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9780415462402/|publisher=[[Routledge]]|pages=3, [https://books.google.com/books?id=rft8AgAAQBAJ&lpg=PA92&pg=PA85#v=onepage&q&f=false 85-96]|isbn=978-0415686174}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Bevins |first1=Vincent|author-link=Vincent Bevins |title= [[The Jakarta Method|The Jakarta Method: Washington's Anticommunist Crusade and the Mass Murder Program that Shaped Our World]]|chapter= Jakarta Is Coming|date=2020 |publisher= [[PublicAffairs]]|pages=181–209 |isbn= 978-1541742406}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=McSherry |first1=J. Patrice|author-link1= J. Patrice McSherry |editor1=Esparza, Marcia |editor-first2=Henry R. |editor-last2=Huttenbach |editor-first3=Daniel |editor-last3=Feierstein |title=State Violence and Genocide in Latin America: The Cold War Years (Critical Terrorism Studies) |chapter=Chapter 5: "Industrial repression" and Operation Condor in Latin America |page=[https://books.google.com/books?id=acGNAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA107 107] |publisher=Routledge |year=2011 |isbn=978-0-415-66457-8 |chapter-url=https://www.routledge.com/State-Violence-and-Genocide-in-Latin-America-The-Cold-War-Years/Esparza-Huttenbach-Feierstein/p/book/9780415496377}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Valentino |first=Benjamin A. |date=2005 |title=Final Solutions: Mass Killing and Genocide in the 20th Century |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ZNy55BHupsoC&pg=PA27 |publisher=Cornell University Press |page=27 |isbn=978-0-8014-7273-2}}</ref> The country has not ratified as many international human rights treaties as other [[liberal democracies]] have, it has also not ratified the 1969 [[Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties]].<ref name=Boyle89>{{cite journal |last=Boyle |first=Francis A. |author-link=Francis Boyle |title=The Hypocrisy and Racism Behind the Formulation of U.S. Human Rights Foreign Policy: In Honor of Clyde Ferguson |journal=Social Justice |volume=16 |issue=1 (35) |date=1989 |pages=71–93 |url=http://www.jstor.org/stable/29766443 |jstor=29766443}}</ref>

===Treaties ratified===
:''See also [[International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights#United States|International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights - United States]]''

The U.S. has signed and ratified the following human rights treaties:
* [[International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights]] (ICCPR) (ratified with 5 [[reservation (law)|reservations]], 5 understandings, and 4 declarations.)<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www1.umn.edu/humanrts/usdocs/civilres.html|title=University of Minnesota Human Rights Library|website=www1.umn.edu}}</ref>
* [[Optional protocol on the involvement of children in armed conflict]]
* [[International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination]]
* [[United Nations Convention Against Torture|Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment]]
* [[Protocol relating to the Status of Refugees]]<ref name="autogenerated1">{{cite web|url=http://academic.udayton.edu/race/06hrights/unitednations/USStatus.htm|title=Selected Human Rights Treaties and US Status|website=academic.udayton.edu}}</ref>
* [[Optional Protocol to the Convention on the Rights of the Child on the Sale of Children, Child Prostitution and Child Pornography]]<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.unhchr.ch/tbs/doc.nsf/newhvstatbytreaty?OpenView|title=unhchr.ch|website=unhchr.ch}}</ref>

Non-binding documents voted for:
* [[Universal Declaration of Human Rights]]<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.unhchr.ch/udhr/miscinfo/carta.htm|title=unhchr.ch|website=unhchr.ch}}</ref>

===International Bill of Rights===
:''See also [[International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights#United States|International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights - United States]]''

The [[International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights]] (ICCPR) and the [[International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights]] (ICESCR) are the legal treaties that enshrine the rights outlined in the [[Universal Declaration of Human Rights]]. Together, and along with the [[First Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights|first]] and [[First Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights|second]] optional protocols of the [[ICCPR]] they constitute the [[International bill of rights]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www2.ohchr.org/english/law/|title=OHCHR International law|publisher=OHCHR|access-date=June 23, 2009}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.unhchr.ch/html/menu6/2/fs2.htm|title=unhchr.ch|website=unhchr.ch}}</ref> The US has not ratified the [[ICESCR]] or either of the optional protocols of the [[ICCPR]].

The US's ratification of the [[ICCPR]] was done with five [[Reservation (law)|reservations]] – or limits – on the treaty, 5 understandings and 4 declarations. Among these is the rejection of sections of the treaty that prohibit [[capital punishment]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www2.ohchr.org/english/bodies/ratification/docs/DeclarationsReservationsICCPR.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080528125237/http://www2.ohchr.org/english/bodies/ratification/docs/DeclarationsReservationsICCPR.pdf|url-status=dead|title=OHCHR Reservations and declarations on ratifications|archive-date=May 28, 2008}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.twnside.org.sg/title/1893-cn.htm|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071015051238/http://www.twnside.org.sg/title/1893-cn.htm|url-status=dead|title=America'S Problem With Human Rights<!-- Bot generated title -->|archive-date=October 15, 2007}}</ref> Included in the Senate's ratification was the declaration that "the provisions of Article 1 through 27 of the Covenant are not self-executing",<ref>138 Cong. Rec. S4781-84 (1992)</ref> and in a Senate Executive Report stated that the declaration was meant to "clarify that the Covenant will not create a private cause of action in U.S. Courts."<ref>S. Exec. Rep. No. 102-23 (1992)</ref> This way of ratifying the treaty was criticized as incompatible with the Supremacy Clause by [[Louis Henkin]].<ref>Louis Henkin, U.S. Ratification of Human Rights Treaties: The Ghost of Senator Bricker, 89 Am. J. Int'l L. 341, 346 (1995)</ref>

===International Criminal Court===
{{Further|United States and the International Criminal Court}}

The United States has not ratified the [[Rome Statute]] of the [[International Criminal Court]] (ICC), which was drafted for prosecuting individuals above the authority of national courts in the event of accusations of [[genocide]], [[crimes against humanity]], [[war crimes]], and [[crime of aggression]]. Nations that have accepted the Rome Statute can defer to the jurisdiction of the ICC or must surrender their jurisdiction when ordered.

The U.S. rejected the Rome Statute after its attempts to include the nation of origin as a party in international proceedings failed, and after certain requests were not met, including recognition of gender issues, "rigorous" qualifications for judges, viable definitions of crimes, protection of national security information that might be sought by the court, and jurisdiction of the UN Security Council to halt court proceedings in special cases.<ref name="US objections to RS"/> Since the passage of the statute, the U.S. has actively encouraged nations around the world to sign "bilateral immunity agreements" prohibiting the surrender of U.S. personnel before the ICC<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.iccnow.org/?mod=bia|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061011134834/http://www.iccnow.org/?mod=bia|url-status=usurped|archive-date=October 11, 2006|title=Coalition for the International Criminal Court - Global justice for atrocities|website=iccnow.org}}</ref> and actively attempted to undermine the [[Rome Statute]] of the [[International Criminal Court]].<ref name="hrw.org">{{cite web|url=https://www.hrw.org/campaigns/icc/us.htm|title=HRW: ICC: The U.S. and the ICC|website=hrw.org}}</ref> The U.S. Congress also passed a law, [[American Service-Members' Protection Act]] (ASPA), authorizing the use of military force to free any U.S. personnel that are brought before the court rather than its own court system.<ref>Human Rights Watch, "[https://www.hrw.org/press/2002/08/aspa080302.htm U.S.: 'Hague Invasion Act' Becomes Law]." August 3, 2002. Retrieved January 8, 2007.</ref><ref>John Sutherland, "[https://www.theguardian.com/Archive/Article/0,4273,4456801,00.html Who are America's real enemies?]" ''The Guardian'', July 8, 2002. Retrieved January 8, 2007.</ref> Human Rights Watch criticized the United States for removing itself from the Statute.<ref name="BBC News">{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/americas/1970312.stm|title=US renounces world court treaty|date=May 6, 2002|via=BBC News}}</ref>

Objections to the Rome Statute have revolved around issues of jurisdiction and process. A U.S. ambassador for War Crimes Issues to the UN Security Council said that, because the Rome Statute requires only one nation to submit to the ICC, and that this nation can be the country in which an alleged crime was committed rather than defendant's country of origin, military personnel and foreign peaceworkers in more than 100 countries could be tried in international court without the consent of the US. The ambassador stated that "most atrocities are committed internally and most internal conflicts are between warring parties of the same nationality, the worst offenders of international humanitarian law can choose never to join the treaty and be fully insulated from its reach absent a Security Council referral."<ref name="US objections to RS">{{Cite web|url=https://1997-2001.state.gov/www/policy_remarks/1998/980723_scheffer_icc.html|title=Technical Difficulties|website=1997-2001.state.gov}}</ref>

===Other treaties not signed or signed but not ratified===

The U.S. has not ratified the following international human rights treaties:<ref name="autogenerated1"/>
* [[First Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights]] (ICCPR)
* [[Second Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights]], aiming at the abolition of the death penalty
* [[Optional Protocol to the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women|Optional Protocol to CEDAW]]
* [[Optional Protocol to the Convention against Torture]]
* [[Convention relating to the Status of Refugees]] (1951)
* [[Convention Relating to the Status of Stateless Persons]] (1954)
* [[1961 Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness|Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness]] (1961)
* [[United Nations Convention on the Protection of the Rights of All Migrant Workers and Members of Their Families|International Convention on the Protection of the Rights of All Migrant Workers and Members of their Families]]

The US has signed but not ratified the following treaties:

* [[Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women]] (CEDAW)
* [[Convention on the Rights of the Child]] (CRC)
*[[International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights]]
*[[Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities]]

Non-binding documents voted against:
* [[Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples]] in September 2007.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.iwgia.org/sw248.asp|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080110115246/http://www.iwgia.org/sw248.asp|url-status=unfit|title=Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples|archive-date=January 10, 2008|website=www.iwgia.org}}</ref>

===Inter-American human rights system===
The US is a signatory to the 1948 [[American Declaration of the Rights and Duties of Man]] and has signed but not ratified the 1969 [[American Convention on Human Rights]]. It is a member of Inter-American Convention on the Granting of Political Rights to Women (1948). It does not accept the adjudicatory jurisdiction of the [[Costa Rica]]-based [[Inter-American Court of Human Rights]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.cidh.org/Basicos/English/Basic4.Amer.Conv.Ratif.htm|title=Basic Documents - Ratifications of the Convention|website=cidh.org}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://2001-2009.state.gov/p/wha/rls/fs/2007/85564.htm|title=Organization of American States<!-- Bot generated title -->|date=May 30, 2007 }}</ref>

The US has not ratified any of the other regional human rights treaties of the [[Organization of American States]],<ref name="autogenerated1" /> which include:

* [[Protocol to the American Convention on Human Rights to Abolish the Death Penalty]] (1990)
* [[Additional Protocol to the American Convention on Human Rights in the Area of Economic, Social and Cultural Rights]]
* [[Inter-American Convention to Prevent and Punish Torture]] (1985)
* [[Inter-American Convention on the Prevention, Punishment and Eradication of Violence Against Women]] (1994)
* [[Inter-American Convention on Forced Disappearance of Persons]] (1994)
* [[Inter-American Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Persons with Disabilities]]

===Coverage of violations in the media===
Studies have found that ''The New York Times'' coverage of worldwide human rights violations predominately focuses on human rights violations in nations where there is clear U.S. involvement, while having relatively little coverage of the human rights violations in other nations.<ref>{{Cite journal|journal=The Harvard International Journal of Press/Politics|url=http://muse.jhu.edu/login?uri=/journals/harvard_international_journal_of_press_politics/v004/4.4caliendo.html|title=All the News That's Fit to Print? New York Times Coverage of Human-Rights Violations|volume= 4|issue= 4, Fall 1999|pages=48–69|author1=Caliendo, Stephen |author2=Gibney, Mark |author3=Tables, Angela |s2cid = 145716613|access-date=May 28, 2007|doi=10.1177/1081180x9900400404|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.allacademic.com/meta/p152798_index.html|title=Paper presented at the annual meeting of the American Political Science Association|publisher=www.allacademic.com|author1=Caliendo, Stephen|author2=Gibney, Mark|access-date=May 28, 2007|date=August 31, 2006|archive-date=October 7, 2007|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071007020822/http://www.allacademic.com/meta/p152798_index.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> [[Amnesty International]]'s Secretary General [[Irene Khan]] explains, "If we focus on the U.S. it's because we believe that the U.S. is a country whose enormous influence and power has to be used constructively ... When countries like the U.S. are seen to undermine or ignore human rights, it sends a very powerful message to others."<ref name=boston>{{Cite news|url=http://www.boston.com/news/world/europe/articles/2007/05/24/report_hits_us_on_human_rights/?rss_id=Boston+Globe+--+World+News|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090105225113/http://www.boston.com/news/world/europe/articles/2007/05/24/report_hits_us_on_human_rights/?rss_id=Boston+Globe+--+World+News|url-status=dead|archive-date=January 5, 2009|title=Report hits US on human rights|publisher=Associated Press (published on Globe)|first=Raphael|last=Satter|date=May 24, 2007|access-date=May 29, 2007}}</ref>

===Inhumane treatment and torture of foreign prisoners===
{{See also|Torture and the United States|CIA prison system|Senate Intelligence Committee report on CIA torture|Criticism of the war on terrorism}}

[[File:US Senate Report on CIA Detention Interrogation Program.pdf|thumb|The US Senate Report on CIA Detention Interrogation Program that details the use of torture during CIA detention and interrogation]]
