Studies of heart, disease, morality rates, show that black individuals experience, worse outcomes than white individuals, regardless of their education.<ref name=":210"/> A long-term study examining cardiovascular health on that black physicians had a higher prevalence of cardiovascular disease, hypertension, and diabetes, compared to white physicians, despite comparable professional status.<ref name=":116"/>

In the area of maternal health, similar disparities exist. Black women with college degrees face higher pregnancy related mortality rates than white women without high school diplomas these pattern suggests that factors beyond SES, which is including stress related to structural racism and differential treatment within healthcare settings, making contribute to these outcomes.<ref name=":43"/>

In addition to healthcare, racial bias, and employment may also indirectly affect health by limiting access to stable income and employer based health benefits. Studies have found that applicants with names perceived as African-Americans are less likely to receive interview callbacks, compared to those with white sounding names, even when resumes are otherwise identical.<ref name=":116"/> This type of bias can reduce opportunities for economic advancement, which contributes to the disparities in SES it's health related impacts.

Perceived experiences of discrimination within healthcare also very by race. According to a few national surveys, why individuals with higher education and income, tend to report, fewer instances of discrimination and have a greater confidence in receiving appropriate medical treatment. But in contrast, black individuals, even those with higher SES are more likely to report experiencing racial bias or unequal treatment in healthcare environments.<ref name=":010"/>

These patterns reflect the con the very complex ways in which race in  social economic status interact to influence health. While SES is a powerful determine, it does not  remove the effects  of racism or structural and  inequality in healthcare access and quality. Ongoing research is exploring how these interesting factors shape health equity and inform interventions to address both economic and racial disparities and health.<ref name=":43" />

==Specific diseases==
Health disparities are well documented in minority populations such as [[African Americans]], [[Native Americans (US)|Native Americans]], and [[Latinos]].<ref name = "Goldberg_2004">{{cite book | vauthors = Goldberg J, Hayes W, Huntley J |date=November 2004 |title=Understanding Health Disparities |publisher=Health Policy Institute of Ohio |url=http://www.healthpolicyohio.org/pdf/healthdisparities.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070927010615/http://www.healthpolicyohio.org/pdf/healthdisparities.pdf |archive-date=2007-09-27}}{{Page needed|date=September 2010}}</ref> In the year 1985,  a report, known as the Heckler Report, was released to address the state of concern regarding African American and minority populations.<ref name=":6">{{Cite web |last=<!--Not stated--> |date=2012 |title=Fact Sheet: Health Disparities |url=https://www.apa.org/topics/racism-bias-discrimination/health-disparities-defined |access-date=24 April 2021 |website=[[American Psychological Association|APA]] |language=en-US}}</ref> This report sought to look at statistical data that showed its prevalence and the action towards bridging this health equity gap.  The report identified six areas of health concern: cancer, cardiovascular disease and stroke, chemical dependency related to cirrhosis of the liver, diabetes, homicides and accidents, and infant mortality.<ref name=":6" />  When compared to [[European Americans]] and [[Asian Americans]], these minority groups have higher incidence of chronic diseases, higher mortality, and poorer health outcomes.<ref name = "Goldberg_2004" /> More importantly noted are the number of lives that could have been saved if healthcare were the same between both populations.<ref name=":6" /> That is, African Americans and minority populations having access to healthcare that meets their needs and seek to address this much needed change.

Minorities often have higher rates of [[cardiovascular disease]], [[HIV/AIDS]], and [[infant mortality]] than whites.<ref name = "Goldberg_2004" /> U.S. ethnic groups can exhibit substantial average differences in disease incidence, disease severity, disease progression, and response to treatment.<ref>Thomas Alexis LaVeist, ''[https://books.google.com/books?id=_FJ4C9uv3YkC Race, Ethnicity, and Health: A Public Health Reader]'' (San Francisco: Jossey-Bass, 2002).</ref>
* African Americans have higher rates of mortality than does any other racial or ethnic group for 8 of the top 10 causes of death.<ref name=hummer2004/> The cancer incidence rate among African Americans is 10% higher than among European Americans and the mortality rate from asthma is twice the rate of European Americans.<ref name=":18">{{Cite journal |last1=Israel |first1=Elliot |last2=Cardet |first2=Juan-Carlos |last3=Carroll |first3=Jennifer K. |last4=Fuhlbrigge |first4=Anne L. |last5=She |first5=Lilin |last6=Rockhold |first6=Frank W. |last7=Maher |first7=Nancy E. |last8=Fagan |first8=Maureen |last9=Forth |first9=Victoria E. |last10=Yawn |first10=Barbara P. |last11=Arias Hernandez |first11=Paulina |date=2022-04-21 |title=Reliever-Triggered Inhaled Glucocorticoid in Black and Latinx Adults with Asthma |journal=New England Journal of Medicine |language=en |volume=386 |issue=16 |pages=1505–1518 |doi=10.1056/NEJMoa2118813 |pmid=35213105 |pmc=10367430 |s2cid=247106044 |issn=0028-4793 |doi-access=free}}</ref>
* African Americans are found to have some of the highest rates of chronic Hepatitis C and Hepatitis C-related deaths in comparison to other populations.<ref name=":13">{{Cite web |title=Minority Health {{!}} NIH: National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases |url=https://www.niaid.nih.gov/research/minority-health |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160918023429/http://www.niaid.nih.gov/research/minority-health |archive-date=September 18, 2016 |access-date=2021-04-24 |website=www.niaid.nih.gov |language=en}}</ref>
* U.S. Latinos have higher rates of death from diabetes, liver disease, asthma, and infectious diseases than do non-Latinos.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Vega WA, Amaro H |title=Latino outlook: good health, uncertain prognosis |journal=Annual Review of Public Health |volume=15 |issue=1 |pages=39–67 |year=1994 |pmid=8054092 |doi=10.1146/annurev.pu.15.050194.000351 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name=":18" />
* In 2015, nearly 2.2 million Hispanics/Latinos nationwide reported having asthma, with Puerto Rican Americans possessing almost tripled the asthma rate of the overall Hispanic population. A part of this disparity can be said to be due to the higher rates of pollution found in communities of people of color.<ref name=":13" />
* Adult African Americans and Latinos have approximately twice the risk as European Americans of developing diabetes.
* Asian Americans are 60% more likely to being at risk of developing diabetes in comparison to European Americans and are more likely to develop the disease at lower BMIs and lower body weights. South Asians are especially more likely to developing diabetes as it is estimated South Asians are four times more likely to developing the disease in comparison to European Americans.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://aadi.joslin.org/content/asian/why-are-asians-higher-risk-diabetes |title=Why Do People of Asian Descent Get Diabetes? |publisher=Asian Diabetes Prevention Initiative |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150430065604/http://aadi.joslin.org/content/asian/why-are-asians-higher-risk-diabetes |archive-date=2015-04-30}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://asiandiabetesprevention.org/what-is-diabetes/why-are-asians-higher-risk |title=Why are Asians at Higher Risk? |publisher=Asian Diabetes Prevention Initiative |access-date=2014-09-19 |archive-date=2019-12-23 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191223030351/http://asiandiabetesprevention.org/what-is-diabetes/why-are-asians-higher-risk }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=McNeely MJ, Boyko EJ |title=Type 2 diabetes prevalence in Asian Americans: results of a national health survey |journal=Diabetes Care |volume=27 |issue=1 |pages=66–9 |date=January 2004 |pmid=14693968 |doi=10.2337/diacare.27.1.66 |url=http://care.diabetesjournals.org/content/27/1/66 |doi-access=free |access-date=2014-09-19 |archive-date=2024-07-12 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240712165238/https://diabetesjournals.org/care/article/27/1/66/26735/Type-2-Diabetes-Prevalence-in-Asian-Americans |url-status=live |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.pamf.org/southasian/risk/concerns/diabetes.html |title=Type 2 Diabetes in South Asians |author=Palo Alto Medical Foundation |access-date=2014-09-19 |archive-date=2014-09-04 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140904184654/http://www.pamf.org/southasian/risk/concerns/diabetes.html |url-status=live }}</ref>
* Native Americans usually suffer from higher rates of diabetes, tuberculosis, pneumonia, influenza, and alcoholism than does the rest of the U.S. population.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Mahoney MC, Michalek AM |title=Health status of American Indians/Alaska Natives: general patterns of mortality |journal=Family Medicine |volume=30 |issue=3 |pages=190–5 |date=March 1998 |pmid=9532441}}</ref> Disparities in diabetes and cardiovascular disease have been hypothesized to be linked to higher rates of suboptimal sleep in this population.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Nuyujukian DS |title=Sleep Duration and Diabetes Risk in American Indian and Alaska Native Participants of a Lifestyle Intervention Project |journal=Sleep |volume=39 |issue=11 |pages=1919–1926 |date=2016 |doi=10.5665/sleep.6216 |pmid=27450685 |pmc=5070746}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Nuyujukian DS, Anton-Culver H, Manson SM, Jiang L |title=Associations of sleep duration with cardiometabolic outcomes in American Indians and Alaska Natives and other race/ethnicities: results from the BRFSS |url=https://www.sleephealthjournal.org/article/S2352-7218(19)30026-9/fulltext |journal=Sleep Health |date=2019 |volume=5 |issue=4 |pages=344–351 |doi=10.1016/j.sleh.2019.02.003 |pmid=30987947 |pmc=6935393 |access-date=2020-04-04 |archive-date=2020-06-26 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200626070441/https://www.sleephealthjournal.org/article/S2352-7218(19)30026-9/fulltext |url-status=live }}</ref>
* European Americans die more often from heart disease and cancer than do Native Americans, Asian Americans, or Hispanics.<ref name=hummer2004>{{cite journal |vauthors=Hummer RA, Ellison CG, Rogers RG, Moulton BE, Romero RR |title=Religious involvement and adult mortality in the United States: review and perspective |journal=Southern Medical Journal |volume=97 |issue=12 |pages=1223–30 |date=December 2004 |pmid=15646761 |doi=10.1097/01.SMJ.0000146547.03382.94 |s2cid=6053725}}</ref>
* White Americans have far higher incident rates of melanoma of the skin or skin cancer than any other race/ethnicity in the US. In 2007 incident rates among white American males were approximately 25/100,000 people, whereas the next highest group (Hispanics and natives) has an incidence rate of approximately 5/100,000 people.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.cdc.gov/cancer/skin/statistics/race.htm |title=Skin Cancer Rates by Race and Ethnicity |publisher=Centers for Disease Control |access-date=2012-04-09 |archive-date=2020-02-17 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200217133742/https://www.cdc.gov/cancer/skin/statistics/race.htm |url-status=live }}</ref>
* Asian Americans are at higher risk for [[hepatitis B]], [[liver cancer]], [[tuberculosis]], and [[lung cancer]].<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Chen MS, Hawks BL |s2cid=22775032 |title=A debunking of the myth of healthy Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders |journal=American Journal of Health Promotion |volume=9 |issue=4 |pages=261–8 |year=1995 |pmid=10150729 |doi=10.4278/0890-1171-9.4.261}}</ref> The subgroup of [[Filipino American]]s suffer health risks similar to that of African Americans and European Americans combined.<ref>{{cite book |vauthors=Gatewood JV, Zhou M |title=Contemporary Asian America: a multidisciplinary reader |url=https://archive.org/details/contemporaryasia00zhou |url-access=registration |publisher=New York University Press |location=New York |year=2000 |isbn=978-0-8147-9691-7}}</ref>
* According to the NIH, African Americans are more likely to develop diabetes. Usually, type 2 diabetes is more prominent in middle-aged adults. Being obese or having a family history can also affect this. Over the past 30 years in the US, "black adults are nearly twice as likely as white adults to develop type 2 diabetes."<ref name=":1">{{cite web |title=Factors contributing to higher incidence of diabetes for black Americans |url=https://www.nih.gov/news-events/nih-research-matters/factors-contributing-higher-incidence-diabetes-black-americans |publisher=United States National Institutes of Health (NIH) |date=2018-01-08 |access-date=2019-04-25 |archive-date=2020-06-15 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200615231812/https://www.nih.gov/news-events/nih-research-matters/factors-contributing-higher-incidence-diabetes-black-americans |url-status=live }}</ref> Besides this difference just being between black and white adults, we see the greatest margin of comparison between black and white women.
* In 2015, 87 percent of all TB cases in the United States occurred in those that are identified as racial and ethnic minorities, especially Hispanics, Asians, and African Americans.<ref name=":13" /> Even more recently, African Americans are considered the group with the highest rate of infection, totaling more than 1,000 cases in 2019. Socioeconomic factors are the related cause, alongside it presenting barriers to treatment in the disease.<ref name=":6" />
* [[Sickle cell disease]] is more susceptible to be found in those of descent from places such as those in the Mediterranean, Italy, Turkey, and Greece, as well as Africa and regions of South and Central America.<ref name=":2">{{cite web |title=Sickle cell disease |url=https://medlineplus.gov/genetics/condition/sickle-cell-disease/ |work=Genetics Home Reference |publisher=U.S. Department of Health & Human Services, National Institutes of Health, National Library of Medicine |access-date=2019-04-25 |archive-date=2016-05-15 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160515204041/https://ghr.nlm.nih.gov/condition/sickle-cell-disease |url-status=live }}</ref>  The disease affects how oxygen is delivered to the red blood cells and is often diagnosed at a young age, discovered through a diagnosis of anemia.
* In a 2019 study on [[racial discrimination]] and [[Dental Health|dental health]] in the U.S. the authors found that the "emotional impact of racial discrimination" results in fewer visits to a dentist.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Sabbah W, Gireesh A, Chari M, Delgado-Angulo EK, Bernabé E | title = Racial Discrimination and Uptake of Dental Services among American Adults | journal = International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health | volume = 16 | issue = 9 | page = 1558 | date = May 2019 | pmid = 31060202 | pmc = 6540199 | doi = 10.3390/ijerph16091558 | doi-access = free }}</ref>
* According to the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey data, childhood obesity is more common among Hispanic (25.8%) and Black children (22.0%) compared to white children (14.1%).<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = McGuire S | title = Shields M., Carroll M.D., Ogden C.L. adult obesity prevalence in Canada and the United States. NCHS data brief no. 56, Hyattsville, MD: National Center for Health Statistics, 2011 | journal = Advances in Nutrition | volume = 2 | issue = 4 | pages = 368–9 | date = July 2011 | pmid = 22332078 | doi = 10.3945/an.111.000497 | pmc = 3125686 | doi-access = free }}</ref>  In other studies the same results are seen in adults from the same race and ethnicity.
* A 2021 systematic review on hearing loss in adults found an absence of racial and ethnic diversity in studies that did not represent the diversity of the US population.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Pittman |first1=Corinne A. |last2=Roura |first2=Raúl |last3=Price |first3=Carrie |last4=Lin |first4=Frank R. |last5=Marrone |first5=Nicole |last6=Nieman |first6=Carrie L. |date=2021-07-01 |title=Racial/Ethnic and Sex Representation in US-Based Clinical Trials of Hearing Loss Management in Adults: A Systematic Review |url=https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamaotolaryngology/fullarticle/2779267 |journal=JAMA Otolaryngology–Head & Neck Surgery |language=en |volume=147 |issue=7 |pages=656–662 |doi=10.1001/jamaoto.2021.0550 |pmid=33885733 |s2cid=233351877 |issn=2168-6181|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
* The likelihood of developing kidney, liver, stomach, and cervical cancers among Native Americans is two to three times higher than among white people.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Dunbar |first1=Marina |title=Cancer cases rising for women and younger adults in US, report finds |url=https://www.theguardian.com/society/2025/jan/16/cancer-young-women-adults |agency=The Guardian |date=16 Jan 2025}}</ref>

== African Americans ==

===History===
{{further|Seasoning (slavery)|Slave health on plantations in the United States|Slavery hypertension hypothesis}}
Disparities in health and lifespan among blacks and whites in the US have long existed. Many [[African Americans]] and minorities weren't subjects of outreach, nor attended to for medical conditions. Several incidents throughout early history show maltreatment, neglect, and being denied healthcare in comparison to the white population. Foregoing early treatment progresses infection, leads to disability, or ultimately death, dependent upon the disease. One of those events was the flu epidemic of 1918.<ref name=":14">{{Cite web |last=Brooks |first=Rodney A. |title=Why African Americans Were More Likely to Die During the 1918 Flu Pandemic |url=https://www.history.com/news/1918-flu-pandemic-african-americans-healthcare-black-nurses |access-date=2021-04-24 |website=HISTORY |date=5 October 2020 |language=en}}</ref> Black communities were either refused care, received subpar attention, or, where available, expected and pursued aid from black nurses. Although current information reflects that minorities in the United States have lower life expectancies and encounter a larger number of health conditions than their white counterparts, the health of black people has not always been documented.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The American Journal of Public Health (AJPH) from the American Public Health Association (APHA) publications |url=http://ajph.aphapublications.org/ |access-date=2021-04-24 |website=American Public Health Association (APHA) publications |language=en |archive-date=2019-05-14 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190514164604/https://ajph.aphapublications.org/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Accurate numbers show the number of African Americans infected, disabled, or died—or succumbed to it—aren't available; records remain scarce, since so few of those victims were able to get to institutional healthcare providers or agencies.<ref name=":14" /> David R. Williams and Chiquita Collins wrote that, although racial taxonomies are socially constructed and arbitrary, race is still one of the major bases of division in American life. Throughout U.S. history racial disparities in health has been pervasive.<ref>{{cite journal| vauthors = Williams DR, Collins C |title=US Socioeconomic and Racial Differences in Health: Patterns and Explanations |journal=Annual Review of Sociology |date=August 1995 |volume=21 |issue=1 |pages=349–386  |doi=10.1146/annurev.so.21.080195.002025}}</ref> In a 2001 paper, Williams and Collins also argued that, although it is no longer being legally enforced, racial segregation is still one of the primary causes of racial disparities in health because it determines [[socioeconomic status]] by limiting access to education and employment opportunities.<ref name=wc2001>{{cite journal | vauthors = Williams DR, Collins C | title = Racial residential segregation: a fundamental cause of racial disparities in health | journal = Public Health Reports | volume = 116 | issue = 5 | pages = 404–16 | date = 2001 | pmid = 12042604 | pmc = 1497358 | doi = 10.1093/phr/116.5.404 | doi-broken-date = 1 July 2025 }}</ref> Clayton and Byrd write that there have been two periods of health reform specifically addressing the correction of race-based health disparities. The first period (1865–1872) was linked to [[Freedmen's Bureau]] legislation and the second (1965–1975) was a part of the [[Civil Rights Movement]]. Both had dramatic and positive effects on black health status and outcome, but were discontinued. Even though African-American health status and outcome is slowly improving, black health has generally stagnated or deteriorated compared to whites since 1980.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Clayton LA, Byrd WM | title = Race: a major health status and outcome variable 1980-1999 | journal = Journal of the National Medical Association | volume = 93 | issue = 3 Suppl | pages = 35S–54S | date = March 2001 | pmid = 12653396 | pmc = 2593960 }}</ref>

The Tuskegee study was another example of health disparities among African Americans.<ref name = "Olansky_1954">{{cite journal | vauthors = Olansky S, Simpson L, Schuman SH | title = Environmental factors in the Tuskegee study of untreated syphilis | journal = Public Health Reports | volume = 69 | issue = 7 | pages = 691–8 | date = July 1954 | pmid = 13177831 | doi = 10.2307/4588864 | jstor = 4588864 | pmc = 2024316 }}</ref> The study showed lack of medical treatment and discrimination among blacks.<ref name = "Olansky_1954" /> African Americans find it difficult to participant in clinical trials due to lack of understanding and knowledge received by researchers.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Freimuth VS, Quinn SC, Thomas SB, Cole G, Zook E, Duncan T | title = African Americans' views on research and the Tuskegee Syphilis Study | journal = Social Science & Medicine | volume = 52 | issue = 5 | pages = 797–808 | date = March 2001 | pmid = 11218181 | doi = 10.1016/s0277-9536(00)00178-7 | hdl = 1903/22694 | hdl-access = free }}</ref>

In 1932, the Tuskegee study involved 600 black men, 399 with syphilis and 201 with no disease.<ref name="cdc.gov">{{Cite web |date=2020-12-10 |title=Tuskegee Study - Timeline - CDC - NCHHSTP |url=https://www.cdc.gov/tuskegee/timeline.htm |access-date=2021-04-09 |website=www.cdc.gov |language=en-us |archive-date=2011-09-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110903161044/http://www.cdc.gov/tuskegee/timeline.htm |url-status=live }}</ref> Researchers told the men that they were being treated for "bad blood," a term used in the study to describe several ailments, including syphilis, anemia, and fatigue.<ref name="cdc.gov"/> The men were told by researchers and health professionals that they would be participating in a study to cure their current illnesses.<ref name="cdc.gov"/> The men in the study later found they were not being treated for the purpose they agreed upon. This study resulted in a class action lawsuit due to lack of evidence, no consent, misleading information, and medical neglect.<ref name="cdc.gov"/> As a result of lack of treatment, by July 1972 when the study ended, over 100 participants had died, 40 spouses had been diagnosed, and disease had been passed to 19 children at birth.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Nix |first=Elizabeth |title=Tuskegee Experiment: The Infamous Syphilis Study |url=https://www.history.com/news/the-infamous-40-year-tuskegee-study |access-date=2021-04-09 |website=HISTORY |date=16 May 2017 |language=en |archive-date=2021-04-08 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210408051619/https://www.history.com/news/the-infamous-40-year-tuskegee-study |url-status=live }}</ref>

In one study, researchers found that medical professionals perceive black patients to be less susceptible to pain than their white patients. White patients are given better treatment and access than black patients. As a result, black patients are more vulnerable to disease than white counterparts.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Royles|first=Dan|title=Perspective {{!}} Years of medical abuse make Black Americans less likely to trust the coronavirus vaccine|language=en-US|newspaper=Washington Post|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/outlook/2020/12/15/years-medical-abuse-make-black-americans-less-likely-trust-covid-vaccine/|access-date=2021-04-09|issn=0190-8286|archive-date=2021-04-09|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210409005335/https://www.washingtonpost.com/outlook/2020/12/15/years-medical-abuse-make-black-americans-less-likely-trust-covid-vaccine/|url-status=live}}</ref>

Sickle cell is a blood disease that is very prevalent in the African American community. This disease cannot be seen with the naked eye. Because of this illness's invisibility, African American patients can be suffering and most likely to be ignored by healthcare providers.<ref>{{Cite book |title=Dying in the city of blues: Sickle Cell Anemia and the politics of race and health |author=Wailoo, K. | year=2001 | publisher= University of North Carolina Press}}</ref> Sickle cell was not discovered in the west until 1910.<ref>{{Cite web |title=History of Sickle cell |url=https://www.redcrossblood.org/donate-blood/blood-types/diversity/african-american-blood-donors/history-of-sickle-cell-disease.html }}</ref> Although sickle cell is not the only invisible disease, it is an example of an invisible illness and how it affects some African Americans. There are many other diseases and illnesses that cannot be seen visibly, causing people to get discriminated against, not only because of their illness but also because of how they look.

Demographic changes can have broad effects on the health of ethnic groups. Cities in the United States have undergone major social transitions during the 1970s, 1980s, and 1990s. Notable factors in these shifts have been sustained rates of black poverty and intensified racial segregation, often as a result of [[redlining]].<ref name="eastny">{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=TWo8OFJpFtAC |title=How East New York Became a Ghetto |vauthors=Thabit W |isbn=978-0-8147-8267-5 |page=42 |year=2003 |publisher=NYU Press |access-date=2016-09-24 |archive-date=2024-07-12 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240712165237/https://books.google.com/books?id=TWo8OFJpFtAC |url-status=live }}</ref> Indications of the effect of these social forces on black-white differentials in health status have begun to surface in the research literature.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Laveist TA |title=Segregation, poverty, and empowerment: health consequences for African Americans |journal=The Milbank Quarterly |volume=71 |issue=1 |pages=41–64 |year=1993 |pmid=8450822 |doi=10.2307/3350274 |jstor=3350274}}</ref>

Race has played a decisive role in shaping systems of medical care in the United States. The divided health system persists, in spite of federal efforts to end segregation, health care remains widely segregated both exacerbating and distorting racial disparities.<ref>{{cite book |title=Health Care Divided: Race and Healing a Nation |vauthors=Smith DB |year=1999 |publisher=University of Michigan Press |isbn=978-0-472-10991-3}}{{Page needed|date=September 2010}}</ref> Furthermore, the risks for many diseases are elevated for socially, economically, and politically disadvantaged groups in the United States, suggesting to some that environmental factors and not genetics are the causes of most of the differences.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Cooper RS, Kaufman JS, Ward R |title=Race and genomics |journal=The New England Journal of Medicine |volume=348 |issue=12 |pages=1166–70 |date=March 2003 |pmid=12646675 |doi=10.1056/NEJMsb022863}}</ref><ref name=cooper2003>Cooper RS, "Genetic factors in ethnic disparities in health," in Anderson NB, Bulatao RA, Cohen B, eds., ''Critical perspectives on racial and ethnic differences in health in later life'', (Washington DC: National Academy Press, 2004), 267–309.</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lin |first1=Jielu |last2=Thompson |first2=Martie P. |last3=Kaslow |first3=Nadine J. |date=May 2009 |title=The mediating role of social support in the community environment—psychological distress link among low-income African American women |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/jcop.20307 |journal=Journal of Community Psychology |language=en |volume=37 |issue=4 |pages=459–470 |doi=10.1002/jcop.20307 |issn=0090-4392 |access-date=2024-03-25 |archive-date=2024-03-25 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240325172226/https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/jcop.20307 |url-status=live |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

There was a trend in health discrimination throughout the COVID-19 pandemic. Data has shown that African Americans have higher rates of contracting COVID-19 as well as dying from it. These rates are mainly high in majority black communities; oftentimes because these communities are more population dense and have higher rates of individuals living with no health insurance, low socioeconomic status, and chronic diseases. Structural racism has forced a majority of African Americans to live in low SES communities and has limited their ability to thrive due to less resources. Because of these lack of resources many African Americans were unable to sustain things like social isolation, transportation, and food.<ref>{{Cite journal |author-link=Peek, Monica E.; Simons, Russell A.; Parker, William F.; Ansell, David A.; Rogers, Selwyn O.; Edmonds, Brownsyne Tucker |title=COVID-19 among African Americans: An action plan for mitigating disparities |journal=American Journal of Public Health}}</ref>

===Racism===
{{Main|Racism against black Americans}}

{{see also|Minority stress|John Henryism|Slavery hypertension hypothesis|Weathering hypothesis}}

Racial differences in health often persist even at equivalent socioeconomic levels. Individual and institutional discrimination, along with the stigma of inferiority, can adversely affect health. Racism can also directly affect health in multiple ways.<ref name="urlBlack doctor's death becomes a symbol of racism in coronavirus care | Coronavirus | The Guardian">{{cite web |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2020/dec/26/black-doctors-death-becomes-a-symbol-of-racism-in-coronavirus-care |title=Black doctor's death becomes a symbol of racism in coronavirus care &#124; Coronavirus &#124; The Guardian |website=[[TheGuardian.com]] |date=26 December 2020 |access-date=4 January 2021 |archive-date=12 July 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240712165237/https://www.theguardian.com/world/2020/dec/26/black-doctors-death-becomes-a-symbol-of-racism-in-coronavirus-care |url-status=live }}</ref> Residence in poor neighborhoods, racial bias in medical care, the stress of experiences of discrimination and the acceptance of the societal stigma of inferiority can have deleterious consequences for health.<ref name=autogenerated1>{{cite journal | vauthors = Williams DR | title = Race, socioeconomic status, and health. The added effects of racism and discrimination | journal = Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences | volume = 896 | issue = 1 | pages = 173–88 | year = 1999 | pmid = 10681897 | doi = 10.1111/j.1749-6632.1999.tb08114.x | bibcode = 1999NYASA.896..173W | hdl = 2027.42/71908 | s2cid = 26852165 | url = https://deepblue.lib.umich.edu/bitstream/2027.42/71908/1/j.1749-6632.1999.tb08114.x.pdf | hdl-access = free | access-date = 2019-09-01 | archive-date = 2012-01-26 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20120126203618/http://deepblue.lib.umich.edu/bitstream/2027.42/71908/1/j.1749-6632.1999.tb08114.x.pdf | url-status = live }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Williams DR, Mohammed SA | title = Discrimination and racial disparities in health: evidence and needed research | journal = Journal of Behavioral Medicine | volume = 32 | issue = 1 | pages = 20–47 | date = February 2009 | pmid = 19030981 | pmc = 2821669 | doi = 10.1007/s10865-008-9185-0 }}</ref> Racism is a key determinant of socioeconomic status (SES) in the United States, and SES, in turn, is a fundamental cause of racial inequities in health.<ref>{{cite journal| vauthors = Phelan JC, Link BG |date=2015|title=Is Racism a Fundamental Cause of Inequalities in Health?|journal=Annual Review of Sociology |volume=41 |issue=1|pages=311–330|doi=10.1146/annurev-soc-073014-112305|doi-access=free}}</ref> Using [[Psychometrics of racism|The Schedule of Racist Events]] (SRE), an 18-item self-report inventory that assesses the frequency of racist discrimination. [[Hope Landrine]] and Elizabeth A. Klonoff found that racist discrimination was frequent in the lives of African Americans and is strongly correlated to psychiatric symptoms.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=[[Hope Landrine|Landrine H]], Klonoff EA |s2cid=145535500 |doi=10.1177/00957984960222002 |title=The Schedule of Racist Events: A Measure of Racial Discrimination and a Study of Its Negative Physical and Mental Health Consequences |year=1996 |journal=Journal of Black Psychology |volume=22 |pages=144–168 |issue=2}}</ref>

A study on racist events in the lives of African American women found that lifetime racism was positively correlated to lifetime history of both physical disease and frequency of recent common colds. These relationships were largely unaccounted for by other variables. Demographic variables such as income and education were not related to experiences of racism. The results suggest that racism can be detrimental to African Americans' well-being.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Kwate NO, Valdimarsdottir HB, Guevarra JS, Bovbjerg DH |title=Experiences of racist events are associated with negative health consequences for African American women |journal=Journal of the National Medical Association |volume=95 |issue=6 |pages=450–60 |date=June 2003 |pmid=12856911 |pmc=2594553}}</ref> The physiological stress caused by racism has been documented in studies by [[Claude Steele]], Joshua Aronson, and Steven Spencer on what they term "[[stereotype threat]]."<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Blascovich J, Spencer SJ, Quinn D, Steele C |title=African Americans and high blood pressure: the role of stereotype threat |journal=Psychological Science |volume=12 |issue=3 |pages=225–9 |date=May 2001 |pmid=11437305 |doi=10.1111/1467-9280.00340 |s2cid=2590855}}</ref>

Kennedy et al. found that both measures of collective disrespect were strongly correlated with black mortality (r = 0.53 to 0.56), as well as with white mortality (r = 0.48 to 0.54). A 1 percent increase in the prevalence of those who believed that blacks lacked innate ability was associated with an increase in age-adjusted black mortality rate of 359.8 per 100,000 (95% confidence interval: 187.5 to 532.1 deaths per 100,000).  These data suggest that racism, measured as an ecologic characteristic, is associated with higher mortality in both blacks and whites.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Kennedy BP, Kawachi I, Lochner K, Jones C, Prothrow-Stith D |title=(Dis)respect and black mortality |journal=Ethnicity & Disease |volume=7 |issue=3 |pages=207–14 |year=1997 |pmid=9467703}}</ref>

Two local governments in the US have issued declarations stating that racism constitutes a [[Public health emergency (United States)|public health emergency]]: the [[Milwaukee County, Wisconsin]] executive in May 2019, and the [[Cleveland City Council]], in June 2020.<ref>{{Cite web |vauthors=Dirr A |title=Milwaukee County executive signs resolution declaring racism a public health crisis |url=https://www.jsonline.com/story/news/local/milwaukee/2019/05/20/abele-signs-resolution-declaring-racism-public-health-crisis/3741809002/ |access-date=2020-06-28 |website=Milwaukee Journal Sentinel |language=en-US |archive-date=2019-10-08 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191008033529/https://www.jsonline.com/story/news/local/milwaukee/2019/05/20/abele-signs-resolution-declaring-racism-public-health-crisis/3741809002/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |vauthors=Goist R |date=2020-06-28 |title=What happens after declaring racism a public health crisis? A Wisconsin county offers a clue |url=https://www.cleveland.com/news/2020/06/what-happens-after-a-city-or-county-declares-racism-a-public-health-crisis-a-wisconsin-county-offers-a-clue.html |access-date=2020-06-28 |website=Cleveland.com |language=en |archive-date=2020-06-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200629185106/https://www.cleveland.com/news/2020/06/what-happens-after-a-city-or-county-declares-racism-a-public-health-crisis-a-wisconsin-county-offers-a-clue.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

Princeton Survey Research Associates found that in 1999 most whites were unaware that race and ethnicity may affect the quality and ease of access to health care.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Lillie-Blanton M, Brodie M, Rowland D, Altman D, McIntosh M |title=Race, ethnicity, and the health care system: public perceptions and experiences |journal=Medical Care Research and Review |volume=57 Suppl 1 |issue=4 suppl |pages=218–35 |year=2000 |pmid=11092164 |doi=10.1177/1077558700574010 |url=http://mcr.sagepub.com/cgi/pmidlookup?view=long&pmid=11092164 |access-date=2011-03-25 |archive-date=2024-07-12 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240712165238/https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/1077558700057001S10 |url-status=live |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

===Inequalities in health care===
{{Main|Medical racism in the United States}}

{{further|Racial biases in medical decision-making tools}}
Inequalities and inequities within healthcare often arise as a result of social determinants of health.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Racial and Ethnic Health Care Disparities |url=https://medicareadvocacy.org/medicare-info/health-care-disparities/ |access-date=2025-07-30 |website=Center for Medicare Advocacy |language=en-US}}</ref> These determinants influence health disparities, including the quality of care received. Race and ethnicity play a significant role in access to health services, and treatment within the healthcare system can sometimes lead to worse health outcomes. Health care inequality's and inequities are shaped by obstacles such as poverty, discrimination, and lack of access. In 2021, California reported that one in ten Latino's had no health insurance, and more than 25% reported being in poor health.<ref>{{Cite web |last=ifroman |date=2025-02-14 |title=Health Disparities by Race and Ethnicity in California Almanac — 2024 Edition |url=https://www.chcf.org/resource/health-disparities-by-race-and-ethnicity-in-california-almanac/ |access-date=2025-07-30 |website=California Health Care Foundation |language=en-US}}</ref> According to the California Health Interview Survey (CHIS) in 2022, one in four black participants reported believing they would have received better care if they were of a different race or ethnicity. The Oklahoma Department of Public Health released an improvement plan in 2020 emphasizing the role of social determinants of health in contributing to racial health disparities.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Health Disparities Overview |url=https://www.ncsl.org/health/health-disparities-overview |access-date=2025-07-30 |website=www.ncsl.org |language=en-US}}</ref>

There is a great deal of research into [[inequalities in health care]]. In 2003, the [[Institute of Medicine]] released a report showing that race and ethnicity were significantly associated with the quality of healthcare received, even after controlling for socioeconomic factors such as access to care.<ref>{{cite book |url=http://www.nap.edu/catalog/10260/unequal-treatment-confronting-racial-and-ethnic-disparities-in-health-care |title=Unequal Treatment: Confronting Racial and Ethnic Disparities in Health Care |date=2003 |access-date=24 March 2016 |doi=10.17226/10260 |isbn=978-0-309-08532-8 |archive-date=21 March 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160321172044/http://www.nap.edu/catalog/10260/unequal-treatment-confronting-racial-and-ethnic-disparities-in-health-care |url-status=live }}</ref> In some cases these inequalities are a result of income and a lack of health insurance, a barrier to receiving services. Almost two-thirds (62 percent) of Hispanic adults aged 19 to 64 (15 million people) were uninsured at some point during the past year, a rate more than triple that of working-age white adults (20 percent). One-third of working-age black adults (more than 6 million people) were also uninsured or experienced a gap in coverage during the year. Blacks had the most problems with [[medical debt]], with 31 percent of black adults aged 18 to 64 reporting Past-Due Medical Debt, vs. 23 percent of whites and 24 percent of Hispanics.<ref>{{cite web |vauthors=Karpman M, Caswell KJ |title=Past-due medical debt among nonelderly adults, 2012–15. |location=Washington, DC |publisher=Urban Institute |date=March 2017 |url=https://article.images.consumerreports.org/prod/content/dam/consumerist/2017/03/past_due_medical_debt.pdf |access-date=2019-07-19 |archive-date=2019-07-19 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190719193104/https://article.images.consumerreports.org/prod/content/dam/consumerist/2017/03/past_due_medical_debt.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref>

Compared with white women, black women are twice as likely and Hispanic women are nearly three times as likely to be uninsured.<ref>{{cite web |title=Health Care for Minority Women: Recent Findings |series=Program Brief. AHRQ Publication No. 09-PB003 |date=April 2009 |publisher=Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality |location=Rockville, MD |url=http://www.ahrq.gov/research/minority.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110523163218/http://www.ahrq.gov/research/minority.htm |archive-date=2011-05-23 }}</ref> However, a survey conducted in 2009, which examined whether patient race influences physician's prescribing, found that racial differences in outpatient prescribing patterns for hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, and diabetes are likely attributable to factors other than prescribing decisions based on patient race. Medications were recommended at comparable rates for hypercholesterolemia, hypertension and diabetes between Whites and African Americans.<ref name=rathore>{{cite journal | vauthors = Rathore SS, Ketcham JD, Alexander GC, Epstein AJ | title = Influence of patient race on physician prescribing decisions: a randomized on-line experiment | journal = Journal of General Internal Medicine | volume = 24 | issue = 11 | pages = 1183–91 | date = November 2009 | pmid = 19705205 | pmc = 2771231 | doi = 10.1007/s11606-009-1077-7 }}</ref>

It has been argued that other cases of inequalities in health care reflect a [[systemic bias]] in the way medical procedures and treatments are prescribed for different ethnic groups. Raj Bhopal writes that the history of [[Scientific racism|racism in science]] and medicine shows that people and institutions behave according to the ethos of their times and warns of dangers to avoid in the future.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Bhopal R | title = Spectre of racism in health and health care: lessons from history and the United States | journal = BMJ | volume = 316 | issue = 7149 | pages = 1970–3 | date = June 1998 | pmid = 9641943 | pmc = 1113412 | doi = 10.1136/bmj.316.7149.1970 }}</ref>
[[Nancy Krieger]] contended that much modern research supported the assumptions needed to justify racism. Racism contributes to unexplained inequities in health care, including treatment for heart disease,<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Oberman A, Cutter G | title = Issues in the natural history and treatment of coronary heart disease in black populations: surgical treatment | journal = American Heart Journal | volume = 108 | issue = 3 Pt 2 | pages = 688–94 | date = September 1984 | pmid = 6332513 | doi = 10.1016/0002-8703(84)90656-2 }}</ref> renal failure,<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Kjellstrand CM | title = Age, sex, and race inequality in renal transplantation | journal = Archives of Internal Medicine | volume = 148 | issue = 6 | pages = 1305–9 | date = June 1988 | pmid = 3288159 | doi = 10.1001/archinte.1988.00380060069016 }}</ref> bladder cancer,<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Mayer WJ, McWhorter WP | title = Black/white differences in non-treatment of bladder cancer patients and implications for survival | journal = American Journal of Public Health | volume = 79 | issue = 6 | pages = 772–5 | date = June 1989 | pmid = 2729474 | pmc = 1349641 | doi = 10.2105/AJPH.79.6.772 }}</ref> and pneumonia.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Yergan J, Flood AB, LoGerfo JP, [[Paula Diehr|Diehr P]] | title = Relationship between patient race and the intensity of hospital services | journal = Medical Care | volume = 25 | issue = 7 | pages = 592–603 | date = July 1987 | pmid = 3695664 | doi = 10.1097/00005650-198707000-00003 | s2cid = 11637921 }}</ref> Raj Bhopal writes that these inequalities have been documented in numerous studies.  The consistent and repeated findings that black Americans receive less health care than white Americans—particularly where this involves expensive new technology—is an indictment of American health care.<ref>{{cite journal | title = Black-white disparities in health care | journal = JAMA | volume = 263 | issue = 17 | pages = 2344–6 | date = May 1990 | pmid = 2182918 | doi = 10.1001/jama.263.17.2344 | author1 = Council on Ethical Judicial Affairs }}</ref>

The infant mortality rate for African Americans is approximately twice the rate for European Americans, but, in a study that looked at members of these two groups who belonged to the military and received care through the same medical system, their infant mortality rates were essentially equivalent.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Rawlings JS, Weir MR | title = Race- and rank-specific infant mortality in a US military population | journal = American Journal of Diseases of Children | volume = 146 | issue = 3 | pages = 313–6 | date = March 1992 | pmid = 1543178 | doi = 10.1001/archpedi.1992.02160150053020 }}</ref> Recently a study was conducted by the KFF, the Henry J Kaiser Family Foundation, in order to learn more about the infant mortality rate throughout the United States. All fifty states were surveyed. Different distributions of racial categories used in the study includes, "Non-Hispanic White, Non-Hispanic Black, American Indian or Alaska Native, Asian or Pacific Islander, or Hispanic".<ref name=":3">"Infant Mortality Rate by Race/Ethnicity". The Henry J. Kaiser Family Foundation. 2018-06-04. Retrieved 2018-10-13.</ref>
The infant mortality rate was compiled by the number of infant deaths per one thousand live births. In 2015, on an average nationwide, the United States reported that for Non-Hispanic white had an infant mortality rate of NSD meaning there as not enough sufficient data, Non-Hispanic black's rate was 11.3, Indian or Alaska Native's was 8.3, Pacific Islander was 4.2, and the infant mortality rate on average for Hispanic was 5.0.<ref name=":3" />

Recent immigrants to the United States from Mexico have better indicators on some measures of health than do Mexican Americans who are more assimilated into American culture.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Franzini L, Ribble J, Spears W | title = The effects of income inequality and income level on mortality vary by population size in Texas counties | journal = Journal of Health and Social Behavior | volume = 42 | issue = 4 | pages = 373–87 | date = December 2001 | pmid = 11831138 | doi = 10.2307/3090185 | jstor = 3090185 }}</ref> The number of Native Americans diagnosed increased by 29% just between the years of 1990 and 1997. The prevalence of this among women and men shows that women more often have diabetes than men, especially in communities of Native American people.<ref name="pmid11128353">{{cite journal | vauthors = Burrows NR, Geiss LS, Engelgau MM, Acton KJ | title = Prevalence of diabetes among Native Americans and Alaska Natives, 1990-1997: an increasing burden | journal = Diabetes Care | volume = 23 | issue = 12 | pages = 1786–90 | date = December 2000 | pmid = 11128353 | doi = 10.2337/diacare.23.12.1786 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

A report from Wisconsin's Department of Health and Family Services showed that while black women are more likely to die from [[breast cancer]], white women are more likely to be diagnosed with breast cancer. Even after diagnosis, black women are less likely to get treatment compared to white women.<ref>''[http://dhfs.wisconsin.gov/wcrs/pdf/cancerwi0004.pdf Wisconsin Cancer Incidence and Mortality, 2000-2004] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080530004014/http://dhfs.wisconsin.gov/wcrs/pdf/cancerwi0004.pdf |date=2008-05-30 }}'' Wisconsin Department of Health and Family Services</ref> University of Wisconsin African-American studies Professor Michael Thornton said the report's results show [[racism]] still exists today. "There's a lot of research that suggests that who gets taken seriously in hospitals and doctors' offices is related to race and gender," Thornton said. "It's related to the fact that many black women are less likely to be taken seriously compared to the white women when they go in for certain illnesses."<ref>''[http://badgerherald.com/news/2007/10/24/breast_cancer_rates_.php Breast cancer rates differ in races] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100213225528/http://badgerherald.com/news/2007/10/24/breast_cancer_rates_.php |date=2010-02-13 }}'' by Amanda Villa
Wednesday, October 24, 2007. Badger Herald</ref>

Krieger writes that given growing appreciation of how race is a social, not biological, construct, some epidemiologists are proposing that studies omit data on "race" and instead collect better socioeconomic data. Krieger writes that this suggestion ignores a growing body of evidence on how noneconomic as well as economic aspects of racial discrimination are embodied and harm health across the lifecourse.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Krieger N | s2cid = 45756159 | title = Refiguring "race": epidemiology, racialized biology, and biological expressions of race relations | journal = International Journal of Health Services | volume = 30 | issue = 1 | pages = 211–6 | year = 2000 | pmid = 10707306 | doi = 10.2190/672J-1PPF-K6QT-9N7U }}</ref> [[Gilbert C. Gee]]'s study ''A Multilevel Analysis of the Relationship Between Institutional and Individual Racial Discrimination and Health Status'' found that individual (self-perceived) and institutional (segregation and [[redlining]]) racial discrimination is associated with poor health status among members of an ethnic group.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Gee GC | title = A multilevel analysis of the relationship between institutional and individual racial discrimination and health status | journal = American Journal of Public Health | volume = 92 | issue = 4 | pages = 615–23 | date = April 2002 | pmid = 11919062 | pmc = 1447127 | doi = 10.2105/AJPH.92.4.615 }}</ref>

In the 2020 covid pandemic, a disproportionate rate in the amount of covid deaths in the African American communities compared to other racial groups has been demonstrated in some part of the United States. Many cases such as covid and AIDs has led more African Americans to lose trust in healthcare intuitions and the government that is supposed to protect their rights.  Milwaukee County is just one of many examples of such communities that were hit hard by covid. African American represented three fourths of covid deaths. This has been a common factor for many parts of the countries major populated cities that have has high percentage of African Americans.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Wells|first=Lindsay|title=A Legacy of Mistrust: African Americans and the US Healthcare System|url=https://proceedings.med.ucla.edu/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/Wells-A200421LW-rko-Wells-Lindsay-M.D.-BLM-formatted.pdf|access-date=2021-12-10|archive-date=2021-12-10|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211210011953/https://proceedings.med.ucla.edu/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/Wells-A200421LW-rko-Wells-Lindsay-M.D.-BLM-formatted.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Race-Based Diagnoses ===
[[Race (human categorization)|Racial groups]], especially [[minority group]]s, are frequently exposed to different types of barriers when in need of medical treatment. The [[World Health Organization]] identifies some of these barriers, including unequal access to health services, lack of [[cultural sensitivity]], differing quality of services, timeliness of access to such services, and general [[Health equity|discrimination in healthcare]] systems.<ref>{{Cite web |last=World Health Organization |date=August 2001 |title=WHO's Contribution to the World Conference Against Racism, Racial Discrimination, Xenophobia and Related Intolerance |url=http://apps.who.int/iris/bitstream/handle/10665/66891/WHO_SDE_HDE_HHR_01.2.pdf;jsessionid=354408353DCE8B94047C97433E72FB01?sequence=1 |access-date=2022-02-24}}</ref> Certain racial groups can receive different courses of treatment, diagnoses, and [[Prescription drug|prescription medications]] than those that self-identify as other races.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Pharmacogenetics, personalized medicine, and race {{!}} Learn Science at Scitable |url=http://www.nature.com/scitable/topicpage/pharmacogenetics-personalized-medicine-and-race-744 |access-date=2022-02-24 |website=www.nature.com |language=en |archive-date=2024-07-12 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240712165312/https://www.nature.com/scitable/topicpage/pharmacogenetics-personalized-medicine-and-race-744/ |url-status=live }}</ref> These differences can be commonly linked to correction factors in [[medical calculator]]s, [[algorithm]]s that are unable to account for variables rooted in social disparities, and [[drug]]s designed for specific racial populations. [[BiDil]] is a drug used to treat congestive [[heart failure]] in [[black people]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=BiDil (isosorbide dinitrate/hydralazine HCl) Heart Failure Medication |url=https://www.bidil.com/ |access-date=2022-02-24 |website=www.bidil.com |archive-date=2022-02-24 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220224061132/https://www.bidil.com/ |url-status=live }}</ref> The [[Food and Drug Administration]] initially rejected applications of the medication since their clinical trials did not demonstrate any efficacy for a general racial population within the [[United States]], except for [[African Americans]].<ref name=":02">{{Cite journal |last1=Sankar |first1=Pamela |last2=Kahn |first2=Jonathan |date=2005-01-01 |title=BiDil: Race Medicine Or Race Marketing? |url=https://www.healthaffairs.org/doi/10.1377/hlthaff.W5.455 |journal=Health Affairs |volume=24 |issue=Suppl1 |pages=W5–455 |doi=10.1377/hlthaff.W5.455 |pmid=16219647 |issn=0278-2715 |access-date=2022-03-01 |archive-date=2024-07-12 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240712165241/https://www.healthaffairs.org/doi/10.1377/hlthaff.W5.455 |url-status=live |url-access=subscription }}</ref> BiDil's manufacturer, NitroMed, then completed a clinical trial that solely enrolled African Americans. They found a decrease in mortality for this exclusive group and in 2005, the FDA approved the drug's usage exclusively for black patients.<ref name=":02" /> It is currently still in use with the same stipulation.

BiDil has been considered to be a "race drug"<ref name=":17">{{Cite journal |last=Krimsky |first=Sheldon |date=2012-01-14 |title=The short life of a race drug |journal=The Lancet |language=English |volume=379 |issue=9811 |pages=114–115 |doi=10.1016/S0140-6736(12)60052-X |issn=0140-6736 |pmid=22256352|s2cid=30592769 |doi-access=free }}</ref> by some in the medical community. Backlash stems from a debate on whether race can be a reliable factor in making diagnoses and prescriptions. Those that oppose its usage believe its prescription process to be unscientific. With respect to BiDil's racialization, [[Sheldon Krimsky]] wrote, "'self-identified race' is a subjective term, influenced by cultural factors, and not even grounded in the ancestral [[genomics]]."<ref name=":17" />

Ziad Obermeyer M.D., et al. found that a specific algorithm, which determines what patients need further care, favors additional medical attention towards [[white people]] over black people.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Obermeyer |first1=Ziad |last2=Powers |first2=Brian |last3=Vogeli |first3=Christine |last4=Mullainathan |first4=Sendhil |date=2019-10-25 |title=Dissecting racial bias in an algorithm used to manage the health of populations |journal=Science |volume=366 |issue=6464 |pages=447–453 |language=EN |doi=10.1126/science.aax2342|pmid=31649194 |bibcode=2019Sci...366..447O |s2cid=204881868 |doi-access=free }}</ref> This analysis was based on data concerning average [[health costs]] that are incurred by these specific races. The same article puts forward the claim, "Bias occurs because the algorithm uses health costs as a proxy for health needs," as African Americans have been found to face disproportionate poverty levels in the United States and are forced to spend less on [[Health care in the United States|healthcare]] than white patients.<ref>{{Cite web |publisher=United States Census Bureau |title=Inequalities Persist Despite Decline in Poverty For All Major Race and Hispanic Origin Groups |url=https://www.census.gov/library/stories/2020/09/poverty-rates-for-blacks-and-hispanics-reached-historic-lows-in-2019.html |access-date=2022-02-24 |website=Census.gov |archive-date=2020-09-17 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200917070757/https://www.census.gov/library/stories/2020/09/poverty-rates-for-blacks-and-hispanics-reached-historic-lows-in-2019.html |url-status=live }}</ref> This bias caused the algorithm to find that black patients are generally healthier than white patients and a conclusion was created by the algorithm that black patients do not need extra care in such instances.

Estimated [[glomerular filtration rate]] (eGFR) is a scored measurement of a patient's [[kidney]] function. Once measured, healthcare providers can utilize the test score to determine the quality of kidneys' filtering ability in a given patient. According to a study by Dr. Darshali Vyas, et al., the equation for eGFR reports a higher score for black patients by a factor of 1.210,<ref name=":23">{{Cite journal |last1=Vyas |first1=Darshali A. |last2=Eisenstein |first2=Leo G. |last3=Jones |first3=David S. |date=2020-06-17 |title=Hidden in Plain Sight — Reconsidering the Use of Race Correction in Clinical Algorithms |journal=New England Journal of Medicine |volume=383 |issue=9 |pages=874–882 |language=en |doi=10.1056/NEJMms2004740|pmid=32853499 |s2cid=221359557 |doi-access=free }}</ref> which the study's authors doubt the validity of. The algorithm's developers backed the results, citing that black people have higher [[creatinine]] levels, which can be a [[Confounding|lurking variable]] in eGFR calculations. Vyas makes a rebuttal to this idea, stating, "Explanations that have been given for this finding include the notion that black people release more creatinine into their blood at baseline, in part because they are reportedly more muscular." In reality, this [[generalization]] may not be the case and can be harmful to minorities that encounter such correction factors.

Similarly, the [[Delivery after previous caesarean section|vaginal birth after Caesarean section]] (VBAC) medical calculator is used to estimate the probability that a patient will successfully complete a [[Vaginal delivery|vaginal birth]] if they have already had a birth via [[Caesarean section]]. There are correction factors based on race that have been commonly used in this calculator; self-reported African American patients' results are multiplied by a factor of 0.671.<ref name=":23" /> The VBAC calculator is in the process of being altered by the Maternal-Fetal Medicine Units Network, as of December 2021, to omit race and ethnicity in the interest of ignoring such "[[Social constructionism|socially constructed]] variables"<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Grobman |first1=William A. |last2=Sandoval |first2=Grecio |last3=Rice |first3=Madeline Murguia |last4=Bailit |first4=Jennifer L. |last5=Chauhan |first5=Suneet P. |last6=Costantine |first6=Maged M. |last7=Gyamfi-Bannerman |first7=Cynthia |last8=Metz |first8=Torri D. |last9=Parry |first9=Samuel |last10=Rouse |first10=Dwight J. |last11=Saade |first11=George R. |date=2021-12-01 |title=Prediction of vaginal birth after cesarean delivery in term gestations: a calculator without race and ethnicity |url=https://www.ajog.org/article/S0002-9378(21)00587-1/abstract |journal=American Journal of Obstetrics & Gynecology |language=English |volume=225 |issue=6 |pages=664.e1–664.e7 |doi=10.1016/j.ajog.2021.05.021 |issn=0002-9378 |pmid=34043983 |pmc=8611105 |access-date=2022-03-01 |archive-date=2024-07-12 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240712165240/https://www.ajog.org/article/S0002-9378(21)00587-1/abstract |url-status=live }}</ref> that may be inaccurate.

=== Mental health ===
Stress can be derived from many individualistic factors or experiences, has multiple effects on health.  Stress is also associated with chronic diseases. Stress that is derived from racism has specific contextual factors, which adds a daily burden to African-Americans and other demographic groups that are discriminated against. These demographic groups do not often realize that these stressors may be contributing to the state of their mental health.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.apa.org/pi/oema/resources/ethnicity-health/racism-stress.aspx|title=Physiological & Psychological Impact of Racism and Discrimination for African-Americans|website=American Psychological Association|access-date=9 November 2018}}</ref> Groups of people are also affected in ways that may not be outward acts of racism by another person, but through education, economics, the justice system, and largely through law enforcement. It is also possible that people who hold racist ideals have mental health problems as well, such as self-centeredness, inability to empathize, and paranoia over groups of people they are discriminating against. Individuals can develop complexes about ethnic groups and races, automatically displaying emotions without learning about the people themselves, and will cut off all friendliness to them.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/blog/the-pacific-heart/201708/after-charlottesville-is-racism-mental-illness|title=After Charlottesville: Is Racism a Mental Illness?| vauthors = Chandra R |website= Psychology Today|access-date=9 November 2018}}</ref>

There are many [[Obstacles to receiving mental health services among African American youth|barriers]] that exist in the relationship for African Americans accessing mental health services. These barriers can range from family dynamics, institutional racism, socioeconomic status, and a host of other reasons.  This is particularly true for African Americans in need of mental health services who could benefit from effective treatment. "Effective treatment exists for many mental disorders, an indicator of need for mental health services (MHS), receive any treatment. This underutilization is more pronounced among African Americans than Non Hispanic whites (Villatoro & Aneshensel, 2014).<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Villatoro AP, Aneshensel CS | title = Family Influences on the Use of Mental Health Services among African Americans | journal = Journal of Health and Social Behavior | volume = 55 | issue = 2 | pages = 161–180 | date = June 2014 | pmid = 24872466 | pmc = 4395552 | doi = 10.1177/0022146514533348 }}</ref> There is something to be said about the lack of utilization of mental health services amongst African Americans. There are several possible explanations for the state of mental health use in African American communities. While many African Americans do not receive mental health services, those who do receive services are negatively impacted by the institutional bias that exists between them and non-black counselors. In a study of 47 clinicians and 129 African Americans who sought therapy, researchers found that African Americans tend to have a healthy cultural paranoia about their non-black therapists. Interviews with them found Black patients simultaneously engaged in and ''scanned'' the encounter for feelings of comfort; safety in disclosing personal information; being trustful of the provider; and being listened to, understood, and respected by the provider. For some patients, judgments about the initial encounter seem to have less to do with clinical expertise or experience of the provider and more with perceptions of empathy and the quality of the interpersonal connection between the two individuals (Earl, Alegría, Mendieta, & Diaz Linhart, 2011<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Earl TR, Alegría M, Mendieta F, Linhart YD | title = "Just be straight with me:" an exploration of Black patient experiences in initial mental health encounters | journal = The American Journal of Orthopsychiatry | volume = 81 | issue = 4 | pages = 519–25 | date = October 2011 | pmid = 21977937 | pmc = 3220950 | doi = 10.1111/j.1939-0025.2011.01123.x }}</ref>). In order to improve the outcomes of therapy for African Americans, it is imperative that non-black therapists are culturally competent. Increasing cultural competence of mental health clinicians will help foster an empathetic relationship between clinicians and their clients.

In addition, the social environment in which African Americans live in plays a role in their mental health. Ecological approaches that aim to systematically modify how the world interacts with blackness, life experiences that African Americans perceive as stressful, depression, and perceived racial discrimination may have the greatest impact on mental health in African Americans and may lead to additional improvements in the holistic well-being of African Americans.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Mama SK, Li Y, Basen-Engquist K, Lee RE, Thompson D, Wetter DW, Nguyen NT, Reitzel LR, McNeill LH | title = Psychosocial Mechanisms Linking the Social Environment to Mental Health in African Americans | journal = PLOS ONE | volume = 11 | issue = 4 | article-number = e0154035 | date = 2016-04-27 | pmid = 27119366 | pmc = 4847864 | doi = 10.1371/journal.pone.0154035 | bibcode = 2016PLoSO..1154035M | doi-access = free }}</ref>

African American millennial's mental health has also raised concerns due to the lack of being able to find employment. African American males between the age of twenty and twenty-four were studied and were found to experience unemployment at almost double the rate of their white peers. Mental issues are presented in the form of addictions such alcohol and smoking. Conditions of depression have reported as well. Societal pressure of gender norm is one factor that leads to mental health issues for African American males.<ref>{{Cite web|date=August 2018|title=Black Male Millennial Unemployment and Mental Health|url=https://www.apa.org/advocacy/health-disparities/black-male-unemployment.pdf|access-date=2021-12-10|archive-date=2021-12-10|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211210023604/https://www.apa.org/advocacy/health-disparities/black-male-unemployment.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Maternal and child health ===
{{Main|Black maternal mortality in the United States|Race and maternal health in the United States}}

[[File:Tamara W. talks about being ignored as a Black mother.ogg|thumb|Tamara speaks about feeling "ignored" as a Black mother in the United States in 2019.]]
African American women are three to four times more likely to die in childbirth than white women, while their babies are twice as likely to die than white babies, even when controlled for many factors such as education, income, and health. Danyelle Solomon argues that "White racism" is the highest cause of unrest in communities, pushing them further apart, and causing more black women and infants to die because of it.<ref name="americanprogress.org">{{cite web|url=https://www.americanprogress.org/issues/race/reports/2018/04/18/449774/racism-evergreen-toxin-killing-black-mothers-infants/|title=Racism: The Evergreen Toxin Killing Black Mothers and Infants|vauthors=Solomon D|website=Center for American Progress|date=18 April 2018|access-date=9 November 2018|archive-date=9 November 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181109112033/https://www.americanprogress.org/issues/race/reports/2018/04/18/449774/racism-evergreen-toxin-killing-black-mothers-infants/|url-status=live}}</ref> Racism affects several components of a black woman's life in regards to being able to give birth or currently carrying. Racism found in the delivery of health care and social service means black women often receive substandard care in comparison to white women.<ref name="ReferenceA">{{Cite web|last1=Taylor|first1=Jamila|last2=Novoa|first2=Cristina|last3=Hamm|first3=Katie|last4=Phadke|first4=Shilpa|title=Eliminating Racial Disparities in Maternal and Infant Mortality|url=https://www.americanprogress.org/issues/women/reports/2019/05/02/469186/eliminating-racial-disparities-maternal-infant-mortality/|access-date=2021-04-24|website=Center for American Progress|date=2 May 2019|language=en-US|archive-date=2021-04-24|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210424005845/https://www.americanprogress.org/issues/women/reports/2019/05/02/469186/eliminating-racial-disparities-maternal-infant-mortality/|url-status=live}}</ref> As well, denial of care to black women that seek help when enduring pain, or that health care and social service providers fail to treat them with dignity and respect when it comes to their wellbeing.<ref name="ReferenceA"/> African American women face greater chances than white women to have chronic stress which can stem from living in impoverished neighborhoods or encountering discrimination. These embedded stressors as a result of societal inequities and prejudice could largely explain the underlying health disparities in negative birth outcomes. Although studies examining the effects of prenatal stress are limited, for a few reasons, evidence does support the consequences of high levels of stress or anxiety.<ref name=":15">{{Cite web|last=Poggi|first=E.|date=May 3, 2006|title=Prenatal Exposure to Stress and Stress Hormones Influences Child Development|url=https://www.du.edu/neurodevelopment/media/documents/prenatalstress_development.pdf|access-date=March 17, 2021|website=University of Denver|archive-date=July 9, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200709181747/https://www.du.edu/neurodevelopment/media/documents/prenatalstress_development.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref> Women are said to bear low birth weight or preterm infants from elevated stress or anxiety, and even more so with a lack of social support.<ref name=":15" /> In the aftermath, newborns become predisposed to issues, such poor physical development, from the mother's stress during pregnancy. With that being said, stress from racism not only affects mental and physical wellbeing, but disproportionately place black infants at a disadvantage for future attainment.

Black women in the United States are three to four times more likely to die during childbirth and two to three times more likely to experience severe pregnancy-related illnesses, than white women.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hailu |first1=Elleni M. |last2=Maddali |first2=Sai Ramya |last3=Snowden |first3=Jonathan M. |last4=Carmichael |first4=Suzan L. |last5=Mujahid |first5=Mahasin S. |date=November 2022 |title=Structural racism and adverse maternal health outcomes: A systematic review |journal=Health & Place |volume=78 |article-number=102923 |doi=10.1016/j.healthplace.2022.102923 |issn=1873-2054 |pmc=11216026 |pmid=36401939}}</ref> Research shows that these disparities persist regardless of education level or socioeconomic status; for example, a Black women with a college degree remains at higher risk of pregnancy complications than a White woman without a high school diploma.<ref name=":24">{{Cite journal |last1=Dayo |first1=Elizabeth |last2=Christy |first2=Kayonne |last3=Habte |first3=Ruth |date=2023-01-01 |title=Health in colour: black women, racism, and maternal health |journal=The Lancet Regional Health - Americas |language=English |volume=17 |article-number=100408 |doi=10.1016/j.lana.2022.100408 |pmid=36531129 |issn=2667-193X|pmc=9735204 }}</ref> Scholars and health experts cite the United States' history of racism and discrimination as major factors influencing maternal health disparities.<ref name=":24" /> Maternal health advocates support the expansion of Medicaid benefits, as 65% of Black mothers in the U.S. rely on Medicaid for coverage.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-05-12 |title=Solving the Black Maternal Health Crisis {{!}} Johns Hopkins {{!}} Bloomberg School of Public Health |url=https://publichealth.jhu.edu/2023/solving-the-black-maternal-health-crisis |access-date=2025-07-30 |website=publichealth.jhu.edu |language=en}}</ref> Recent studies indicate that policies restricting reproductive health care, such as those following the Supreme Court's ''Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization'' decision, are likely to worsen maternal mortality overall, with disproportionate effects on Black Women <ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-05-29 |title=Clear and Growing Evidence That Dobbs Is Harming Reproductive Health and Freedom {{!}} Guttmacher Institute |url=https://www.guttmacher.org/2024/05/clear-and-growing-evidence-dobbs-harming-reproductive-health-and-freedom |access-date=2025-07-30 |website=www.guttmacher.org |language=en}}</ref>''.''

Racism in education has decreased significantly over the past century, however this does not help increase the income for black people, and increased incomes do not provide better health opportunities, especially for mothers and infants.<ref name="americanprogress.org" /> Higher education and income levels for black mothers does not affect this mortality rate. There are also higher chances that a complication will occur during birth. Solomon argues that the 'toxin' of these rates is racism, which has created a toxic environment for minority groups to live in with multiple stressors that effect health.<ref name="americanprogress.org" />

In 2012, a study was conducted on early pregnancy women which followed their children from birth to 5 years old to determine the risk factors of obesity among low-income black children.<ref name = "Janjua_2012">{{cite journal | vauthors = Janjua NZ, Mahmood B, Islam MA, Goldenberg RL | title = Maternal and Early Childhood Risk Factors for Overweight and Obesity among Low-Income Predominantly Black Children at Age Five Years: A Prospective Cohort Study | journal = Journal of Obesity | volume = 2012 | article-number = 457173 | date = 2012 | pmid = 23056928 | doi = 10.1155/2012/457173 | pmc = 3465910 | doi-access = free }}</ref> However, the study showed that children of overweight and obese mothers are more than likely to become obese or overweight by the age of 5.<ref name = "Janjua_2012" /> According to the ''U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office of Minority,'' African American women have the highest rates of obesity or being overweight compared to any other groups in the United States.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Obesity and African Americans - The Office of Minority Health|url=http://minorityhealth.hhs.gov/omh/browse.aspx?lvl=4&lvlid=25|access-date=2021-03-04|website=www.minorityhealth.hhs.gov|archive-date=2021-02-27|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210227211104/https://minorityhealth.hhs.gov/omh/browse.aspx?lvl=4&lvlid=25|url-status=live}}</ref>

===Cardiovascular disease===
{{See also|Cardiovascular disease}}
Research has explored the effect of encounters with racism or discrimination on physiological activity.  Most of the research has focused on traits that cause exaggerated responses, such as neuroticism, strong racial identification, or hostility.<ref name="pmid12554577">{{cite journal | vauthors = Harrell JP, Hall S, Taliaferro J | title = Physiological responses to racism and discrimination: an assessment of the evidence | journal = American Journal of Public Health | volume = 93 | issue = 2 | pages = 243–8 | date = February 2003 | pmid = 12554577 | pmc = 1447724 | doi = 10.2105/AJPH.93.2.243 }}</ref>  Several studies suggest that [[high blood pressure|higher blood pressure]] levels are associated with a tendency not to remember or report racist and discriminatory incidents.<ref name="pmid12554577" /> Personal experiences of racist behaviors increase stress and blood pressure.<ref name="pmid12554577" />

Although the relationship racism and health is unclear and findings have been inconsistent, three likely mechanisms for cardiovascular damage have been identified:<ref name="pmid12811228">{{cite journal | vauthors = Wyatt SB, Williams DR, Calvin R, Henderson FC, Walker ER, Winters K | s2cid = 6145121 | title = Racism and cardiovascular disease in African Americans | journal = The American Journal of the Medical Sciences | volume = 325 | issue = 6 | pages = 315–31 | date = June 2003 | pmid = 12811228 | doi = 10.1097/00000441-200306000-00003 }}</ref>
* [[Institutional racism]] leads to limited opportunities for socioeconomic mobility, differential access to goods and resources, and poor living conditions.
* Personal experiences of racism acts as a [[stressor]] and can induce psychophysiological reactions that negatively affect cardiovascular health.
* Negative self-evaluations and accepting negative cultural stereotypes as true ([[internalized racism]]) can harm cardiovascular health.

According to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office of Minority Health, in 2018, African Americans were 30% more likely to die from heart disease than non-Hispanic whites.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Heart Disease and African Americans - The Office of Minority Health|url=http://minorityhealth.hhs.gov/omh/browse.aspx?lvl=4&lvlid=19|access-date=2021-03-04|website=www.minorityhealth.hhs.gov|archive-date=2021-03-04|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210304171920/https://minorityhealth.hhs.gov/omh/browse.aspx?lvl=4&lvlid=19|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Alzheimer's disease ===
{{See also|Alzheimer's disease in African Americans}}
[[Alzheimer's disease]] (AD) is a progressive, irreversible neurodegenerative disease and it is the leading cause of dementia.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.alz.org/alzheimers-dementia/what-is-alzheimers|title=What is Alzheimer's Disease?
