<!-- Note: All citations are listed in the article body, as per [[WP:LEADCITE]]; indicate with in-line {{citation needed|date=October 2017}} if in doubt. -->
'''Singapore''',{{efn|{{IPAc-en|audio=En-us-Singapore.ogg|ˈ|s|ɪ|ŋ|(|g|)|ə|p|ɔːr}} {{respell|SING|(g)ə|por}}}} officially the '''Republic of Singapore''', is an [[island country]] and [[city-state]] in [[Southeast Asia]]. Its territory comprises a [[Singapore (island)|main island]], [[List of islands of Singapore|over 60 satellite islands and islets]], and [[Pedra Branca, Singapore|one outlying islet]]. The country is about one [[degree of latitude]] ({{Convert|137|km|disp=or}}) north of the [[equator]], off the southern tip of the [[Malay Peninsula]], bordering the [[Strait of Malacca]] to the west, the [[Singapore Strait]] to the south along with the [[Riau Islands]] in [[Indonesia]], the [[South China Sea]] to the east and the [[Straits of Johor]] along with the [[Johor|State of Johor]] in [[Malaysia]] to the north.

In [[Early history of Singapore|its early history]], Singapore was a maritime [[Emporium (antiquity)|emporium]] known as ''[[Temasek]]''; subsequently, it was a major constituent of several successive [[thalassocratic]] empires. Its contemporary era began in 1819, when [[Stamford Raffles]] established Singapore as an [[entrepôt|entrepôt trading post]] of the [[British Empire]]. In 1867, Singapore came under direct British control as part of the [[Straits Settlements]]. During [[World War II]], Singapore was [[Japanese occupation of Singapore|occupied by Japan]] in 1942 and returned to Britain as a [[Colony of Singapore|Crown colony]] following [[Surrender of Japan|Japan's surrender]] in 1945. Singapore gained [[Self-governance of Singapore|self-governance]] in 1959 and in [[Malaysia Agreement|1963]] became part of the new federation of [[Malaysia]], alongside [[Federation of Malaya|Malaya]], [[Crown Colony of North Borneo|North Borneo]] and [[Crown Colony of Sarawak|Sarawak]]. [[State of Singapore (Malaysia)|Ideological differences]] led to Singapore's expulsion from the federation two years later; it became an independent [[Sovereign state|sovereign country]] in 1965. After early years of [[History of the Republic of Singapore#1965 to Late 1970s|turbulence]] and despite lacking natural resources and a [[hinterland]], the nation rapidly developed to become one of the [[Four Asian Tigers]].

As a highly [[developed country]], Singapore has the [[List of countries by GDP (PPP) per capita|highest PPP-adjusted GDP per capita]] in the world and is the only country in Asia with an AAA [[Credit rating#Sovereign credit ratings|sovereign credit rating]] from [[Big Three (credit rating agencies)|all major rating agencies]]. Identified as a [[tax haven]], it is a major [[Airline hub|aviation]], [[Financial centre|financial]] and [[Port|maritime shipping]] hub and has consistently been ranked as one of the [[List of most expensive cities for expatriate employees|most expensive cities]] for [[expatriate]]s and [[foreign worker]]s. Singapore ranks highly in key social indicators: [[Education in Singapore|education]], [[Healthcare in Singapore|healthcare]], [[public housing in Singapore|housing]], [[Global Peace Index|peacefulness]], [[Henley Passport Index|passport strength]], [[Crime in Singapore|personal safety]] and [[infrastructure]], with a high [[List of countries by home ownership rate|home-ownership rate]]. [[Singaporeans]] enjoy one of the [[List of countries by life expectancy|longest life expectancies]], [[List of countries by Internet connection speeds|fastest Internet connection speeds]], [[List of countries by infant and under-five mortality rates|lowest infant mortality rates]] and [[Corruption Perceptions Index|lowest levels of corruption]] in the world. Singapore is [[Administrative divisions of Singapore|organised]] into five [[Regions of Singapore|regions]], 55 [[Planning areas of Singapore|planning areas]] and hundreds of [[Subzones of Singapore|subzones]]. It has the [[List of countries and dependencies by population density|second highest population density of any country]], although there are numerous green and recreational spaces as a result of [[urban planning]]. With a multicultural population and in recognition of the cultural identities of the country's major ethnic groups, Singapore has four [[Languages of Singapore|official languages]]: [[Singaporean English|English]], [[Malay language|Malay]], [[Singaporean Mandarin|Mandarin]] and [[Tamil language|Tamil]]. English is the [[lingua franca|common language]], with exclusive use in numerous [[public service]]s. [[multiculturalism|Multi-racialism]] is enshrined in the constitution and continues to shape [[Race in Singapore|national policies]].

Singapore is a [[parliamentary republic]] and its legal system is based on [[common law]]. While it is [[Constitution of Singapore|constitutionally]] a [[List of political parties in Singapore|multi-party democracy]] where [[Elections in Singapore|free elections]] are regularly held, it functions as a ''[[de facto]]'' [[one-party dominant state]], with the [[People's Action Party]] (PAP) maintaining continuous political dominance since [[1959 Singaporean general election|1959]]. The PAP's longstanding control has resulted in limited [[Pluralism (political theory)|political pluralism]] and a highly centralised governance structure over national institutions. One of the five founding members of [[ASEAN]], Singapore is also the headquarters of the [[Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation]] Secretariat, the [[Pacific Economic Cooperation Council]] Secretariat and is the host city of many [[MICE (Meetings, Incentives, Conferences, Exhibitions) tourism|international conferences and events]]. Singapore is also a member of the [[United Nations]], the [[World Trade Organization]], the [[East Asia Summit]], the [[Non-Aligned Movement]] and the [[Commonwealth of Nations]].

== Name and etymology ==
{{Main|Names of Singapore}}

The [[English language|English]] name of "Singapore" is an [[anglicisation]] of the native [[Malay language|Malay]] name for the country, {{lang|ms|Singapura}} ({{IPA|ms|siŋapura|audio|LL-Q9237 (msa)-Noaius Paticus-Singapura.wav}}), which was in turn derived from the [[Sanskrit]] word for 'lion city' ({{langx|sa|सिंहपुर}}; <small>[[International Alphabet of Sanskrit Transliteration|romanised:]]</small> {{lang|sa-Latn|Siṃhapura}}; [[Brahmi script|Brahmi]]: {{lang|sa-Brah|𑀲𑀺𑀁𑀳𑀧𑀼𑀭}}; literally "lion city"; {{wikt-lang|sa|सिंह|siṃha|script=Latn}} means 'lion', {{wikt-lang|sa|पुर|pura|script-Latn}} means 'city' or 'fortress').<ref>{{cite web |title=Singapore |url=http://www.bartleby.com/61/46/S0424600.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20010411060419/http://www.bartleby.com/61/46/S0424600.html |archive-date=11 April 2001 |access-date=13 May 2020 |publisher=Bartleby}}</ref> ''Pulau Ujong'' was one of the earliest names for the island of Singapore, which corresponds to a Chinese account from the third century referred to a place as ''[[Pulau Ujong|Pú Luó Zhōng]]'' ({{lang-zh|c=[[wikt:蒲|蒲]] [[wikt:羅|羅]] [[wikt:中|中]]}}), a transcription of the Malay name for 'island at the end of [[Malay Peninsula|a peninsula]]'.<ref>{{cite web |title=Singapore: History, Singapore 1994 |url=http://inic.utexas.edu/asnic/countries/singapore/Singapore-History.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070323095958/http://inic.utexas.edu/asnic/countries/Singapore/Singapore-History.html |archive-date=23 March 2007 |access-date=13 May 2020 |publisher=Asian Studies @ University of Texas at Austin}}</ref> Early references to the name ''[[Temasek]]'' (or ''Tumasik'') are found in the [[Nagarakretagama]], a [[Java (island)|Javanese]] [[eulogy]] written in 1365, and a [[Vietnam]]ese source from the same time period. The name possibly means ''Sea Town'', being derived from the Malay {{lang|ms|tasek}}, meaning 'sea' or 'lake'.<ref name="Brenda Yeoh-2013">{{cite book |author1=Victor R Savage |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=DTOJAAAAQBAJ&pg=PA381 |title=Singapore Street Names: A Study of Toponymics |author2=Brenda Yeoh |date=15 June 2013 |publisher=Marshall Cavendish |isbn=9789814484749 |page=381 |access-date=28 July 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230412012131/https://books.google.com/books?id=DTOJAAAAQBAJ&pg=PA381 |archive-date=12 April 2023 |url-status=live}}</ref> The [[Chinese people|Chinese]] traveller [[Wang Dayuan]] visited a place around 1330 named ''Danmaxi'' ({{lang-zh|c=淡馬錫|p= Dànmǎxí|w=Tan Ma Hsi}}) or ''Tam ma siak'', depending on pronunciation; this may be a transcription of ''Temasek'', alternatively, it may be a combination of the Malay {{lang|ms|Tanah}} meaning 'land' and [[Chinese language|Chinese]] {{lang|zh-Latn|xi}} meaning '[[tin]]', which was traded on the island.<ref>{{cite book |author=John N. Miksic |author1-link=John N. Miksic |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=bMt3BgAAQBAJ&pg=PA173 |title=Singapore and the Silk Road of the Sea, 1300–1800 |date=15 November 2013 |publisher=NUS Press |isbn=978-9971695743 |pages=171–182 |access-date=19 June 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240305143007/https://books.google.com/books?id=bMt3BgAAQBAJ&pg=PA173#v=onepage&q&f=false |archive-date=5 March 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Brenda Yeoh-2013" />

Variations of the name {{lang|sa-Latn|Siṃhapura}} were used for a number of cities throughout the region prior to the establishment of the [[Kingdom of Singapura]]. In [[Buddhism and Hinduism|Hindu–Buddhist culture]], lions were associated with power and protection, which may explain the attraction of such a name.{{sfn |Miksic |2013 |pp=[https://books.google.com/books?id=bMt3BgAAQBAJ&pg=PA151 151–152]}}<ref>{{cite news |author=Joshua Lee |date=6 December 2016 |title=5 other places in Asia which are also called Singapura |url=https://mothership.sg/2016/12/5-other-places-in-asia-which-are-also-called-singapura/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230406022412/https://mothership.sg/2016/12/5-other-places-in-asia-which-are-also-called-singapura/ |archive-date=6 April 2023 |access-date=13 May 2020 |work=Mothership}}</ref> The name ''Singapura'' supplanted ''[[Temasek]]'' sometime before the 15th century, after the establishment of the Kingdom of Singapura on the island by a fleeing Sumatran ''[[Raja]]'' (prince) from [[Palembang]]. However, the precise time and reason for the name change is unknown. The semi-historical [[Malay Annals]] state that Temasek was christened ''Singapura'' by [[Sang Nila Utama]], a 13th-century Sumatran ''Raja'' from Palembang. The Annals state that Sang Nila Utama encountered a strange beast on the island that he took to be a lion. Seeing this as an omen, he established the town of ''Singapura'' where he encountered the beast.<ref>{{cite book |url=https://archive.org/details/sejarah-melayu-cheah-boon-kheng/page/n1/mode/2up?q= |title=Sejarah Melayu The Malay Annals MS RAFFLES No. 18 Edisi Rumi Baru/New Romanised Edition |date=1998 |publisher=Academic Art & Printing Services Sdn. Bhd. |isbn=967-9948-13-7 |editor-last1=Kheng |editor-first1=Cheah Boon |editor-last2=Ismail |editor-first2=Abdul Rahman Haji}}</ref>{{Rp|37, 88–92}}<ref>{{cite journal |last=Brown |first=C.C. |date=October 1952 |title=The Malay Annals translated from Raffles MS 18 |url=https://archive.org/details/malay-annals-C.-C.-Brown/page/n1/mode/2up?q= |journal=Journal of the Malayan Branch of the Royal Asiatic Society |volume=25 |issue=2&3 |pages=1–276}}</ref>{{Rp|30–31}} The second hypothesis, drawn from [[Tomé Pires#The Suma Oriental|Portuguese sources]], postulates that this mythical story is based on the real life [[Parameswara (king)|Parameswara]] of Palembang. Parameswara declared independence from [[Majapahit]] and mounted a Lion Throne. After then being driven into exile by the [[Javanese people|Javanese]], he usurped control over ''Temasek''. He may have rechristened the area as ''Singapura'', recalling the throne he had been driven from.<ref name="Turnbull-2009">{{cite book |last=Turnbull |first=C.M. |author-link=C. M. Turnbull |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Y9yvBgAAQBAJ&pg=PA22 |title=A History of Modern Singapore, 1819–2005 |publisher=NUS Press |year=2009 |isbn=978-9971-69-430-2 |pages=21–22 |access-date=13 January 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240305143058/https://books.google.com/books?id=Y9yvBgAAQBAJ&pg=PA22#v=onepage&q&f=false |archive-date=5 March 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref>

Under [[Japanese occupation of Singapore|Japanese occupation]], Singapore was renamed {{Nihongo|''Syonan-to''|[[wikt:昭|昭]] [[wikt:南|南]]|Shōnan|lead=yes}}, meaning 'light of the south'.<ref>{{cite book |last=Abshire |first=Jean |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=AHF59oExO80C&pg=PA104 |title=The History of Singapore |publisher=ABC-CLIO |year=2011 |isbn=978-0-313-37743-3 |page=104 |access-date=21 November 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240211000704/https://books.google.com/books?id=AHF59oExO80C&pg=PA104 |archive-date=11 February 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Blackburn |first1=Kevin |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=TUC2qveu-b8C&pg=PA132 |title=Did Singapore Have to Fall?: Churchill and the Impregnable Fortress |last2=Hack |first2=Karl |publisher=[[Routledge]] |year=2004 |isbn=978-0-203-40440-9 |page=132 |access-date=21 November 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240211000739/https://books.google.com/books?id=TUC2qveu-b8C&pg=PA132 |archive-date=11 February 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref> Singapore is sometimes referred to by the nickname the "Garden City", in reference to its parks and tree-lined streets.<ref>{{cite encyclopedia |title=Singapore <!-- this is a guess fixing a bollixed ref --> |encyclopedia=The New Encyclopædia Britannica |location=Chicago |date=1991 |edition=15th |page=832 |bibcode=1991neb..book.....G |isbn=978-0-85229-529-8 |quote="Singapore, known variously as the 'Lion City,' or 'Garden City,' the latter for its many parks and tree-lined streets |last1=Goetz |first1=Philip W.}}</ref> Another informal name, the "[[Little red dot|Little Red Dot]]", was adopted after an article in the ''[[The Wall Street Journal Asia|Asian Wall Street Journal]]'' of 4 August 1998 said that [[Indonesia]]n President [[B. J. Habibie]] referred to Singapore as a red dot on a map.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Glennie |first1=Charlotte |last2=Ang |first2=Mavis |last3=Rhys |first3=Gillian |last4=Aul |first4=Vidhu |last5=Walton |first5=Nicholas |date=6 August 2015 |title=50 reasons Singapore is the best city in the world |url=https://edition.cnn.com/travel/article/singapore-50-reasons |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200807045157/http://edition.cnn.com/travel/article/singapore-50-reasons |archive-date=7 August 2020 |access-date=13 May 2020 |publisher=[[CNN]] |quote="The Lion City. The Garden City. The Asian Tiger. The 'Fine' City. All venerable nicknames, and the longtime favourite is the 'Little Red Dot'"}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |date=16 July 2015 |title=A little red dot in a sea of green |url=https://www.economist.com/news/special-report/21657610-sense-vulnerability-has-made-singapore-what-it-today-can-it-now-relax-bit |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171016175357/https://www.economist.com/news/special-report/21657610-sense-vulnerability-has-made-singapore-what-it-today-can-it-now-relax-bit |archive-date=16 October 2017 |access-date=16 October 2017 |newspaper=[[The Economist]] |location=London |quote="..with a characteristic mixture of pride and paranoia, Singapore adopted 'little red dot' as a motto"}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |date=8 September 2017 |title=Editorial: The mighty red dot |url=http://www.thejakartapost.com/academia/2017/09/08/editorial-the-mighty-red-dot.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200128071756/https://www.thejakartapost.com/academia/2017/09/08/editorial-the-mighty-red-dot.html |archive-date=28 January 2020 |access-date=13 May 2020 |work=[[The Jakarta Post]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |date=20 September 2006 |title=Habibie truly admired the 'Little Red Dot' |newspaper=[[Today (Singapore newspaper)|Today]]}}.</ref>

== History ==
{{Main|History of Singapore}}

=== Ancient Singapore ===
{{Further|Early history of Singapore}}
In 1299, according to the ''[[Malay Annals]]'', the [[Kingdom of Singapura]] was founded on the island by [[Sang Nila Utama]].<ref>{{cite book |author=<!--unknown; old historical document--> |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=J9JAAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA43 |title=Malay Annals |date=1821 |page=43 |translator-last=Leyden |translator-first=John}}</ref> Although the historicity of the accounts as given in the ''Malay Annals'' is the subject of academic debates,{{sfn |Miksic |2013 |p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=bMt3BgAAQBAJ&pg=PA154 154]}} it is nevertheless known from various documents that Singapore in the 14th century, then known as ''[[Temasek]]'', was a trading port under the influence of both the [[Majapahit]] Empire and the [[Ayutthaya Kingdom|Siamese]] kingdoms,{{sfn |Miksic |2013 |pp=[https://books.google.com/books?id=bMt3BgAAQBAJ&pg=PA184 183–185]}} and was a part of the [[Indosphere]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Dixon |first1=Robert M.W. |url=https://archive.org/details/adjectiveclasses00dixo_002 |title=Adjective Classes: A Cross-linguistic Typology |last2=Alexandra |first2=Y. |publisher=Oxford University Press |year=2004 |isbn=0-19-920346-6 |page=[https://archive.org/details/adjectiveclasses00dixo_002/page/n96 74] |url-access=limited}}</ref><ref>{{Citation |last=Matisoff |first=James |title=On Megalocomparison |journal=Language |volume=66 |issue=1 |pages=106–120 |year=1990 |doi=10.2307/415281 |jstor=415281 |author-link=James Matisoff}}</ref><ref>{{Citation |last=Enfield |first=N.J. |title=Areal Linguistics and Mainland Southeast Asia |journal=Annual Review of Anthropology |volume=34 |pages=181–206 |year=2005 |url=http://pubman.mpdl.mpg.de/pubman/item/escidoc:57458/component/escidoc:57459/Enfield_2005_areal.pdf |access-date=5 August 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170816071246/http://pubman.mpdl.mpg.de/pubman/item/escidoc:57458/component/escidoc:57459/Enfield_2005_areal.pdf |archive-date=16 August 2017 |url-status=dead |doi=10.1146/annurev.anthro.34.081804.120406 |hdl=11858/00-001M-0000-0013-167B-C |hdl-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lavy |first1=Paul A. |year=2003 |title=As in Heaven, So on Earth: The Politics of Visnu Siva and Harihara Images in Preangkorian Khmer Civilisation |url=https://www.academia.edu/2635407 |url-status=live |journal=Journal of Southeast Asian Studies |publisher=Academia |volume=34 |issue=1 |pages=21–39 |doi=10.1017/S002246340300002X |issn=0022-4634 |s2cid=154819912 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210812222402/https://www.academia.edu/2635407 |archive-date=12 August 2021 |access-date=23 December 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Results of the 1995–1996 Archaeological Field Investigations at Angkor Borei, Cambodia |url=http://www.anthropology.hawaii.edu/people/faculty/stark/pdfs/AP1999%20article.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150923172419/http://www.anthropology.hawaii.edu/People/Faculty/Stark/pdfs/AP1999%20article.pdf |archive-date=23 September 2015 |access-date=5 July 2015 |publisher=University of Hawai'i-Manoa}}</ref> These Indianised kingdoms were characterised by surprising resilience, political integrity and administrative stability.<ref>Pierre-Yves Manguin, "From Funan to Sriwijaya: Cultural continuities and discontinuities in the Early Historical maritime states of Southeast Asia", in ''25 tahun kerjasama Pusat Penelitian Arkeologi dan Ecole française d'Extrême-Orient,'' Jakarta, Pusat Penelitian Arkeologi / EFEO, 2002, p. 59–82.</ref> Historical sources also indicate that around the end of the 14th century, its ruler [[Parameswara (king)|Parameswara]] was attacked by either the Majapahit or the Siamese, forcing him to move to [[Malacca]] where he founded the [[Sultanate of Malacca]].{{sfn |Miksic |2013 |pp=[https://books.google.com/books?id=bMt3BgAAQBAJ&pg=PA162 155–163]}} Archaeological evidence suggests that the main settlement on [[Fort Canning Hill]] was abandoned around this time, although a small trading settlement continued in Singapore for some time afterwards.<ref name="Turnbull-2009" /> In 1613, [[Portuguese people|Portuguese]] raiders burned down the settlement, and the island faded into obscurity for the next two centuries.<ref>{{cite book |last=Borschberg |first=P. |title=The Singapore and Melaka Straits. Violence, Security and Diplomacy in the 17th century |publisher=NUS Press |year=2010 |isbn=978-9971-69-464-7 |location=Singapore |pages=157–158}}</ref> By then, Singapore was nominally part of the [[Johor Sultanate]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Country Studies: Singapore: History |url=http://countrystudies.us/singapore/3.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060923070753/http://countrystudies.us/singapore/3.htm |archive-date=23 September 2006 |access-date=1 May 2007 |publisher=U.S. Library of Congress}}</ref> The wider maritime region and much trade was under Dutch control for the following period after the 1641 [[Dutch Malacca|Dutch conquest of Malacca]].<ref>{{cite book |url=http://countrystudies.us/singapore/ |title=Singapore: A Country Study |publisher=GPO for tus/singapore/4.htm |year=1989 |editor-last=Leitch Lepoer |editor-first=Barbara |series=Country Studies |access-date=18 February 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091015211019/http://countrystudies.us/singapore/ |archive-date=15 October 2009 |url-status=live}}</ref>

=== British colonisation ===
{{Main|Founding of modern Singapore|Singapore in the Straits Settlements}}

[[File:Letter from William Farquhar to Sultan Muhammad Kanzul Alam, the Sultan of Brunei, dated 28 November 1819.jpg|thumb|Letter from [[William Farquhar]] to Sultan Muhammad Kanzul Alam, the 21st [[List of sultans of Brunei|Sultan of Brunei]], dated 28 November 1819. In the first line, Farquhar mentions that Sultan Hussein Shah and Temenggong Abdul Rahman allowed the [[East India Company|British East India Company]] to establish a [[Factory (trading post)|factory]] in Singapore on 6 February 1819.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Nicholl |first1=Robert |title=From Buckfast to Borneo: Essays Presented to Father Robert Nicholl on the 85th Anniversary of His Birth, 27 March 1995 |last2=King |first2=Victor T. |last3=Horton |first3=A. V. H. |publisher=University of Hull |year=1995 |isbn=978-0-85958-836-2 |location=Hull, England |pages=219 |chapter=Malay sources for the history of the Sultanate of Brunei in the early nineteenth century: some letters from the reign of Sultan Muhammad Kanzul Alam (Annabel Teh Gallop) |oclc=35366675 |access-date=24 April 2022 |chapter-url=https://www.academia.edu/11507827 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240211000715/https://www.academia.edu/11507827 |archive-date=11 February 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |url=http://www.bl.uk/manuscripts/Viewer.aspx?ref=add_ms_12398_f019r |title=Farquhar Letterbook (Add MS 12398) |year=1842 |pages=39–40 |language=ms |chapter=Ini kupia surat kepada Raja Barunai |trans-chapter=This is a copy of the letter to the Raja of Brunei |access-date=24 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220424173837/http://www.bl.uk/manuscripts/Viewer.aspx?ref=add_ms_12398_f019r |archive-date=24 April 2022 |url-status=live}}</ref>]]
The British governor [[Stamford Raffles]] arrived in Singapore on 28 January 1819 and soon recognised the island as a natural choice for the new port.<ref>{{cite book |author1=Mun Cheong Yong |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ZdZo5Ui8oS4C&pg=PA3 |title=Singapore-India Relations: A Primer |author2=V. V. Bhanoji Rao |publisher=NUS Press |year=1995 |isbn=978-9971-69-195-0 |page=3 |access-date=14 September 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240211000734/https://books.google.com/books?id=ZdZo5Ui8oS4C&pg=PA3#v=onepage&q&f=false |archive-date=11 February 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref> The island was then nominally ruled by [[Abdul Rahman Muazzam Shah of Johor|Tengku Abdul Rahman]], the [[Sultan of Johor]], who was controlled by the [[Dutch Empire|Dutch]] and the [[Bugis]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Trocki |first=Carl A. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vA-CAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA73 |title=Singapore: Wealth, Power and the Culture of Control |publisher=Routledge |year=2009 |isbn=978-1-134-50243-1 |page=73 |access-date=14 September 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240211000706/https://books.google.com/books?id=vA-CAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA73#v=onepage&q&f=false |archive-date=11 February 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref> However, the [[Sultanate]] was weakened by factional division: [[Temenggong Abdul Rahman|Abdul Rahman]], the [[Temenggong of Johor]] to Tengku Abdul Rahman, as well as his officials, were loyal to the Sultan's elder brother [[Hussein Shah of Johor|Tengku Long]], who was living in [[exile]] in [[Penyengat Island]], [[Riau Islands]]. With the Temenggong's help, Raffles managed to smuggle Tengku Long back into Singapore. Raffles offered to recognise Tengku Long as the rightful Sultan of Johor, under the title of Sultan Hussein, as well as provide him with a yearly payment of $5000 and another $3000 to the Temenggong; in return, Sultan Hussein would grant the British the right to establish a trading post on Singapore.<ref>{{cite web |title=Singapore – Founding and Early Years |url=http://countrystudies.us/singapore/4.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221117143728/http://countrystudies.us/singapore/4.htm |archive-date=17 November 2022 |access-date=18 July 2006 |publisher=[[U.S. Library of Congress]]}}</ref> The [[1819 Singapore Treaty|Treaty of Singapore]] was signed on 6 February 1819.<ref>{{cite web |last=Ng |first=Jenny |date=7 February 1997 |title=1819 – The February Documents |url=http://www.mindef.gov.sg/imindef/about_us/history/overview/the_early_years/v01n02b_history.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170717065310/https://www.mindef.gov.sg/imindef/about_us/history/overview/the_early_years/v01n02b_history.html |archive-date=17 July 2017 |access-date=18 July 2006 |publisher=[[Ministry of Defence (Singapore)|Ministry of Defence]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Milestones in Singapore's Legal History |url=http://app.supremecourt.gov.sg/default.aspx?pgID=39 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070927183512/http://app.supremecourt.gov.sg/default.aspx?pgID=39 |archive-date=27 September 2007 |access-date=18 July 2006 |publisher=[[Supreme Court, Singapore]]}}</ref>

In 1824, a further treaty with the Sultan led to the entire island becoming a part of the [[British Empire]].<ref name="Ministry of Information, Communications and the Arts">{{cite web |title=Founding of Modern Singapore |url=http://app.www.sg/who/32/Founding-of-Modern-Singapore.aspx |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090508135636/http://app.www.sg/who/32/Founding-of-Modern-Singapore.aspx |archive-date=8 May 2009 |access-date=13 April 2011 |publisher=[[Ministry of Information, Communications and the Arts]]}}</ref> In 1826, Singapore became part of the [[Straits Settlements]], then under the jurisdiction of [[British India]]. Singapore became the regional capital in 1836.<ref>{{cite web |title=East & South-East Asia Titles: Straits Settlements Annual Reports (Singapore, Penang, Malacca, Labuan) 1855–1941 |url=http://www.archiveeditions.co.uk/titledetails.asp?tid=17 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120609014003/http://www.archiveeditions.co.uk/titledetails.asp?tid=17 |archive-date=9 June 2012 |access-date=31 July 2012 |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]]}}</ref> Prior to Raffles' arrival, there were only about a thousand people living on the island, mostly indigenous [[Malays (ethnic group)|Malays]] along with a handful of [[Overseas Chinese|Chinese]].<ref>{{cite web |title=The Malays |url=http://yesterday.sg/discover-more/communities-festivals/communities/the-malays/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110223000344/http://yesterday.sg/discover-more/communities-festivals/communities/the-malays/ |archive-date=23 February 2011 |access-date=28 July 2011 |publisher=National Heritage Board 2011}}</ref> By 1860 the population had swelled to over 80,000, more than half being [[Chinese Singaporeans|Chinese]].<ref name="Ministry of Information, Communications and the Arts" /> Many of these early immigrants came to work on the pepper and [[Uncaria gambir|gambier]] plantations.<ref>{{cite book |last=Sanderson |first=Reginald |url=https://archive.org/stream/cu31924023134368#page/n227/mode/2up |title=Twentieth century impressions of British Malaya: its history, people, commerce, industries, and resources |date=1907 |editor1-last=Wright |editor1-first=Arnold |pages=220–221 |editor2-last=Cartwright |editor2-first=H.A.}}</ref> In 1867, the Straits Settlements were separated from British India, coming under the direct control of [[United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland|Britain]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Singapore attains crown colony status – Singapore History |url=https://www.nlb.gov.sg/main/article-detail?cmsuuid=372a4e72-9f1b-4eb4-9ec6-58cad02000f0 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210414171544/https://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/history/events/372a4e72-9f1b-4eb4-9ec6-58cad02000f0 |archive-date=14 April 2021 |access-date=22 December 2025 |website=nlb.gov.sg}}</ref> Later, in the 1890s, when the rubber industry became established in [[State of Singapore (Malaysia)|Malaya]] and Singapore,<ref>{{cite web |title=First Rubber Trees are Planted in Singapore – 1877 |url=https://www.nlb.gov.sg/main/article-detail?cmsuuid=a8ceea4c-1c8b-4c9a-885c-b85038b39e4c |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180614122517/http://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/history/events/a8ceea4c-1c8b-4c9a-885c-b85038b39e4c |archive-date=14 June 2018 |access-date=28 December 2025 |website=History SG |publisher=National Library Board Singapore}}</ref> the island became a global centre for rubber sorting and export.<ref name="Ministry of Information, Communications and the Arts" />
[[File:Singapore 1865 SLNSW FL15083916.jpg|thumb|A lithograph by [[Vincent Brooks, Day & Son|Vincent Brooks]] of [[City of Singapore (historical entity)|Singapore City]] in 1865 from the former Mount Wallich]]

Singapore was not greatly affected by the [[First World War]] (1914–1918), as the conflict did not spread to [[Southeast Asia]]. The only significant event during the war was the [[1915 Singapore Mutiny]] by [[Muslim]] [[sepoys]] from British India, who were garrisoned in Singapore.<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cON5DwAAQBAJ&pg=PA17 |title=The Indian Army in the Two World Wars |date=14 October 2011 |publisher=[[Brill Publishers]] |isbn=978-90-04-21145-2 |pages=17–18 |access-date=14 September 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240211000843/https://books.google.com/books?id=cON5DwAAQBAJ&pg=PA17#v=onepage&q&f=false |archive-date=11 February 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref> After hearing rumours that they were to be sent to fight the [[Ottoman Empire]], a Muslim state, the soldiers rebelled, killing their officers and several British civilians before the mutiny was suppressed by non-Muslim troops arriving from [[Johore]] and [[Burma]].<ref>{{cite web |title=1915 Singapore Mutiny |url=https://www.nlb.gov.sg/main/article-detail?cmsuuid=82db2bb0-b99c-4a9f-9beb-b25626cb3f87 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210225200105/https://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/infopedia/articles/SIP_570_2005-01-24.html |archive-date=25 February 2021 |access-date=28 December 2025 |website=National Library Board |publisher=National Library Board Singapore}}</ref>

[[File:HMS-Repulse-Battlecruiser-IWM-collections.jpg|thumb|[[Battlecruiser]] [[HMS Repulse (1916)|HMS Repulse]], one of the few capital ships sent by Churchill to Singapore to defend it]]
After [[World War I]], the British built the large [[Singapore Naval Base]] as part of the defensive [[Singapore strategy]].<ref name="Stille-2016">{{cite book |last=Stille |first=Mark |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gHe9DAAAQBAJ&pg=PA5 |title=Malaya and Singapore 1941–42: The fall of Britain's empire in the East |publisher=Bloomsbury Publishing |year=2016 |isbn=978-1-4728-1124-0 |pages=5–6 |access-date=14 September 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240211000710/https://books.google.com/books?id=gHe9DAAAQBAJ&pg=PA5#v=onepage&q&f=false |archive-date=11 February 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref> Originally announced in 1921, the construction of the base proceeded at a slow pace until the [[Japanese invasion of Manchuria]] in 1931. Costing $60&nbsp;million and not fully completed in 1938, it was nonetheless the largest [[dry dock]] in the world, the third-largest [[floating dock (jetty)|floating dock]], and had enough fuel tanks to support the entire British navy for six months.<ref name="Stille-2016" /><ref>{{cite book |last=Tan |first=Kevin |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BH88kpvyrdYC&pg=PA90 |title=Marshall of Singapore: A Biography |publisher=Institute of Southeast Asian Studies |year=2008 |isbn=978-981-230-878-8 |pages=90–}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Hobbs |first=David |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FVEgDAAAQBAJ&pg=PA5 |title=The British Pacific Fleet: The Royal Navy's Most Powerful Strike Force |publisher=Naval Institute Press |year=2017 |isbn=978-1-61251-917-3 |page=5 |access-date=14 September 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240211001300/https://books.google.com/books?id=FVEgDAAAQBAJ&pg=PA5#v=onepage&q&f=false |archive-date=11 February 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref> The base was defended by heavy {{convert|15|in|mm|adj=on}} naval guns stationed at [[Fort Siloso]], [[Fort Canning]] and Labrador, as well as a [[Royal Air Force]] airfield at [[Tengah Air Base]]. [[Winston Churchill]] touted it as the "[[Gibraltar]] of the East", and military discussions often referred to the base as simply "[[East of Suez]]". However, the [[British Home Fleet]] was stationed in Europe, and the British could not afford to build a second fleet to protect their interests in Asia. The plan was for the Home Fleet to sail quickly to Singapore in the event of an emergency. After [[World War II]] broke out in 1939, the fleet was fully occupied with defending Britain, leaving Singapore vulnerable to [[Japanese occupation of Singapore|Japanese invasion]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Lamb |first1=Margaret |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4izcCwAAQBAJ&pg=PA39 |title=From Versailles to Pearl Harbor: The Origins of the Second World War in Europe and Asia |last2=Tarling |first2=Nicholas |date=2001 |publisher=Macmillan International Higher Education |isbn=978-1-4039-3772-8 |page=39 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200818180438/https://books.google.com/books?id=4izcCwAAQBAJ&pg=PA39 |archive-date=18 August 2020 |url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Tan |first=Kevin |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BH88kpvyrdYC&pg=PA90 |title=Marshall of Singapore: A Biography |publisher=Institute of Southeast Asian Studies |year=2008 |isbn=978-981-230-878-8}}</ref>

=== Japanese occupation ===
{{Main|Japanese occupation of Singapore}}

[[File:Evacuation of British POWs, Kallang Airport, Singapore - 19450908.jpg|thumb|right|British prisoners of war evacuating in 1945 following the [[Japanese surrender]] at [[Kallang Airport]]. The airport's control tower, located near the city, has been conserved.]]
During the [[Pacific War]], the Japanese [[Malayan campaign|invasion of Malaya]] culminated in the [[Battle of Singapore]]. When the British force of 60,000 troops surrendered on 15 February 1942, British prime minister Winston Churchill called the defeat "the worst disaster and largest capitulation in British history".<ref>{{cite news |date=15 February 1942 |title=On This Day&nbsp;– 15 February 1942: Singapore forced to surrender |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/onthisday/hi/dates/stories/february/15/newsid_3529000/3529447.stm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190519174009/http://news.bbc.co.uk/onthisday/hi/dates/stories/february/15/newsid_3529000/3529447.stm |archive-date=19 May 2019 |access-date=1 May 2007 |publisher=BBC News}}</ref> British and Empire losses during the fighting for Singapore were heavy, with a total of nearly 85,000 personnel captured.{{sfn |Wigmore |1957 |p=382}} About 5,000 were killed or wounded,<ref>{{cite web |title=Battle of Singapore |url=http://www.historynet.com/battle-of-singapore |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150512181020/http://www.historynet.com/battle-of-singapore |archive-date=12 May 2015 |access-date=8 May 2015 |publisher=World History Group}}</ref> of which [[Australians]] made up the majority.{{sfn |Legg |1965 |p=248}}<ref>{{cite news |last=Ooi |first=Teresa |date=17 January 1995 |title=1,000 Aussie victims of WWII join suit against Japan |newspaper=[[The Straits Times]] |location=Singapore}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |date=12 September 1946 |title=South West Pacific War: Australia's Fine Record |url=http://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/newspapers/Digitised/Article/straitstimes19460912-1.2.47?ST=1&AT=search&k=battle%20of%20singapore,%20world%20war%20ii,%20australians&QT=battle,of,singapore,world,war,ii,australians&oref=article |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191220093327/https://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/newspapers/Digitised/Article/straitstimes19460912-1.2.47?ST=1&AT=search&k=battle%20of%20singapore,%20world%20war%20ii,%20australians&QT=battle,of,singapore,world,war,ii,australians&oref=article |archive-date=20 December 2019 |access-date=22 October 2019 |newspaper=The Straits Times |location=Singapore}}</ref> Japanese casualties during the fighting in Singapore amounted to 1,714 killed and 3,378 wounded.{{sfn |Wigmore |1957 |p=382}}{{efn|The breakdown of British Empire losses included 38,496 United Kingdom, 18,490 Australian, 67,340 Indian and 14,382 local volunteer troops. Total Australian casualties included 1,789 killed and 1,306 wounded.{{sfn |Wigmore |1957 |p=382}}}} The occupation was to become a major turning point in the histories of several nations, including those of [[Japan]], [[United Kingdom|Britain]], and Singapore. Japanese newspapers triumphantly declared the victory as deciding the general situation of the war.{{sfn |Toland |1970 |p=277}}<ref>{{cite news |last=Zaccheus |first=Melody |date=21 January 2017 |title=Japanese Occupation newspaper in library portal |url=https://www.straitstimes.com/singapore/japanese-occupation-newspaper-in-library-portal |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220819024819/https://www.straitstimes.com/singapore/japanese-occupation-newspaper-in-library-portal |archive-date=19 August 2022 |access-date=22 October 2019 |newspaper=The Straits Times |location=Singapore}}</ref> Between 5,000 and 25,000 ethnic Chinese people were killed in the subsequent [[Sook Ching massacre]].<ref>{{cite web |last=Leitch Lepoer |first=Barbara |year=1989 |title=Singapore, Shonan: Light of the South |url=http://lcweb2.loc.gov/cgi-bin/query/r?frd/cstdy:@field(DOCID+sg0027) |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170629230435/http://lcweb2.loc.gov/cgi-bin/query/r?frd/cstdy:@field(DOCID+sg0027) |archive-date=29 June 2017 |access-date=29 January 2011 |website=[[Library of Congress Country Studies]] |publisher=[[United States Government Printing Office|Government Printing Office]] |location=Washington, DC}}</ref> British forces had [[Operation Mailfist|planned to liberate Singapore]] in 1945/1946; however, the war ended before these operations could be carried out.{{sfn |Bose |2010 |pp=18–20}}<ref name="The Sunday Times-2005">{{cite news |date=4 September 2005 |title=The real Japanese surrender |url=http://staff.science.nus.edu.sg/~sivasothi/blog/pdf/jap_surrender-st04sep2005.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://wayback.archive-it.org/all/20080119210334/http://staff.science.nus.edu.sg/~sivasothi/blog/pdf/jap_surrender-st04sep2005.pdf |archive-date=19 January 2008 |access-date=22 October 2019 |newspaper=The Sunday Times |location=Singapore}}</ref>

=== Post-war period ===
{{Main|Colony of Singapore}}

[[File:Map of Singapore City in 1951.png|thumb|right|Map of the [[City of Singapore (historical entity)|City of Singapore]] in 1951]]
After the [[Surrender of Japan|Japanese surrender]] to the [[Allies of World War II|Allies]] on 15 August 1945, Singapore fell into a brief state of violence and disorder; looting and [[revenge killing]]s particularly against [[Wartime collaboration|collaborators]] were widespread.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Keo |first1=Bernard Z |date=6 February 2025 |title=Malaya Transformed: Upheaval in Post-War Malaya, 1945–1946 |url=https://academic.oup.com/book/59235/chapter/499141301 |journal=Imagining Malaya |pages=54–76 |doi=10.1093/9780198917113.003.0003 |url-access=subscription |access-date=14 January 2026|doi-access=free }}</ref> British, Australian, and Indian troops led by Lord [[Louis Mountbatten]] [[Operation Tiderace|returned to Singapore]] to receive the formal surrender of Japanese forces in the region from General [[Seishirō Itagaki]] on behalf of General [[Hisaichi Terauchi]] on 12 September 1945.{{sfn |Bose |2010 |pp=18–20}}<ref name="The Sunday Times-2005" /> Meanwhile, [[Tomoyuki Yamashita]] was tried by a US military commission for war crimes, but not for crimes committed by his troops in Malaya or Singapore. He was convicted and hanged in the [[Commonwealth of the Philippines|Philippines]] on 23 February 1946.{{sfn |Smith |2006 |pp=556–557}}<ref>{{cite news |date=23 February 1946 |title=Yamashita Hanged |url=http://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/newspapers/Digitised/Article/maltribune19460223-1.2.12 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191022150250/http://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/newspapers/Digitised/Article/maltribune19460223-1.2.12 |archive-date=22 October 2019 |access-date=22 October 2019 |work=Malaya Tribune |location=Singapore}}</ref>

Much of the infrastructure in Singapore had been destroyed during the war, including those needed to supply utilities. A shortage of food led to malnutrition, disease, and rampant crime and violence. A series of strikes in 1947 caused massive stoppages in public transport and other services. However, by late 1947 the economy began to recover, facilitated by a growing international demand for tin and rubber.<ref name="U.S. Library of Congress-2">{{cite web |title=Singapore – Aftermath of War |url=http://countrystudies.us/singapore/9.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110514010408/http://countrystudies.us/singapore/9.htm |archive-date=14 May 2011 |access-date=16 May 2020 |publisher=U.S. Library of Congress}}</ref> The failure of Britain to successfully defend its colony against the Japanese changed its image in the eyes of Singaporeans. The [[British Military Administration (Malaya)|British Military Administration]] ended on 1 April 1946, and Singapore became a separate [[crown colony]] in its own right, as the [[Straits Settlements]] were formally dissolved that year.<ref name="U.S. Library of Congress-2" /> In July 1947, an [[Cabinet of Singapore#History|Executive]] and [[Legislative Council of Singapore|Legislative Council]] (LegCo) were reconstituted and the election of six members of the LegCo was scheduled for [[1948 Singaporean general election|1948]]. Only one political party, the [[Progressive Party (Singapore)|Progressive Party]], contested in the highly restricted general election, which continued in [[1951 Singaporean general election|1951]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Towards Self-government |url=http://www.sg/explore/history_towards.htm |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060713023113/http://www.sg/explore/history_towards.htm |archive-date=13 July 2006 |access-date=18 June 2006 |publisher=Ministry of Information, Communications and the Arts, Singapore}}</ref>

During the 1950s, [[Malayan Communist Party|Chinese communists]], with strong ties to the trade unions and Chinese schools, waged a [[Guerrilla warfare|guerrilla war]] against the government, leading to the [[Malayan Emergency]]. The [[1954 National Service riots]], 1955 [[Hock Lee bus riots]], and 1956 [[Chinese middle schools riots]] in Singapore were all linked to these events.<ref>{{cite web |title=Communism |url=http://library.thinkquest.org/12405/19.htm |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20000409182924/http://library.thinkquest.org/12405/19.htm |archive-date=9 April 2000 |access-date=29 January 2012 |website=Thinkquest}}</ref> [[David Marshall (Singaporean politician)|David Marshall]], pro-independence leader of the [[Labour Front]], won Singapore's [[1955 Singaporean general election|general election in 1955]] which had an expanded but not universal [[suffrage]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Low |first=James |date=2004 |title=Kept in Position: The Labour Front-Alliance Government of Chief Minister David Marshall in Singapore, April 1955 – June 1956 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/20072556 |url-status=live |journal=Journal of Southeast Asian Studies |volume=35 |issue=1 |pages=41–64 |doi=10.1017/S0022463404000037 |issn=0022-4634 |jstor=20072556 |s2cid=154326049 |url-access=subscription |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210419081147/https://www.jstor.org/stable/20072556 |archive-date=19 April 2021 |access-date=20 February 2021}}</ref> During his [[Chief ministership of David Marshall|chief ministership]], he led a delegation to London for complete self-rule, but Britain had rejected his demand. He subsequently resigned and was replaced by [[Lim Yew Hock]] in 1956, and after further negotiations, Britain agreed to grant Singapore full internal [[Self-governance of Singapore|self-government]] for all matters except defence and foreign affairs on 3 June 1959.<ref name="U.S. Library of Congress">{{cite web |title=Country studies: Singapore: Road to Independence |url=http://countrystudies.us/singapore/10.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140704220519/http://countrystudies.us/singapore/10.htm |archive-date=4 July 2014 |access-date=16 May 2020 |publisher=U.S. Library of Congress}}</ref> Days before, in the [[1959 Singaporean general election|general election of 30 May]] which had [[universal suffrage]], the PAP won a landslide victory under [[Lee Kuan Yew]].<ref>{{cite news |date=2 December 1990 |title=Headliners; Retiring, Semi |url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9D0CE4DD123DF931A35751C1A966958260 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090318035148/http://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9D0CE4DD123DF931A35751C1A966958260 |archive-date=18 March 2009 |access-date=27 December 2008 |newspaper=[[The New York Times]]}}</ref> [[Governor of Singapore|Governor]] [[William Goode (colonial administrator)|William Goode]] served as the first head of state, also known as the [[Yang di-Pertuan Negara of Singapore|Yang di-Pertuan Negara]].<ref>{{cite web |title=The Singapore Legal System |url=http://www.singaporelaw.sg/content/LegalSyst1.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110603225639/http://www.singaporelaw.sg/content/LegalSyst1.html |archive-date=3 June 2011 |access-date=26 June 2011 |publisher=Singapore Academy of Law}}</ref>

=== Within Malaysia ===
{{Main|State of Singapore (Malaysia)}}

[[File:SingaporeRiver-bumboats-196009.jpg|thumb|Singapore thrived as an entrepôt. In the 1960s, [[bumboat]]s were used to transport cargoes and supplies between nearshore ships and Singapore River.]]
[[File:Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew of Singapore Making a Toast at a State Dinner Held in His Honor, 1975.jpg|thumb|upright=0.68|[[Lee Kuan Yew]], the first prime minister of Singapore from 1959 to 1990]]
PAP leaders believed that Singapore's future lay with Malaya, due to strong ties between the two. It was thought that reuniting with Malaya would benefit the economy by creating a common market, alleviating ongoing unemployment woes in Singapore. However, a sizeable left-wing faction of the PAP was strongly opposed to the merger, fearing a loss of influence, and hence formed the [[Barisan Sosialis]], after being kicked out from the PAP.<ref>{{cite book |last=Lee |first=T. H |title=The Open United Front: The Communist Struggle in Singapore, 1954–1966 |publisher=Singapore: South Seas Society |year=1996}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Bloodworth |first=D |url=https://archive.org/details/tigertrojanhorse00bloo |title=The Tiger and the Trojan Horse |publisher=Singapore: Times Books International |year=1986 |url-access=registration}}</ref> The ruling party of Malaya, [[United Malays National Organisation]] (UMNO), was staunchly anti-communist, and it was suspected UMNO would support the non-communist factions of PAP. UMNO, initially sceptical of the idea of a merger due to distrust of the PAP government and concern that the large ethnic Chinese population in Singapore would alter the racial balance in Malaya on which their political power base depended, became supportive of the idea of the merger due to joint fear of a communist takeover.<ref name="Singapore Standard-1959">{{cite news |date=18 February 1959 |title=MCA: Wipe out extremists |newspaper=Singapore Standard}}</ref>

On 27 May 1961, Malaya's prime minister, [[Tunku Abdul Rahman]], made a surprise proposal for a new Federation called [[Malaysia]], which would unite the current and former [[British possessions]] in the region: the [[Federation of Malaya]], Singapore, [[Brunei]], [[North Borneo (British Crown colony)|North Borneo]], and [[Sarawak (British Crown colony)|Sarawak]].<ref name="Singapore Standard-1959" /><ref>{{cite news |date=28 May 1961 |title=Big 'Unity' Plan – Tengku on closer ties with S'pore, Borneo and Brunei |url=https://www.straitstimes.com/multimedia/graphics/assets/images/ST175/NewspaperSG/1961-05-28/full.jpg |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220309061422/https://www.straitstimes.com/multimedia/graphics/assets/images/ST175/NewspaperSG/1961-05-28/full.jpg |archive-date=9 March 2022 |access-date=9 March 2022 |work=The Straits Times |publisher=[[Singapore Press Holdings]] |page=1}}</ref> UMNO leaders believed that the additional Malay population in the Bornean territories would balance Singapore's Chinese population.<ref name="U.S. Library of Congress" /> The British government, for its part, believed that the merger would prevent Singapore from becoming a haven for communism.<ref>{{cite news |date=28 March 1962 |title=Appeal To Singapore |url=http://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/newspapers/Digitised/Article/straitstimes19620328-1.2.70.1?ST=1&AT=advanced |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180319214737/http://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/newspapers/Digitised/Article/straitstimes19620328-1.2.70.1?ST=1&AT=advanced |archive-date=19 March 2018 |access-date=19 August 2017 |newspaper=The Straits Times |location=Singapore |page=10}}</ref> To obtain a mandate for a merger, the PAP held a [[1962 Merger Referendum of Singapore|referendum on the merger]]. This referendum included a choice of different terms for a merger with Malaysia and had no option for avoiding merger altogether.<ref>{{cite news |date=2 September 1962 |title=Yes – What a win for Premier Lee |url=https://www.straitstimes.com/multimedia/graphics/assets/images/ST175/NewspaperSG/1962-09-02/full.jpg |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220309061847/https://www.straitstimes.com/multimedia/graphics/assets/images/ST175/NewspaperSG/1962-09-02/full.jpg |archive-date=9 March 2022 |access-date=9 March 2022 |work=The Straits Times |publisher=Singapore Press Holdings |page=1}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |date=3 September 1962 |title=Merger "Yes" |url=https://www.straitstimes.com/multimedia/graphics/assets/images/ST175/NewspaperSG/1962-09-03/full.jpg |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220309061616/https://www.straitstimes.com/multimedia/graphics/assets/images/ST175/NewspaperSG/1962-09-03/full.jpg |archive-date=9 March 2022 |access-date=9 March 2022 |work=The Straits Times |publisher=Singapore Press Holdings |page=1}}</ref> On 16 September 1963, Singapore joined with Malaya, the North Borneo, and Sarawak to form the new Federation of Malaysia under the terms of the [[Malaysia Agreement]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Abisheganaden |first1=Felix |date=16 September 1963 |title=Hail Malaysia! |url=https://www.straitstimes.com/multimedia/graphics/assets/images/ST175/NewspaperSG/1963-09-16/full.jpg |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220309062748/https://www.straitstimes.com/multimedia/graphics/assets/images/ST175/NewspaperSG/1963-09-16/full.jpg |archive-date=9 March 2022 |access-date=9 March 2022 |work=[[The Straits Times]] |publisher=[[Singapore Press Holdings]] |page=1}}</ref> Under this Agreement, Singapore had a relatively high level of autonomy compared to the other states of Malaysia.<ref>{{cite web |title=Singapore becomes part of Malaysia |url=http://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/history/events/1dab53ea-788c-461c-acfb-ca625b974c9c |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170207040425/http://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/history/events/1dab53ea-788c-461c-acfb-ca625b974c9c |archive-date=7 February 2017 |access-date=6 February 2017 |publisher=HistorySG}}</ref>

[[Indonesia]] opposed the formation of Malaysia due to its own claims over Borneo and launched [[Konfrontasi|''Konfrontasi'']]  in response to the formation of Malaysia.<ref>{{cite book |last1=James |first1=Harold |title=The Undeclared War: The Story of the Indonesian Confrontation 1962–1966 |last2=Sheil-Small |first2=Denis |publisher=Rowman and Littlefield |year=1971 |isbn=978-0-87471-074-8 |location=Totowa}}{{cite book |last=Mackie |first=J.A.C. |year=1974 |title=Konfrontasi: The Indonesia-Malaysia Dispute 1963–1966 |location=Kuala Lumpur |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-638247-0}}</ref> On 10 March 1965, [[MacDonald House bombing|a bomb planted by Indonesian saboteurs]] on a mezzanine floor of [[MacDonald House]] exploded, killing three people and injuring 33 others. It was the deadliest of at least 42 bomb incidents which occurred during the ''Konfrontasi''.<ref>{{cite news |date=16 May 1965 |title=Record of the Wreckers |url=http://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/newspapers/Digitised/Article/straitstimes19650516-1.2.85 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170819065549/http://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/newspapers/Digitised/Article/straitstimes19650516-1.2.85 |archive-date=19 August 2017 |access-date=19 August 2017 |newspaper=The Straits Times |location=Singapore}}</ref> Two members of the [[Indonesian Marine Corps]], [[Osman bin Haji Mohamed Ali]] and [[Harun bin Said]], were eventually convicted and executed for the crime.<ref>{{cite news |date=6 April 1965 |title=Mac Donald House blast: Two for trial |url=http://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/newspapers/Digitised/Article/straitstimes19650406-1.2.99 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170819064442/http://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/newspapers/Digitised/Article/straitstimes19650406-1.2.99 |archive-date=19 August 2017 |access-date=19 August 2017 |newspaper=The Straits Times |location=Singapore}}</ref> The explosion caused US$250,000 ({{Inflation|US|250000|1965|fmt=eq|cursign=[[United States dollar|US$]]}}) in damages to MacDonald House.<ref>{{cite web |author=Tan Lay Yuan |title=MacDonald House bomb explosion |url=http://infopedia.nl.sg/articles/SIP_62_2004-12-17.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111215082844/http://infopedia.nl.sg/articles/SIP_62_2004-12-17.html |archive-date=15 December 2011 |website=Singapore Infopedia |publisher=National Library Board}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |date=9 October 1965 |title=Mac Donald House suffered $250,000 bomb damage |url=http://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/newspapers/Digitised/Article/straitstimes19651009-1.2.46 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170819065124/http://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/newspapers/Digitised/Article/straitstimes19651009-1.2.46 |archive-date=19 August 2017 |access-date=19 August 2017 |newspaper=The Straits Times |location=Singapore}}</ref>

Even after the merger, the [[People's Action Party–United Malays National Organisation relations|Singaporean government and the Malaysian central government disagreed]] on many political and economic issues.<ref name="Road to Independence-1998">{{cite news |year=1998 |title=Road to Independence |url=http://ourstory.asia1.com.sg/merger/merger.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131013002423/http://ourstory.asia1.com.sg/merger/merger.html |archive-date=13 October 2013 |publisher=[[AsiaOne]]}}</ref> Despite an agreement to establish a common market, Singapore continued to face restrictions when trading with the rest of Malaysia. In retaliation, Singapore did not extend to [[Sabah]] and [[Sarawak]] the full extent of the loans agreed to for economic development of the two eastern states. Talks soon broke down, and abusive speeches and writing became rife on both sides. This led to communal strife in Singapore, culminating in the [[1964 race riots in Singapore|1964 race riots]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Lau |first=A |title=A moment of anguish: Singapore in Malaysia and the politics of disengagement |publisher=Times Academic Press |year=2000 |location=Singapore}}</ref> On 7 August 1965, after series of secret negotiations between the Malaysian and Singaporean leaders, a [[Independence of Singapore Agreement 1965|separation agreement]] was signed, paving way for a sudden but planned independence for Singapore.<ref>{{Cite news |date=19 September 1998 |title=which split the nation |url=https://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/newspapers/digitised/article/straitstimes19980919-1.2.63.4 |access-date=5 December 2025 |work=The Straits Times |pages=51}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Fong |first=Leslie |date=9 August 1990 |others=Illustrations by Jose Tence Ruiz |title=The Week Before Separation |url=https://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/newspapers/digitised/article/straitstimes19900809-1.2.109.3 |access-date=5 December 2025 |work=The Straits Times |pages=5–15}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Tin Seng |first=Lim |date=August 2019 |title=Singapore's separation from Malaysia |url=https://www.nlb.gov.sg/main/article-detail?cmsuuid=9641f35d-3ae5-41d8-9fa6-7ca8b845ea53 |access-date=5 December 2025 |website=National Library Board Singapore}}</ref> On 9 August 1965, [[Members of the Dewan Rakyat, 2nd Malaysian Parliament|the Malaysian Parliament]] voted 126 to 0 to pass [[Constitution and Malaysia (Singapore Amendment) Act 1965|a constitutional amendment bill]], thereby separating Singapore from Malaysia, which left Singapore as a newly independent country.<ref name="U.S. Library of Congress" /><ref>{{cite web |last=Leitch Lepoer |first=Barbara |year=1989 |title=Singapore as Part of Malaysia |url=http://lcweb2.loc.gov/cgi-bin/query/r?frd/cstdy:@field(DOCID+sg0033) |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170629223526/http://lcweb2.loc.gov/cgi-bin/query/r?frd/cstdy:@field(DOCID+sg0033) |archive-date=29 June 2017 |access-date=29 January 2011 |website=Library of Congress Country Studies |publisher=Government Printing Office |location=Washington, DC}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=A Summary of Malaysia-Singapore History |url=http://www.europe-solidaire.org/spip.php?article7878 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120529081759/http://www.europe-solidaire.org/spip.php?article7878 |archive-date=29 May 2012 |access-date=29 January 2012 |website=europe-solidaire}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Singapore separates from Malaysia and becomes independent – Singapore History |url=http://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/history/events/dc1efe7a-8159-40b2-9244-cdb078755013#27 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201111210312/https://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/history/events/dc1efe7a-8159-40b2-9244-cdb078755013#27 |archive-date=11 November 2020 |access-date=12 May 2017 |publisher=National Library Board |quote=Negotiations were, however, done in complete secrecy... (Tunku moved) a bill to amend the constitution that would provide for Singapore's departure from the Federation. Razak was also waiting for the fully signed separation agreement from Singapore to allay possible suggestions that Singapore was expelled from Malaysia.}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Episode 0: Trailer |url=https://thehistoryofsingapore.com/2015/07/31/episode-0-trailer/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210920150336/https://thehistoryofsingapore.com/2015/07/31/episode-0-trailer/ |archive-date=20 September 2021 |access-date=14 August 2022}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last1=Lim |first1=Edmund |date=22 December 2015 |title=Secret documents reveal extent of negotiations for Separation |url=https://www.straitstimes.com/opinion/secret-documents-reveal-extent-of-negotiations-for-separation |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210920150329/https://www.straitstimes.com/opinion/secret-documents-reveal-extent-of-negotiations-for-separation |archive-date=20 September 2021 |access-date=15 August 2022 |newspaper=The Straits Times}}</ref>

=== Republic of Singapore ===
{{See also|Independence of Singapore Agreement 1965}}
[[File:153 Singapore, Jan 1978 (52023517826).jpg|thumb|right|Facing the [[Central Area, Singapore|Central Area]] of Singapore in 1978]]
[[File:Marina Bay Sands 20250903 (1).jpg|thumb|right|The [[Marina Bay Sands]], one of Singapore's two [[casino hotel|integrated resorts]]]]

After its expulsion from Malaysia, Singapore became independent as the "Republic of Singapore" on 9 August 1965,<ref name="Road to Independence-1998" /><ref>{{cite news |last1=Abisheganaden |first1=Felix |date=10 August 1965 |title=Singapore is out |url=https://www.straitstimes.com/multimedia/graphics/assets/images/ST175/NewspaperSG/1965-08-10/full.jpg |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220221051204/https://www.straitstimes.com/multimedia/graphics/assets/images/ST175/NewspaperSG/1965-08-10/full.jpg |archive-date=21 February 2022 |access-date=21 February 2022 |work=[[The Straits Times]] |publisher=[[Singapore Press Holdings]]}}</ref> with [[Lee Kuan Yew]] and [[Yusof bin Ishak]] as the first prime minister and president respectively.<ref>{{cite web |author=Vernon Cornelius |title=Past and present leaders of Singapore |url=https://www.nlb.gov.sg/main/article-detail?cmsuuid=3520aab7-25a2-452d-bdd3-2e75b1989866 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260127080909/https://www.nlb.gov.sg/main/article-detail?cmsuuid=3520aab7-25a2-452d-bdd3-2e75b1989866 |archive-date=27 January 2026 |access-date=27 January 2026 |publisher=National Library Board}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=1 February 1960 |title=Yusof to be the first President |url=https://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/newspapers/Digitised/Article/straitstimes19651215-1.2.60 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200807064731/https://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/newspapers/Digitised/Article/straitstimes19651215-1.2.60 |archive-date=7 August 2020 |access-date=28 May 2020 |website=The Straits Times |location=Singapore |via=National Libraries Board}}</ref> In 1967, the country co-founded the [[Association of Southeast Asian Nations]] (ASEAN).<ref>{{cite wikisource|Bangkok Declaration}}</ref> Race riots [[1969 race riots of Singapore|erupted again]] in 1969 as a spillover from the [[13 May incident]] in Malaysia. On this occasion, the unrest was more firmly contained.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Sandhu |first1=Kernial Singh |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ldKwPQ2PyBAC&pg=PA107 |title=Management of Success: The Moulding of Modern Singapore |last2=Wheatley |first2=Paul |publisher=Institute of Southeast Asian Studies |year=1989 |isbn=978-981-3035-42-3 |page=107}}</ref> Lee's emphasis on rapid economic growth, racial integration, promotion of business entrepreneurship and curbs on democratic freedoms by governing with extensive legal powers shaped Singapore's policies for the next half century.<ref>Terry McCarthy, "Lee Kuan Yew." ''Time ''154: 7–8 (1999). [https://web.archive.org/web/20150402104451/http://madeinthoughts.com/pdf/LeeKuanYew.pdf online]</ref><ref name="The Straits Times-2015" /> Economic growth continued throughout the 1980s, with the unemployment rate falling to 3% and real GDP growth averaging at about 8% up until 1999. During the 1980s, Singapore began to shift towards high-tech industries, such as the [[wafer fabrication]] sector, in order to remain competitive as neighbouring countries began manufacturing with cheaper labour. [[Singapore Airlines]] was formed in 1972 and [[Changi Airport]] was opened in 1981, replacing the international airport at [[Paya Lebar Air Base|Paya Lebar]].<ref>{{cite web |title=History of Changi Airport |url=http://www.changiairport.com.sg/changi/en/about_us/history_changi.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060629014047/http://www.changiairport.com.sg/changi/en/about_us/history_changi.html |archive-date=29 June 2006 |publisher=Civil Aviation Authority of Singapore}}</ref> Lee's government capitalised on Singapore's favourable geographical position to develop the [[Port of Singapore]] into one of the world's busiest ports, while the service and tourism industries also expanded significantly during this period.<ref>{{cite web |title=Lunch Dialogue on 'Singapore as a Transport Hub' |url=https://lkyspp.nus.edu.sg/news-events/events/details/lunch-dialogue-on-singapore-as-a-transport-hub |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181117104954/https://lkyspp.nus.edu.sg/news-events/events/details/lunch-dialogue-on-singapore-as-a-transport-hub |archive-date=17 November 2018 |access-date=17 November 2018 |website=Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Lam |first1=Yin Yin |date=26 January 2017 |title=Three factors that have made Singapore a global logistics hub |url=http://blogs.worldbank.org/transport/three-factors-have-made-singapore-global-logistics-hub |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181117105041/http://blogs.worldbank.org/transport/three-factors-have-made-singapore-global-logistics-hub |archive-date=17 November 2018 |access-date=17 November 2018 |website=The World Bank Blogs}}</ref>

The PAP has remained in power since 1959. Often described as a ''de facto'' [[one-party dominant state]] because of its uncommon longevity for a nominal [[liberal democracy]], some activists and opposition politicians view the PAP government's tight regulation of political and media activities, along with its stringent laws, as an infringement on political rights.<ref>{{cite news |date=5 May 2006 |title=Singapore elections |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/world/asia-pacific/4976536.stm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090115181132/http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/asia-pacific/4976536.stm |archive-date=15 January 2009 |access-date=28 July 2017 |publisher=[[BBC News]]}}</ref>{{additional citations needed|date=October 2026}} In response, the PAP introduced several significant political changes, including the creation of the [[Non-constituency Members of Parliament]] (NCMPs) scheme from the [[1984 Singaporean general election|1984 election]], which allowed a limited number of the best performing losing opposition candidates to be appointed as MPs. [[Group representation constituencies]] (GRCs) were subsequently introduced in the [[1988 Singaporean general election|1988 election]] as multi-member electoral divisions intended to guarantee minority representation in parliament, although the opposition has accused the scheme of enabling [[gerrymandering]].<ref>{{Singapore legislation|title=Parliamentary Elections Act|cap=218|titlelink=Parliamentary Elections Act (Singapore)}}</ref> In addition, [[Nominated Members of Parliament]] (NMPs) were introduced in 1990 to allow non-elected and non-partisan representatives from diverse professional fields to serve in parliament.<ref>Ho Khai Leong (2003). ''Shared Responsibilities, Unshared Power: The Politics of Policy-Making in Singapore''. Eastern Univ Pr. {{ISBN|978-981-210-218-8}}</ref> The [[Constitution of Singapore|constitution]] was amended in 1991 to provide for an [[President of Singapore|elected president]] with veto powers over the use of [[Reserves of the Government of Singapore|past reserves]] and key public service appointments. The first such election was held in [[1993 Singaporean presidential election|1993]].<ref>{{cite web |date=18 April 2006 |title=Presidential Elections |url=http://www.elections.gov.sg/presidential_elections.htm |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080827213801/http://www.elections.gov.sg/presidential_elections.htm |archive-date=27 August 2008 |publisher=Elections Department Singapore}}</ref>

In 1990, [[Goh Chok Tong]] succeeded Lee and became Singapore's second prime minister, leading the PAP into the [[1991 Singaporean general election|1991 election]].<ref>{{cite book |url=http://eservice.nlb.gov.sg/item_holding_s.aspx?bid=12751459 |title=Encyclopedia of Singapore |date=2006 |publisher=Tailsman Publishing |isbn=978-981-05-5667-9 |location=Singapore |page=82 |access-date=19 August 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170707102725/http://eservice.nlb.gov.sg/item_holding_s.aspx?bid=12751459 |archive-date=7 July 2017 |url-status=live}}</ref> During Goh's tenure, the country went through the [[1997 Asian financial crisis]] and the [[2002–2004 SARS outbreak]].<ref>{{cite news |last=Yeoh |first=En-Lai |date=9 April 2003 |title=Singapore Woman Linked to 100 SARS Cases |agency=[[Associated Press]]}}</ref><ref name="National Library Board">{{cite web |title=Goh Chok Tong |url=http://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/infopedia/articles/SIP_860_2004-12-27.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230729194333/https://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/infopedia/articles/SIP_860_2004-12-27.html |archive-date=29 July 2023 |access-date=6 February 2017 |publisher=National Library Board}}</ref> In 2004, [[Lee Hsien Loong]], the eldest son of [[Lee Kuan Yew]], became the country's third prime minister.<ref name="National Library Board" /> Lee Hsien Loong's tenure included the [[2008 financial crisis]], the resolution of a [[Malaysia–Singapore Points of Agreement of 1990|dispute over land ownership]] at [[Tanjong Pagar railway station]] between Singapore and Malaysia, the introduction of the two [[integrated resort]]s (IRs) located at the [[Marina Bay Sands]] and [[Resorts World Sentosa]] as well as the [[COVID-19 pandemic in Singapore|COVID-19 pandemic]].<ref>{{cite news |date=15 July 2009 |title=Country profile: Singapore |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-asia-15961759 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081229042533/http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/world/asia-pacific/country_profiles/1143240.stm |archive-date=29 December 2008 |access-date=22 April 2010 |publisher=BBC News}}</ref> The PAP experienced its [[2011 Singaporean general election|worst electoral performance]] in 2011, securing only 60% of the vote. While this would be considered a [[landslide victory]] in many countries since it preserved the party's [[supermajority]], it was regarded locally as a poor outcome, reflecting public debate over issues such as the high rates of [[Immigration to Singapore|immigration]] and the rising [[cost of living]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Hui Min |first=Chew |date=28 August 2015 |title=GE2015: A look back at the last 5 general elections from 1991 to 2011 |url=https://www.straitstimes.com/politics/ge2015-a-look-back-at-the-last-5-general-elections-from-1991-to-2011 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181007073757/https://www.straitstimes.com/politics/ge2015-a-look-back-at-the-last-5-general-elections-from-1991-to-2011 |archive-date=7 October 2018 |access-date=7 October 2018 |work=The Straits Times}}</ref> On 23 March 2015, Lee Kuan Yew [[Death and state funeral of Lee Kuan Yew|died]], and a one-week period of public mourning was observed nationwide.<ref name="The Straits Times-2015">{{cite news |date=25 March 2015 |title=Lee Kuan Yew: Our chief diplomat to the world |url=http://www.straitstimes.com/singapore/remembering-lee-kuan-yew-our-chief-diplomat-to-the-world |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151026020834/http://www.straitstimes.com/singapore/remembering-lee-kuan-yew-our-chief-diplomat-to-the-world |archive-date=26 October 2015 |access-date=8 November 2015 |work=The Straits Times |location=Singapore}}</ref> Subsequently, the PAP regained its dominance in Parliament through the [[2015 Singaporean general election|September general election]], receiving 69.9% of the popular vote,<ref>{{cite news |last1=Lee |first1=U-Wen |title=PAP racks up landslide win, takes 83 out of 89 seats |url=http://www.businesstimes.com.sg/government-economy/singapore-general-election/pap-racks-up-landslide-win-takes-83-out-of-89-seats |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150913023301/http://www.businesstimes.com.sg/government-economy/singapore-general-election/pap-racks-up-landslide-win-takes-83-out-of-89-seats |archive-date=13 September 2015 |access-date=13 September 2015 |work=Business Times (Singapore)}}</ref> although this remained lower than the [[2001 Singaporean general election|2001]] tally of 75.3%<ref>{{cite news |last=Heng |first=Janice |date=12 September 2015 |title=For PAP, the numbers hark back to 2001 polls showing |url=http://www.straitstimes.com/politics/for-pap-the-numbers-hark-back-to-2001-polls-showing |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150912094804/http://www.straitstimes.com/politics/for-pap-the-numbers-hark-back-to-2001-polls-showing |archive-date=12 September 2015 |newspaper=The Straits Times |location=Singapore}}</ref> and the [[1968 Singaporean general election|1968]] tally of 86.7%.<ref>{{cite web |title=History of general elections in Singapore |url=https://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/infopedia/articles/SIP_549_2004-12-28.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200204130922/https://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/infopedia/articles/SIP_549_2004-12-28.html |archive-date=4 February 2020 |access-date=4 February 2020 |publisher=National Library Board}}</ref> The [[2020 Singaporean general election|2020 election]] held in July during COVID saw the PAP drop to 61% of the vote, while the [[Workers' Party (Singapore)|Workers' Party]] (WP) took 10 of the 93 seats, including its leader [[Pritam Singh]] becoming the first ''de jure'' [[Leader of the Opposition (Singapore)|leader of the opposition]] since independence.<ref name="The Economist-2020">{{cite news |date=18 July 2020 |title=Why so many Singaporeans voted for the opposition |url=https://www.economist.com/asia/2020/07/18/why-so-many-singaporeans-voted-for-the-opposition |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200720041203/https://www.economist.com/asia/2020/07/18/why-so-many-singaporeans-voted-for-the-opposition |archive-date=20 July 2020 |access-date=20 July 2020 |newspaper=The Economist}}</ref> On 15 May 2024, [[Lawrence Wong]] became Singapore's fourth prime minister and the first born after independence.<ref>{{cite news |date=14 May 2024 |title=Singapore to swear in Lawrence Wong as new prime minister |url=https://sg.news.yahoo.com/singapore-swear-lawrence-wong-prime-212009750.html |url-status=live
