== Demographics ==
{{Main|Demographics of Singapore|Singaporeans}}

{{See also|Race in Singapore}}
[[File:KITLV - 103763 - Chinese and Malaysian women at Singapore - circa 1890.tif|upright|thumb|Chinese ([[East Asian people|East Asian]]), Malay ([[Indigenous peoples of Southeast Asia|Southeast Asian]]), and Indian ([[South Asian ethnic groups|South Asian]]) women in Singapore, {{Circa|1890}}. To promote racial harmony among the three races, a unique [[Racial Harmony Day]] is celebrated on 21 July every year.]]
As of mid-2025, Singapore's total population stood at 6,110,200, of whom 3,660,200 (59.9%) were [[Singaporean nationality law|citizens]] and the remaining 2,450,000 (40.1%) were either [[Permanent residency in Singapore|permanent residents]] (543,800, 8.9%) or [[international student]]s, [[foreign worker]]s, or [[dependant]]s (1,906,700, 31.2%).<ref name="Singapore Department of Statistics"/> It is the [[city-state|world's largest and most populous city-state]].<ref name="mw"/><ref name="Singapore Department of Statistics"/>

The 2020 census reported that about 74.3% of residents were of Chinese descent, 13.5% of Malay descent, 9.0% of Indian descent, and 3.2% of other descent (such as [[Eurasians in Singapore|Eurasian]]); this proportion was virtually identical to the 2010 census, with slight increases among Chinese and Malay (0.2% and 0.1% respectively) and minor decreases in Indian and others (0.2% and 0.1%).<ref>[https://www.parliament.gov.sg/docs/default-source/default-document-library/cop2020sr1.pdf Singapore Department of Statistics | Census of Population 2020 Statistical Release 1 – Demographic Characteristics, Education, Language and Religion], '''p. 20'''.</ref><ref>{{cite report |url=http://www.singstat.gov.sg/pubn/popn/c2010acr.pdf |title=Census of Population 2010 Advance Census Release |year=2010 |publisher=Singapore Department of Statistics |pages=13–16 |isbn=978-981-08-6819-2 |access-date=2 July 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120327064912/http://www.singstat.gov.sg/pubn/popn/c2010acr.pdf |archive-date=27 March 2012 |url-status=dead}}</ref> Prior to 2010, each person could register as a member of only one race, by default that of their father; therefore, mixed-race persons were solely grouped under their father's race in government censuses. From 2010 onward, people may register using a multi-racial classification, in which they may choose one primary race and one secondary race, but no more than two.<ref>{{cite news |author=Hoe Yeen Nie |date=12 January 2010 |title=Singaporeans of mixed race allowed to 'double barrel' race in IC |url=http://www.channelnewsasia.com/stories/singaporelocalnews/view/1030142/1/.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100206100917/http://www.channelnewsasia.com/stories/singaporelocalnews/view/1030142/1/.html |archive-date=6 February 2010 |access-date=18 February 2011 |publisher=Channel NewsAsia |location=Singapore}}</ref>

Like other developed countries in Asia, Singapore experienced a rapid decline in its [[total fertility rate]] (TFR) beginning in the 1980s.<ref name="IMF">{{Cite web |title=Lessons from Singapore on Raising Fertility Rates – IMF F&D |url=https://www.imf.org/en/Publications/fandd/issues/2020/03/lessons-from-singapore-on-raising-fertility-rates-tan |access-date=22 January 2024 |website=IMF}}</ref> Since 2010, its TFR has largely plateaued at 1.1 children per woman, which is among the lowest in the world and well below the 2.1 needed to replace the population.<ref>{{Cite web |title=World Bank Open Data |url=https://data.worldbank.org/ |access-date=22 January 2024 |website=World Bank Open Data |quote=Fertility rate, total (births per woman) – Singapore; ( 1 ) United Nations Population Division. World Population Prospects: 2022 Revision. ( 2 ) Census reports and other statistical publications from national statistical offices, ( 3 ) Eurostat: Demographic Statistics, ( 4 ) United Nations Statistical Division. Population and Vital Statistics Report ( various years ), ( 5 ) U.S. Census Bureau: International Database, and ( 6 ) Secretariat of the Pacific Community: Statistics and Demography Programme.}}</ref> Consequently, the median age of Singaporean residents is among the highest in the world, at 42.8 in 2022 compared to 39.6 ten years earlier.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Singapore: citizen population median age 1970–2022 |url=https://www.statista.com/statistics/1304574/singapore-citizen-population-median-age/ |access-date=22 January 2024 |website=Statista}}</ref> Starting in 2001, the government [[Population planning in Singapore|introduced a series of programmes]] to increase fertility, including paid maternity leave, childcare subsidies, tax relief and rebates, one-time cash gifts, and grants for companies that implement flexible work arrangements;<ref name="IMF"/> nevertheless, live births have continued to decline, hitting a record low in 2022.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Jacob |first=Charmaine |date=18 September 2023 |title=Singapore's birth rate is at a record low — but 'throwing money' at the problem won't solve it |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2023/09/18/singapores-birth-rate-is-falling-and-throwing-money-at-the-problem-wont-solve-it-.html |access-date=22 January 2024 |website=CNBC}}</ref> Singapore's immigration policy is designed to alleviate the decline and maintain its working-age population.<ref>{{cite news |last=Ng |first=Julia |date=7 February 2007 |title=Singapore's birth trend outlook remains dismal |url=http://www.channelnewsasia.com/stories/singaporelocalnews/view/257208/1/.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120105180711/http://www.channelnewsasia.com/stories/singaporelocalnews/view/257208/1/.html |archive-date=5 January 2012 |access-date=22 April 2010 |publisher=Channel NewsAsia |location=Singapore}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=O'Callaghan |first1=John |date=31 August 2012 |title=Tiny Singapore risks economic gloom without big baby boom |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/uk-singapore-babies/tiny-singapore-risks-economic-gloom-without-big-baby-boom-idUKLNE87U00H20120831 |access-date=17 May 2021 |work=Reuters}}</ref><ref>Jessica Pan and Walter Theseira, [https://thedocs.worldbank.org/en/doc/080a4bc64cc8a9eb8a2a0e98d97a260a-0050062023/original/WDR-Immigration-in-Singapore-FORMATTED.pdf Immigration in Singapore] – Background paper to the World Development Report 2023: Migrants, Refugees, and Societies (April 2023)</ref>

91% of resident households (i.e. households headed by a Singapore citizen or permanent resident) own the homes they live in, and the average household size is 3.43 persons (which include dependants who are neither citizens nor permanent residents).<ref>{{cite web |title=Statistics Singapore – Latest Data – Households & Housing |url=https://www.singstat.gov.sg/find-data/search-by-theme/households/households/latest-data |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250122211547/https://www.singstat.gov.sg/find-data/search-by-theme/households/households/latest-data |archive-date=22 January 2025 |access-date=27 February 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |year=2014 |title=Statistics Singapore – Latest Data – Households & Housing |url=http://www.singstat.gov.sg/statistics/latest-data#20 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151129094649/http://www.singstat.gov.sg/statistics/latest-data#20 |archive-date=29 November 2015 |access-date=20 April 2015 |publisher=Statistics Singapore}}</ref> However, due to scarcity of land, 78.7% of resident households live in [[Public housing in Singapore|subsidised, high-rise, public housing apartments]] developed by the [[Housing and Development Board]] (HDB). Also, 75.9% of resident households live in properties that are equal to, or larger than, a four-room (i.e. three bedrooms plus one living room) HDB flat or in private housing.<ref>{{cite web |title=Singapore Resident Households by dwellings |url=https://www.singstat.gov.sg/modules/infographics/-/media/Files/visualising_data/infographics/Population/singapore-population13022019 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200215160407/https://www.singstat.gov.sg/modules/infographics/-/media/Files/visualising_data/infographics/Population/singapore-population13022019 |archive-date=15 February 2020 |access-date=15 February 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=HDB InfoWEB: HDB Wins the 2010 UN-HABITAT Scroll of Honour Award |url=http://www.hdb.gov.sg/fi10/fi10320p.nsf/w/HDBWinsUNAward?OpenDocument |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111211145036/http://www.hdb.gov.sg/fi10/fi10320p.nsf/w/HDBWinsUNAward?OpenDocument |archive-date=11 December 2011 |access-date=14 October 2013 |publisher=Hdb.gov.sg}}</ref> Live-in foreign [[domestic worker]]s are quite common in Singapore, with about 224,500 foreign domestic workers there, as of December 2013.<ref>{{cite news |date=5 August 2014 |title=More than 1.3&nbsp;million foreigners working in Singapore: Tan Chuan-Jin |url=http://www.channelnewsasia.com/news/singapore/more-than-1-3-million/1297688.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140914232514/http://www.channelnewsasia.com/news/singapore/more-than-1-3-million/1297688.html |archive-date=14 September 2014 |access-date=26 October 2014 |publisher=Channel NewsAsia |location=Singapore}}</ref>

{{Main|Languages of Singapore}}

English is the [[lingua franca]]<ref>{{cite journal |last=Gupta |first=A.F. |title=Epistemic modalities and the discourse particles of Singapore |url=http://www.leeds.ac.uk/english/staff/afg/pragp3.doc |url-status=dead |format=DOC |journal=Approaches to Discourse Particles |location=Amsterdam |publisher=Elsevier |pages=244–263 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110205010214/http://www.leeds.ac.uk/english/staff/afg/pragp3.doc |archive-date=5 February 2011 |access-date=2 February 2011 |editor=Fischer, K.}}</ref><ref name="Dixon" /><ref>{{cite press release |url=http://www.moe.gov.sg/media/speeches/2000/sp31032000a.htm |date=31 March 2000 |title=Global Literacy: The advantage of speaking good English |publisher=Ministry of Education |access-date=27 January 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120306034004/http://www.moe.gov.sg/media/speeches/2000/sp31032000a.htm|archive-date=6 March 2012|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>Tan, Sherman, p. 340–341. "The four recognised official languages are English, Mandarin, Tamil, and Malay, but in practice, English is Singapore's default lingua franca."</ref> and the main language used in business, government, law and education.<ref>{{cite web |date=October 2010 |title=Education UK Partnership&nbsp;– Country focus |url=http://www.britishcouncil.org/eumd-partnership-webzine-october-2010-country-focus.htm#singapore |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110402172957/http://www.britishcouncil.org/eumd-partnership-webzine-october-2010-country-focus.htm |archive-date=2 April 2011 |access-date=27 February 2011 |publisher=[[British Council]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |date=19 April 2010 |title=Speech by Mr S. Iswaran, Senior Minister of State, Ministry of Trade and Industry and Ministry of Education |url=http://www.moe.gov.sg/media/speeches/2010/04/19/speech-by-mr-s-iswaran-at-the-apec-relc-int-seminar-opening-ceremony.php |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110519070557/http://www.moe.gov.sg/media/speeches/2010/04/19/speech-by-mr-s-iswaran-at-the-apec-relc-int-seminar-opening-ceremony.php |archive-date=19 May 2011 |publisher=Ministry of Education}}</ref> The [[Constitution of Singapore]] and all government legislation is written in English, and [[Language interpretation|interpreters]] are required if a language other than English is used in the [[Judicial system of Singapore|Singaporean courts]].<ref>{{cite web |title=What do I do if I can't speak English? |url=http://app.subcourts.gov.sg/criminal/page.aspx?pageid=64541#faq13-9 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100709074333/http://app.subcourts.gov.sg/criminal/page.aspx?pageid=64541 |archive-date=9 July 2010 |access-date=11 October 2011 |publisher=Singapore Subordinate Courts}}</ref><ref name="Singapore Statutes Online" /> [[Statutory corporation]]s conduct their businesses in English, while any official documents written in a non-English official language such as Malay, Mandarin, or Tamil are typically translated into English to be accepted for use.<ref>{{cite web |date=6 January 2015 |title=Public Agencies |url=http://www.careers.gov.sg/the-singapore-public-service/public-agencies |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150106063743/http://www.careers.gov.sg/the-singapore-public-service/public-agencies |archive-date=6 January 2015 |access-date=21 September 2018}}</ref><ref name="Dixon">Dixon, L. Quentin. (2005). The Bilingual Education Policy in Singapore: Implications for Second Language Acquisition. In James Cohen, J., McAlister, K. T., Rolstad, K., and MacSwan, J (Eds.), ''ISB4: Proceedings of the 4th International Symposium on Bilingualism''. p. 625–635, Cascadilla Press, Somerville, MA.</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=31 March 2000 |url=http://www.moe.gov.sg/media/speeches/2000/sp31032000a.htm |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120306034004/http://www.moe.gov.sg/media/speeches/2000/sp31032000a.htm |archive-date=6 March 2012 |access-date=27 January 2011 |publisher=Moe.gov.sg}}</ref>

[[Malay language|Malay]] was designated as a national language by the Singaporean government after independence from Britain in the 1960s to avoid friction with Singapore's Malay-speaking neighbours of Malaysia and Indonesia.<ref name="Lee Kuan Yew-2012" /> It has a symbolic, rather than functional purpose.<ref name="Republic of Singapore Independence Act 1965" /><ref>{{cite book |last1=Afendras |first1=Evangelos A. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=CQgjrpgdU6gC&pg=PA42 |title=Language and society in Singapore |last2=Kuo |first2=Eddie C.Y. |publisher=Singapore University Press |year=1980 |isbn=978-9971-69-016-8 |access-date=27 February 2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Ammon |first1=Ulrich |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=LMZm0w0k1c4C&pg=PA2018 |title=Sociolinguistics: An international handbook of the science of language and society |last2=Dittmar |first2=Norbert |last3=Mattheier |first3=Klaus J. |publisher=Walter de Gruyter |year=2006 |isbn=978-3-11-018418-1 |volume=3 |location=Berlin |access-date=27 February 2011}}</ref> It is used in the national anthem ''[[Majulah Singapura]]'',<ref>{{Singapore legislation |title=Singapore Arms and Flag and National Anthem Act |cap=296 |ed=1985}}</ref> in citations of [[Singaporean orders and decorations]] and in military commands.<ref>{{cite web |title=Literacy and Language |url=http://www.singstat.gov.sg/pubn/papers/people/c2000adr-literacy.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091113162718/http://www.singstat.gov.sg/pubn/papers/people/c2000adr-literacy.pdf |archive-date=13 November 2009 |access-date=27 February 2011 |publisher=Singapore Statistics}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |year=2015 |title=General Household Survey 2015 |url=https://www.singstat.gov.sg/docs/default-source/default-document-library/publications/publications_and_papers/GHS/ghs2015/findings.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171215063843/http://www.singstat.gov.sg/docs/default-source/default-document-library/publications/publications_and_papers/GHS/ghs2015/findings.pdf |archive-date=15 December 2017 |access-date=15 November 2016}}</ref> Singaporean Malay is officially written in the Latin-based [[Rumi script]], though some Singaporean Malays also learn the Arabic-based [[Jawi alphabet|Jawi script]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Cook |first1=Vivian |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=yDLVaYJkyHUC |title=Second Language Writing Systems |last2=Bassetti |first2=Benedetta |date=2005 |publisher=Multilingual Matters |isbn=978-1-85359-793-0 |page=359}}</ref> Jawi is considered an ethnic script for use on Singaporean identity cards.<ref>{{cite web |title=Update Change of Name in IC |url=https://www.ica.gov.sg/page.aspx?pageid=140 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170202101218/https://www.ica.gov.sg/page.aspx?pageid=140 |archive-date=2 February 2017 |access-date=29 January 2017 |publisher=Immigration and Checkpoints Authority}}</ref>

Singaporeans are mostly [[bilingual]], typically with English as their common language and their [[mother-tongue]] as a second language taught in schools, in order to preserve each individual's ethnic identity and values. According to the 2025 census, English was the language most spoken at home, used by 58.1% of the population; Mandarin was next, spoken at home by 26.6%.<ref>{{cite news |date=30 June 2026 |title=More young Singapore residents staying single as family sizes shrink |url=https://www.channelnewsasia.com/singapore/household-survey-singles-married-english-dialect-religion-6220661 |work=[[CNA (TV network)]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Oi |first=Mariko |date=5 October 2010 |title=Singapore's booming appetite to study Mandarin |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/business-11468401 |access-date=27 February 2011 |publisher=BBC News}}</ref> Nearly half a million speak other ancestral Southern [[varieties of Chinese]], mainly [[Hokkien]], [[Teochew dialect|Teochew]], and [[Cantonese]], as their home language, although the use of these is declining in favour of Mandarin or just English.<ref>{{cite web |year=2005 |title=General Household Survey 2005, Statistical Release 1: Socio-Demographic and Economic Characteristics |url=https://www.singstat.gov.sg/find-data/search-by-theme/population/education-language-spoken-and-literacy/visualising-data |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120326052305/http://www.singstat.gov.sg/pubn/popn/ghsr1/chap2.pdf |archive-date=26 March 2012 |access-date=11 November 2010 |publisher=Singapore Statistics}}</ref> [[Singapore Chinese characters]] are [[simplified Chinese characters|simplified characters]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Fagao Zhou |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NEzEo5Y8B3oC |title=Papers in Chinese Linguistics and Epigraphy |date=1986 |publisher=Chinese University Press |isbn=978-962-201-317-9 |page=56 |access-date=31 January 2017}}</ref>

[[Singapore English|Singaporean English]] is largely based on [[British English]], owing to the country's status as a former [[Colony of Singapore|crown colony]].<ref>{{cite web |date=18 April 2008 |title=What are some commonly misspelled English words? |url=http://blogs.nlb.gov.sg/ask/children/481 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120303222846/https://blogs.nlb.gov.sg/ask/children/481 |archive-date=3 March 2012 |access-date=18 February 2011 |publisher=National Library Board |location=Singapore}}</ref> However, forms of English spoken in Singapore range from [[Singapore Standard English|Standard Singapore English]] to a colloquial form known as [[Singlish]], which is discouraged by the government as it claims it to be a "bad language" that handicaps Singaporeans, presenting an obstacle to learning standard English and rendering the speaker incomprehensible to everyone except to another Singlish speaker.<ref>{{cite news |author=Tan Hwee Hwee |date=22 July 2002 |title=A war of words is brewing over Singlish |url=http://www.time.com/time/magazine/article/0,9171,501020729-322685,00.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070429011917/http://www.time.com/time/magazine/article/0,9171,501020729-322685,00.html |archive-date=29 April 2007 |access-date=18 February 2011 |newspaper=Time |location=New York}}</ref> Standard Singapore English is fully understandable to all [[Standard English]] speakers, while most English-speaking people do not understand Singlish. Nevertheless, Singaporeans have a strong sense of identity and connection to Singlish, whereby the existence of Singlish is recognised as a distinctive cultural marker for many Singaporeans.<ref name="Harbeck-2016">{{cite web |last=Harbeck |first=James |date=19 September 2016 |title=The language the government tried to suppress |url=https://www.bbc.com/culture/article/20160919-the-language-the-government-tried-to-suppress |access-date=1 May 2022 |publisher=[[BBC]]}}</ref> As such, in recent times, the government has tolerated the [[diglossia]] of both Singlish and Standard English (only for those who are fluent in both), whilst continuously reinforcing the importance of Standard English amongst those who speak only Singlish (which is not [[Mutual intelligibility|mutually intelligible]] with the Standard English of other [[English-speaking country|English-speaking countries]]).<ref name="Harbeck-2016" />

=== Religion ===
{{Main|Religion in Singapore}}

[[Buddhism in Singapore|Buddhism]] is the most widely practised religion, with 30.9% of residents declaring themselves adherents in the 2020 census. [[Christianity in Singapore|Christianity]] was the second largest religion at 17.1%, followed by [[Islam in Singapore|Islam]] (15.0%), [[Taoism in Singapore|Taoism]] and [[Chinese folk religion|folk beliefs]] (7.3%) and [[Hinduism in Singapore|Hinduism]] (5.4%). Over one-fifth of the population had no religious affiliation.<ref name="Singapore Department of Statistics-2025"/> The proportion of Christians, Muslims, and the nonreligious slightly increased between 2010 and 2020, while the proportion of Buddhists and Taoists slightly decreased; Hinduism and other faiths remained largely stable in their share of the population.<ref>{{Cite news |date=16 June 2021 |title=More S'poreans have no religious affiliation: Population census |url=https://www.straitstimes.com/singapore/more-sporeans-have-no-religious-affiliation-population-census#:~:text=Among%20Singapore%20residents%20aged%2015%20years%20and,share%20of%20Buddhists%20and%20Taoists%20decreased%20slightly. |access-date=8 July 2025 |work=The Straits Times |issn=0585-3923}}</ref><ref>{{cite press release |url=http://www.singstat.gov.sg/news/news/press12012011.pdf |title=Census of population 2010: Statistical Release 1 on Demographic Characteristics, Education, Language and Religion |publisher=Singapore Department of Statistics |date=12 January 2011 |access-date=16 January 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20110124160522/http://www.singstat.gov.sg/news/news/press12012011.pdf |archive-date=24 January 2011}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=16 June 2021 |title=More Singapore residents identifying as having no religion: census |url=https://sg.news.yahoo.com/more-singapore-residents-no-religion-census-064808058.html |access-date=8 July 2025 |website=Yahoo News}}</ref>

Singapore hosts monasteries and [[Dharma]] centres from all three major traditions of Buddhism: [[Theravada]], [[Mahayana]], and [[Vajrayana]]. Most Buddhists in Singapore are Chinese and adhere to the Mahayana tradition,<ref>{{cite book |author=Khun Eng Kuah |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=GBdX2ELnkXQC&pg=PR8 |title=State, society, and religious engineering: toward a reformist Buddhism in Singapore |publisher=Institute of Southeast Asian Studies |year=2009 |isbn=978-981-230-865-8 |location=Singapore |access-date=1 November 2010}}</ref> owing to decades of missionary activity from China. However, [[Buddhism in Thailand|Thailand's Theravada Buddhism]] has seen growing popularity among the populace (not only the Chinese) during the past decade. [[Soka Gakkai International]], a Japanese Buddhist organisation, is practised by many people in Singapore, and mostly by those of Chinese descent. [[Tibetan Buddhism]] has also made slow inroads into the country in recent years.<ref>{{cite news |date=2 December 1995 |title=Modernity in south-east Asia |publisher=Informaworld}}</ref>

=== Education ===
{{Main|Education in Singapore}}

{{See also|List of primary schools in Singapore|List of secondary schools in Singapore|List of universities in Singapore}}
[[File:Singapore University of Technology and Design (SUTD) campus.jpg|thumb|253x253px|[[Singapore University of Technology and Design]] (SUTD) campus]]
Education for primary, secondary, and tertiary levels is mostly supported by the state. All institutions, public and private, must be registered with the [[Ministry of Education (Singapore)|Ministry of Education]] (MOE).<ref>{{cite web |year=2011 |title=Private Education in Singapore |url=http://www.moe.gov.sg/education/private-education/ |access-date=2 July 2011 |publisher=Ministry of Education}}</ref> English is the language of instruction in all public schools,<ref>{{cite web |title=International Student Admissions: General Information on Studying in Singapore |url=http://www.moe.gov.sg/education/admissions/international-students/general-info/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110304134017/http://www.moe.gov.sg/education/admissions/international-students/general-info/ |archive-date=4 March 2011 |access-date=27 February 2011 |publisher=Ministry of Education}}</ref> and all subjects are taught and examined in English except for the "[[mother tongue]]" language paper.<ref>{{cite web |title=ASEAN Scholarships: Frequently Asked Questions |url=http://www.moe.gov.sg/education/scholarships/asean/faq/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080406231811/http://www.moe.gov.sg/education/scholarships/asean/faq/ |archive-date=6 April 2008 |access-date=27 February 2011 |publisher=Ministry of Education}}</ref> While the term "mother tongue" in general refers to the first language internationally, in Singapore's education system, it is used to refer to the second language, as English is the first language.<ref>{{cite press release |url=http://www.moe.gov.sg/media/speeches/2003/sp20030215a.htm |title=Speech by Tharman Shanmugaratnam, Senior Minister of State for Trade & Industry and Education at the Seminar on 'The Significance of Speaking Skills For Language Development', organised by the Tamil Language and Culture Division of Nie on 15 February 2003 |publisher=Ministry of Education |date=2 January 2008|access-date=27 February 2011|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110515193809/http://www.moe.gov.sg/media/speeches/2003/sp20030215a.htm|archive-date=15 May 2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |date=26 June 2010 |title=Mandarin is important but remains a second language in S'pore MM Lee |url=http://www.channelnewsasia.com/stories/singaporelocalnews/view/1065927/1/.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170630180427/http://www.channelnewsasia.com/stories/singaporelocalnews/view/1065927/1/.html |archive-date=30 June 2017 |access-date=27 February 2011 |publisher=Channel NewsAsia |location=Singapore}}</ref> Students who have been abroad for a while, or who struggle with their "Mother Tongue" language, are allowed to take a simpler syllabus or drop the subject.<ref>{{cite web |title=Returning Singaporeans – Mother-Tongue Language Policy |url=http://www.moe.gov.sg/education/admissions/returning-singaporeans/mother-tongue-policy/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080408195106/http://www.moe.gov.sg/education/admissions/returning-singaporeans/mother-tongue-policy/ |archive-date=8 April 2008 |access-date=27 February 2011 |publisher=Ministry of Education}}</ref><ref>{{cite press release |url=http://www.moe.gov.sg/media/press/2004/pr20040109.htm |title=Refinements to Mother Tongue Language Policy |publisher=Ministry of Education|access-date=27 February 2011|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110224021851/http://www.moe.gov.sg/media/press/2004/pr20040109.htm|archive-date=24 February 2011}}</ref>

Education takes place in three stages: primary, secondary, and pre-university education, with the primary education being compulsory. Students begin with six years of primary school, which is made up of a four-year foundation course and a two-year orientation stage. The curriculum is focused on the development of English, the mother tongue, [[mathematics]], and [[natural science|science]].<ref name="Ministry of Education-2011a">{{cite web |year=2011 |title=Primary Education |url=http://www.moe.gov.sg/education/primary/ |access-date=2 July 2011 |publisher=Ministry of Education}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |year=2011 |title=Primary School Curriculum |url=http://www.moe.gov.sg/education/primary/curriculum/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080407095703/http://www.moe.gov.sg/education/primary/curriculum/ |archive-date=7 April 2008 |access-date=2 July 2011 |publisher=Ministry of Education}}</ref> Secondary school lasts from four to five years, and is divided between Express, Normal (Academic), and Normal (Technical) streams in each school, depending on a student's ability level.<ref name="Ministry of Education-2011b">{{cite web |year=2011 |title=Secondary Education |url=http://www.moe.gov.sg/education/secondary/ |access-date=2 July 2011 |publisher=Ministry of Education}}</ref> The basic coursework breakdown is the same as in the primary level, although classes are much more specialised.<ref>{{cite web |year=2011 |title=Special/Express Courses Curriculum |url=http://www.moe.gov.sg/education/secondary/express/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080407202048/http://www.moe.gov.sg/education/secondary/express/ |archive-date=7 April 2008 |access-date=2 July 2011 |publisher=Ministry of Education}}</ref> Pre-university education takes place at either [[Junior college (Singapore)|Junior Colleges]] (JCs) or the [[Millennia Institute]] (MI), over a period of two and three years respectively.<ref>{{cite web |year=2011 |title=Pre-University Education |url=http://www.moe.gov.sg/education/pre-u/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080405194544/http://www.moe.gov.sg/education/pre-u/ |archive-date=5 April 2008 |access-date=2 July 2011 |publisher=Ministry of Education}}</ref> As alternatives to pre-university education, however, courses are offered in other post-secondary education institutions, including at [[Institute of technology#Singapore|polytechnics]] and [[Institute of Technical Education]] (ITE) colleges. Singapore has six public universities,<ref>{{cite news |date=3 March 2015 |title=How Singapore's six public universities differ |url=http://www.straitstimes.com/singapore/education/how-singapores-six-public-universities-differ |access-date=23 September 2016 |newspaper=The Straits Times |location=Singapore}}</ref> of which the [[National University of Singapore]] (NUS) and [[Nanyang Technological University]] (NTU) are among the top 20 universities in the world.<ref>{{cite web |date=11 September 2015 |title=QS World University Rankings 2015/16 |url=http://www.topuniversities.com/university-rankings/world-university-rankings/2015 |access-date=15 November 2016 |publisher=QS}}</ref>

National examinations are standardised across all schools, with a test taken after each stage. After the first six years of education, students take the [[Primary School Leaving Examination]] (PSLE),<ref name="Ministry of Education-2011a" /> which determines their placement at secondary school. At the end of the secondary stage, [[Singapore-Cambridge GCE Ordinary Level|GCE O-Level]] or [[Singapore-Cambridge GCE Normal Level|GCE N-Level]] exams are taken;<ref>{{cite web |title=Secondary |url=https://www.moe.gov.sg/education/secondary |access-date=2 December 2016 |publisher=Ministry of Education}}</ref> at the end of the following pre-university stage, the [[Singapore-Cambridge GCE Advanced Level|GCE A-Level]] exams are taken.<ref>{{cite web |title=Singapore's Education System: An Overview |url=https://www.moe.gov.sg/images/default-source/default-album/sg-education-landscape-print9e3a5a33f22f6eceb9b0ff0000fcc945.jpg |access-date=6 December 2016 |publisher=Ministry of Education}}</ref> Some schools have a degree of freedom in their curriculum and are known as autonomous schools, for [[Secondary education in Singapore|secondary education]] level and above.<ref name="Ministry of Education-2011b" /> Singapore is also an education hub, with more than 80,000 international students in 2006.<ref>{{cite web |year=2011 |title=Developing Asian education hubs |url=http://www.eahep.org/asiahigher-education/asian-policy-drivers/127-developing-asian-education-hubs.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111023215241/http://www.eahep.org/asiahigher-education/asian-policy-drivers/127-developing-asian-education-hubs.html |archive-date=23 October 2011 |access-date=12 October 2011 |publisher=EU-Asia Higher Education Platform}}</ref> 5,000 Malaysian students cross the [[Johor–Singapore Causeway]] daily to attend schools in Singapore.<ref>{{cite news |date=7 May 2006 |title=The long, long ride |work=New Straits Times |location=Kuala Lumpur}} [http://jaring.general.narkive.com/l1ulIlar/the-long-long-ride Alt URL] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260228175943/https://jaring.general.narkive.com/l1ulIlar/the-long-long-ride |date=28 February 2026 }}</ref> In 2009, 20% of all students in Singaporean universities were international students—the maximum cap allowed, a majority from [[ASEAN]], China and India.<ref>{{cite web |year=2011 |title=Foreign Students in Singapore |url=http://www.moe.gov.sg/media/parliamentary-replies/2009/03/foreign-students-in-singapore.php |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090409150704/http://www.moe.gov.sg/media/parliamentary-replies/2009/03/foreign-students-in-singapore.php |archive-date=9 April 2009 |access-date=12 October 2011 |publisher=Ministry of Education}}</ref>

Singapore students have excelled in many of the world education benchmarks in maths, science and reading. In 2015, both its primary and secondary students rank first in [[Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development|OECD]]'s global school performance rankings across 76 countries—described as the most comprehensive map of education standards.<ref>{{cite news |date=13 May 2015 |title=Singapore tops OECD's global school ranking, US placed 28th |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2015/05/13/singapore-tops-oecds-global-school-ranking-us-placed-28th.html |publisher=CNBC}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |date=13 May 2015 |title=Singapore tops biggest global education rankings published by OECD |url=http://www.straitstimes.com/singapore/education/singapore-tops-biggest-global-education-rankings-published-by-oecd |newspaper=The Straits Times |location=Singapore}}</ref> In 2016, Singapore students topped both the [[Programme for International Student Assessment]] (PISA)<ref>{{cite news |date=7 December 2016 |title=Pisa tests: Singapore top in global education rankings |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/education-38212070 |publisher=BBC News}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |date=6 December 2016 |title=PISA: Singapore teens top global education ranking |url=https://edition.cnn.com/2016/12/06/world/pisa-global-education-rankings/ |publisher=CNN}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |date=22 July 2016 |title=Why Singapore's kids are so good at maths |url=https://www.ft.com/content/2e4c61f2-4ec8-11e6-8172-e39ecd3b86fc |url-access=subscription |url-status=live |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20221210/https://www.ft.com/content/2e4c61f2-4ec8-11e6-8172-e39ecd3b86fc |archive-date=10 December 2022 |work=Financial Times |location=London}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |date=6 December 2016 |title=S'pore students top in science, maths and reading in Pisa test |url=http://www.todayonline.com/singapore/spore-teens-top-second-global-test-maths-science-reading |newspaper=Today |location=Singapore}}</ref> and the [[Trends in International Mathematics and Science Study]] (TIMSS).<ref>{{cite news |date=6 December 2016 |title=Singapore students top in maths, science and reading in Pisa international benchmarking test |url=http://www.straitstimes.com/singapore/education/singapore-students-top-in-maths-science-and-reading-in-international |work=The Straits Times |location=Singapore}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |date=6 |work=The Guardian |location=London}}</ref> In the 2016 EF English Proficiency Index taken in 72 countries, Singapore placed 6th and has been the only Asian country in the top 10.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Nylander |first=Johan |date=14 November 2016 |title=Singaporeans among top English speakers; Hong Kong slides |url=https://asiatimes.com/article/singaporeans-among-top-english-speakers-hong-kong-slides/ |access-date=16 November 2016 |newspaper=Asia Times Online |location=Hong Kong}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170713204753/http://nordic.businessinsider.com/the-nordics-have-the-highest-english-proficiency-in-the-world---and-its-boosting-their-tech-and-innovation-2016-11
