In the United States, eighteen states require the clinician to be physically present during the administration of medications for abortion which effectively bans telehealth of medication abortion: five states explicitly ban telemedicine for medication abortion, while thirteen states require the prescriber (usually required to be a physician) to be physically present with the patient.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Jones RK, Jerman J | title = Abortion Incidence and Service Availability In the United States, 2014 | journal = Perspectives on Sexual and Reproductive Health | volume = 49 | issue = 1 | pages = 17–27 | date = March 2017 | pmid = 28094905 | pmc = 5487028 | doi = 10.1363/2019.30760 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|date=2020-06-08|title=Medication Abortion and Telemedicine: Innovations and Barriers During the COVID-19 Emergency|url=https://www.kff.org/policy-watch/medication-abortion-telemedicine-innovations-and-barriers-during-the-covid-19-emergency/|access-date=2020-08-03|website=KFF|language=en-US}}</ref> In the UK, the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists approved a no-test protocol for medication abortion, with mifepristone available through a minimal-contact pick-up or by mail.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Coronavirus (COVID-19) infection and abortion care|url=https://www.rcog.org.uk/en/guidelines-research-services/guidelines/coronavirus-abortion/|access-date=2020-08-03|website=Royal College of Obstetricians & Gynaecologists|language=en-US}}</ref>

===Other specialist care delivery===
Telemedicine can facilitate specialty care delivered by [[primary care physician]]s according to a controlled study of the treatment of [[hepatitis C]].<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Arora S, Thornton K, Murata G, Deming P, Kalishman S, Dion D, Parish B, Burke T, Pak W, Dunkelberg J, Kistin M, Brown J, Jenkusky S, Komaromy M, Qualls C | title = Outcomes of treatment for hepatitis C virus infection by primary care providers | journal = The New England Journal of Medicine | volume = 364 | issue = 23 | pages = 2199–2207 | date = June 2011 | pmid = 21631316 | pmc = 3820419 | doi = 10.1056/NEJMoa1009370 }}</ref> Various specialties are contributing to telemedicine, in varying degrees.Other specialist conditions for which telemedicine has been used include perinatal mental health.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sun |first1=Yaoyao |last2=Li |first2=Yanyan |last3=Wang |first3=Juan |last4=Chen |first4=Qingyi |last5=Bazzano |first5=Alessandra N |last6=Cao |first6=Fenglin |title=Effectiveness of Smartphone-Based Mindfulness Training on Maternal Perinatal Depression: Randomized Controlled Trial |journal=Journal of Medical Internet Research |date=27 January 2021 |volume=23 |issue=1 |article-number=e23410 |doi=10.2196/23410 |doi-access=free |pmid=33502326 |pmc=7875700 }}</ref>

In light of the COVID-19 pandemic, primary care physicians have relied on telehealth to continue to provide care in outpatient settings.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.cdc.gov/coronavirus/2019-ncov/hcp/telehealth.html|title = Healthcare Workers|date = 11 February 2020}}</ref> The transition to virtual health has been beneficial in providing patients access to care (especially care that does not require a physical exam e.g. medication changes, minor health updates) and avoid putting patients at risk of COVID-19. This included providing services to pediatric patients during the pandemic, where issues of last minute cancelation and rescheduling were frequently related to a lack of technicality and engagement, two factors often understudied in the literature.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sezgin |first1=Emre |last2=Huang |first2=Yungui |last3=Lin |first3=Deborah |last4=Ramtekkar |first4=Ujjwal |last5=Pauline |first5=Lindsey |last6=Lin |first6=Simon |title=Documented Reasons of Cancellation and Rescheduling of Telehealth Appointments During the Pandemic |journal=Telemedicine and e-Health |date=October 2021 |volume=27 |issue=10 |pages=1143–1150 |doi=10.1089/tmj.2020.0454 |pmid=33373553 }}</ref>

Telemedicine has also been beneficial in facilitating medical education to students while still allowing for adequate social distancing during the COVID-19 pandemic. Many medical schools have shifted to alternate forms of virtual curriculum and are still able to engage in meaningful telehealth encounters with patients.<ref>{{cite report |type=Preprint |doi=10.35542/osf.io/9urcd |title=Designing Virtual Medical Student Ambulatory Rotations in Light of the Coronavirus Pandemic: A Pilot Project |last1=Louis |first1=Shreya |last2=Isaacson |first2=J. Harry |last3=Yepes-Rios |first3=Monica |last4=Mehta |first4=Neil }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | vauthors = Murphy B | date = 17 September 2020 | title = How Medical Students are Innovating During COVID-19 | url = https://www.ama-assn.org/residents-students/medical-school-life/how-medical-students-are-innovating-during-covid-19 | publisher = American Medical Association }}</ref>

Medication assisted treatment (MAT) is the treatment of [[opioid use disorder]] (OUD) with medications, often in combination with behavioral therapy<ref name="Medication Assisted Treatment (MAT)">{{cite web |title=Information on Medication-Assisted Treatment (MAT) |url=https://www.samhsa.gov/medication-assisted-treatment |website=SAMHSA|date=21 July 2015 }}</ref> As a response to the COVID-19 pandemic the use of telemedicine has been granted by the [[Drug Enforcement Administration]] to start or maintain people OUD on [[buprenorphine]] (trade name Suboxone) via [[telemedicine]] without the need for an initial in-person examination.<ref>{{cite web |title=Use of Telephone Evaluations to Initiate Buprenorphine Prescribing |url=https://www.deadiversion.usdoj.gov/GDP/(DEA-DC-022)(DEA068)%20DEA%20SAMHSA%20buprenorphine%20telemedicine%20%20(Final)%20+Esign.pdf |website=DEA Information Page}}</ref> On March 31, 2020, [[QuickMD]] became the first national [[TeleMAT]] service in the United States to provide Medication-assisted Treatment with Suboxone online – without the need of an in-person visit; with others announcing to follow soon.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Jane |date=2020-07-21 |title=I am Addicted to Opioids and in my Desperation I Turned to the Internet — Here is What happened |url=https://medium.com/@jane1/how-i-beat-my-opioid-addiction-online-suboxone-quickmd-telemat-medication-assisted-treatment-buprenorphine-7d459d14f59e |access-date=2020-07-22 |website=Medium |language=en}}</ref>

== Major developments ==

=== In policy ===
Telehealth is a modern form of health care delivery. Telehealth breaks away from traditional health care delivery by using modern telecommunication systems including wireless communication methods.<ref>{{cite thesis |last1=Altharthi |first1=Mansour Saeed |title=Telehealth practice in eight countries: New Zealand, Australia, the USA, Canada, UK, Malaysia, China and India: a thesis presented in partial fulfillment of the requirements of degree of Master in Information Science at Massey University, Albany campus, Auckland, New Zealand |date=2012 |hdl=10179/3538 |hdl-access=free |oclc=1085527078 }}{{pn|date=July 2025}}</ref><ref name="García-Rojo-2016">{{cite journal | vauthors = García-Rojo M | title = International Clinical Guidelines for the Adoption of Digital Pathology: A Review of Technical Aspects | journal = Pathobiology | volume = 83 | issue = 2–3 | pages = 99–109 | pmid = 27100834 | doi = 10.1159/000441192 | year = 2016 | doi-access = free }}</ref> Traditional health is legislated through policy to ensure the safety of medical practitioners and patients. Consequently, since telehealth is a new form of health care delivery that is now gathering momentum in the health sector, many organizations have started to legislate the use of telehealth into policy.<ref name="García-Rojo-2016" /> In New Zealand, the Medical Council has a statement about telehealth on their website. This illustrates that the medical council has foreseen the importance that telehealth will have on the health system and have started to introduce telehealth legislation to practitioners along with government.<ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.mcnz.org.nz/assets/News-and-Publications/Statement-on-telehealthv3.pdf |title=Statement on telehealth | date=2013 |publisher=Medical Council of New Zealand }}</ref>

=== Transition to mainstream ===
{{See also|Remote patient monitoring}}

Traditional use of telehealth services has been for specialist treatment. However, there has been a paradigm shift and telehealth is no longer considered a specialist service.<ref>{{cite thesis |last1=Lucas |first1=Julie Anne |title=Clinicians' Perceptions of Telemedicine: Opportunities and Barriers for Emergency Medicine |date=2013 |hdl=2292/20430 |hdl-access=free }}{{pn|date=July 2025}}</ref> This development has ensured that many access barriers are eliminated, as medical professionals and patients are able to use wireless communication technologies to deliver health care.<ref name="Bazzano-2024">{{Cite journal |last1=Bazzano |first1=Alessandra N. |last2=Patel |first2=Tejal |last3=Nauman |first3=Elizabeth |last4=Cernigliaro |first4=Dana |last5=Shi |first5=Lizheng |date=2024-01-01 |title=Optimizing Telehealth for Diabetes Management in the Deep South of the United States: Qualitative Study of Barriers and Facilitators on the Patient and Clinician Journey |journal=Journal of Medical Internet Research |language=EN |volume=26 |issue=1 |article-number=e43583 |doi=10.2196/43583|doi-access=free |pmid=37976468 |pmc=10790202 }}</ref> This is evident in [[Rural health|rural communities]]. Rural residents typically have to travel to longer distances to access healthcare than urban counterparts due to physician shortages and healthcare facility closures in these areas.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Transportation to Support Rural Healthcare Overview - Rural Health Information Hub |url=https://www.ruralhealthinfo.org/topics/transportation#travel-burdens |access-date=2024-04-14 |website=www.ruralhealthinfo.org |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Healthcare Access in Rural Communities Overview - Rural Health Information Hub |url=https://www.ruralhealthinfo.org/topics/healthcare-access |access-date=2024-04-14 |website=www.ruralhealthinfo.org |language=en}}</ref> Telehealth eliminates this barrier as health professionals are able to conduct medical consultations through the use of wireless communication technologies. However, this process is dependent on both parties having internet access and comfort level with technology, which poses barriers for many low-income and rural communities.<ref name="Bazzano-2024" /><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Possemato K, Bishop TM, Willis MA, Lantinga LJ | title = Healthcare utilization and symptom variation among veterans using Behavioral Telehealth Center services | journal = The Journal of Behavioral Health Services & Research | volume = 40 | issue = 4 | pages = 416–26 | date = October 2013 | pmid = 23616251 | doi = 10.1007/s11414-013-9338-y }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Darkins A, Foster L, Anderson C, Goldschmidt L, Selvin G | title = The design, implementation, and operational management of a comprehensive quality management program to support national telehealth networks | journal = Telemedicine Journal and e-Health | volume = 19 | issue = 7 | pages = 557–64 | date = July 2013 | pmid = 23705961 | doi = 10.1089/tmj.2012.0263 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Telehealth and Health Information Technology in Rural Healthcare Overview - Rural Health Information Hub |url=https://www.ruralhealthinfo.org/topics/telehealth-health-it#:~:text=Challenges%20for%20providing%20telehealth%20services,and%20access%20to%20broadband%20services. |access-date=2024-04-14 |website=www.ruralhealthinfo.org |language=en}}</ref>

Telehealth allows the patient to be monitored between physician office visits which can improve patient health. Telehealth also allows patients to access expertise which is not available in their local area. This remote patient monitoring ability enables patients to stay at home longer and helps avoid unnecessary hospital time. In the long-term, this could potentially result in less burdening of the healthcare system and consumption of resources.<ref name="Office for the Advancement of Telehealth-2022" /><ref name="Maheu-2002" />

During the COVID-19 pandemic, there were large increases in the use of telemedicine for primary care visits within the United States, increasing from an average of 1.4 million visits in Q2 of 2018 and 2019 to 35 million visits in Q2 2020, according to data from [[IQVIA]].<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Alexander GC, Tajanlangit M, Heyward J, Mansour O, Qato DM, Stafford RS | title = Use and Content of Primary Care Office-Based vs Telemedicine Care Visits During the COVID-19 Pandemic in the US | journal = JAMA Network Open | volume = 3 | issue = 10 | pages = e2021476 | date = October 2020 | pmid = 33006622 | pmc = 7532385 | doi = 10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2020.21476  | doi-access = free}}</ref> The telehealth market is expected to grow at 40% a year in 2021. Use of telemedicine by General Practitioners in the UK rose from 20 to 30% pre-COVID to almost 80% by the beginning of 2021. More than 70% of practitioners and patients were satisfied with this.<ref>{{cite news |title=Telemedicine is here to stay |url=https://www.buildingbetterhealthcare.com/news/article_page/Telemedicine_is_here_to_stay/178218/cn164706 |access-date=26 September 2021 |publisher=Building Better Healthcare |date=11 August 2021}}</ref> [[Boris Johnson]] was said to have "piled pressure on GPs to offer more in-person consultations" supporting a campaign largely orchestrated by the ''[[Daily Mail]]''. The [[Royal College of General Practitioners]] said that a patient "right" to have face-to-face appointments if they wish was "undeliverable".<ref>{{cite news |title=Prime Minister says GPs should see patients face to face |url=https://www.pulsetoday.co.uk/news/breaking-news/prime-minister-says-gps-should-see-patients-face-to-face/ |access-date=26 September 2021 |publisher=Pulse |date=21 September 2021}}</ref>

=== Technology advancement ===
{{See also|Technology|Emerging technologies}}

The technological advancement of wireless communication devices is a major development in telehealth.<ref name="Vockley-2015">{{cite journal | vauthors = Vockley M | title = The Rise of Telehealth: 'Triple Aim,' Innovative Technology, and Popular Demand Are Spearheading New Models of Health and Wellness Care | journal = Biomedical Instrumentation & Technology | volume = 49 | issue = 5 | pages = 306–20 | date = 2015-10-01 | pmid = 26443907 | doi = 10.2345/0899-8205-49.5.306 }}</ref> This allows patients to self-monitor their health conditions and to not rely as much on health care professionals. Furthermore, patients are more willing to stay on their treatment plans as they are more invested and included in the process as the decision-making is shared.<ref name="Kvedar-2014">{{cite journal | vauthors = Kvedar J, Coye MJ, Everett W | title = Connected health: a review of technologies and strategies to improve patient care with telemedicine and telehealth | journal = Health Affairs | volume = 33 | issue = 2 | pages = 194–9 | date = February 2014 | pmid = 24493760 | doi = 10.1377/hlthaff.2013.0992 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref name="Hirani-2017">{{cite journal |last1=Hirani |first1=Shashivadan P |last2=Rixon |first2=Lorna |last3=Beynon |first3=Michelle |last4=Cartwright |first4=Martin |last5=Cleanthous |first5=Sophie |last6=Selva |first6=Abi |last7=Sanders |first7=Caroline |last8=Newman |first8=Stanton P |last9=WSD |first9=investigators |title=Quantifying beliefs regarding telehealth: Development of the Whole Systems Demonstrator Service User Technology Acceptability Questionnaire |journal=Journal of Telemedicine and Telecare |date=May 2017 |volume=23 |issue=4 |pages=460–469 |doi=10.1177/1357633X16649531 |pmid=27224997 }}</ref> Technological advancement also means that health care professionals are able to use better technologies to treat patients for example in maternal care<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Cantor AG, Jungbauer RM, Totten AM, Tilden EL, Holmes R, Ahmed A, Wagner J, Hermesch AC, McDonagh MS | title = Telehealth Strategies for the Delivery of Maternal Health Care: A Rapid Review | journal = Annals of Internal Medicine | volume = 175 | issue = 9 | pages = 1285–1297 | date = September 2022 | pmid = 35878405 | doi = 10.7326/M22-0737 }}</ref> and [[surgery]]. A 2023 study published in the ''[[Journal of the American College of Surgeons]]'' showed telemedicine as making a positive impact, with expectations exceeded for those physicians and patients who had consulted online for surgeries.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.medicaleconomics.com/view/telemedicine-better-than-expected-for-consulting-on-surgeries|author=Richard Payerchin|title=Telemedicine better than expected for consulting on surgeries|website=Medical Economics|date=January 20, 2023}}</ref> Technological developments in telehealth are essential to improve health care, especially the delivery of healthcare services, as resources are finite along with an ageing population that is living longer.<ref name="Vockley-2015" /><ref name="Kvedar-2014" /><ref name="Hirani-2017" />

== Licensing ==
=== U.S. licensing and regulatory issues ===
Restrictive licensure laws in the United States require a practitioner to obtain a full license to deliver telemedicine care across state lines. Typically, states with restrictive licensure laws also have several exceptions (varying from state to state) that may release an out-of-state practitioner from the additional burden of obtaining such a license. A number of states require practitioners who seek compensation to frequently deliver interstate care to acquire a full license.

If a practitioner serves several states, obtaining this license in each state could be an expensive and time-consuming proposition. Even if the practitioner never practices medicine face-to-face with a patient in another state, he/she still must meet a variety of other individual state requirements, including paying substantial licensure fees, passing additional oral and written examinations, and traveling for interviews.

In 2008, the U.S. passed the Ryan Haight Act which required face-to-face or valid telemedicine consultations prior to receiving a prescription.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.govtech.com/health/Ryan-Haight-Act-will.html|title=Ryan Haight Act will Require Tighter Restrictions on Internet Pharmacies|website=www.govtech.com|date=27 July 2010|access-date=7 March 2016}}</ref>

[[:Category:Medical licensing boards in the United States|State medical licensing boards]] have sometimes opposed telemedicine; for example, in 2012 electronic consultations were illegal in Idaho, and an Idaho-licensed general practitioner was punished by the board for prescribing an antibiotic, triggering reviews of her licensure and board certifications across the country.<ref name=":0b">{{cite web|url=http://www.spokesman.com/stories/2015/aug/22/telemedicine-sanction-in-idaho-clouds-doctors/|title=Telemedicine sanction in Idaho clouds doctor's future|website=Spokesman.com|access-date=7 March 2016}}</ref> Subsequently, in 2015 the state legislature legalized electronic consultations.<ref name=":0b" />

In 2015, Teladoc filed suit against the [[Texas Medical Board]] over a rule that required in-person consultations initially; the judge refused to dismiss the case, noting that antitrust laws apply to state medical boards.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.modernhealthcare.com/article/20151214/NEWS/151219924|title=Teladoc case against Texas Medical Board will move forward, judge rules|website=Modern Healthcare|date=14 December 2015|access-date=7 March 2016}}</ref>

=== EU licensing and regulatory issues ===
In the European Union, telemedicine service providers are primarily subject to the regulatory requirements that apply at their place of establishment (country of origin principle).<ref>{{cite SSRN |last1=Hahn |first1=Erik |last2=Liddell |first2=Kathleen |last3=Aboy |first3=Mateo |last4=Cohen |first4=I. Glenn |title=Cross-border telemedicine - A reason to 'smile'? also comment on ECJ, judgment of 11 September 2025 -C-115/24 (UJ/Austrian Dental Association) |date=24 November 2025 |ssrn=5798224 |ssrn-access=free}}</ref>

== Major implications and impacts ==
Telehealth allows multiple, varying disciplines to merge and deliver a potentially more uniform level of care, using technology. As telehealth proliferates mainstream healthcare, it challenges notions of traditional healthcare delivery. Some populations experience better quality, access and more personalized health care.<ref name="Elsevier-2012">{{Cite book|title=Telemental Health: Clinical, Technical, and Administrative Foundations for Evidence-Based Practice|date=2012-09-20|publisher=Elsevier|isbn=978-0-12-416048-4 | veditors = Myers K, Turvey C |edition=1  }}</ref><ref name="Umefjord-2006">{{cite thesis |last1=Umefjord |first1=Göran |title=Internet consultation in medicine: studies of a text-based Ask the doctor service |date=2006 |url=https://urn.kb.se/resolve?urn=urn:nbn:se:umu:diva-854 }}{{pn|date=July 2025}}</ref>

=== Health promotion ===
{{See also|Health promotion}} [[File:SmallWorldSocial BreastfeedingSupportProject GeorgiawithBabyEve.jpg|thumb|Baby Eve with Georgia for the Breastfeeding Support Project]]Telehealth can also increase health promotion efforts. These efforts can now be more personalised to the target population and professionals can extend their help into homes or private and safe environments in which patients of individuals can practice, ask and gain health information.<ref name="Maheu-2002" /><ref name="Hirani-2017" /><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Kahn JM | title = Virtual visits--confronting the challenges of telemedicine | journal = The New England Journal of Medicine | volume = 372 | issue = 18 | pages = 1684–1685 | date = April 2015 | pmid = 25923547 | doi = 10.1056/NEJMp1500533 }}</ref> Health promotion using telehealth has become increasingly popular in [[Developing country|underdeveloped countries]] where there are very poor physical resources available. There has been a particular push toward [[mHealth]] applications as many areas, even underdeveloped ones have mobile phone and smartphone coverage.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Goggin |first1=Gerard |title=Cell Phone Culture: Mobile Technology in Everyday Life |date=2006 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-36743-1 }}{{pn|date=July 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Donner |first1=Jonathan |last2=Mechael |first2=Patricia |title=MHealth in Practice: Mobile Technology for Health Promotion in the Developing World |date=2013 |publisher=A&C Black |isbn=978-1-78093-229-3 }}{{pn|date=July 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Ben-Zeev D, Brian RM, Jonathan G, Razzano L, Pashka N, Carpenter-Song E, Drake RE, Scherer EA | title = Mobile Health (mHealth) Versus Clinic-Based Group Intervention for People With Serious Mental Illness: A Randomized Controlled Trial | journal = Psychiatric Services | volume = 69 | issue = 9 | pages = 978–985 | date = September 2018 | pmid = 29793397 | doi = 10.1176/appi.ps.201800063 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

In a 2015 article reviewing research on the use of a mobile health application in the United Kingdom,<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Hardinge M, Rutter H, Velardo C, Shah SA, Williams V, Tarassenko L, Farmer A | title = Using a mobile health application to support self-management in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: a six-month cohort study | journal = BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making | volume = 15 | issue = 1 | article-number = 46 | date = June 2015 | pmid = 26084626 | pmc = 4472616 | doi = 10.1186/s12911-015-0171-5 | doi-access = free }}</ref> authors describe how a home-based application helped patients manage and monitor their health and symptoms independently. The mobile health application allows people to rapidly self-report their symptoms – 95% of patients were able to report their daily symptoms in less than 100 seconds, which is less than the 5 minutes (plus commuting) taken to measure vital signs by nurses in hospitals.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Dall'Ora C, Griffiths P, Hope J, Briggs J, Jeremy J, Gerry S, Redfern OC | title = How long do nursing staff take to measure and record patients' vital signs observations in hospital? A time-and-motion study | journal = International Journal of Nursing Studies | volume = 118 | article-number = 103921 | date = June 2021 | pmid = 33812297 | pmc = 8249906 | doi = 10.1016/j.ijnurstu.2021.103921 }}</ref> Online applications allow patients to remain at home to keep track of the progression of their chronic illnesses. The downside of using mHealth applications is that not everyone, especially in developing countries, has daily access to internet or electronic devices.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-11-29 |title=Facts and Figures 2021: 2.9 billion people still offline |url=https://www.itu.int/hub/2021/11/facts-and-figures-2021-2-9-billion-people-still-offline/ |access-date=2022-05-10 |website=ITU Hub |language=en-US}}</ref>

In [[Developed country|developed countries]], health promotion efforts using telehealth have been met with some success. The [[Google Glass breastfeeding app trial|Australian hands-free breastfeeding Google Glass application]] reported promising results in 2014. This application made in collaboration with the Australian Breastfeeding Association and a tech startup called [[Small World Social]], helped new mothers learn how to [[Breastfeeding|breastfeed]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.hlntv.com/article/2014/04/23/breastfeeding-google-glass-app?sr=fb042414breastfeed10photolink|title=Google Glass can help you breastfeed | date=2014|publisher=HLN Staff}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.breastfeeding.asn.au/breastfeeding-and-google-glass-application-trial|title=Breastfeeding and Google Glass application trial|work=Australian Breastfeeding Association |date=2016|publisher=The Australian Breastfeeding Association|access-date=2016-06-16|archive-date=2019-04-10|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190410075803/https://www.breastfeeding.asn.au/breastfeeding-and-google-glass-application-trial}}</ref><ref name="SWS Website-2015">{{Cite web|url=https://www.smallworldsocial.com/breastfeeding-support-project/|title=Breastfeeding Support Program Through Google Glass |work=SWS Website | date=2015|publisher=Small World}}</ref> Breastfeeding is beneficial to infant health and [[maternal health]] and is recommended by the [[World Health Organization|World Health Organisation]] and health organisations all over the world.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Horta |first1=Bernardo L. |last2=Bahl |first2=Rajiv |last3=Martinés |first3=José Carlos |last4=Victora |first4=Cesar G. |last5=Organization |first5=World Health |title=Evidence on the long-term effects of breastfeeding: systematic review and meta-analyses. |date=2007 |publisher=World Health Organization |isbn=978-92-4-159523-0 |hdl=10665/43623 |hdl-access=free }}{{pn|date=July 2025}}</ref><ref name="Victora-2016">{{cite journal | vauthors = Victora CG, Bahl R, Barros AJ, França GV, Horton S, Krasevec J, Murch S, Sankar MJ, Walker N, Rollins NC | title = Breastfeeding in the 21st century: epidemiology, mechanisms, and lifelong effect | journal = Lancet | volume = 387 | issue = 10017 | pages = 475–490 | date = January 2016 | pmid = 26869575 | doi = 10.1016/S0140-6736(15)01024-7 | doi-access = free | hdl = 10072/413175 | hdl-access = free }}</ref> Widespread breastfeeding can prevent 820,000 infant deaths globally but the practice is often stopped prematurely or intents to do are disrupted due to lack of social support, know-how or other factors.<ref name="Victora-2016" /> This application gave mother's hands-free information on breastfeeding, instructions on how to breastfeed and also had an option to call a lactation consultant over Google Hangout. When the trial ended, all participants were reported to be confident in breastfeeding.<ref name="SWS Website-2015" />

=== Health care quality and barriers to adoption ===
{{See also|Health care quality}}

A [[scientific review]] indicates that, in general, outcomes of telemedicine are or can be as good as in-person care with health care use staying similar.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Albritton J, Ortiz A, Wines R, Booth G, DiBello M, Brown S, Gartlehner G, Crotty K | title = Video Teleconferencing for Disease Prevention, Diagnosis, and Treatment: A Rapid Review | journal = Annals of Internal Medicine | volume = 175 | issue = 2 | pages = 256–266 | date = February 2022 | pmid = 34871056 | doi = 10.7326/m21-3511 }}</ref>

[[File:Diagnosis By Radio, 1925 (telemedicine).webp|thumb|Telemedicine as predicted in 1925<ref>{{cite web | vauthors = Novak M |title=Telemedicine Predicted in 1925 |url=https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/telemedicine-predicted-in-1925-124140942/ |website=Smithsonian Magazine |access-date=1 February 2022 |language=en}}</ref>]]
Advantages of the nonexclusive adoption of already existing telemedicine technologies such as smartphone [[videotelephony]] may include reduced infection risks,<ref name="COVID-19 Reducing the Risks: Teleme">{{cite journal | vauthors = Gillman-Wells CC, Sankar TK, Vadodaria S | title = COVID-19 Reducing the Risks: Telemedicine is the New Norm for Surgical Consultations and Communications | journal = Aesthetic Plastic Surgery | volume = 45 | issue = 1 | pages = 343–348 | date = February 2021 | pmid = 32885319 | pmc = 7471549 | doi = 10.1007/s00266-020-01907-8 }}</ref> increased control of disease during epidemic conditions,<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Monaghesh E, Hajizadeh A | title = The role of telehealth during COVID-19 outbreak: a systematic review based on current evidence | journal = BMC Public Health | volume = 20 | issue = 1 | article-number = 1193 | date = August 2020 | pmid = 32738884 | pmc = 7395209 | doi = 10.1186/s12889-020-09301-4 | doi-access = free }}</ref> improved access to care,<ref name="aafp-tele">{{cite web |title=Telehealth Key to Maintaining Access to Addiction Recovery |url=https://www.aafp.org/news/opinion/20220111guested-telemedsud.html |website=www.aafp.org |access-date=27 January 2022}}</ref> reduced stress and exposure to other pathogens<ref name="10.1016/j.jaip.2020.03.008">{{cite journal | vauthors = Portnoy J, Waller M, Elliott T | title = Telemedicine in the Era of COVID-19 | journal = The Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology. In Practice | volume = 8 | issue = 5 | pages = 1489–1491 | date = May 2020 | pmid = 32220575 | pmc = 7104202 | doi = 10.1016/j.jaip.2020.03.008 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Benefits of Telemedicine |url=https://www.hopkinsmedicine.org/health/treatment-tests-and-therapies/Benefits-of-Telemedicine |website=www.hopkinsmedicine.org |date=18 January 2022 |access-date=1 February 2022 |language=en}}</ref> during illness for better recovery, reduced time<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Molfenter T, Boyle M, Holloway D, Zwick J | title = Trends in telemedicine use in addiction treatment | journal = Addiction Science & Clinical Practice | volume = 10 | issue = 1 | article-number = 14 | date = May 2015 | pmid = 26016484 | pmc = 4636787 | doi = 10.1186/s13722-015-0035-4 | doi-access = free }}</ref> and labor costs, efficient more accessible matching of patients with particular symptoms and clinicians who are experts for such, and reduced travel while disadvantages may include privacy breaches (e.g. due to software backdoors and vulnerabilities or sale of data), dependability on Internet access<ref name="COVID-19 Reducing the Risks: Teleme"/> and, depending on various factors, increased health care use.{{additional citation needed|date=January 2022}}

Theoretically, the whole health system could benefit from telehealth. There are indications telehealth consumes fewer resources and requires fewer people to operate it with shorter training periods to implement initiatives.<ref name="The Center for Connected Health Policy" /> Commenters suggested that lawmakers may fear that making telehealth widely accessible, without any other measures, would lead to patients using unnecessary health care services.<ref name="aafp-tele"/> Telemedicine could also be used for connected networks between health care professionals.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Hyder MA, Razzak J | title = Telemedicine in the United States: An Introduction for Students and Residents | journal = Journal of Medical Internet Research | volume = 22 | issue = 11 | article-number = e20839 | date = November 2020 | pmid = 33215999 | pmc = 7690251 | doi = 10.2196/20839 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

Telemedicine also can eliminate the possible transmission of [[infectious disease]]s or [[parasite]]s between patients and medical staff. This is particularly an issue where [[MRSA]] is a concern. Additionally, some patients who feel uncomfortable in a doctors office may do better remotely. For example, [[white coat syndrome]] may be avoided. Patients who are home-bound and would otherwise require an ambulance to move them to a clinic are also a consideration.

However, whether or not the standard of health care quality is increasing is debatable, with some literature refuting such claims.<ref name="Umefjord-2006" /><ref name="Bardsley-2013">{{cite journal | vauthors = Bardsley M, Steventon A, Doll H | title = Impact of telehealth on general practice contacts: findings from the whole systems demonstrator cluster randomised trial | journal = BMC Health Services Research | volume = 13 | article-number = 395 | date = October 2013 | pmid = 24099334 | pmc = 3852608 | doi = 10.1186/1472-6963-13-395 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref name="pmid23444424">{{cite journal | vauthors = Cartwright M, Hirani SP, Rixon L, Beynon M, Doll H, Bower P, Bardsley M, Steventon A, Knapp M, Henderson C, Rogers A, Sanders C, Fitzpatrick R, Barlow J, Newman SP | title = Effect of telehealth on quality of life and psychological outcomes over 12 months (Whole Systems Demonstrator telehealth questionnaire study): nested study of patient reported outcomes in a pragmatic, cluster randomised controlled trial | journal = BMJ | volume = 346 | pages = f653 | date = February 2013 | pmid = 23444424 | pmc = 3582704 | doi = 10.1136/bmj.f653 }}</ref> Research has reported that clinicians find the process difficult and complex to deal with.<ref name="Bardsley-2013" /><ref name="pmid22834978">{{cite journal | vauthors = Sanders C, Rogers A, Bowen R, Bower P, Hirani S, Cartwright M, Fitzpatrick R, Knapp M, Barlow J, Hendy J, Chrysanthaki T, Bardsley M, Newman SP | title = Exploring barriers to participation and adoption of telehealth and telecare within the Whole System Demonstrator trial: a qualitative study | journal = BMC Health Services Research | volume = 12 | article-number = 220 | date = July 2012 | pmid = 22834978 | pmc = 3413558 | doi = 10.1186/1472-6963-12-220 | doi-access = free }}</ref> Furthermore, there are concerns around informed consent, legality issues as well as legislative issues. A recent study also highlighted that the swift and large-scale implementation of telehealth across the United Kingdom NHS Allied Health Professional (AHP) services might increase disparities in health care access for vulnerable populations with limited digital literacy.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Eddison N, Leone E, Healy A, Royse C, Chockalingam N | title = The potential impact of allied health professional telehealth consultations on health inequities and the burden of treatment | journal = International Journal for Equity in Health | volume = 21 | issue = 1 | article-number = 91 | date = June 2022 | pmid = 35773695 | pmc = 9245876 | doi = 10.1186/s12939-022-01689-2 | doi-access = free }}</ref> Although health care may become affordable with the help of technology, whether or not this care will be "good" is the issue.<ref name="Umefjord-2006" /> Many studies indicate high satisfaction with telemedicine among patients.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Waller M, Stotler C | title = Telemedicine: a Primer | journal = Current Allergy and Asthma Reports | volume = 18 | issue = 10 | article-number = 54 | date = August 2018 | pmid = 30145709 | doi = 10.1007/s11882-018-0808-4 }}</ref> Among the factors associated with a good trust in telemedicine, the use of known and user-friendly video services and confidence in the [[Information privacy|data protection]] policies were the two variables contributing most to trust in telemedicine.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Costantino |first1=Andrea |last2=Caprioli |first2=Flavio |last3=Elli |first3=Luca |last4=Roncoroni |first4=Leda |last5=Stocco |first5=Davide |last6=Doneda |first6=Luisa |last7=Nandi |first7=Nicoletta |last8=Conforti |first8=Francesco Simone |last9=Noviello |first9=Daniele |last10=Penagini |first10=Roberto |last11=Vecchi |first11=Maurizio |title=Determinants of patient trust in gastroenterology televisits: Results of machine learning analysis |journal=Informatics in Medicine Unlocked |date=2022 |volume=29 |article-number=100867 |doi=10.1016/j.imu.2022.100867 }}</ref>

Public health practitioners also face broader challenges in scaling telehealth services, including limited digital skills among certain patient groups, variability in technology access, concerns around data privacy, and the difficulty of integrating remote-care workflows into existing health systems.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Addressing Challenges Faced by Public Health |date=19 September 2024 |url=https://tau.edu.zm/blog/challenges-faced-by-public-health-professionals/}}</ref>

Major problems with increasing adoption include technically challenged staff, resistance to change or habits<ref name="10.1016/j.jaip.2020.03.008"/> and age of patient. Focused policy could eliminate several barriers.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Scott Kruse C, Karem P, Shifflett K, Vegi L, Ravi K, Brooks M | title = Evaluating barriers to adopting telemedicine worldwide: A systematic review | journal = Journal of Telemedicine and Telecare | volume = 24 | issue = 1 | pages = 4–12 | date = January 2018 | pmid = 29320966 | pmc = 5768250 | doi = 10.1177/1357633X16674087 }}</ref>

A review lists a number of potentially good practices and pitfalls, recommending the use of "virtual handshakes" for [[authentication|confirming identity]], taking consent for conducting remote consultation over a conventional meeting, and professional standardized norms for protecting patient privacy and confidentiality.<ref name="10.1016/j.dsx.2020.06.007">{{cite journal | vauthors = Iyengar K, Jain VK, Vaishya R | title = Pitfalls in telemedicine consultations in the era of COVID 19 and how to avoid them | journal = Diabetes & Metabolic Syndrome | volume = 14 | issue = 5 | pages = 797–799 | date = 1 September 2020 | pmid = 32534432 | pmc = 7280804 | doi = 10.1016/j.dsx.2020.06.007 }}</ref> It also found that the [[COVID-19 pandemic]] substantially increased, voluntarily, the adoption of telephone or video consultation and suggests that telemedicine technology "is a key factor in delivery of health care in the future".<ref name="10.1016/j.dsx.2020.06.007"/>

=== Geriatric population ===

Technologies' growing involvement in health care has led to continuous improvement in access, efficiency and quality of care, but numerous challenges lie with addressing the barriers that impair the geriatric population from benefitting from the use of this new technology.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Alverson |first1=Dale C. |last2=Krupinski |first2=Elizabeth A. |last3=Erps |first3=Kristine A. |last4=Rowe |first4=Nancy S. |last5=Weinstein |first5=Ronald S. |title=The Third National Telemedicine & Telehealth Service Provider Showcase Conference: Advancing Telehealth Partnerships |journal=Telemedicine and e-Health |date=April 2019 |volume=25 |issue=4 |pages=332–340 |doi=10.1089/tmj.2018.0096 |pmid=29851367 |pmc=6482893 }}</ref> With the COVID-19 pandemic, rapid implementation of telehealth in geriatric outpatient clinics occurred. Although time efficiency greatly improved and increased access to geriatric patients with lack of transportation to the clinic, there were complications that arose during and after implementation with many appointments requiring rescheduling due to language barrier, poor connection, hard of hearing, or inability to perform assessments.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Callisaya |first1=Michele L. |last2=Lee |first2=Angel Hui-Ching |last3=Khushu |first3=Anjali |title=Rapid implementation of telehealth in geriatric outpatient clinics due to COVID-19 |journal=Internal Medicine Journal |date=July 2021 |volume=51 |issue=7 |pages=1151–1155 |doi=10.1111/imj.15306 |pmid=34143563 |pmc=8444941 }}</ref> Studies also show that patients and their family member often preferred in-person visits. Even though patients were able to meet with a provider sooner and had access to high-quality audio and video as well as family participation during visits, patients and family noted preferences for in-person visits due to the difficulty in using the service.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Groom |first1=Lisa L. |last2=McCarthy |first2=Margaret M. |last3=Stimpfel |first3=Amy Witkoski |last4=Brody |first4=Abraham A. |title=Telemedicine and Telehealth in Nursing Homes: An Integrative Review |journal=Journal of the American Medical Directors Association |date=September 2021 |volume=22 |issue=9 |pages=1784–1801.e7 |doi=10.1016/j.jamda.2021.02.037 |pmid=33819450 |pmc=9626369 }}</ref> Improvements are being made to help ease the complications of telehealth for geriatric patients. These include integrated captions on video calls for the hearing impaired, virtual interpreters that will attend the calls for language differences, government assisted internet services, and increased training to medical providers and patients on telehealth use.{{citation needed|date=September 2025}}

=== Economic evaluations ===
Due to its digital nature, it is often assumed that telehealth saves the health system money. However, the evidence to support this is varied. When conducting economic evaluations of telehealth services, the individuals evaluating them need to be aware of potential outcomes and extraclinical benefits of the telehealth service.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Snoswell C, Smith AC, Scuffham PA, Whitty JA | title = Economic evaluation strategies in telehealth: Obtaining a more holistic valuation of telehealth interventions | journal = Journal of Telemedicine and Telecare | volume = 23 | issue = 9 | pages = 792–796 | date = October 2017 | pmid = 27789615 | doi = 10.1177/1357633x16671407 | doi-access = free }}</ref> Economic viability relies on the funding model within the country being examined (public vs private), the consumers willingness-to-pay, and the expected remuneration by the clinicians or commercial entities providing the services (examples of research on these topics from teledermoscopy in Australia)<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Snoswell CL, Whitty JA, Caffery LJ, Loescher LJ, Gillespie N, Janda M | title = Direct-to-consumer mobile teledermoscopy for skin cancer screening: Preliminary results demonstrating willingness-to-pay in Australia | journal = Journal of Telemedicine and Telecare | volume = 24 | issue = 10 | pages = 683–689 | date = December 2018 | pmid = 30343653 | doi = 10.1177/1357633x18799582 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Snoswell CL, Caffery LJ, Whitty JA, Soyer HP, Gordon LG | title = Cost-effectiveness of Skin Cancer Referral and Consultation Using Teledermoscopy in Australia | journal = JAMA Dermatology | volume = 154 | issue = 6 | pages = 694–700 | date = June 2018 | pmid = 29801161 | pmc = 6145645 | doi = 10.1001/jamadermatol.2018.0855 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Snoswell CL, Whitty JA, Caffery LJ, Finnane A, Soyer HP | title = What do Australian dermatologists expect to be paid for store-and-forward teledermoscopy? A preliminary investigation | journal = Journal of Telemedicine and Telecare | volume = 25 | issue = 7 | pages = 438–444 | date = August 2019 | pmid = 29933722 | doi = 10.1177/1357633x18776766 | url = https://ueaeprints.uea.ac.uk/id/eprint/68175/1/Accepted_manuscript.pdf }}</ref>

In a UK telehealth trial done in 2011, it was reported that the cost of health could be dramatically reduced with the use of telehealth monitoring. The usual cost of [[in vitro fertilisation]] (IVF) per cycle would be around $15,000; with telehealth it was reduced to $800 per patient.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Chausiaux O, Hayes J, Long C, Morris S, Williams G, Husheer S | title = Pregnancy Prognosis in Infertile Couples on the DuoFertility Programme Compared with In Vitro Fertilisation/Intracytoplasmic Sperm Injection. | journal = European Obstetrics & Gynaecology | date = 2011 | volume = 6 | issue = 2 | pages = 92–94 }}</ref> In [[Alaska Federal Health Care Access Network|Alaska the Federal Health Care Access Network]], which connects 3,000 healthcare providers to communities, engaged in 160,000 telehealth consultations from 2001 and saved the state $8.5 million in travel costs for just [[Medicaid]] patients.<ref>{{cite web |date=2013 |title=Telehealth Improves Access and Quality of Care for Alaska Natives. |url=https://innovations.ahrq.gov/perspectives/telehealth-improves-access-and-quality-care-alaska-natives |work=The Innovations Exchange Team.}}</ref>

[[Use of technology in treatment of mental disorders|Digital interventions for mental health conditions]] seem to be cost-effective compared to no intervention or non-therapeutic responses such as monitoring. However, when compared to in-person therapy or medication their added value is currently uncertain.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Gega L, Jankovic D, Saramago P, Marshall D, Dawson S, Brabyn S, Nikolaidis GF, Melton H, Churchill R, Bojke L | title = Digital interventions in mental health: evidence syntheses and economic modelling | journal = Health Technology Assessment | volume = 26 | issue = 1 | pages = 1–182 | date = January 2022 | pmid = 35048909 | pmc = 8958412 | doi = 10.3310/RCTI6942 | publisher = National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) }}</ref>

===Beneficial enablements===
Telemedicine can be beneficial to patients in isolated communities and remote regions, who can receive care from doctors or specialists far away without the patient having to travel to visit them.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Berman M, Fenaughty A | title = Technology and managed care: patient benefits of telemedicine in a rural health care network | journal = Health Economics | volume = 14 | issue = 6 | pages = 559–573 | date = June 2005 | pmid = 15497196 | doi = 10.1002/hec.952 | publisher = [[John Wiley & Sons|Wiley]] }}</ref> Recent developments in [[mobile collaboration]] technology can allow healthcare professionals in multiple locations to share information and discuss patient issues as if they were in the same place.<ref>{{cite news | vauthors = Van't Haaff C | title = Virtually On-sight | page = 22 | publisher = Just for Canadian Doctors | date = March–April 2009 | url = http://www.justforcanadiandoctors.com/pastissues/JFCD2009/JFCD-Mar-Apr2009.pdf | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20120324052954/http://www.justforcanadiandoctors.com/pastissues/JFCD2009/JFCD-Mar-Apr2009.pdf | archive-date = 2012-03-24 }}</ref> Remote patient monitoring through [[mobile technology]] can reduce the need for outpatient visits and enable remote prescription verification and drug administration oversight, potentially significantly reducing the overall cost of medical care.<ref name="MobilePatient">{{cite book | title = The Mobile Wave: How Mobile Intelligence Will Change Everything | url = https://archive.org/details/mobilewavehowmob0000sayl | url-access = registration | vauthors = Saylor M | year = 2012 | publisher = Perseus Books/Vanguard Press | page=[https://archive.org/details/mobilewavehowmob0000sayl/page/153 153]| isbn = 978-1-59315-720-3 }}</ref> It may also be preferable for patients with limited mobility, for example, patients with Parkinson's disease.<ref name="Teleneurology and mobile technologi"/> Telemedicine can also facilitate medical education by allowing workers to observe experts in their fields and share best practices more easily.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Conde JG, De S, Hall RW, Johansen E, Meglan D, Peng GC | title = Telehealth innovations in health education and training | journal = Telemedicine Journal and e-Health | volume = 16 | issue = 1 | pages = 103–106 | date = January–February 2010 | pmid = 20155874 | pmc = 2937346 | doi = 10.1089/tmj.2009.0152 }}</ref>

====During war and disasters====
{{Expand section|date=July 2022}}
[[Remote surgery]] and types of videoconferencing for sharing expertise (e.g. [[Latin tag#Ad hoc|ad hoc]] assistance) have been and could be used to support doctors in Ukraine during the [[2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine]].<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Best J | title = From Ukraine to remote robotics: how videoconferencing and next generation technology are transforming surgery | journal = BMJ | volume = 377 | article-number = o1078 | date = May 2022 | pmid = 35504650 | doi = 10.1136/bmj.o1078 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

==== Nonclinical uses ====
* [[Distance education]] including continuing medical education, grand rounds, and patient education<ref name="CFP">{{cite journal | vauthors = Masson M | title = Benefits of TED Talks | journal = Canadian Family Physician | volume = 60 | issue = 12 | page = 1080 | date = December 2014 | pmid = 25500595 | pmc = 4264800 }}</ref>
* administrative uses including meetings among telehealth networks, supervision, and presentations
* research on telehealth
* online information and [[health data]] management
* healthcare system integration
* asset identification, listing, and patient to asset matching, and movement
* overall healthcare system management
* patient movement and remote admission
* Physical distancing to prevent transmission of communicable diseases<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Snoswell CL, Caffery LJ, Haydon HM, Thomas EE, Smith AC | title = Telehealth uptake in general practice as a result of the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic | journal = Australian Health Review | volume = 44 | issue = 5 | pages = 737–740 | date = September 2020 | pmid = 32853536 | doi = 10.1071/AH20183 | doi-access = free | hdl = 11343/274283 | hdl-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Smith AC, Thomas E, Snoswell CL, Haydon H, Mehrotra A, Clemensen J, Caffery LJ | title = Telehealth for global emergencies: Implications for coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) | journal = Journal of Telemedicine and Telecare | volume = 26 | issue = 5 | pages = 309–313 | date = June 2020 | pmid = 32196391 | pmc = 7140977 | doi = 10.1177/1357633x20916567 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Zhou X, Snoswell CL, Harding LE, Bambling M, Edirippulige S, Bai X, Smith AC | title = The Role of Telehealth in Reducing the Mental Health Burden from COVID-19 | journal = Telemedicine Journal and e-Health | volume = 26 | issue = 4 | pages = 377–379 | date = April 2020 | pmid = 32202977 | doi = 10.1089/tmj.2020.0068 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

== Limitations and restrictions ==
While many branches of medicine have wanted to fully embrace telehealth for a long time, there are certain risks and barriers which bar the full amalgamation of telehealth into [[best practice]]. For a start, it is dubious as to whether a practitioner can fully leave the "hands-on" experience behind.<ref name="Umefjord-2006" /> Although it is predicted that telehealth will replace many consultations and other health interactions, it cannot yet fully replace a physical examination, this is particularly so in [[Medical diagnosis|diagnostics]], [[Physical medicine and rehabilitation|rehabilitation]] or [[mental health]].<ref name="Umefjord-2006" /> To minimise safety issues, researchers have suggested not offering remote consultations for some conditions (breathing problems, new psychosis, or acute chest pain, for example), when a parent is very concerned about a child, when a condition has not resolved as expected or has worsened, or to people who might struggle to understand or be understood (such as those with limited English or learning difficulties).<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Payne |first1=Rebecca |last2=Clarke |first2=Aileen |last3=Swann |first3=Nadia |last4=van Dael |first4=Jackie |last5=Brenman |first5=Natassia |last6=Rosen |first6=Rebecca |last7=Mackridge |first7=Adam |last8=Moore |first8=Lucy |last9=Kalin |first9=Asli |last10=Ladds |first10=Emma |last11=Hemmings |first11=Nina |last12=Rybczynska-Bunt |first12=Sarah |last13=Faulkner |first13=Stuart |last14=Hanson |first14=Isabel |last15=Spitters |first15=Sophie |last16=Wieringa |first16=Sietse |last17=Dakin |first17=Francesca H |last18=Shaw |first18=Sara E |last19=Wherton |first19=Joseph |last20=Byng |first20=Richard |last21=Husain |first21=Laiba |last22=Greenhalgh |first22=Trisha |title=Patient safety in remote primary care encounters: multimethod qualitative study combining Safety I and Safety II analysis |journal=BMJ Quality & Safety |date=September 2024 |volume=33 |issue=9 |pages=573–586 |doi=10.1136/bmjqs-2023-016674 |pmc=11347200 |pmid=38050161 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |date=1 October 2024 |title=How to make remote consultations safer |url=https://evidence.nihr.ac.uk/alert/how-to-make-remote-consultations-safer/ |journal=NIHR Evidence}}</ref>

The benefits posed by telehealth challenge the normative means of healthcare delivery set in both legislation and practice. Therefore, the growing prominence of telehealth is starting to underscore the need for updated regulations, guidelines and legislation which reflect the current and future trends of healthcare practices.<ref name="Shaw-2009" /><ref name="Umefjord-2006" /> Telehealth enables timely and flexible care to patients wherever they may be which reduces travel time; although this is a benefit, it also poses threats to [[privacy]], [[safety]] [[Medical license|, medical licensing]] and [[reimbursement]], even so it still increases healthcare access and reduces costs. When a clinician and patient are in different locations, it is difficult to determine which laws apply to the context.<ref name="pmid24820794">{{cite journal | vauthors = Keck CS, Doarn CR | title = Telehealth technology applications in speech-language pathology | journal = Telemedicine Journal and E-health | volume = 20 | issue = 7 | pages = 653–9 | date = July 2014 | pmid = 24820794 | doi = 10.1089/tmj.2013.0295 }}</ref> Once healthcare crosses borders different state bodies are involved in order to regulate and maintain the level of care that is warranted to the patient or telehealth consumer. As it stands, telehealth is complex with many grey areas when put into practice especially as it crosses borders. This effectively limits the potential benefits of telehealth.<ref name="Shaw-2009" /><ref name="Umefjord-2006" />

An example of these limitations include the current American reimbursement infrastructure, where [[Medicare (United States)|Medicare]] will reimburse for telehealth services only when a patient is living in an area where specialists are in shortage, or in particular rural counties. The area is defined by whether it is a medical facility as opposed to a patient's' home. The site that the practitioner is in, however, is unrestricted. Medicare will only reimburse live video (synchronous) type services, not store-and-forward, mhealth or remote patient monitoring (if it does not involve live-video). Some insurers currently will reimburse telehealth, but not all yet. So providers and patients must go to the extra effort of finding the correct insurers before continuing. Again in America, states generally tend to require that clinicians are licensed to practice in the surgery' state, therefore they can only provide their service if licensed in an area that they do not live in themselves.<ref name=":0b" />

More specific and widely reaching laws, legislations and regulations will have to evolve with the technology. They will have to be fully agreed upon, for example, will all clinicians need full licensing in every community they provide telehealth services too, or could there be a limited use telehealth licence? Would the limited use licence cover all potential telehealth interventions, or only some? Who would be responsible if an emergency was occurring and the practitioner could not provide immediate help – would someone else have to be in the room with the patient at all consult times? Which state, city or country would the law apply in when a breach or malpractice occurred?<ref name="Umefjord-2006" /><ref name="Paul-2006">{{cite journal |last1=Paul |first1=David L. |title=Collaborative Activities in Virtual Settings: A Knowledge Management Perspective of Telemedicine |journal=Journal of Management Information Systems |date=2006 |volume=22 |issue=4 |pages=143–176 |doi=10.2753/MIS0742-1222220406 |jstor=40398816 }}</ref>

A major legal action prompt in telehealth thus far has been issues surrounding online prescribing and whether an appropriate clinician-patient relationship can be established online to make prescribing safe, making this an area that requires particular scrutiny.<ref name="Elsevier-2012" /> It may be required that the practitioner and patient involved must meet in person at least once before online prescribing can occur, or that at least a live-video conference must occur, not just impersonal questionnaires or surveys to determine need.<ref name="Cascella-2014">{{cite magazine |last1=Cascella |first1=Laura M |title=Virtual risk: An overview of telehealth from a risk management perspective |magazine=Protector |date=Spring 2014 |pages=2–13 }}</ref>

Telehealth has some potential for facilitating self-management techniques in health care, but for patients to benefit from it, the appropriate contact with, and relationship, between doctor and patient must be established first.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Luz PL | title = Telemedicine and the Doctor/Patient Relationship | journal = Arquivos Brasileiros de Cardiologia | volume = 113 | issue = 1 | pages = 100–102 | date = August 2019 | pmid = 31411296 | pmc = 6684176 | doi = 10.5935/abc.20190117 }}</ref> This would start with an online consultation, providing patients with techniques and tools that help them participate in healthy behaviors, and initiating a collaborative partnership between health care professionals and patient.<ref name="ReferenceA">{{cite journal | vauthors = Dineen-Griffin S, Garcia-Cardenas V, Williams K, Benrimoj SI | title = Helping patients help themselves: A systematic review of self-management support strategies in primary health care practice | journal = PLOS ONE | volume = 14 | issue = 8 | article-number = e0220116 | date = 2019-08-01 | pmid = 31369582 | pmc = 6675068 | doi = 10.1371/journal.pone.0220116 | bibcode = 2019PLoSO..1420116D | doi-access = free | veditors = Leroyer C }}</ref> Self-management strategies fall into a broader category called patient activation, which is defined as a "patients' willingness and ability to take independent actions to manage their health."<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Hibbard JH, Greene J | title = What the evidence shows about patient activation: better health outcomes and care experiences; fewer data on costs | journal = Health Affairs | volume = 32 | issue = 2 | pages = 207–214 | date = February 2013 | pmid = 23381511 | doi = 10.1377/hlthaff.2012.1061 }}</ref> It can be achieved by increasing patients' knowledge and confidence in coping with and managing their own disease through a "regular assessment of progress [...] and problem-solving support."<ref name="ReferenceA"/> Teaching patients about their conditions and ways to cope with chronic illnesses will allow them to be knowledgeable about their disease and willing to manage it, improving their everyday life. Without a focus on the doctor-patient relationship and on the patient's understanding, telehealth cannot improve the quality of life of patients, despite the benefit of allowing them to do their medical check-ups from the comfort of their home.

The downsides of telemedicine include the cost of telecommunication and data management equipment and of technical training for medical personnel who will employ it. Virtual medical treatment also entails potentially decreased human interaction between medical professionals and patients, an increased risk of error when medical services are delivered in the absence of a registered professional, and an increased risk that [[protected health information]] may be compromised through electronic storage and transmission.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Hjelm NM | title = Benefits and drawbacks of telemedicine | journal = Journal of Telemedicine and Telecare | volume = 11 | issue = 2 | pages = 60–70 | date = 1 March 2005 | pmid = 15829049 | doi = 10.1258/1357633053499886 }}</ref> There is also a concern that telemedicine may actually decrease time efficiency due to the difficulties of assessing and treating patients through virtual interactions; for example, it has been estimated that a [[teledermatology]] consultation can take up to thirty minutes, whereas fifteen minutes is typical for a traditional consultation.<ref>{{cite web | url = http://www.rrh.org.au/publishedarticles/article_print_1581.pdf | title = Barriers to the up-take of telemedicine in Australia – a view from providers | work = The University of Queensland, School of Medicine | vauthors = Moffatt JJ | date = February 2011}}</ref> Additionally, potentially poor quality of transmitted records, such as images or patient progress reports, and decreased access to relevant clinical information are quality assurance risks that can compromise the quality and continuity of patient care for the reporting doctor.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Strehle EM, Shabde N | title = One hundred years of telemedicine: does this new technology have a place in paediatrics? | journal = Archives of Disease in Childhood | volume = 91 | issue = 12 | pages = 956–9 | date = December 2006 | pmid = 17119071 | pmc = 2082971 | doi = 10.1136/adc.2006.099622 }}</ref> Other obstacles to the implementation of telemedicine include unclear legal regulation for some telemedical practices and difficulty claiming reimbursement from insurers or government programs in some fields.<ref name="Angaran">{{cite journal | vauthors = Angaran DM | title = Telemedicine and telepharmacy: current status and future implications | journal = American Journal of Health-System Pharmacy | volume = 56 | issue = 14 | pages = 1405–26 | date = July 1999 | pmid = 10428449 | doi = 10.1093/ajhp/56.14.1405 | doi-access = free }}</ref> Some medical organizations have delivered position statement on the correct use of telemedicine in their field.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Omboni |first1=Stefano |last2=McManus |first2=Richard J. |last3=Bosworth |first3=Hayden B. |last4=Chappell |first4=Lucy C. |last5=Green |first5=Beverly B. |last6=Kario |first6=Kazuomi |last7=Logan |first7=Alexander G. |last8=Magid |first8=David J. |last9=Mckinstry |first9=Brian |last10=Margolis |first10=Karen L. |last11=Parati |first11=Gianfranco |last12=Wakefield |first12=Bonnie J. |title=Evidence and Recommendations on the Use of Telemedicine for the Management of Arterial Hypertension: An International Expert Position Paper |journal=Hypertension |date=November 2020 |volume=76 |issue=5 |pages=1368–1383 |doi=10.1161/HYPERTENSIONAHA.120.15873 |pmid=32921195 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Daniel |first1=Hilary |last2=Sulmasy |first2=Lois Snyder |title=Policy Recommendations to Guide the Use of Telemedicine in Primary Care Settings: An American College of Physicians Position Paper |journal=Annals of Internal Medicine |date=17 November 2015 |volume=163 |issue=10 |pages=787–789 |doi=10.7326/M15-0498 |pmid=26344925 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Dramburg |first1=Stephanie |last2=Walter |first2=Uso |last3=Becker |first3=Sven |last4=Casper |first4=Ingrid |last5=Röseler |first5=Stefani |last6=Schareina |first6=Astrid |last7=Wrede |first7=Holger |last8=Klimek |first8=Ludger |title=Telemedicine in allergology: practical aspects: A position paper of the Association of German Allergists (AeDA) |journal=Allergo Journal International |date=June 2021 |volume=30 |issue=4 |pages=119–129 |doi=10.1007/s40629-021-00167-5 |pmid=33758744 |pmc=7977487 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Costantino |first1=Andrea |last2=Bortoluzzi |first2=Francesco |last3=Giuffrè |first3=Mauro |last4=Vassallo |first4=Roberto |last5=Montalbano |first5=Luigi Maria |last6=Monica |first6=Fabio |last7=Canova |first7=Daniele |last8=Checchin |first8=Davide |last9=Fedeli |first9=Paolo |last10=Marmo |first10=Riccardo |last11=Elli |first11=Luca |title=Correct use of telemedicine in gastroenterology, hepatology, and endoscopy during and after the COVID-19 pandemic: Recommendations from the Italian association of hospital gastroenterologists and endoscopists (AIGO) |journal=Digestive and Liver Disease |date=October 2021 |volume=53 |issue=10 |pages=1221–1227 |doi=10.1016/j.dld.2021.06.032 |pmid=34312103 }}</ref>

Another disadvantage of telemedicine is the inability to start treatment immediately. For example, a patient with a bacterial infection might be given an [[antibiotic]] [[hypodermic injection]] in the clinic, and observed for any reaction, before that antibiotic is prescribed in pill form.

Equitability is also a concern. Many families and individuals in the United States, and other countries, do not have internet access in their homes or the proper electronic devices to access services such as a laptop or smartphone.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Krupinski |first1=Elizabeth A. |last2=Abbey |first2=Dana |last3=Muralidaran |first3=Mala |last4=Steele |first4=Faith |last5=Strawley |first5=George |date=2025-01-01 |title=Libraries as Telehealth Hubs: Bridging the Digital Divide and Expanding Health care Access |url=https://doi.org/10.1089/tmr.2024.0075 |journal=Telemedicine Reports |volume=6 |issue=1 |pages=1–5 |doi=10.1089/tmr.2024.0075 |pmid=39991645 |pmc=11839511 |issn=2692-4366}}</ref>

== Ethical issues ==
{{See also|Informed consent|Medical ethics}}

''[[Informed consent]]'' is another issue. When telehealth includes the possibility for technical problems such as transmission errors, security breaches, or storage issues, it can impact the system's ability to communicate. It may be wise to obtain informed consent in person first, as well as having backup options for when technical issues occur. In person, a patient can see who is involved in their care (namely themselves and their clinician in a consult), but online there will be other involved such as the technology providers, therefore consent may need to involve disclosure of anyone involved in the transmission of the information and the security that will keep their information private, and any legal malpractice cases may need to involve all of those involved as opposed to what would usually just be the practitioner.<ref name="Elsevier-2012" /><ref name="Paul-2006" /><ref name="Cascella-2014" />

== State of the market ==
The rate of adoption of telehealth services in any jurisdiction is frequently influenced by factors such as the adequacy and cost of existing conventional [[health care|health services]] in meeting [[patient|patient needs]]; the policies of governments and/or insurers with respect to coverage and payment for telehealth services; and medical licensing requirements that may inhibit or deter the provision of telehealth second opinions or primary consultations by physicians.

Projections for the growth of the telehealth market are optimistic, and much of this optimism is predicated upon the increasing demand for remote medical care. According to a recent survey, nearly three-quarters of U.S. consumers say they would use telehealth.<ref name="healthdata">{{cite web|url=http://www.healthdatamanagement.com/news/telemedicine-38701-1.html|title=Survey: Consumers Keen on Telemedicine|access-date=2010-04-26|archive-date=2010-04-29|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100429075350/http://www.healthdatamanagement.com/news/telemedicine-38701-1.html}}</ref> At present, several major companies along with a bevvy of startups are working to develop a leading presence in the field.

In the UK, the Government's Care Services minister, Paul Burstow, has stated that telehealth and [[telecare]] would be extended over the next five years (2012–2017) to reach three million people.

===United States===
In the United States, telemedicine companies are collaborating with health insurers and other telemedicine providers to expand marketshare and patient access to telemedicine consultations.

{{as of|2019}}, 95% of employers believe their organizations will continue to provide health care benefits over the next five years.<ref>''[https://www.willistowerswatson.com/en-US/Insights/2019/11/2019-best-practices-in-health-care-employer-survey-highlights 2019 Best Practices in Health Care Employer Survey Highlights]'', Willis Towers Watson, November 5, 2019</ref>

The COVID-19 pandemic drove increased usage of telehealth services in the U.S. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported a 154% increase in telehealth visits during the last week of March 2020, compared to the same dates in 2019.<ref>''[https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/69/wr/mm6943a3.htm?s_cid=mm6943a3_e&ACSTrackingID=USCDC_921-DM41453&ACSTrackingLabel=This%20Week%20in%20MMWR%20-%20Vol.%2069%2c%20October%2030%2c%202020&deliveryName=USCDC_921-DM41453 Trends in the Use of Telehealth During the Emergence of the COVID-19 Pandemic — United States, January–March 2020]'', Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report (MMWR), October 30, 2020</ref>

=== Switzerland ===
From 1999 to 2018, the [[University Hospital of Zürich|University Hospital of Zurich]] (USZ) offered clinical telemedicine and online medical advice on the Internet. A team of doctors answered around 2500 anonymous inquiries annually, usually within 24 to 48 hours. The team consisted of up to six physicians who are specialists in clinical telemedicine at the USZ and have many years of experience, particularly in internal and general medicine. In the entire period, 59360 inquiries were sent and answered.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Kessler SH, Schmidt-Weitmann S | title = Diseases and Emotions: An Automated Content Analysis of Health Narratives in Inquiries to an Online Health Consultation Service | journal = Health Communication | volume = 36 | issue = 2 | pages = 226–235 | date = February 2021 | pmid = 36112901 | doi = 10.1080/10410236.2019.1673950 | url = https://www.zora.uzh.ch/id/eprint/175841/1/Schmidt_Manuskript_Diseases_and_Emotions.pdf }}</ref> The majority of the users were female and on average 38 years old. However, in the course of time, considerably more men and older people began to use the service. The diversity of medical queries covered all categories of the [[International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems]] (ICD) and correlated with the statistical frequency of diseases in hospitals in Switzerland. Most of the inquiries concerned unclassified symptoms and signs, services related to reproduction, respiratory diseases, skin diseases, health services, diseases of the eye and nervous systems, injuries and disorders of the female genital tract. As with the Swedish online medical advice service,<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Umefjord G, Sandström H, Malker H, Petersson G | title = Medical text-based consultations on the Internet: a 4-year study | journal = International Journal of Medical Informatics | volume = 77 | issue = 2 | pages = 114–121 | date = February 2008 | pmid = 17317292 | doi = 10.1016/j.ijmedinf.2007.01.009 }}</ref> one-sixth of the requests related to often shameful and [[Social stigma|stigmatised]] diseases of the genitals, gastrointestinal tract, sexually transmitted infections, obesity and mental disorders. By providing an anonymous space where users can talk about (shameful) diseases, online telemedical services empower patients and their health literacy is enhanced by providing individualized health information. The Clinical Telemedicine and Online Counselling service of the University Hospital of Zurich is currently being revised and will be offered in a new form in the future.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.usz.ch/Seiten/Telemedizin.aspx|title=Willkommen am UniversitätsSpital Zürich|website=www.usz.ch|language=de-CH|access-date=2020-01-23|archive-date=2020-01-17|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200117122940/http://www.usz.ch/Seiten/Telemedizin.aspx}}</ref>

== Developing countries ==
For developing countries, telemedicine and [[eHealth]] can be the only means of healthcare provision in remote areas. For example, the difficult financial situation in many African states and lack of trained health professionals has meant that the majority of the people in sub-Saharan Africa are badly disadvantaged in medical care, and in remote areas with low population density, direct healthcare provision is often very poor<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20160205083116/http://euroafrica-ict.org.sigma-orionis.com/downloads/Coop_Forum/SessionC/Adesina_Iluyemi.pdf ''Refocusing Europe-Africa Strategy: Strategic Importance of eHealth''] NEPAD. Accessed 28 January 2016.</ref> However, provision of telemedicine and eHealth from urban centers or from other countries is hampered by the lack of communications infrastructure, with no landline phone or broadband internet connection, little or no mobile connectivity, and often not even a reliable electricity supply.<ref>Gerhard Bethscheider [http://www.worldteleport.org/news/249029/Satellite-Is-Vital-For-A-Unified-Global-e-Health-System...-An-SES-Techcom-Services-Perspective-.htm ''Satellite is vital for a unified, global, E-Health system''] September 2015 World Teleport Association. Accessed 28 January 2016.</ref>

=== Telemedicine in developing countries ===

==== Telemedicine in India ====
India has broad rural-urban population and rural India is bereaved from medical facilities, giving telemedicine a space for growth in India. Deprived education and medical professionals in rural areas is the reason behind government's ideology to use technology to bridge this gap. Remote areas not only present a number of challenges for the service providers but also for the families who are accessing these services. Since 2018, telemedicine has expanded in India. It has undertaken a new way for doctor consultations. On 25 March 2020, in the wake of COVID-19 pandemic, the [[Ministry of Health and Family Welfare]] issued India's Telemedicine Practice Guidelines.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Telemedicine Practice Guidelines of India |url=https://www.reclica.com/telemedicine-guidelines.html}}</ref> The Board of Governors entasked by the Health Ministry published an amendment to the [[Indian Medical Council]] (Professional Conduct, Etiquette and Ethics) Regulations, 2002 that gave much-needed statutory support for the practice of telemedicine in India. This sector is at an ever-growing stage with high scope of development.<ref name="economictimes">{{cite news |title=The future of Telemedicine in India |url=https://health.economictimes.indiatimes.com/news/health-it/outlook-2019-the-future-of-telemedicine-in-india/67366188 |access-date=19 May 2020}}</ref> In April 2020, the union health ministry launched the eSanjeevani telemedicine service that operates at two levels: the doctor-to-doctor telemedicine platform, and the doctor-to-patient platform. This service crossed five million tele-consultations within a year of its launch indicating a conducive environment for acceptability and growth of telemedicine in India.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-05-14 |title= Govt's telemedicine service crosses 5 million consultations |url=https://www.hindustantimes.com/india-news/govts-telemedicine-service-crosses-5-million-consultations-101620965457038.html |access-date=2021-10-10|website=Hindustan Times|language=en}}</ref>

==== Telemedicine in Sub-Saharan Africa ====
[[File:Travel Time to the Nearest Health-Care Facility for adults aged 60 years or older, by sub-Saharan African region.jpg|thumb|Travel time to the nearest health-care facility by Sub-Saharan African region, for adults aged 60 years or older]]
Sub-Saharan Africa is marked by the massive introduction of new technologies and internet access.<ref>{{cite book |doi=10.1109/istafrica.2015.7190589 |chapter=On bringing governance into technology: Case of Internet governance and implications for Africa |title=2015 IST-Africa Conference |date=2015 |last1=Kanjo |first1=Chipo |last2=Jere |first2=Towela |pages=1–12 |isbn=978-1-9058-2451-9 }}</ref> Urban areas are facing a rapid change and development, and access to internet and health is rapidly improving. Population in remote areas however, still lack access to healthcare and modern technologies. Some people in rural regions must travel more between 2 and 6 hours to reach the closest healthcare facilities of their country.<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Geldsetzer P, Reinmuth M, Ouma PO, Lautenbach S, Okiro EA, Bärnighausen T, Zipf A |title=Mapping physical access to health care for older adults in sub-Saharan Africa and implications for the COVID-19 response: A cross-sectional analysis |journal=The Lancet Healthy Longevity |date=2020 |volume=1 |issue=1 |pages=e32–e42 |doi=10.1016/s2666-7568(20)30010-6 |pmid=34173615 |pmc=7574846 |medrxiv=10.1101/2020.07.17.20152389}}</ref> leaving room for telehealth to grow and reach isolated people in the near future.

=== Internet via satellite in rural areas ===
The Satellite African eHEalth vaLidation (SAHEL) demonstration project has shown how [[Satellite Internet access|satellite broadband]] technology can be used to establish telemedicine in such areas. SAHEL was started in 2010 in Kenya and Senegal, providing self-contained, solar-powered internet terminals to rural villages for use by community nurses for collaboration with distant health centers for training, diagnosis and advice on local health issues.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20160203143432/http://www.ses.com/14444955/SES_Broadband_SAHEL_case_study_EN.pdf ''Helping to build sustainable eHealth services in Africa''] SES Broadband. Company brochure. Accessed 28 January 2016.</ref> Those methods can have major impact on both health professionals to get and provide training from remote areas, and on the local population who can receive care without traveling long distances. Some non-profits provide internet to rural places around the world using a mobile VSAT terminal. This VSAT terminal equips remote regions allowing them to alert the world when there is a medical emergency, resulting in a rapid deployment or response from developed countries.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wilk-Jakubowski |first1=Jacek |title=A review on information systems engineering using vsat networks and their development directions |journal=Yugoslav Journal of Operations Research |date=2021 |volume=31 |issue=3 |pages=409–428 |doi=10.2298/yjor200215015w |doi-access=free }}</ref> Technologies such as the ones used by MAF allows health professionals in remote clinics to have internet access, making consultations much easier, both for patients and doctors.
