{{Alternative medical systems|fringe}}

'''Facilitated communication''' ('''FC'''), or '''supported typing''', is a scientifically discredited technique<ref name="Vyse 2">{{cite web |last1=Vyse |first1=Stuart |title=Autism Wars: Science Strikes Back |url=https://www.csicop.org/specialarticles/show/autism_wars_science_strikes_back |date=7 August 2018 |website=Skeptical Inquirer Online |publisher=Skeptical Inquirer |access-date=28 November 2018 |archive-date=22 March 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190322040631/https://www.csicop.org/specialarticles/show/autism_wars_science_strikes_back |url-status=live }}</ref> that claims to allow non-verbal people, such as those with [[autism]], to communicate. The technique involves a facilitator guiding the disabled person's arm or hand in an attempt to help them type on a keyboard or other such device that they are unable to properly use if unfacilitated.<ref name="Facilitated Communication Is a Cult That Won't Die">{{cite web|last1=Auerbach|first1=David|title=Facilitated Communication Is a Cult That Won't Die|url=http://www.slate.com/articles/health_and_science/medical_examiner/2015/11/facilitated_communication_pseudoscience_harms_people_with_disabilities.html|website=Slate|access-date=30 November 2015|date=12 November 2015|archive-date=26 September 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180926044147/http://www.slate.com/articles/health_and_science/medical_examiner/2015/11/facilitated_communication_pseudoscience_harms_people_with_disabilities.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

There is widespread agreement within the scientific community and among disability advocacy organizations that FC is a [[pseudoscience]].<ref name="Review 2018">{{cite journal |last1=Hemsley |first1=Bronwyn |author-link=Bronwyn Hemsley |last2=Bryant |first2=Lucy |last3=Schlosser |first3=Ralf |last4=Shane |first4=Howard |last5=Lang |first5=Russell |last6=Paul |first6=Diane |last7=Benajee |first7=Meher |last8=Ireland |first8=Marie |date=2018 |title=Systematic review of facilitated communication 2014-2018 finds no new evidence that messages delivered using facilitated communication are authored by the person with the disability |journal=Autism and Developmental Language Impairments |volume=3 |pages=239694151882157 |article-number=2396941518821570 |doi=10.1177/2396941518821570 |doi-access=free}}</ref>  Research indicates that the facilitator is the source of the messages obtained through FC, rather than the disabled person. The facilitator may believe they are not the source of the messages due to the [[ideomotor effect]], which is the same effect that guides a [[Ouija board]] and [[dowsing]] rods.<ref name="Why debunked autism treatment fads persist">{{cite web|last1=Lilienfeld|date=26 February 2015|title=Why debunked autism treatment fads persist|url=https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2015/02/150226154644.htm|website=Science Daily|publisher=Emory University|access-date=10 November 2015|display-authors=etal|archive-date=31 May 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190531003343/https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2015/02/150226154644.htm|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Ganz/Katsiyannis/Morin">{{cite journal|last1=Ganz|first1=Jennifer B.|last2=Katsiyannis|first2=Antonis|last3=Morin|first3=Kristi L.|title=Facilitated Communication: The Resurgence of a Disproven Treatment for Individuals With Autism |journal=Intervention in School and Clinic|volume=54|date=February 2017|pages=52–56|doi=10.1177/1053451217692564|doi-access=free}}</ref> Studies have consistently found that FC is unable to provide the correct response to even simple questions when the facilitator does not know the answers to the questions (e.g., showing the patient but not the facilitator an object).<ref name="An experimental analysis of facilitated communication">{{cite journal|last1=Montee|first1=B B|last2=Miltenberger|first2=R G|last3=Wittrock|first3=D|last4=Watkins|first4=N|last5=Rheinberger|first5=A|last6=Stackhaus|first6=J|title=An experimental analysis of facilitated communication.|journal=Journal of Applied Behavior Analysis|date=1995|volume=28|issue=2|pages=189–200|doi=10.1901/jaba.1995.28-189|pmid=7601804|pmc=1279809}}</ref> In addition, in numerous cases disabled persons have been assumed by facilitators to be typing a coherent message while the patient's eyes were closed or while they were looking away from or showing no particular interest in the letter board.<ref name="Making contact with a helping hand">{{cite news|last1=Goldacre|first1=Ben|title=Making contact with a helping hand|url=https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2009/dec/05/bad-science-ben-goldacre-column|newspaper=[[The Guardian]]|access-date=10 November 2015|date=5 December 2009|archive-date=7 May 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200507234242/https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2009/dec/05/bad-science-ben-goldacre-column|url-status=live}}</ref>

James Todd called facilitated communication "the single most scientifically discredited intervention in all of developmental disabilities".<ref name="Wichert"/> Some promoters of the technique have claimed that FC cannot be clearly disproven because a testing environment [[Observer's paradox|might cause the subject to lose confidence]].<ref name="Palfreman, Jon (1993)">{{cite web|last1=Palfreman|first1=Jon|author-link1=Jon Palfreman|date=October 19, 1993|title=Frontline: Prisoners of Silence|url=https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/pages/frontline/programs/transcripts/1202.html|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180622144420/http://www.pbs.org/wgbh//pages/frontline/programs/transcripts/1202.html|archive-date=June 22, 2018|website=[[PBS]]|publisher=WGBH Educational Foundation}}</ref> However, there is a [[scientific consensus]] that facilitated communication is not a valid communication technique, and its use is strongly discouraged by most speech and language disability professional organizations.<ref name="Review 2018" /> There have been a large number of [[List of abuse allegations made through facilitated communication|false abuse allegations made through facilitated communication]].

==Overview==
Facilitated communication is promoted as a means to assist people with severe communication disabilities in pointing to letters on an alphabet board, keyboard, or other device so that they can communicate independently. It has also been called "supported typing",<ref name="ISAAC Position Statement (2014)">{{cite journal|title=ISAAC Position Statement on Facilitated Communication: International Society for Augmentative and Alternative Communication|journal=Augmentative and Alternative Communication|date=2014|volume=30|issue=4|pages=357–358|doi=10.3109/07434618.2014.971492|pmid=25379709|author1=International Society for Augmentative Alternative Communication|doi-access=free|hdl=10536/DRO/DU:30072729|hdl-access=free}}<!--|access-date=March 18, 2015--></ref> "progressive kinesthetic feedback",<ref name="Lilienfeld, Marshall, Todd, Shane (2015)">{{cite journal|last1=Lilienfeld|first1=Scott O.|author-link=Scott Lilienfeld|last2=Marshall|first2=Julia|last3=Todd|first3=James T.|last4=Shane|first4=Howard C.|date=2 February 2015|title=The persistence of fad interventions in the face of negative scientific evidence: Facilitated Communication for autism as a case example|journal=Evidence-Based Communication Assessment and Intervention|volume=8|issue=2|pages=62–101|doi=10.1080/17489539.2014.976332|s2cid=145366255}}</ref> and "written output communication enhancement".<ref name="Lilienfeld, Marshall, Todd, Shane (2015)"/> It is related to the [[Rapid Prompting Method]] (RPM),<ref name="Burling, Stacey (2004)">{{cite news|last1=Burling|first1=Stacey|title=A pacesetting technique style for the autistic. She used the technique on her son. Some doubt the value of her methods.|url=http://articles.philly.com/2004-05-17/news/25382897_1_autistic-children-autistic-disorder-autistic-person|access-date=March 18, 2015|work=[[The Philadelphia Inquirer]]|date=May 17, 2004|location=Philadelphia, PA|page=C.1|archive-date=March 4, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304065609/http://articles.philly.com/2004-05-17/news/25382897_1_autistic-children-autistic-disorder-autistic-person|url-status=dead}}</ref> also known as "informative pointing",<ref name="Lilienfeld, Marshall, Todd, Shane (2015)" /> which also has no evidence of efficacy.<ref name="Wombles, Kimberly (2015)">{{cite journal|last1=Wombles|first1=Kimberly|title=Some fads never die – they only hide behind other names: Facilitated Communication is not and never will be Augmentative Communication|journal=Evidence-Based Communication Assessment and Intervention|date=18 February 2015|url=http://www.tandfonline.com/loi/tebc20|access-date=March 18, 2015|doi=10.1080/17489539.2015.1012780|volume=8|pages=181–186|issue=4|s2cid=143959563|archive-date=12 January 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200112170921/https://www.tandfonline.com/loi/tebc20|url-status=live|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref name="AshaLeaderBlog">{{cite journal|last1=Travers|first1=Jason|title=The Pseudoscientific Phenom{{and}}Facilitated Communication{{and}}Makes a Comeback|url=http://blog.asha.org/2015/05/19/the-pseudoscientific-phenom-facilitated-communication-makes-a-comeback/|journal=Leader Live|publisher=American-Speech-Language-Hearing Association|access-date=10 April 2016|date=19 May 2015|archive-date=21 May 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150521234217/http://blog.asha.org/2015/05/19/the-pseudoscientific-phenom-facilitated-communication-makes-a-comeback/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="science20">{{cite web|last1=Wombles|first1=Kim|title=Why Rapid Prompting Method Still Doesn't Pass the Evidence-Based Test|url=http://www.science20.com/countering_tackling_woo/blog/why_rapid_prompting_method_still_doesn't_pass_evidencebased_test-68146|website=Science 2.0|date=27 August 2014 |publisher=ION Publications LLC|access-date=10 April 2016|archive-date=11 December 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191211180033/https://www.science20.com/countering_tackling_woo/blog/why_rapid_prompting_method_still_doesn%E2%80%99t_pass_evidencebased_test-68146|url-status=live}}</ref>

The person with disabilities, who is often unable to rely on speech to communicate, is called the ''communication partner'', while the person holding their arm is called the ''facilitator''. The facilitator holds or touches the communication partner's elbow, wrist, hand, sleeve or other parts of the body<ref name="Biklen, Douglas (1990)">{{cite journal|last1=Biklen|first1=Douglas|title=Communication Unbound: Autism and Praxis|journal=Harvard Educational Review|date=1990|volume=60|pages=291–314|doi=10.17763/haer.60.3.013h5022862vu732|issue=3}}<!--|access-date=March 18, 2015--></ref> while the communication partner points to letters of the alphabet on a keyboard or other device.<ref name="Schwiegert, Mary Beth">{{cite news|last1=Schwiegert|first1=Mary Beth|title=Will to succeed Lititz man battles autism{{snd}}and goes to college|work=Lancaster New Era|date=28 December 2000|location=Lancaster, Pennsylvania|page=D-1}}</ref><ref name="Lilienfeld, Marshall, Todd, Shane (2015)" /> Biklen describes FC as provision of "physical supports under the forearm, under or above the wrist, or by helping a person to isolate the index finger to facilitate the use of communication aid" and contrasts it with "typing independently, with support by a hand on a shoulder, or hand on a sleeve, leg, or elsewhere".<ref name="Biklen, Douglas (1990)" />

One device popular with early FC users was the Canon Communicator, which printed a tape of letters when activated.<ref name="Biklen, Morton, Gold, Berrigan, Swaminatham (1992)">{{cite journal|last1=Biklen|first1=Douglas|last2=Morton|first2=Mary Winston|last3=Gold|first3=Deborah|last4=Berrigan|first4=Carol|last5=Swaminathan|first5=Sudha|title=Facilitated Communication: implications for individuals with autism|journal=Topics in Language Disorders|date=1992|volume=12|issue=4|pages=1–28|doi=10.1097/00011363-199208000-00003|s2cid=143895378}}<!--|access-date=March 18, 2015--></ref><ref name="Dillon, Kathleen M. (1993)">{{cite journal|last1=Dillon|first1=Kathleen M.|title=Facilitated Communication, Autism and Ouija|journal=Skeptical Inquirer|date=1993|volume=17|issue=3|pages=281–287}}</ref><ref name="Dineen, Janice (1991)">{{cite news|last1=Dineen|first1=Janice|title=How autistic Chloe stunned the medical world|work=Toronto Star|issue=SA2 Edition|date=December 21, 1991|location=Toronto, Ontario|page=A1}}</ref> However, two American companies were later charged by the [[Federal Trade Commission]] for making "false and unsubstantiated claims" that the device could enable disabled people to communicate using FC. The companies settled and stopped mentioning FC in their advertising campaigns.<ref name="Boodman, Sandra (1995)">{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/wellness/1995/01/17/can-autistic-children-be-reached-through-facilitated-communication-scientists-say-no/0f703028-81ac-4d4a-877e-daf6f98cd0fc/|title=Can autistic children be reached through 'Facilitated Communication'? Scientists say no|date=January 17, 1995|newspaper=The Washington Post|issue=Final Edition|location=Washington, D.C.|page=z01|last1=Boodman|first1=Sandra G.|access-date=March 18, 2015|archive-date=March 2, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170302015807/https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/wellness/1995/01/17/can-autistic-children-be-reached-through-facilitated-communication-scientists-say-no/0f703028-81ac-4d4a-877e-daf6f98cd0fc/|url-status=live}}</ref>

Proponents of FC claim that the reason people with autism cannot communicate effectively involves motor issues such as [[apraxia]], and that they "lack confidence in their abilities"<ref name="Biklen, Douglas (1990)" /><ref name="Green, Gina (1994)" /> but physical support helps them overcome this limitation. However, this claim is unsubstantiated. Research indicates that many non-verbal people with [[autism spectrum disorder]] are unable to communicate due to [[intellectual disability]].<ref name="Lilienfeld, Marshall, Todd, Shane (2015)" />

The facilitator is depicted as helping the patient with pointing to letters, controlling involuntary arm movements, avoiding mistakes, initiating movement,<ref name="Jacobson, Mulick, Schwartz (1995)" /> verbal prompts, and moral support.<ref name="Schwiegert, Mary Beth" /><ref name="Mangiacasale, Angela">{{cite news|last1=Mangiacasale|first1=Angela|title=New voice: system lets disabled communicate|work=The Ottawa Citizen|issue=Final Edition|date=January 23, 1992|page=D3}}</ref><ref name="Mostert, Mark (2012)">{{cite journal|last1=Mostert|first1=Mark P.|author-link=Mark Mostert|title=Facilitated Communication: The empirical imperative to prevent further professional malpractice|journal=Evidence-Based Communication Assessment and Intervention|date=18 June 2012|volume=6|issue=1|pages=18–27|doi=10.1080/17489539.2012.693840|s2cid=143959332}}</ref><ref name="von Tetzchner, Stephen (1997)">{{cite journal|last1=von Tetzchner|first1=Stephen|title=Historical issues in intervention research: hidden knowledge and facilitating techniques in Denmark|journal=European Journal of Disorders of Communication|date=1997|volume=32|pages=1–18|doi=10.3109/13682829709021453|pmid=9135710|issue=1}}</ref><ref name="Greenbaum, Kurt (1992)">{{cite news|last1=Greenbaum|first1=Kurt|title=Autistic Method Disputed Researcher Says Child Not Helped|work=[[Sun-Sentinel]]|date=September 27, 1992|location=Fort Lauderdale, Florida|page=8B}}</ref> It is also claimed that the facilitator must believe in the patient's ability to communicate.<ref name="Kim, Rose (1992)">{{cite news|last1=Kim|first1=Rose|title=The magic touch keyboard technique helps severely disabled students learn to communicate|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1992-06-17-mn-480-story.html|access-date=March 18, 2015|work=Los Angeles Times|issue=Home Edition|date=17 June 1992|location=Los Angeles, California|page=3|archive-date=2015-04-02|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402174750/http://articles.latimes.com/1992-06-17/news/mn-480_1_severely-disabled-students|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Green, Gina (1995)">{{cite journal|last1=Green|first1=Gina|title=An ecobehavioral interpretation of the facilitated communication phenomenon|journal=Psychology in Mental Retardation and Developmental Disabilities|date=Fall 1995|volume=21|issue=2|pages=1–8}}</ref><ref name="Libman, Gary (1992)">{{cite news|last1=Libman|first1=Gary|title=A controversial technique may be the key to providing sufferers with a way to communicate unlocking autism|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1992-11-17-vw-788-story.html|access-date=March 18, 2015|work=[[Los Angeles Times]]|issue=Home Edition|date=17 November 1992|page=1|archive-date=2015-04-02|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402221033/http://articles.latimes.com/1992-11-17/news/vw-788_1_facilitated-communication|url-status=live}}</ref> Former facilitator Janyce Boynton, who came to reject the technique after taking part in blind testing, later reported that her training<ref name="Facilitated Communication—what harm it can do: Confessions of a former facilitator" /><ref name="How facilitators control words" /> took for granted that the process worked, and that the complexity of facilitation made it hard to realise that messages were coming from her expectations and not from her patients: {{blockquote|When you're facilitating, you're so distracted by other things. You're carrying on conversations, you're asking and answering questions, you're trying to look at the person to see if they're looking at the keyboard...Your brain is so engaged that you lose sight of what's happening with your hand...that's what makes it feel like it's working because the more you practice it, the more the movements feel really fluid.<ref name="Facilitated Communication—what harm it can do: Confessions of a former facilitator">{{cite journal|last1=Boynton|first1=Janyce|s2cid=144642290|title=Facilitated Communication{{snd}}what harm it can do: Confessions of a former facilitator|journal=Evidence-Based Communication Assessment and Intervention|date=March 2012|volume=6|issue=1|pages=3–13|doi=10.1080/17489539.2012.674680}}</ref><ref name="Double Talk"/><ref name="How facilitators control words">{{cite web|last1=Burke|first1=Michael|title=How facilitators control words typed in facilitated communication without realizing|url=http://dailyorange.com/2016/04/how-facilitators-control-words-typed-in-facilitated-communication-without-realizing/|website=Daily Orange|access-date=17 March 2018|date=2016-04-11|archive-date=2016-04-15|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160415200726/http://dailyorange.com/2016/04/how-facilitators-control-words-typed-in-facilitated-communication-without-realizing/|url-status=live}}</ref>}}

[[Scott Lilienfeld]], the Dobbs Professor of Psychology at Emory University, writing in ''The Neuroethics Blog'', admonishes practitioners of mental health practice not to ignore their "''epistemic duties'' – responsibilities to seek out and possess accurate knowledge about the world", and wrote:
{{blockquote|Ultimately, the proponents of facilitated communication very much wanted to help individuals with autism. But the facilitated communication tragedy teaches us that good intentions are not sufficient. Good intentions paired with grossly inaccurate knowledge and an absence of a self-critical mindset can be disastrous. This tragedy also teaches us that by not attending to their epistemic duties, professionals can do grave harm without intending to do so.<ref name=lilienfeld-2016>{{cite web |last1=Lilienfeld |first1=S.O. |title=The Ethical Duty to Know: Facilitated Communication for Autism as a Tragic Case Example |url=http://www.theneuroethicsblog.com/2016/03/the-ethical-duty-to-know-facilitated.html |website=The Neuroethics Blog |date=8 March 2016 |publisher=Emory Center For Ethics |access-date=22 July 2019 |archive-date=22 July 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190722162328/http://www.theneuroethicsblog.com/2016/03/the-ethical-duty-to-know-facilitated.html |url-status=live }}</ref>}}

==History==
[[File:dynawrite.jpg|right|thumb|alt=a communication device resembling a computer keyboard with a small liquid-crystal display attached to the top| Keyboard of the type used in facilitated communication]]
Techniques similar to FC appeared around the 1960s, with early observations regarding facilitated teaching of children with autism being published by Else Hansen (Denmark), [[Lorna Wing]] (England), and Rosalind Oppenheim (U.S.).<ref name=":1">{{cite web|last=Pilvang|first=Maureen|date=August 2002|title=Facilitated Communication in Denmark|url=http://fc2000.dk/wp-content/uploads/2015/07/Pilvang-Facilitated-Communication-in-Denmark.pdf|work=Seventh Biennial ISAAC Research Symposium|access-date=2020-10-04|archive-date=2022-01-04|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220104030040/http://fc2000.dk/wp-content/uploads/2015/07/Pilvang-Facilitated-Communication-in-Denmark.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref> Studies were made in Denmark in the 1960s and 1970s,<ref name="von Tetzchner, Stephen (1997)" /> but did not have an impact outside of the country,<ref name="von Tetzchner, Stephen (1997)" /> and the debate there died out in the early 1980s due to a lack of scientific evidence.<ref name="von Tetzchner, Stephen (1997)" />{{rp|11}}

In Australia, Special educator [[Rosemary Crossley]] independently created facilitated communication in 1977,<ref name="von Tetzchner, Stephen (1997)" />{{rp|12}} where it became popular largely due to her efforts.<ref name="Dillon, Kathleen M. (1993)" /><ref name="lilienfeld-2016" /><ref name="Alferink, Larry A.">{{cite journal|last1=Alferink|first1=Larry A.|title=Educational Practices, Superstitious Behavior and Mythed Opportunities |journal=Scientific Review of Mental Health Practice|date=Fall–Winter 2007|volume=5|issue=2|pages=21–30}}</ref><ref name="Palfreman, Jon (2012)">{{cite journal|last1=Palfreman|first1=Jon|author-link1=Jon Palfreman|title=The dark legacy of FC|journal=Evidence-Based Communication Assessment and Intervention|date=11 May 2012|volume=6|issue=1|pages=14–17|doi=10.1080/17489539.2012.688343|s2cid=144395085}}</ref><ref name="Well, Judith (1994)">{{cite news|last1=Well|first1=Judith|title=Facilitation: How much of a helping hand? |work=Jerusalem Post|date=March 9, 1994|location=Jerusalem|page=07}}</ref> It was popularized in the United States beginning in the late 1980s by [[Arthur Schawlow]] and [[Douglas Biklen]].<ref name="Wright, Pearce (1999)">{{cite news|last1=Wright|first1=Pearce|title=Obituary: How the laser changed our world: Arthur Schawlow|url=https://www.theguardian.com/news/1999/may/11/guardianobituaries|access-date=March 18, 2015|work=The Guardian|date=11 May 1999|location=London, England|page=18|archive-date=12 January 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200112170833/https://www.theguardian.com/news/1999/may/11/guardianobituaries|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Green, Gina (1994)">{{cite journal|last1=Green|first1=Gina|title=Mental Miracle or Sleight of Hand? |journal=Skeptic|date=1994|volume=2|issue=3 |pages=68–76}}</ref><ref name="Biklen, Douglas (1990)" /><ref name="Dillon, Kathleen M. (1993)" /><ref name="Jacobson, Mulick, Schwartz (1995)">{{cite journal|last1=Jacobson|first1=John W.|last2=Mulick|first2=James A.|last3=Schwartz|first3=Allen A.|title=A History of Facilitated Communication: Science, Pseudoscience, and Antiscience: Science Working Group on Facilitated Communication|journal=American Psychologist|date=September 1995|volume=50|issue=9|pages=750–765|doi=10.1037/0003-066x.50.9.750}}<!--|access-date=March 18, 2015--></ref> FC has also received attention in Asia and Europe.<ref name="Lilienfeld, Marshall, Todd, Shane (2015)" /><ref name="Alferink, Larry A." /><ref name="Gifford, Aaron (2000)">{{cite news|last1=Gifford|first1=Aaron|title=SU professor still pushes to validate his method|work=The Post-Standard|issue=Final Edition|date=October 9, 2000|location=Syracuse, New York|page=B2}}</ref>

Early users of facilitated communication praised it for its apparent simplicity.<ref name="Green, Gina (1994)" /><ref name="Kim, Rose (1992)" /><ref name="Green, Gina (1995)" /><ref name="Celiberti, David (2010)">{{cite journal|last1=Celiberti|first1=David |title=Facilitate This: Part 1 of a Two-Part Interview with Dr. James Todd|journal=Science in Autism Treatment|date=Spring 2010|volume=7|issue=2}}</ref><ref name="Ballon, Diana (1992)">{{cite news|last1=Ballon|first1=Diana |title=A ray of sunshine for the Rain Man. A new technique for communicating with autistic children is being greeted with skepticism by some experts - but the anecdotal evidence is compelling|work=The Globe and Mail |date=April 25, 1992|location=Toronto, Ontario|page=D.8}}</ref> It was promoted as a "teaching strategy"<ref name="Stengle, Bernice">{{cite news|last1=Stengle|first1=Bernice|title=Michael casts a spell|work=St. Petersburg Times|issue=City Edition|date=5 September 1993|location=St. Petersburg, Florida}}</ref> that did not require objective evaluation or close monitoring.<ref name="Green, Gina (1995)" /> However, as early as 1991, more than 40 peer-reviewed studies had not only failed to demonstrate FC's efficacy, but indicated that any successes reported were due to facilitator influence.<ref name="MostertActivist">{{cite journal|last=Mostert|first=Mark|author-link=Mark Mostert|date=2014|title=An Activist Approach to Debunking FC|journal=Research and Practice for Persons with Severe Disabilities|volume=39|issue=3|pages=203–210|doi=10.1177/1540796914556779|doi-access=free}}<!--|access-date=14 May 2015--></ref> This influence is usually attributed to non-conscious movements,<ref name="Spitz, Herman">{{cite book|last1=Spitz|first1=Herman|title=Nonconscious Movements: From Mystical Messages to Facilitated Communication|year=1997|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-0-805-82564-0|url=http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9780805825633/|access-date=March 18, 2015|archive-date=2 April 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402204124/http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9780805825633/|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="von Tetzchner, Stephen (2012)">{{cite journal|last1=von Tetzchner|first1=Stephen|title=Understanding facilitated communication: Lessons from a former facilitator - Comments on Boynton, 2012|journal=Evidence-Based Communication Assessment and Intervention|date=June 25, 2012|volume=6|issue=1|pages=28–35 |doi=10.1080/17489539.2012.699729|s2cid=217511582}}</ref> and it is thought that facilitators are genuinely unaware that they are controlling the communications.<ref name="Boodman, Sandra (1995)" /><ref name=BW>{{cite news|last1=Brasier|first1=L.L.|last2=Wisely|first2=John|title=Abuse case hinges on a keyboard|url=http://archive.freep.com/article/20071218/NEWS03/712180304/Abuse-case-hinges-keyboardWest-Bloomfield|access-date=March 18, 2015|work=McClatchy-Tribune Business News|date=December 18, 2007|location=Washington, D.C.|archive-date=April 2, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402101625/http://archive.freep.com/article/20071218/NEWS03/712180304/Abuse-case-hinges-keyboardWest-Bloomfield|url-status=live}}</ref>

In 1994, the [[American Psychological Association]] (APA),<ref name="Rising, Gerry">{{cite news|last1=Rising|first1=Gerry|date=8 January 2001|title='Miraculous' autism treatment stirs concern|page=2B|work=Buffalo News|issue=Final Edition|location=Buffalo, New York}}</ref><ref name="Riggott, Julie">{{cite journal |last1=Riggott |first1=Julie |date=Spring–Summer 2005 |title=Pseudoscience in Autism Treatment: Are the News and Entertainment Media Helping or Hurting? |url=http://srmhp.org/0401/media-watch.html |journal=Scientific Review of Mental Health Practice |volume=4 |issue=1 |pages=58–60 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060707074823/http://srmhp.org/0401/media-watch.html |archive-date=7 July 2006 |quote=This issue's Media Watch article is an adapted version of a piece originally published in the ''Pasadena Weekly'' (May 19, 2005) by staff writer Julie Riggott.}}</ref> passed a resolution cautioning against the use of facilitated communication, citing the lack of scientific evidence.<ref name="Boodman, Sandra (1995)" /> They also stated that information obtained via FC should not be used to confirm or deny allegations of abuse or to make diagnostic or treatment decisions.<ref name=BW/><ref name="Mann, Lisa Barrett (2005)">{{cite news |last1=Mann |first1=Lisa Barrett |date=February 22, 2005 |title=Oscar Nominee: Documentary or Fiction? Film Resurrects Discredited Autism Tactic |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/wellness/2005/02/22/oscar-nominee-documentary-or-fiction/f576a9ae-d062-4a68-9726-92a6d97efa0d/ |access-date=March 18, 2015 |newspaper=The Washington Post |page=F01, Health |issue= |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230610101217/https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/wellness/2005/02/22/oscar-nominee-documentary-or-fiction/f576a9ae-d062-4a68-9726-92a6d97efa0d/ |archive-date=10 June 2023 }}</ref><ref name="The Times (July 2000)">{{cite news|title=Facilitated communication not reliable as evidence|work=The Times|date=July 29, 2000|location=London, England}}</ref> In recognition of the continued scientific evidence against the technique, this was followed by similar statements from the [[American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry]] (AACAP),<ref name="Riggott, Julie" /> [[American Speech-Language-Hearing Association]] (ASHA),<ref name="Jacobson, Mulick, Schwartz (1995)" /><ref name=ECE>{{cite news|last1=Emery Jr.|first1=C. Eugene|title=FC Message Technique for the Handicapped Unproven, experts say *A national group of speech and language experts votes to warn its 80,000 members that tests show facilitated communication lacks scientific validity|work=Providence Journal|date=November 30, 1994|location=Providence, Rhode Island|page=D-09}}</ref><ref name="Duchan, Judith (2001)">{{cite journal|last1=Duchan|first1=Judith F.|last2=Calculator |first2=Stephen |last3=Sonnenmeier|first3=Rae|last4=Diehl|first4=Sylvia |last5=Cumley|first5=Gary D.|title=A Framework for Managing Controversial Practices |journal=Language, Speech, and Hearing Services in Schools|volume=32|pages=133–141|doi=10.1044/0161-1461(2001/011) |pmid=27764404|issue=3 |year=2001}}<!--|access-date=March 18, 2015 --></ref> and the [[International Society for Augmentative and Alternative Communication]] (ISAAC)<ref name=Schlosser_et_al_2014>{{cite journal|last1=Schlosser|first1=R.|last2=Balandin |first2=S.|last3=Hemsley |first3=B.|last4=Iacono|first4=T.|last5=Probst|first5=P.|last6=von Tetzchner|first6=S.|s2cid=207470234|title=Facilitated Communication and Authorship: A Systematic Review|journal=Augmentative and Alternative Communication|date=2014|volume=30 |issue=4|pages=359–368|doi=10.3109/07434618.2014.971490|pmid=25384895}}</ref> In 1998, a British government report concluded that "the phenomenon fails to materialise once facilitator effects have been controlled. It would be hard to justify further research on this".<ref name="Making contact with a helping hand" /><ref name="Educational Interventions for Children With Autism: A Literature Review of Recent And Current Research">{{cite web|last1=Jordan, Jones & Murray|title=Educational Interventions for Children With Autism: A Literature Review of Recent And Current Research|url=http://dera.ioe.ac.uk/15770/1/RR77.pdf|website=Institute of Education|publisher=DfEE|access-date=10 November 2015|archive-date=17 April 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160417200921/http://dera.ioe.ac.uk/15770/1/RR77.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref> By 2001, it was reported in a comprehensive review of peer-reviewed literature that "Facilitated Communication (FC) had largely been empirically discredited as an effective intervention for previously uncommunicative persons with disabilities, especially those with autism and related disorders. Key empirical findings consistently showed that the facilitator and not the client initiated communication."<ref name="Mostert, Mark P. (2010)" />

Many people believed FC had passed its peak,<ref name="Oswald, Donald P. (1996)">{{cite journal|last1=Oswald|first1=Donald P.|title=Book Review: Facilitated Communication: The Clinical and Social Phenomenon. Edited by Howard C. Shane. San Diego, CA: Singular Publishing Group. 1994. pp. 323|journal=Journal of Behavioral Education|date=September 1996|volume=6|issue=3|pages=355–357|jstor=41824137|doi=10.1007/BF02110136|s2cid=195215616}}</ref> characterizing it as a fad<ref name="Oswald, Donald P. (1996)" /> and [[pseudoscientific]].<ref name="Wombles, Kimberly (2015)" /><ref name="Normand, Matthew P. (2008)">{{cite journal|last1=Normand|first1=Matthew P.|title=Science, Skepticism, and Applied Behavior Analysis|journal=Behavior Analysis in Practice|date=Winter 2008|volume=1|issue=2|pages=42–49|pmid=22477687|pmc=2846586|doi=10.1007/BF03391727}}</ref> However, promotion of the technique continued, with supporters dismissing empirical investigations as irrelevant, flawed, or unnecessary, and calling FC an "effective and legitimate intervention".<ref name="Mostert, Mark P. (2010)">{{cite journal|last1=Mostert|first1=Mark P.|author-link=Mark Mostert|title=Facilitated Communication and Its Legitimacy - Twenty-first century developments|journal=Exceptionality|date=2010 |volume=18|pages=31–41|doi=10.1080/09362830903462524|issue=1|s2cid=143946477}}<!--|access-date=March 18, 2015--></ref><ref name=MostertActivist /><ref name="Gardner, Martin">{{cite journal|last1=Gardner|first1=Martin |title=Facilitated Communication: A Cruel Farce|journal=Skeptical Inquirer|date=January–February 2001|pages=17–19 }}</ref><ref name="Porter, Kayla">{{cite news|last1=Porter|first1=Kayla|title=Awakening the silence|work=McClatchy-Tribune Business News|date=14 August 2007|location=Washington, D.C.}}</ref> As of 2014, the facilitated communication movement remained popular and it continued to be used in many countries.<ref name="Palfreman, Jon (2012)" /><ref name="Lilienfeld, Marshall, Todd, Shane (2015)" /> Mostert writes:<blockquote>All the newer pro-FC studies operate from the premise that FC works and is a legitimate practice to be used in investigating any number of other phenomena related to people with autism and other related severe communication problems. Such assumptions increasingly morph FC into a valid intervention among readers who are unaware of the empirical dismissal of the intervention and who might not be skilled in distinguishing solid from suspect research. In this regard, it is likely that FC will continue to reinforce the assumptions of efficacy among parents and practitioners. These perceptions will continue to be reinforced by professional organizations such as the Facilitated Communication Institute at Syracuse University, a fairly wide acceptance of FC internationally, and the vacuum created by few if any future solid empirical studies that are likely to dissuade the faithful.<ref name="Mostert, Mark P. (2010)" /></blockquote>Facilitated communication is closely related to the [[rapid prompting method]] (RPM), in which the facilitator holds the letter board instead of touching the patient.<ref name="Chandler, Michael (March 2017)">{{cite news|last1=Chandler|first1=Michael Alison|title=The key to unlock their autistic son's voice|url=https://www.pressreader.com/usa/the-washington-post/20170301/281487866131617|access-date=14 April 2017|newspaper=The Washington Post|date=March 1, 2017|location=Washington, D.C.|page=A.1|archive-date=3 December 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201203130034/https://www.pressreader.com/usa/the-washington-post/20170301/281487866131617|url-status=live}}</ref> Proponents of RPM deny similarities with FC and state that the prompts are "nonspecific".<ref name="Beach, Patrick (January 2008)">{{cite news|last1=Beach|first1=Patrick|title=Understanding Tito|work=Austin Statesman|date=January 20, 2008|location=Austin, Texas|page=J.1}}</ref> However, RPM contains subtle cuing that makes it highly susceptible to influence from the facilitator.<ref name="Chandler, Michael (March 2017)"/>

Other similarities between RPM and FC include: reluctance or refusal to test their claims in [[Scientific control|controlled]] settings (purportedly because the process breaks the trust between facilitator and client), presumed competence, reliance on anecdotal accounts as proof of efficacy, maintenance of practices, techniques and claims that are inconsistent with the known research, claims of extraordinary literacy or intellectual breakthroughs, unconscious verbal or physical cuing by facilitators to obtain the expected responses, and inadequate or non-existent protocols to account for the effects of the facilitator.<ref name="Tostanoski et al (August 2014)">{{cite journal|last1=Tostanoski|first1=Amy|last2=Lang|first2=Russell|last3=Raulston|first3=Tracy|last4=Carnett|first4=Amarie|last5=Davis|first5=Tonya|title=Voices from the past: Comparing the rapid prompting method and facilitated communication|journal=Developmental Neurorehabilitation|date=August 2014|volume=17|issue=4|pages=219–223|doi=10.3109/17518423.2012.749952|pmid=24102487|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="Todd, James (Rapid Prompting)">{{cite book|last1=Todd|first1=James|chapter=Rapid Prompting|title=Encyclopedia of Autism Spectrum Disorders|pages=2497–2503|doi=10.1007/978-1-4419-1698-3_1896|year=2013|isbn=978-1-4419-1697-6}}</ref>

Rapid Prompting Method has been rebranded as Spelling to Communicate (S2C) and Spellers Method.<ref name="safeguarding">{{cite journal |last1=Hemsley |first1=Bronwyn |last2=Beals |first2=Katharine |last3=Lang |first3=Russell |last4=Schlosser |first4=Ralf W. |last5=Shane |first5=Howard |last6=Simmons |first6=William |last7=Skinner |first7=Sharon |last8=Todd |first8=James |title=Safeguarding the communication rights of minimally- or non-speaking people who are vulnerable to Facilitated Communication, Rapid Prompting (Spellers Method) and variants |journal=Research and Practice in Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities |date=3 July 2025 |volume=12 |issue=2 |pages=158–178 |doi=10.1080/23297018.2025.2544116|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="london-2025-10-05">{{cite news |last1=London |first1=William |title=Consumer Health Digest, Issue #25-40 |url=https://quackwatch.org/ncahf/digest25/25-40/ |access-date=28 August 2026 |work=Quackwatch |date=5 Oct 2025}}</ref>

In 2019, a dispute about the use of Spelling to Communicate (S2C) developed between the [[Lower Merion School District]] and the parent of a child attending school there. The parents claimed the child was deprived of a free education because the district declined to pay for a private educational program based on S2C. In December of that year, the hearing officer in the Pennsylvania Office of Dispute Resolution found that there was no evidence that S2C enabled the child to communicate and thus the school district prevailed.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Vyse|first=Stuart|date=March–April 2020|title=A Small Victory of Science in Suburban Philadelphia|url=https://skepticalinquirer.org/2020/03/a-small-victory-for-science-in-suburban-philadelphia/|journal=Skeptical Inquirer|volume=44|pages=5|access-date=2020-03-07|archive-date=2020-05-05|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200505214158/https://skepticalinquirer.org/2020/03/a-small-victory-for-science-in-suburban-philadelphia/|url-status=live}}</ref>

== Organizations supporting and opposing facilitated communication ==

=== Supporters ===
In 2010, ''Autism Spectrum Disorders: A Reference Handbook'' mentioned the Autism National Committee (AutCom), a parent-led nonprofit, as the main example of an organization that continued promoting facilitated communication, despite research in the mid-1990s which found that facilitators were doing the communicating rather than the children themselves.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Bernier |first1=Raphael |title=Autism Spectrum Disorders: A Reference |last2=Gerdts |first2=Jennifer |publisher=ABC–CLIO |year=2010 |isbn=978-1-59884-334-7 |location=Santa Barbara, California |pages=71–72}}</ref> As of 2022, AutCom continues to state on its website that it "[stands] with autistics, along with their families, friends, and allies, and others who know and respect them, who are working to gain a reliable, autonomous voice", and lists methods it supports including "Facilitated Communication Training (FCT), Rapid Prompting Method (RPM), Spelling to Communicate (S2C), or Informative Pointing Method".<ref>{{Cite web |title=AutCom Statement on Facilitated Communication |url=https://www.autcom.org/assets/Right-to-Communicate-Resources-v2.pdf |access-date=2022-10-04 |website=Autism National Committee}}</ref> Other organizations supporting FC have included the Association for Persons with Severe Handicaps (TASH) and the Autistic Self-Advocacy Network (ASAN).<ref>{{Cite news |last=Auerbach |first=David |date=November 12, 2015 |title=Facilitated Communication Is a Cult That Won't Die |work=Slate |url=https://slate.com/technology/2015/11/facilitated-communication-pseudoscience-harms-people-with-disabilities.html |access-date=2022-10-04}}</ref>

=== Opponents ===
Organizations opposing facilitated communication include:
* The [[American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry]] (AACAP)<ref name="Riggott, Julie" />
* The [[American Academy of Pediatrics]] (AAP)<ref name="ISAAC Position Statement (2014)" /><ref name="Riggott, Julie" />
* The [[American Association on Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities]] (AAIDD), previously called the American Association on Mental Retardation (AAMR)<ref name="ISAAC Position Statement (2014)" /><ref name="Riggott, Julie" /><ref name="AAIDD">{{cite web |title=Facilitated Communication and Rapid Prompting Method |url=https://www.aaidd.org/news-policy/policy/position-statements-2/facilitated-communication-and-rapid-prompting-method |website=AAIDD |access-date=19 February 2026 }}</ref>
* The [[American Psychiatric Association]] (APA)<ref name="ISAAC Position Statement (2014)" /><ref name="Riggott, Julie" />
* The [[American Psychological Association]] (APA)<ref name="Rising, Gerry" /><ref name="Riggott, Julie"/>
