==Claims and evidence==
[[File:Anne McDonald Centre.jpg|thumb|The [[Anne McDonald]] Centre, a facilitated communication centre in Melbourne, Australia, directed by [[Rosemary Crossley]]]]
There is widespread agreement within the scientific community and multiple disability advocacy organizations that FC is not a valid technique for communicating with those with autism spectrum disorder.<ref name="Review 2018"/>  Instead, research indicates that the facilitator is the source of the messages obtained through FC (involving [[ideomotor effect]] guidance of the arm of the patient by the facilitator).<ref name="Why debunked autism treatment fads persist" /><ref name="Ganz/Katsiyannis/Morin" /> Studies have consistently found that FC is unable to provide the correct response to even simple questions when the facilitator does not know the answers to the questions (e.g., showing the patient but not the facilitator an object).<ref name="An experimental analysis of facilitated communication"/>

While videotapes exist that appear to show disabled people communicating through FC, or who have used it as a means to learn independent typing, these videos are widely regarded as inaccurate and misleading. According to Gina Green, a former president of the [[Association for Behavior Analysis International]], says "You can edit videotape and show whatever you want. They'll show you a close-up of the finger moving across the keyboard... but you're not getting what else is going on."<ref name="Mann, Lisa Barrett (2005)" />

===Authorship of messages===

Researchers attribute the facilitators' beliefs about authorship to the [[ideomotor effect]] (also called the [[Clever Hans]] or [[Ouija]] effect).<ref name="Hyman, Ray (1999)">{{cite journal|last1=Hyman|first1=Ray|author-link=Ray Hyman|date=Fall–Winter 1999|title=The Mischief Making of Ideomotor Action|url=http://www.quackwatch.com/01QuackeryRelatedTopics/ideomotor.html|journal=The Scientific Review of Alternative Medicine|volume=3|issue=2|access-date=2015-03-23|archive-date=2015-08-20|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150820024646/http://www.quackwatch.com/01QuackeryRelatedTopics/ideomotor.html|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Spitz, Herman" /><ref name="Dillon, Kathleen M. (1993)" /><ref name="Green, Gina (1994)" /> While proponents say that FC should never involve guiding the patient, researchers attending an FC class in 1993 observed that physical force was used to prevent the patients from moving their hand away from the keyboard.<ref name="Mulick et all" /> Facilitators may also influence movements without realizing it.<ref name="Gardner, Martin" /> Researcher Gina Green stated: "Very subtle influence can affect people's behavior. It doesn't even have to be touched. It can be the slightest sound, the slightest visual cue."<ref name="Dillow, Gordon (1993)">{{cite news|last1=Dillow|first1=Gordon|date=24 January 1993|title=Teacher says method that helps disabled ruined him. Courts: Autism sufferers, using a 'facilitator' to communicate, accused teacher of sexual assault. Charges dropped but he plans to sue for $2.5 million|page=1|work=Los Angeles Times|issue=Home Edition|location=Los Angeles, CA}}</ref> Guidelines for facilitators instruct practitioners to expect the emergence of hidden skills and sensitive personal information, to use anecdotal data to validate authorship, and to avoid objective scrutiny.<ref name="Green, Gina (1994)" />

Some observers have reported that while the facilitators were watching the letter board, their communication partners were often distracted, staring off into space, rolling around on the floor,<ref name="Greenbaum, Kurt (1992)" /> falling asleep,<ref name="Green, Gina (1995)" /> or otherwise not paying attention.<ref name="Schwiegert, Mary Beth" /><ref name="Stengle, Bernice" /> In other cases, the communication partners spoke words that conflicted with the words being typed.<ref name="Palfreman, Jon (1993)" /> Individuals described as highly competent would also give wrong answers to simple questions or information that they should have readily known (e.g. the name of the family dog, the names of family members, the spelling of their own name) but which facilitators did not.<ref name="Biklen, Douglas (1990)" /><ref name="MH021692">{{cite news|author1=Paul Heinrichs|date=February 16, 1992|title=Suffering at the hands of the protectors|work=The Sunday Morning Herald|url=http://www.smh.com.au/national/suffering-at-the-hands-of-the-protectors-20090821-esuq|access-date=October 21, 2015|archive-date=January 22, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180122134026/http://www.smh.com.au/national/suffering-at-the-hands-of-the-protectors-20090821-esuq|url-status=live}}</ref>

Proponents of the technique believed that patients who had not been taught reading, writing, or mathematics could write down complex thoughts and solve multiplication problems.<ref name="von Tetzchner, Stephen (1997)" /><ref name="Kim, Rose (1992)" /><ref name="Stengle, Bernice" /><ref name="Biklen, Schubert (1991)">{{cite journal|last1=Biklen|first1=Douglas|last2=Schubert|first2=Annegret|date=November–December 1991|title=New Words: The Communication of Students with Autism|url=http://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ439556|journal=Remedial and Special Education|volume=12|issue=6|pages=46–57|doi=10.1177/074193259101200607|s2cid=145504550|access-date=March 18, 2015|archive-date=April 2, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402174828/http://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ439556|url-status=live|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Patients have also been claimed to write books and poetry,<ref name="Dickerson, Brian (2008)">{{cite news|last1=Dickerson|first1=Brian|date=17 March 2008|title=Brian Dickerson Column: A legal horror show tears Oakland Co. family apart|work=McClatchy-Tribune Business News|location=Washington, D.C.}}</ref><ref name="Reischman, Rick">{{cite news|last1=Reischman|first1=Rick|date=31 December 2007|title=Region Brief|work=Daily Record|location=Wooster, Ohio}}</ref> advocate for better treatment of people with disabilities,<ref name="McKechnie, Howell (1993)">{{cite news|last1=McKechnie|first1=Gary|last2=Howell|first2=Nancy|date=March 14, 1993|title=The world according to David: A controversial new approach may be allowing David Graham Perry and thousands of others to communicate for the first time in their lives or it may be offering false hope|page=10|work=Orlando Sentinel|issue=2* Edition|location=Orlando, Florida}}</ref> express a desire to get married,<ref name="Lilienfeld, Marshall, Todd, Shane (2015)" /><ref name="Libman, Gary (1992)" /> have sexual relations,<ref name="Lilienfeld, Marshall, Todd, Shane (2015)" /><ref name="Todd, James (2012)">{{cite journal|last1=Todd|first1=James T.|date=13 July 2012|title=The moral obligation to be empirical: Comments on Boynton's "Facilitated Communication - what harm it can do: Confessions of a former facilitator."|url=http://www.tandfonline.com/loi/tebc20|journal=Evidence-Based Communication Assessment and Intervention|volume=6|issue=1|pages=36–57|doi=10.1080/17489539.2012.704738|s2cid=143043194|access-date=March 18, 2015|archive-date=12 January 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200112170921/https://www.tandfonline.com/loi/tebc20|url-status=live|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref name="Sundstrom, Kathy (2014)">{{cite news|last1=Sundstrom|first1=Kathy|date=October 17, 2014|title=Carer: "I fell in love": Grandma guilty of indecent dealing|work=Sunshine Coast Daily|location=Queensland, Australia|url=https://www.questia.com/newspaper/1G1-386176050/carer-i-fell-in-love-grandma-guilty-of-indecent|access-date=March 18, 2015|archive-date=January 13, 2020|via=[[Questia]]|url-access=subscription|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200113125204/https://www.questia.com/newspaper/1G1-386176050/carer-i-fell-in-love-grandma-guilty-of-indecent|url-status=dead}}</ref> decide important medical issues, and, in some cases, [[List of abuse allegations made through facilitated communication|report abuses allegedly occurring in their homes]].<ref name="Alferink, Larry A." /><ref name="Papp, Leslie (1996)">{{cite news|last1=Papp|first1=Leslie|date=21 January 1996|title=Autism 'miracle' a nightmare for family|work=The Toronto Star|publisher=Toronto Star Newspapers, Ltd.|issue=Sunday Second Edition|location=Toronto, Ontario, Canada}}</ref><ref name="Spake, Amanda (1992)">{{cite news|last1=Spake|first1=Amanda|date=31 May 1992|title=Skeptics and Believers; The Facilitated Communication Debate|page=W22|newspaper=The Washington Post|url=http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1P2-1008445.html|url-status=usurped|access-date=March 18, 2015|via=[[HighBeam Research]]|url-access=subscription|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402141032/http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1P2-1008445.html|archive-date=2 April 2015}}</ref> According to psychologist Adrienne Perry, "The adult or child with autism is made a 'screen' for a facilitator's hostilities, hopes, beliefs or suspicions".<ref name="Papp, Leslie (1996)" />

===Autism===

While proponents of FC claim that autism is primarily a motor control problem that can be overcome with physical support,<ref name="Biklen, Douglas (1990)" /><ref name="Green, Gina (1995)" /><ref name="Well, Judith (1994)" /> this view is not accepted by the scientific community.<ref name=reviewofcaa>{{cite journal |last1=Beals |first1=Katharine |title=Review of Communication Alternatives in Autism: Perspectives on Typing and Spelling Approaches for the Nonspeaking |journal=Journal of Evidence-Based Social Work |date=2020 |volume=17 |issue=3 |pages=361–367 |doi=10.1080/26408066.2020.1729284|s2cid=239764348 }}</ref><ref name=bealsreview>{{cite journal |last1=Beals |first1=Katharine |title=Book Review: Biklen, D. (2005). Autism and the myth of the person alone |journal=Research on Social Work Practice |date=2021 |pages=1–5 |doi=10.1177/10497315211003952|s2cid=233228576 }}</ref> Autism is often accompanied by [[Intellectual disability|intellectual disabilities]] affecting language and communication which cannot be overcome by supportively holding someone's hand.<ref name="Lilienfeld, Marshall, Todd, Shane (2015)" /><ref name="Calculator, Stephen (1999)" /> Facilitators reject objective data and use public opinion and qualitative studies<ref name="TraversVoice">{{cite journal|last1=Travers|first1=Jason|last2=Tincani|first2=Matt|last3=Lang|first3=Russell|date=September 2014|title=Facilitated Communication Denies People With Disabilities Their Voice|journal=Research and Practice for Persons with Severe Disabilities|volume=39|issue=3|pages=195–202|doi=10.1177/1540796914556778|doi-access=free}}<!--|access-date=17 May 2015--></ref><ref name="CardinalMaturingFC">{{cite journal|last1=Cardinal|first1=Donald|last2=Falvey|first2=Mary|date=September 2014|title=Facilitated Communication Denies People With Disabilities Their Voice|journal=Research and Practice for Persons with Severe Disabilities|volume=39|issue=3|pages=189–194|doi=10.1177/1540796914555581|doi-access=free}}<!--|access-date=17 May 2015--></ref> to promote FC's efficacy despite contradicting a long history of autism research.<ref name="Oswald, Donald P. (1996)" /><ref name="Cuff, John Haslett (1993)">{{cite news|last1=Cuff|first1=John Haslett|date=19 October 1993|title=Television "Prisoners of Silence: A Shocking look at autism research|page=C.4|work=The Globe and Mail|location=Toronto, Ontario}}</ref><ref name="SingerStandardsofProof">{{cite journal|last1=Singer|first1=George|last2=Horner|first2=Robert|last3=Dunlap|first3=Glen|last4=Wang|first4=Mian|date=September 2014|title=Standards of Proof: TASH, Facilitated Communication, and the Science-Based Practices Movement|journal=Research and Practice for Persons with Severe Disabilities|volume=39|issue=3|pages=178–188|doi=10.1177/1540796914558831|s2cid=145757011}}<!--|access-date=17 May 2015--></ref> In some cases, patients learn to give specific responses to cues from the facilitator, such as in cases where the facilitator only touches their shoulder or does not touch the patient at all.<ref name="Riggott, Julie" /> Proponents also say that a few individuals using FC have developed the ability to type independently or with minimal support,<ref name="Broderick, Kasa-Henderson (2001)">{{cite journal|last1=Broderick|first1=Alicia A.|last2=Kasa-Handrickson|first2=Christi|title="Say just one word at first": The emergence of reliable speech in a student labeled with autism|journal=Journal of the Association for Persons with Severe Handicaps|date=Spring 2001|volume=26|issue=1|pages=13–24|url=http://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ629415|access-date=19 March 2015|doi=10.2511/rpsd.26.1.13|s2cid=144645577|archive-date=2 April 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402155606/http://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ629415|url-status=live|url-access=subscription}}</ref> but these claims are anecdotal and have not been substantiated.<ref name="Lilienfeld, Marshall, Todd, Shane (2015)" /><ref name="Wombles, Kimberly (2015)" /><ref name="SPA (2012)">{{cite web|title=Augmentative and Alternative Communication Clinical Guidelines|url=http://www.speechpathologyaustralia.org.au/publications/clinical-guidelines|website=Speech Pathology Australia|publisher=The Speech Pathology Association of Australia Limited|access-date=March 19, 2015|date=September 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150310210835/http://speechpathologyaustralia.org.au/publications/clinical-guidelines|archive-date=2015-03-10|url-status=dead}}</ref> Many facilitators deny they are influencing their communication partners' movements, even when faced with evidence to the contrary.<ref name="Palfreman, Jon (2012)" /><ref name="Riggott, Julie" />

According to the [[American Academy of Pediatrics]] (AAP) clinical report, ''Identification, Evaluation, and Management of Children With Autism Spectrum Disorder'', published in January, 2020, the "Current scientific evidence does not support the use of facilitated communication in which a nonverbal individual is guided to communicate. This differs from [[augmentative and alternative communication]], in which the individual is taught to communicate independently."<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Hyman|first1=Susan L.|last2=Levy|first2=Susan E.|last3=Myers|first3=Scott M.|last4=Council on Children with Disabilities|first4=Section on Developmental and Behavioral Pediatrics|date=2020-01-01|title=Identification, Evaluation, and Management of Children With Autism Spectrum Disorder|journal=Pediatrics|language=en|volume=145|issue=1|pages=e20193447|doi=10.1542/peds.2019-3447|issn=0031-4005|pmid=31843864|doi-access=free}}</ref>

Belief in facilitated communication is promoted by its status as a claimed "miracle cure" presented when parents are undergoing stress and grief from learning that their child has a disability. The only evidence of success is the transcript of apparent communication.<ref name="Mulick et all"/> In some cases of autism, parents reject the diagnosis and say that their child's disability is physical rather than developmental, and with FC or RPM, their beliefs are confirmed.<ref name="Vyse2018">{{cite journal|last1=Vyse|first1=Stuart|date=2018|title=The Enduring Legend of the Changeling|journal=Skeptical Inquirer|volume=42|issue=4|pages=23–26}}</ref><ref name=bealsreview /> Researchers James Mulick, John Jacobson and Frank Kobe state that FC is used to "...stroke their hopes with empty promises, regardless of their sincerity, while reaping personal or political rewards and working hard to prevent systematic verification of their claims". They add that "people with handicaps can be valued members of their families and communities without resorting to appeals to miracle cures" and that genuine help is available, but "advances in treatment and understanding come at the price of rigorous training, dedication to accuracy and scientific standards, and objective verification of all treatment claims".<ref name="Mulick et all">{{cite journal|last1=Mulick|first1=James|last2=Jacobson|first2=John|last3=Kobe|first3=Frank|title=Anguished Silence and Helping Hands: Autism and Facilitated Communication|journal=Skeptical Inquirer|date=1993|volume=17|issue=3|pages=270–280}}</ref>

[[Bernard Rimland]], a research psychologist who founded the [[Autism Research Institute]] of San Diego and the [[Autism Society of America]], asked "How is it possible that an autistic kid can pick up the last tiny crumbs of potato chips off a plate but not have sufficient motor coordination to type the letter E?"<ref name="Boodman, Sandra (1995)" /> [[Howard Shane]], director of the Center for Communication Enhancement at Children's Hospital in Boston and an associate professor at Harvard Medical School, finds it "curious that those being facilitated can only create [these] insightful comments" when helped by an assistant.<ref name="Healey, Michelle (2011)">{{cite news|last1=Healey|first1=Michelle|date=6 April 2011|title=New film gives voice to a nearly silent minority|page=ARC|work=Gannett News|url=http://usatoday30.usatoday.com/LIFE/usaedition/2011-04-07-autism07_ST_U.htm|access-date=March 18, 2015|archive-date=2015-04-03|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150403220528/http://usatoday30.usatoday.com/LIFE/usaedition/2011-04-07-autism07_ST_U.htm|url-status=live}}</ref> Why, when technology allowed people with severe disabilities the opportunity to access independent communication with even the slightest movement (e.g., an eye wink, movement of an eyebrow, a puff of air into a straw), would a facilitator need to hold their hand?<ref name="Palfreman, Jon (1993)" /><ref name="Lilienfeld, Marshall, Todd, Shane (2015)" />

Testifying in the Anna Stubblefield court case, psychology professor James Todd called facilitated communication "the single most scientifically discredited intervention in all of developmental disabilities" and that every methodologically sound study of FC has shown it to be invalid.<ref name="Wichert">{{cite web|url=http://www.nj.com/essex/index.ssf/2015/10/professor_found_guilty_of_sexually_assaulting_disa.html|title=Professor found guilty of sexually assaulting disabled man|last1=Wichert|first1=Bill|website=NJ.com|access-date=4 October 2015|date=2015-10-02|archive-date=2019-02-07|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190207215734/https://www.nj.com/essex/index.ssf/2015/10/professor_found_guilty_of_sexually_assaulting_disa.html|url-status=live}}</ref> Writing about that case in the journal "Disability and Society", Mark Sherry voiced similar concerns about FC's lack of scientific validity, calling it a "sham", "hoax" and a "fraud." Sherry's was the first article published in a Disability Studies journal which thoroughly critiqued Stubblefield's actions, a noteworthy contribution because Stubblefield had also been in Disability Studies and had previously published about FC in the journal ''Disability Studies Quarterly''.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Sound and Fury: When Opposition to Facilitated Communication Functions as Hate Speech|date=25 October 2011|journal=Disability Studies Quarterly|volume=31|issue=4|doi=10.18061/dsq.v31i4.1729 | last1 = Stubblefield | first1 = Anna|doi-access=free}}</ref> Sherry suggested that some of the defenders of Stubblefield (and FC more broadly) are either her personal friends or work in institutions which receive substantial income from providing FC.<ref>{{cite journal | doi = 10.1080/09687599.2016.1218152 | volume=31 | issue=7 | title=Facilitated communication, Anna Stubblefield and disability studies | year=2016 | journal=Disability & Society | pages=974–982 | last1 = Sherry | first1 = Mark| doi-access=free }}</ref> A newspaper editorial from [[Syracuse University]], where the techniques relevant to the case had been taught, called it "inexcusable" and "embarrassing" that the university continues to support FC after over 25 years of research has discredited it.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Editorial Board|title=Syracuse University's reinforcement of facilitated communication inexcusable, concerning|url=http://dailyorange.com/2016/04/syracuse-universitys-reinforcement-of-facilitated-communication-inexcusable-concerning/|website=The Daily Orange|publisher=Syracuse University|access-date=13 April 2016|date=2016-04-12|archive-date=2016-04-15|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160415182457/http://dailyorange.com/2016/04/syracuse-universitys-reinforcement-of-facilitated-communication-inexcusable-concerning|url-status=live}}</ref>

===Opposition to research===

Members of the FC movement rely on anecdotal and observational data (e.g., the existence of unique spellings or unexpected skills or revelations made during the communication session)<ref name="Biklen, Morton, Gold, Berrigan, Swaminatham (1992)" /><ref name="Jacobson, Mulick, Schwartz (1995)" /> in order to back up their claims.<ref name="Biklen, Douglas (1990)" /><ref name=ECE/> However, because cueing is often subtle and it is not always possible to observe the influence of the facilitator, informal observations and facilitator reports have proven unreliable in determining authorship.<ref name="Riggott, Julie" /><ref name=reviewofcaa />

Parents and researchers who questioned FC's effectiveness and supported evaluating FC by objective methods have been accused of being "oppressors of the disabled", told they were narrow-minded, outmoded, evil, jealous they were not the ones to discover FC,<ref name="Green, Gina (1995)" /> and, in some cases, accused of hate speech for advocating a more studied approach.<ref name="Wombles, Kimberly (2015)" /><ref name="Mostert, Mark (2012)" /><ref name="Stubblefield, Anna (2011)">{{cite journal|last1=Stubblefield|first1=Anna|title=Sound and Fury: When Opposition to Facilitated Communication Functions as Hate Speech|journal=Disability Studies Quarterly|date=2011|volume=31|issue=4|doi=10.18061/dsq.v31i4.1729|url=http://dsq-sds.org/article/view/1729|access-date=March 19, 2015|doi-access=free|archive-date=April 2, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402154722/http://dsq-sds.org/article/view/1729|url-status=live}}</ref> Proponents claim that testing is demeaning to the disabled person,<ref name="Biklen, Douglas (1990)" /> that the testing environment creates performance anxiety,<ref name="Goldman, Daniel (1993)" /> or that those being facilitated may purposely produce nonsense, refuse to respond, or give wrong answers to counteract the negative attitudes of those who are skeptical of the technique.<ref name="Crossley, Remington-Gurney (1992)">{{cite journal|last1=Crossley|first1=Rosemary|author1-link=Rosemary Crossley|last2=Remington-Gurney|first2=Jane|title=Getting the words out: Facilitated communication training|journal=Topics in Language Disorders|date=August 1992|volume=12|issue=4|pages=29–45|url=http://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ451558|access-date=March 19, 2015|doi=10.1097/00011363-199208000-00004|s2cid=144141846|archive-date=April 2, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402112141/http://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ451558|url-status=live|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

Mostert wrote in 2001, "FC proponents must be encouraged to subject their claims to further scientific verification, the claims of anecdotal evidence notwithstanding. If any small part of FC is ever to be found effective or even plausible, it is abundantly clear that only by careful use of controlled experimental methods will this be established."<ref name="Mostert, Mark (2001)">{{cite journal| last1=Mostert|first1=Mark|author-link=Mark Mostert|title=Facilitated Communication Since 1995: A Review of Published Studies|journal=Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders|date=June 2001|volume=31|issue=3| pages=287–313|pmid=11518483|doi=10.1023/a:1010795219886|s2cid=6842817}}</ref> The only way to determine whether communications are truly independent is to perform controlled testing, where the facilitator does not already know the answers to questions and, therefore, cannot inadvertently or purposefully cue their communication partner to obtain the desired answer.<ref name="Wombles, Kimberly (2015)" /><ref name="Boynton, Janyce">{{cite journal| last1=Boynton|first1=Janyce|s2cid=144642290|title=Facilitated Communication - What harm it can do: Confessions of a former facilitator|journal=Evidence-Based Communication Assessment and Intervention|date=April 17, 2012|volume=6|issue=1|pages=3–13| doi=10.1080/17489539.2012.674680}}</ref><ref name="Goldman, Daniel (1993)">{{cite news|last1=Goldman|first1=Daniel|title=New Treatments for Autism Arouse Hope and Skepticism| url=https://www.nytimes.com/1993/07/13/science/new-treatments-for-autism-arouse-hope-andskepticism.html|access-date=March 19, 2015|work=The New York Times|issue=Late Edition|date=July 13, 1993|page=C.1}}</ref> Even if the facilitator feels like they are not moving the other person's hand, they can still be providing cues that lead to specific letters on the keyboard.<ref name="Dillon, Kathleen M. (1993)" /><ref name="Todd, James (2012)" /><ref name="Kezuka, Emiko">{{cite journal|last1=Kezuka|first1=Emiko|title=The Role of Touch in Facilitated Communication|journal=Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders|date=October 1997|volume=27|issue=5|pages=571–593|doi=10.1023/a:1025882127478|pmid=9403373|s2cid=22082973}}</ref>

In 1992, when FC was fairly new to the United States, Douglas Biklen was quoted in ''[[The Washington Post]]'' as saying he "welcomed scientific studies", but the article went on to say: <blockquote>he doesn't want to do them. He's an educator, not a psychiatrist, and like other educators who have written about facilitated communication, he is comfortable with the fact that there is often a lag time between the application of a new method and its scientific validation.<ref name="Spake, Amanda (1992)" /></blockquote> Although proponents say that FC is difficult or impossible to objectively test, psychologist James T. Todd wrote: <blockquote>the determination of authorship in FC involves a straightforward application of basic experimental methods described comprehensively by [[Mill's Methods|Mill]] (1843) more than a century and half ago, but understood for millennia. We are not speaking of obscure or controversial techniques. We are speaking of authorship validation by selectively presenting different information to two people, then observing what is produced.<ref name="Todd, James (2012)" /></blockquote>

===Blind testing===
Despite the FC community's reluctance to participate in testing, researchers outside the community set up [[blinded experiment]]s to identify who was doing the communicating. Some of the tests were conducted as a direct response to cases involving sexual abuse allegations made through facilitated communication against parents, teachers, and caregivers of people with disabilities.<ref name="von Tetzchner, Stephen (1997)" /><ref name="Dickerson, Brian (2008)"/><ref name="Shane, Kearns (1994)">{{cite journal|last1=Shane|first1=Howard C.|last2=Kearns|first2=Kevin|title=An Examination of the Role of the Facilitator in "Facilitated Communication"|journal=American Journal of Speech-Language Pathology|date=September 1994|volume=3|pages=48–54|doi=10.1044/1058-0360.0303.48|issue=3}}</ref><ref name="Twachtman-Cullen">{{cite book|last1=Twachtman-Cullen|first1=Diane|title=A Passion to Believe|year=1997|publisher=Westview Press|location=Boulder, Colorado|isbn=978-0-813-39098-7|url-access=registration|url=https://archive.org/details/passiontobelieve00twac}}</ref><ref name="Seebach, Linda (2008)">{{cite news|last1=Seebach|first1=Linda|title=Charlatans to the rescue|url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB122212979072465559|access-date=March 19, 2015|work=Wall Street Journal|issue=Eastern Edition|date=23 September 2008|location=New York, New York|page=A.27|archive-date=12 January 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200112170957/https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB122212979072465559|url-status=live}}</ref> However, several controlled evaluations were also conducted by clinicians, researchers, and program administrators who were considering the use of FC, but wanted an objective, empirical basis for deciding what role, if any, FC would have in their programs.<ref name="Green, Gina (1994)" />

The O.D. Heck Center in Schenectady, New York, was one of the first in the United States to go public with their findings,<ref name="Green, Gina (1994)" /> which were that their clients produced meaningful responses through facilitated communication only when their facilitators had access to the correct responses.<ref name=ECE/> The report also ruled out issues of confidence or skepticism on the part of the evaluators. All twelve participants (people with disabilities) were chosen for the evaluation because their facilitators believed in their ability to communicate through FC. The study demonstrated that the communication partners were "systematically and unknowingly" being influenced by their facilitators. The researchers wrote:<blockquote>In fact, the nature of the findings permits us to assert that their output in facilitated communication was not only influenced, but was controlled and determined by the facilitators. To all appearances, these participants had been producing thoughtful communication, and several had consistently engaged in interactive conversations using facilitated communication. Many people serving these individuals believed that this output reflected the valid expressions of the participants.<ref name="Boodman, Sandra (1995)" /><ref name="Wheeler, Jacobson, Paglieri, Schwartz (1993)">{{cite journal|last2=Jacobson|first2=John W.|last3=Paglieri|first3=Raymond A.|last4=Schwartz|first4=Allen A.|date=February 1993|title=An experimental Assessment of Facilitated Communication|journal=American Association on Mental Retardation|volume=31|issue=1|pages=49–60|pmid=8441353|last1=Wheeler|first1=Douglas L.}}</ref></blockquote>The result of the O.D. Heck study seemed so startling, especially in light of the positive response FC was getting in the popular press, that ''[[Frontline (U.S. TV series)|Frontline]]'' featured the story in its 1993 "Prisoners of Silence".<ref name="Palfreman, Jon (1993)" /><ref name="Palfreman, Jon (2012)" /><ref name="Riggott, Julie" /><ref name="Cuff, John Haslett (1993)" /> In 1993, Genae A. Hall, research director for the Behavior Analysis Center for Autism, wrote: <blockquote>The fact that facilitators often control and direct the typing has been called "facilitator influence," which seems to be a misnomer. "Facilitator influence" suggests that the disabled person is emitting verbal behavior, and the facilitator is exerting partial control (or "influence") over that behavior. Although partial control certainly may occur when fading prompts within structured teaching programs, such control has not been demonstrated in most cases of FC. Rather than influencing the typed messages, the facilitator appears to be the sole author of those messages. Thus, the focus of analysis is shifted from the disabled person's behavior to the facilitator's behavior.<ref name="Hall, Genae (1993)">{{cite journal|last1=Hall|first1=Genae A.|date=1993|title=Facilitator control as automatic behavior: a verbal analysis|journal=The Analysis of Verbal Behavior|volume=11|issue=1|pages=89–97|doi=10.1007/bf03392890|pmc=2748555|pmid=22477083}}</ref></blockquote> Multiple other double-blind studies were being conducted at the same time,<ref name="Green, Gina (1995)" /> and whenever conditions were adequately controlled to prevent the facilitator from knowing the answers to questions, the results revealed facilitator influence, if not direct authorship.<ref name="Green, Gina (1994)" /><ref name="von Tetzchner, Stephen (1997)" /><ref name="Heinrich, Paul (February 1992)">{{cite news|last1=Heinrich|first1=Paul|title=State 'tortured' family - Landmark case finds experts' naivety 'tragic'|work=Sunday Age|issue=Late Edition| date=February 16, 1992|location=Melbourne, Australia|page=1}}</ref>

In 1994, Thistledown Regional Centre in Ontario, Canada, conducted an internal study of 20 people with autism and stopped using FC when the results showed facilitator influence was "contaminating the messages being produced."<ref name="Papp, Leslie (1996)" /> By 1995, these results had been replicated by researchers worldwide in at least 24 studies in credible, peer-reviewed research journals using multiple different methods that ensure the facilitator does not know or cannot guess the expected message, or does not look at the letters.<ref name="Green, Gina (1995)" />

In 1997, reflecting on the trajectory FC has taken in several countries, including Denmark, the U.S., and Australia, von Tetzchner wrote:<blockquote>In the struggle to keep up to date with an increasing number of published papers, both researchers and practitioners tend to forget history. To avoid making the same mistakes, the issues and processes underlying the rise and fall of facilitating techniques--as well as other intervention methods--in various countries should have a natural place in research reviews. When an intervention claimed to have exceptional effects disappears, the likely reason is a lack of positive results.<ref name="von Tetzchner, Stephen (1997)" /></blockquote>By 2005, more than 50 controlled studies and blind tests had been conducted, in addition to numerous controlled tests conducted in legal cases. The studies consistently showed "without a doubt" that the messages obtained through facilitated communication were controlled by the facilitators and not their communication partners.<ref name="Riggott, Julie" />

The vast majority of evidence now indicates that facilitated communication is not scientifically valid. However, this information has not stopped many individuals from using this technique under various circumstances and advocating for its effectiveness.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://skepticalinquirer.org/exclusive/syracuse_apple_and_autism_pseudoscience/|title=Syracuse, Apple, and Autism Pseudoscience &#124; Skeptical Inquirer|first=Marc|last=Kreidler|date=April 28, 2016|access-date=June 20, 2019|archive-date=June 20, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190620235635/https://skepticalinquirer.org/exclusive/syracuse_apple_and_autism_pseudoscience/|url-status=live}}</ref> The overwhelming majority of studies conducted on the efficacy of this technique has revealed that any "positive" results indicating that facilitated communication has worked can be attributed to the facilitators themselves.<ref name=reviewofcaa /> Be it the facilitator attributing their own beliefs and views onto the individual, or creating a pseudo-personality for the disabled individual based on their previous encounters with them, it is clear that the facilitator is the one doing all the communicating.<ref name=bealsreviewjaswal>{{cite journal |last1=Beals |first1=Katharine |title=A recent eye-tracking study fails to reveal agency in assisted autistic communication |journal=Evidence-based Communication Assessment and Intervention |date=2021 |volume=15 |issue=1 |pages=46–51 |doi=10.1080/17489539.2021.1918890|s2cid=236600771 }}</ref>

The [[American Psychological Association]] (APA) issued a statement in 1994 that there was "no scientifically demonstrated support for its efficacy."<ref name="APA FC statement">{{cite web|title=Facilitated Communication: Sifting the Psychological Wheat from the Chaff|url=http://www.apa.org/research/action/facilitated.aspx|website=American Psychological Association|access-date=17 March 2018|archive-date=16 November 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201116101557/http://www.apa.org/research/action/facilitated.aspx|url-status=live}}</ref> Finally, even further defining facilitated communication as a pseudoscience, the APA issued a statement indicating that facilitated communication studies have repeatedly demonstrated that it is not a scientifically valid technique and that it is a controversial and unproved communicative procedure with no scientifically demonstrated support for its efficacy.<ref name="APA FC statement" />

==Previous proponents==

Pat Mirenda, a professor in the Department of Educational and Counseling Psychology and Special Education at the University of British Columbia, and co-author [[David Beukelman|David R. Beukelman]], Barkley Professor of Communication Disorders at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln, had included FC in early versions of their textbook ''Augmentative and Alternative Communication: Supporting Children and Adults with Complex Communication Needs.'' These versions are quoted in pro-FC literature. However, they decided not to include FC in revised versions, and in 2015 Mirenda stated that she, "came to recognize (painfully, to be honest) that my advocacy stance biased me to interpret what I saw on videotapes as independent typing even though other explanations were more plausible (e.g., subtle prompting, resulting in an ideomotor effect), and that, even if independent typing did occur subsequent to FC exposure, only correlational—but definitely not causal—evidence exists with regard to its relationship to FC. In short, I do not endorse FC as a communication or instructional technique, and I do not support its use."<ref name="Mirenda, Pat (2015)">{{cite journal|last1=Mirenda|first1=Pat|date=13 January 2015|title=Comments and a personal reflection on the persistence of facilitated communication|journal=Evidence-Based Communication Assessment and Intervention|volume=8|issue=2|pages=102–110|doi=10.1080/17489539.2014.997427|s2cid=144689055}}</ref>

Stephen N. Calculator of the University of New Hampshire, an early proponent of FC, later distanced himself from the movement because he could not replicate claims of independent communication in his own research studies.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Calculator|first1=S|last2=Hatch|first2=E|title=Validation of facilitated communication: A case study and beyond.|journal=American Journal of Speech-Language Pathology|date=1995|volume=4|pages=49–58|issn=1058-0360|doi=10.1044/1058-0360.0401.49|issue=1}}</ref> He described the importance of determining the extent of facilitator influence: "The consequences of falsely attributing messages to communicators, rather than facilitators, continue to have significant financial, social and moral ramifications. Facilitators must take extraordinary precautions to ensure that they are not unduly influencing messages and thereby impinging on communicators' freedom of speech. The rights of individuals to express their thoughts and ideas should not be circumvented by facilitators who communicate for them, unwilling or not."<ref name="Calculator, Stephen (1999)">{{cite journal|last1=Calculator|first1=Stephen|title=Look Who's Pointing Now: Cautions Related to the Clinical Use of Facilitated Communication|journal=Language, Speech, and Hearing Services in Schools| date=October 1999|volume=30|pages=408–414|doi=10.1044/0161-1461.3004.408|pmid=27764351|issue=4}}</ref>

Janyce Boynton, who was once a strong FC proponent, is now one of FC's leading critics. In the early 1990s, she was the facilitator for a non-speaking high school girl with autism who [[List of abuse allegations made through facilitated communication#Wheaton case|seemed to describe]] having been sexually abused by her parents, resulting in the girl and her brother being removed from their home. However, systematic testing by [[Howard Shane]] revealed that the girl could not have been the author of the messages. The case was described in the 1993 PBS [[Frontline (U.S. TV program)|''Frontline'']] documentary "Prisoners of Silence". Unlike many in the FC-proponent community, Boynton accepted the evidence from Shane's testing and other well-controlled scientific studies. She stopped using FC, convinced her school administration to implement a system-wide prohibition on its use, and apologized to the falsely accused parents of the girl she had worked with. In a presentation at the CSICON meetings in 2019, Boynton argued that most FC facilitators are well-meaning but are caught up in a belief system that leads them to discount the overwhelming evidence that FC does not work.<ref name="CSICON2019">{{cite journal |last1=Frazier |first1=Kendrick |title=The foibles of FC |journal=[[Skeptical Inquirer]] |date=April 2020 |volume=44 |issue=2 |pages=12–13}}</ref> She maintains a clearinghouse of professional articles and media coverage about FC, and helped in convincing the University of Northern Iowa to stop sponsoring an annual workshop that included instruction in FC.<ref name="Vyse 2"/>  As stated by another member of that group (Stuart Vyse), "this is just the beginning. There are a number of other universities and governmental organizations that tacitly or explicitly endorse FC and/or its related techniques, and Ms. Boynton and her allies have their eyes on a number of these future targets".<ref name="Vyse 1">{{cite web |last1=Vyse |first1=Stuart |title=An Artist with a Science-Based Mission |url=https://www.csicop.org/specialarticles/show/an_artist_with_a_science-based_mission |website=CSI Online |date=16 November 2018 |publisher=Center for Inquiry |access-date=29 November 2018 |archive-date=1 December 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181201093133/https://www.csicop.org/specialarticles/show/an_artist_with_a_science-based_mission |url-status=live }}</ref>

In 2006, Belgian neurologist [[Steven Laureys]] claimed that [[Rom Houben]], a comatose man, was able to type out thoughts on a keypad with the help of facilitated communications. However, when independent tests demonstrated that FC could not produce the correct answers to questions if the facilitator had not been in the room, he agreed that Houben had not been communicating.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Marshall|first1=Michael|author-link1=Michael Marshall (skeptic)|last2=French|first2=Christopher|author-link2=Chris French|title=Why communication from a 'locked-in' child is a miracle we must question|url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/blog/2018/feb/05/why-communication-from-a-locked-in-child-is-a-miracle-we-must-question|newspaper=The Guardian|publisher=www.theguardian.com|access-date=26 April 2018|date=2018-02-05|archive-date=2018-04-26|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180426144425/https://www.theguardian.com/science/blog/2018/feb/05/why-communication-from-a-locked-in-child-is-a-miracle-we-must-question|url-status=live}}</ref>

== Presentation in the media ==
Stories of purported successes are still reported in magazines such as ''[[Reader's Digest]]'',<ref name="Gardner, Martin" /> in movies<ref name="Palfreman, Jon (2012)" /><ref name="Riggott, Julie" /><ref name="Mann, Lisa Barrett (2005)" /><ref name="Healey, Michelle (2011)" /><ref name="Murray, Steve">{{cite news|last1=Murray|first1=Steve|title=The world of autism as seen from the inside|work=The Atlanta Journal-Constitution|issue=Home Edition|date=May 21, 2005|page=Living; 3C}}</ref><ref name="McCabe, Bruce (1994)">{{cite news|last1=McCabe|first1=Bruce|title=Autism and feelings|work=[[The Boston Globe]]|issue=City Edition|date=16 October 1994| location=Boston, Massachusetts|page=3}}</ref><ref name="Shales, Tom">{{cite news|last1=Shales|first1=Tom|title=Third-place CBS hauls out yet another lame movie on Sunday|work=Buffalo News|issue=City Edition| date=14 October 1994|location=Buffalo, New York|page=C10}}</ref> and plays,<ref name="Ruth, Jim (2001)">{{cite news|last1=Ruth|first1=Jim|title=Will to survive Autistic man's struggle mirrors a new drama|work=Sunday News| date=January 2001|location=Lancaster, Pennsylvania|page=H-1}}</ref> and on television shows such as ABC's [[20/20 (U.S. TV series)|''20/20'']] Prime Time Live with [[Diane Sawyer]].<ref name="Green, Gina (1994)" /><ref name="Mostert, Mark (2012)" /><ref name="Green, Gina (1995)" /><ref name="Palfreman, Jon (2012)" /><ref name=ECE/><ref name="Gorman, Brian J. (1998)">{{cite journal|last1=Gorman|first1=Brian J.|title=Facilitated communication in America: Eight years and counting|journal=Skeptic|date=1998|volume=6|issue=3|page=8}}</ref> Thousands of people—teachers, parents, speech pathologists, psychologists—struggling to find a way to communicate with individuals who, otherwise, demonstrated little ability to use words to communicate—adopted FC with "blinding speed" with little public scrutiny or debate.<ref name="Green, Gina (1994)" /><ref name="Green, Gina (1995)" /> [[Eric Schopler]], then director of an autism education program at the University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill and editor of the Journal of Autism, described promoting facilitated communication with no empirical evidence as "reckless".<ref name="Brown, Molly T. (1992)">{{cite news|last1=Brown|first1=Molly T.|date=28 July 1992|title=The typed voice helping the nonverbal communicate|page=C:1|work=Buffalo News|location=Buffalo, New York}}</ref>

Describing this rapid rise in popularity, particularly in the United States, doctors John W. Jacobson, James A. Mulick, and Allen A. Schwartz wrote: <blockquote>The general acceptance of FC by the public and segments of the professional community has called into question the rigor with which educational and therapeutic interventions are evaluated in publicly funded programs and the ability of many professionals to critically assess the procedures they use. As such, FC serves as a case study in how the public and, alarmingly, some professionals, fail to recognize the role of science in distinguishing truth from falsity and its applicability to assessing the value of treatment modalities.<ref name="Jacobson, Mulick, Schwartz (1995)" /></blockquote>[[James Randi]], a magician familiar with the [[ideomotor effect]] commonly attributed to [[dowsing]] and later linked to FC,<ref name="Spitz, Herman" /><ref name="Burgess, et al (1998)">{{cite journal| last1=Burgess|first1=Cheryl A.|last2=Kirsch|first2=Irving|last3=Shane|first3=Howard C.| last4=Niederauer|first4=Kristen L.|last5=Graham|first5=Steven M.|last6=Bacon|first6=Alyson|s2cid=145631775| title=Facilitated Communication as an Ideomotor Response|journal= Psychological Science| date=January 1998|volume=9|issue=1|pages=71–74| doi=10.1111/1467-9280.00013}}<!--|access-date=March 19, 2015--></ref> was called in to investigate facilitated communication at the University of Wisconsin at Madison in 1992, and later called it "a crock that does more harm than good by raising false hopes among families of autistic children".<ref name="Greenbaum, Kurt (1992)" /><ref name="Gardner, Martin" /> The [[James Randi Educational Foundation]] has offered a million-dollar prize "to a valid demonstration of facilitated communication." In 2009, Randi responded in an interview for the [[Rom Houben]] case, where it was shown that messages from a Belgian man who was believed to be in a coma for 23 years were generated by the facilitator, "Our prize is still there."<ref name="Keim, Brandon">{{cite magazine|last1=Keim|first1=Brandon|title=Reborn Coma Man's Words May Be Bogus|url=https://www.wired.com/2009/11/houben-communication/|magazine=Wired|access-date=March 19, 2015|date=24 November 2009|archive-date=12 January 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140112152411/http://www.wired.com/wiredscience/2009/11/houben-communication/|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Institutional support==

===Syracuse University===
In 1992, [[Syracuse University]] founded the Facilitated Communication Institute to promote the use of FC. Douglas Biklen was appointed as the institute's first director. In 2010, the name was changed to the ''Institute on Communication and Inclusion (ICI)''. It is part of the Center on Disability and Inclusion of the School of Education. According to the ICI website, the Institute "... is an active research, training, and support center, and the nation's leading resource for information about communication and inclusion for individuals who type to communicate." The Institute carries out training and research in FC and publishes scholarly articles, books, and films.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Gorman |first1=Brian J. |title=Facilitated Communication In America: Eight Years and Counting |journal=Skeptic |date=1998 |volume=6 |issue=3 |pages=64–71}}</ref><ref name="Double Talk">{{cite web |last1=Burke |first1=Michael |title=Double Talk |url=http://dailyorange.com/2016/04/double-talk-syracuse-university-institute-continues-to-use-discredited-technique-with-dangerous-effects/ |website=The Daily Orange |access-date=30 October 2019 |date=2016-04-11 |archive-date=2019-11-08 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191108013822/http://dailyorange.com/2016/04/double-talk-syracuse-university-institute-continues-to-use-discredited-technique-with-dangerous-effects/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

===University of Northern Iowa===
From 2014 through 2018, the [[University of Northern Iowa]] (UNI) held the Midwest Summer Institute that focused on "inclusive schools, employment and daily living, as well as communication and supported or facilitated typing for people with autism spectrum disabilit[ies] and other complex communication needs."<ref name="courier-2014">{{cite news |title=UNI to host inclusion, communication event |url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/428959530/ |access-date=29 October 2019 |publisher=The Courier (Waterloo, Iowa) |date=May 5, 2014 |archive-date=29 October 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191029172030/https://www.newspapers.com/image/428959530/ |url-status=live }}</ref> In 2018, following the release of a statement from scientists and academics arguing FC had long been discredited and calling it an "invalidated and demonstrably harmful practice", UNI announced it would stop supporting the conference.<ref name=Gazette1>{{cite web |last1=Miller |first1=Vanessa |title='Facilitated communication' conference draws fire at University of Northern Iowa |url=http://www.thegazette.com/subject/news/education/facilitated-communication-conference-draws-fire-at-university-of-northern-iowa-20180615 |website=The Gazette |publisher=The Gazette, Cedar Rapids, IA |access-date=16 June 2018 |archive-date=16 June 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180616033400/http://www.thegazette.com/subject/news/education/facilitated-communication-conference-draws-fire-at-university-of-northern-iowa-20180615 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name=Gazette2>{{Cite news|url=https://www.thegazette.com/subject/news/education/university-of-northern-iowa-drops-controversial-conference-20181113|title=University of Northern Iowa drops controversial conference|last=Miller|first=Vanessa|date=November 13, 2018|work=The Gazette|access-date=November 13, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181114014955/https://www.thegazette.com/subject/news/education/university-of-northern-iowa-drops-controversial-conference-20181113|archive-date=November 14, 2018}}</ref>

==Abuse allegations and facilitator misconduct==
{{Further|List of abuse allegations made via facilitated communication}}

There have been instances in which facilitated communication produces allegations of sexual or physical abuse.<ref name="Spake, Amanda (1992)"/> Often, the alleged abuse is sexual and contains "extensive, explicit, pornographic details."<ref name="Green, Gina (1994)"/><ref>{{cite book|title=Facilitated Communication: The Clinical and Social Phenomenon|year=1994|publisher=Singular Publishing Group|isbn=978-1-565-93341-5|editor1-last=Shane|editor1-first=Howard C.|url-access=registration|url=https://archive.org/details/facilitatedcommu0000unse}}</ref> It is not known whether FC generates more abuse allegations than other suggestive techniques.<ref name="Hall, Genae (1993)"/><ref name="Lilienfeld, Scott O. (2007)">{{cite journal |last1=Lilienfeld|first1=Scott O. |date=March 2007 |title=Psychological Treatments that Cause Harm |journal=Perspectives on Psychological Science |volume=2 |issue=1 |pages=53–70<!--|citeseerx=10.1.1.531.9405--> |doi=10.1111/j.1745-6916.2007.00029.x |pmid=26151919 |s2cid=26512757}}</ref>

Researchers suspect that facilitators involved in this type of case may, mistakenly, believe there is a link between early abuse and autism, or suspect familial abuse for other reasons.<ref name="Hall, Genae (1993)" /><ref name="Lilienfeld, Scott O. (2007)" /> As Green wrote in a 1995 article:<blockquote>suggestions about sexual abuse permeate the culture. Just watch [[Oprah]] or [[Phil Donahue|Phil [Donahue]]] almost any time or scan the pop psychology section at your local bookstore. Couple that with mandatory abuse reporting laws, mix in a little bit of crusading zeal to "save" people with disabilities from mistreatment, and you have a potent set of antecedents for facilitators to produce allegations.<ref name="Green, Gina (1995)" /></blockquote>In 1993, ''Frontline''<nowiki/>'s "Prisoners of Silence" featured the story of Gerry Gherardi of North Carolina, who was accused, through FC-generated messages, of sexually abusing his son. Despite protestations of innocence, Gherardi was forced to stay away from his home for six months.<ref name="Palfreman, Jon (1993)"/> The charges were dropped when court-ordered double-blind tests showed that Gherardi's son could not write.<ref name="Koehler, Robert (1993)">{{cite news|title=TV Review 'Prisoners' Puts Autism Technique to the Test|last1=Koehler|first1=Robert|date=19 October 1993|work=Los Angeles Times|issue=Home Edition|location=Los Angeles, California|page=9}}</ref> In the same year, Rimland reported in a ''[[The New York Times|New York Times]]'' article that he knew of about 25 cases where families were accused through facilitated communication of sexually abusing their children.<ref name="Goldman, Daniel (1993)"/>

By 1995, there were 60 known cases,<ref name="Lilienfeld, Scott O. (2007)" /><ref name="Margolin, K.N. (1994)">{{cite book|title=Facilitated Communication: The Clinical and Social Phenomenon|last1=Margolin|first1=K.N.|date=1994|publisher=Singular Publishing|isbn=978-1-565-93341-5|editor1-last=Shane|editor1-first=Howard C.|location=San Diego, CA|pages=[https://archive.org/details/facilitatedcommu0000unse/page/227 227–257]|chapter=How Shall Facilitated Communication be Judged? Facilitated Communication and the Legal System|chapter-url=https://archive.org/details/facilitatedcommu0000unse/page/227}}</ref> with many others settled without reaching public visibility. Since then, the number of cases continues to increase. In addition to accusations of sexual abuse, facilitators have reportedly fallen in love with their communication partners and, relying on FC for consent, initiated sexual, physical contact with people in their care,<ref name="Lilienfeld, Marshall, Todd, Shane (2015)"/><ref name="Sundstrom, Kathy (2014)"/> raising serious ethical and legal problems.<ref name="Todd, James (2012)"/>

=== Anna Stubblefield  ===
{{Main|Anna Stubblefield}}

In 2015, [[Anna Stubblefield]], a [[Rutgers University–Newark]] philosophy professor, was found guilty of aggravated sexual assault against a man with severe mental disabilities. A proponent of facilitated communication, Stubblefield's website described her as "certified as a Facilitated Communication Trainer by the FC Institute at the School of Education, Syracuse University. She provides [[motor planning]] support for communication and literacy for adults and children."<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://andromeda.rutgers.edu/~philos1/component/content/component/content/article/8-fac/7-anna.html|title=Archived University Website of Anna Stubblefield|last=Stubblefield|first=Anna|date=June 27, 2010|website=Anna Stubblefield|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100627171006/http://andromeda.rutgers.edu/~philos1/component/content/component/content/article/8-fac/7-anna.html|archive-date=June 27, 2010|url-status=dead|access-date=October 4, 2015}}</ref> At the time the investigation began in 2011, Stubblefield was the chair of Rutgers-Newark's philosophy department, whose professional work centered on ethics, race, and disability rights,<ref name="NYTM102015">{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/10/25/magazine/the-strange-case-of-anna-stubblefield.html|title=The Strange Case of Anna Stubblefield|author1=Daniel Engber|date=October 20, 2015|work=The New York Times Magazine|access-date=October 21, 2015|quote=...the judge ruled that facilitated communication failed New Jersey's test for scientific evidence.|archive-date=October 20, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151020210800/http://www.nytimes.com/2015/10/25/magazine/the-strange-case-of-anna-stubblefield.html|url-status=live}}</ref> but she was subsequently put on administrative leave without pay and removed as chair of the philosophy department.<ref name="Wichert, Bill (2015)" /><ref name="Zambito, Thomas (2014)" />

The victim was identified as D.J., a 33-year-old African-American man with severe mental disabilities who cannot speak, has [[cerebral palsy]], and is unable to stand independently or accurately direct movements of his body. Based on his disability, his mother and brother were appointed his legal guardians.<ref name="NYTM102015" /> Stubblefield stated that she had successfully communicated with him, determining he was of normal intelligence. She subsequently brought him to conferences where she "held him out as a success story". In 2011, she revealed to his mother and brother that she had had sexual relations with D.J. and said that they were in love, attributing consent to messages received while facilitating. Stubblefield stated that the two of them had a mutually consenting relationship established through facilitated communication. However, testing of D.J. by family members failed to establish the ability to communicate, and Stubblefield was thanked but denied further access to D.J. She continued to attempt to maintain contact with D.J. and began challenging control of D.J.'s legal guardians over him.<ref name="NYTM102015" /> In August 2011, the family contacted the police.<ref name="Wichert, Bill (2015)">{{cite news|url=http://www.nj.com/essex/index.ssf/2015/01/judge_approves_document_use_in_trial_of_rutgers_professor_accused_of_sexually_assaulting_mentally_di.html|title=New Jersey: Judge OKs document detailing Rutgers professor's sexual relations with mentally disabled man|last1=Wichert|first1=Bill|date=January 8, 2015|work=NJ Advance Media|access-date=21 March 2015|publisher=New Jersey Online LLC|archive-date=2 April 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402091353/http://www.nj.com/essex/index.ssf/2015/01/judge_approves_document_use_in_trial_of_rutgers_professor_accused_of_sexually_assaulting_mentally_di.html|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Szteinbaum, Sabrina">{{cite news|url=http://www.dailytargum.com/article/2014/04/former-rutgers-newark-philosophydepartment-chairwoman-to-appear-in-court-for-alleged-sexual-abuse-o|title=Former RutgersNewark philosophy department chairwoman to appear in court for alleged sexual abuse of mentally handicapped man|last1=Szteinbaum|first1=Sabrina|work=The Daily Targum|access-date=March 21, 2015|location=New Brunswick, New Jersey|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402171541/http://www.dailytargum.com/article/2014/04/former-rutgers-newark-philosophydepartment-chairwoman-to-appear-in-court-for-alleged-sexual-abuse-o|archive-date=April 2, 2015|url-status=dead}} Dead link as of October 22, 2015</ref>

Stubblefield pleaded not guilty to the charges and said that FC revealed D.J. was mentally capable, while prosecutors said that FC was scientifically discredited and that D.J. did not have the ability to consent to sexual relations.<ref name="Wichert, Bill (2015)" /><ref name="Zambito, Thomas (2014)">{{cite news|url=http://www.nj.com/news/index.ssf/2014/04/judge_questions_consent_defense_in_case_of_rutgersnewark_professor_accused_of_sex_assault.html|title=Judge questions 'consent' defense in case of Rutgers-Newark professor accused of sexual assault|last1=Zambito|first1=Thomas|date=April 25, 2014|work=NJ Advance Media for NJ.com|access-date=March 21, 2015|publisher=New Jersey Online LLC}} Dead link as of October 22, 2015</ref> Experts evaluating D.J. testified he did not have the intellectual ability to consent to sexual activity.<ref name="Wichert"/> Facilitated communication testimony from D.J. was not allowed as the technique was ruled unreliable under New Jersey law.<ref name="NYTM102015" /> After a three-week trial, the jury found Stubblefield guilty of two counts of first-degree aggravated sexual assault.<ref name="NYTM102015" /> After conviction, the judge revoked bail, saying that she was a flight risk,<ref name="NYTM102015" /> and she was sentenced to 12 years in prison.<ref name="startribune.com">{{cite web|url=http://www.startribune.com/sentencing-for-prof-convicted-of-sex-abuse-of-disabled-man/365390581/|title=Professor who abused disabled man sentenced to prison|work=[[Associated Press]] via [[Star Tribune]]|access-date=15 January 2016}}{{Dead link|date=August 2018|bot=InternetArchiveBot|fix-attempted=yes}}</ref> This included requiring her to register as a sex offender.<ref name="startribune.com" /><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.timesunion.com/news/crime/article/Sentencing-for-prof-convicted-of-sex-abuse-of-6760684.php|title=Professor who abused disabled man gets 12 years in prison|author=David Porter, [[Associated Press]]|date=15 January 2016|agency=[[Associated Press]]|publisher=[[Times Union (Albany)|Times Union]]|access-date=16 January 2016}}</ref> In July 2017, an appeals court overturned her conviction and ordered a retrial,<ref>{{cite court |litigants=State of New Jersey v. Stubblefield |vol=162 |reporter=A.3d |opinion=1074 |court=[[New Jersey Superior Court, Appellate Division|N.J. Super. Ct. App. Div]] |date=2017-06-09 |url=https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=2725698065028411594}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{cite news|url=https://www.nj.com/essex/index.ssf/2018/05/anna_stubblefield_sentenced_for_second_time.html|title=No more prison for ex-Rutgers professor who sexually assaulted disabled student|last=Napoliello|first=Alex|date=11 May 2018|access-date=2 October 2018|publisher=NJ.com|archive-date=3 October 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181003014216/https://www.nj.com/essex/index.ssf/2018/05/anna_stubblefield_sentenced_for_second_time.html|url-status=live}}</ref> and in 2018 she pleaded guilty to "third-degree aggravated criminal sexual contact" and was sentenced to time served.<ref name=":0" /> In October 2016, the family was awarded $4 million in a civil lawsuit against Stubblefield.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nj.com/essex/index.ssf/2018/03/ex-rutgers-newark_prof_admits_criminal_sexual_cont.html|title=Ex-Rutgers prof admits it was a crime to have sex with disabled man|last1=Moriarty|first1=Thomas|publisher=NJ.com|access-date=20 March 2018|date=2018-03-19|archive-date=2018-03-19|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180319232326/http://www.nj.com/essex/index.ssf/2018/03/ex-rutgers-newark_prof_admits_criminal_sexual_cont.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

The 2023 documentary film ''[[Tell Them You Love Me]]'' covers the story.<ref>{{cite web |last=Latif |first=Leila |title=Tell Them You Love Me review – this chilling documentary is vital, challenging TV |url=https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio/2024/feb/03/tell-them-you-love-me-review-this-chilling-documentary-is-vital-challenging-tv |website=[[The Guardian]] |archive-url=https://archive.today/20240204032218/https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio/2024/feb/03/tell-them-you-love-me-review-this-chilling-documentary-is-vital-challenging-tv |archive-date=4 February 2024 |date=3 February 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Martina Susanne Schweiger case ===
In 2014, Martina Susanne Schweiger of Queensland, Australia, received an 18-month suspended jail sentence for two counts of indecent dealing with a 21-year-old client with severe autism with whom she worked at a disability services home. The client required 24-hour support and could not speak, write, or use manual sign language.

Schweiger believed the client expressed love for her through FC, which she claimed to reciprocate. She also believed the client, again through FC, indicated a desire to have sex. On one occasion, Schweiger removed her clothes in front of her client. On another, she "play wrestled" with him, touching his penis with her hands and mouth. She confessed her actions to her employer. After hearing reports from Alan Hudson, psychology professor at [[RMIT University]], that FC "did not work for the young man", Judge Gary Long of [[Maroochydore]] District Court found Schweiger guilty of the charges, indicating that FC was neither reliable nor accurate as a method of communication.<ref name="Sundstrom, Kathy (2014)" /><ref name="Sundstrom, Kathy (2014b)">{{cite news|url=http://www.sunshinecoastdaily.com.au/news/mother-angered-by-suspended-sentences/2422829/|title=Mother angered by suspended sentences|last1=Sundstrom|first1=Kathy|date=17 October 2014|work=Sunshine Coast Daily|access-date=March 19, 2015|location=Queensland, Australia|page=4|archive-date=2 April 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402220021/http://www.sunshinecoastdaily.com.au/news/mother-angered-by-suspended-sentences/2422829/|url-status=live}}</ref>
