The creation of these 18 quarters was intended to address [[overcrowding]]. On 11 November 1998, the governor of North Kivu signed Order No. 01/085/CAB/GP-NK/98, which established quarters in the city. It divided Katoyi into Kasika and Katoyi, and Mabanga into Mabanga-Nord and Mabanga-Sud.<ref name=":25">{{Cite web |last=Mussa |first=Kanambe Juakaly |date=2012 |title=L'émergence du M23 au Nord-Kivu et son impact sur la situation socio-économique des habitants de la ville de Goma |trans-title=The emergence of the M23 in North Kivu and its impact on the socio-economic situation of the inhabitants of the city of Goma |url=https://www.memoireonline.com/11/13/7719/m_L-emergence-du-M23-au-Nord-Kivu-et-son-impact-sur-la-situation-socio-economique-des-habitants-de-l9.html |access-date=25 December 2025 |publisher=Institut Supérieur de Développement Rural des Grands Lacs (ISDR-GL) |language=fr |publication-place=Goma, North Kivu, Democratic Republic of the Congo}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Buchekabiri |first=E. C. |date=2013 |title=Analyse de la population de la ville de goma sur les programmes de la radio television communautaire Tayna Â« rtct Â» 2011–2012 |trans-title=Analysis of the population of the city of Goma on the programs of the community radio television Tayna “rtct” 2011–2012 |url=https://www.memoireonline.com/01/17/9500/m_Analyse-de-la-population-de-la-ville-de-goma-sur-les-programmes-de-la-radio-television-communautaire3.html |access-date=7 February 2024 |publisher=Université du CEPROMAD |language=fr |publication-place=Goma, Democratic Republic of the Congo}}</ref>

A subsequent order, No. 10/037/CAB/GP-NK/98, established Bujovu quarter in the Karisimbi commune. Bujovu included the Byahi and Tyazo cells, formerly part of Majengo and Virunga quarters, respectively.<ref name=":25" /><ref name=":1" />

==History==
{{For timeline}}
The village of Ngoma was a port for lake traffic and a crossroads for the overland trade routes between [[Central Africa]] and the [[Indian Ocean]]. In 1894, the explorer [[Gustav Adolf von Götzen]], following the footsteps of an earlier missionary, was traveling to Rwanda from the eastern coast of Africa and passed through the village, which he recorded as Goma.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Charton |first=Edouard |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=pIJQAQAAIAAJ |title=Le Tour du monde: nouveau journal des voyages |publisher=Hachette Livre |year=1892 |location=Paris, France |pages=14–16 |language=fr}}</ref><ref>Koen Vlassenroot, Timothy Raeymaekers, ''Conflict and Social Transformation in Eastern DR Congo'', Academia Press, USA, 2004, p. 105</ref> In 1906, officers of the [[Congo Free State]] established Goma post opposite [[Gisenyi]] as a military outpost to oversee [[Maritime transport|maritime]] activities on [[Lake Kivu]], which later transformed into a civil status office.<ref>{{Cite book |last= |first= |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=TwjqTXt-n2EC |title=Revue des questions scientifiques |publisher=Société scientifique de Bruxelles |year=1914 |location=Brussels, Belgium |pages=336–337 |language=fr}}</ref><ref name=":8">{{Cite web |last=Karumba |first=Janvier Bagula |date=2011 |title=De l'opportunité du développement du tourisme au nord Kivu. Cas de la ville de Goma |trans-title=The opportunity for tourism development in North Kivu. Case of the city of Goma |url=https://www.memoireonline.com/01/14/8505/De-l-opportunite-du-developpement-du-tourisme-au-nord-Kivu-Cas-de-la-ville-de-Goma.html |access-date=14 February 2024 |publisher=Institut Supérieur de Tourisme de Goma (ISTou-Goma) |language=fr |publication-place=Goma, North Kivu, Democratic Republic of the Congo}}</ref> Around 1930, the Goma precinct accommodated camps for laborers of the Eastern Railway (CFE), initially sited along Lake Kivu's eastern shores.<ref name=":8" /> By the mid-20th century, Goma had become an essential hub, and served as the endpoint of the [[Société des Chemins de Fer Vicinaux du Congo|Vici Congo]] road network and a port for the [[transshipment]] of agricultural commodities and [[building material]]s to and from [[Bukavu]].<ref name=":8" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Zihalirwa |first=Etienne Mushagalusa |date=2014 |title=Commercialisation des cartes prepayees par les revendeurs dans la ville de Goma: Cas de la commune de Goma |trans-title=Marketing of prepaid cards by resellers in the city of Goma: Case of the commune of Goma |url=https://www.africmemoire.com/part.4-chapitre-deuxieme-presentation-du-cadre-de-recherche-129.html |access-date=23 January 2025 |publisher=[[Free University of the Great Lakes Countries]] |language=fr |publication-place=Goma, North Kivu, Democratic Republic of the Congo}}</ref> In 1945, it burgeoned into a state post under [[Rutshuru Territory]]'s jurisdiction, experiencing a rapid demographic upsurge with approximately 8,600 inhabitants.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Jouannet |first=Francis |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7h5hSTWUHjwC |title=Le français au Rwanda: enquête lexicale |publisher=Peeters Publishers |year=1984 |isbn=978-2-85297-170-7 |pages=84 |language=fr}}</ref><ref name=":8" /> Goma's prominence as a city grew steadily and earned it the status of an extra-customary center that year.<ref name=":8" /> Educational infrastructure developed in tandem, with institutions such as the "École Royale" (now the Goma Institute or INSTIGO) and the École Primaire d'Application de l'institut de Goma (EPAIGO) catering to European settlers.<ref name=":43">{{Cite web |last=Babonangenda |first=Laetitia |date=2016 |title=Developpement du capital humain et croissance des petites et moyennes entreprises: cas de la ville de Goma de 2013–2015 |trans-title=Human capital development and growth of small and medium-sized enterprises: the case of the city of Goma from 2013–2015 |url=https://www.africmemoire.com/part.6-chapitre-deuxieme-le-secteur-des-pme-dans-la-ville-de-goma-122.html |access-date=22 January 2025 |publisher=[[Free University of the Great Lakes Countries]] |language=fr |publication-place=Goma, North Kivu, Democratic Republic of the Congo}}</ref> Meanwhile, the native population relied on the Saint André School, later renamed Kyeshero Primary School, for [[primary education]].<ref name=":43" /> 

The inception of urbanization in [[Belgian Congo]] was formalized with the promulgation of a decree on 21 February 1949, which instituted entities responsible for evaluating and issuing building permits, overseeing demolitions, modifying [[Land lot|land plots]], and making changes to the urban landscape.<ref name=":18">{{Cite web |last=John |first=Luendo Malira |date=September 2018 |title=Essai d'etude sur le reamenagement urbain de la ville de Goma |trans-title=Study essay on the urban redevelopment of the city of Goma |url=https://www.istougoma.ac.cd/pdf/publication/642ac6221e32a.pdf |access-date=4 October 2024 |publisher=Institut Supérieur de Tourisme de Goma (ISTOU-Goma) |pages=23–24 |language=fr |publication-place=Goma, North Kivu, Democratic Republic of the Congo}}</ref> In 1951, Goma was elevated to the territorial and capital level of North Kivu. This period also witnessed movements advocating for administrative separation between Goma and [[Rutshuru]], leading to the establishment of deliberative and executive bodies in Kirotshe and later in [[Sake, Democratic Republic of the Congo|Sake]].<ref name=":8" />

The urban sprawl of Goma adhered to the archetypal colonial planning paradigm with the demarcation of separate neighborhoods for Europeans (''cité Européenne'') and indigenous Congolese (''cité indigène'').<ref name=":9">{{Cite web |last1=Hendriks |first1=Maarten |last2=Büscher |first2=Karen |date=September 2019 |title=Insecurity in Goma: Experiences, actors and responses |url=https://riftvalley.net/wp-content/uploads/2020/02/Insecurity-in-Goma-by-Maarten-Hendriks-and-Karen-Buscher-RVI-Usalama-Project-2019.pdf |access-date=14 January 2024 |website=Riftvalley.net |publisher=[[Rift Valley Institute]] |page=14 |publication-place=Nairobi, Kenya}}</ref> The latter was limited to contemporary Birere, a densely populated ''quartier'' abutting the Rwandan border. Meanwhile, the ''quartiers'' allocated for European settlers were concentrated within the contemporary city center (''quartier les Volcans'') and an enclave of the Himbi ''quartier'', which persists as the most urbanized, affluent, and wealthy parts of the city.<ref name=":9" />

On 25 December 1966, [[Nord-Kivu District|North Kivu regained its district status]] before becoming a region following the constitutional referendum of June 1967.<ref name=":8" /> By 10 July 1988, North Kivu attained its regional autonomy, promulgating its status as a sovereign entity within the [[Kivu|tripartite division of the Kivu region]] into provinces: [[North Kivu]], [[South Kivu]], and [[Maniema]].<ref name=":8" /> A decree issued on 14 September 1988, outlined critical urban development guidelines, such as construction alignments, the delineation of housing plans and communication routes, and the segregation of sustainable residential districts from native-dominated huts.<ref name=":18" /> This marked the onset of a segregationist urban paradigm, in which Congolese cities became characterized by a dichotomy between modern urban centers and native settlements.<ref name=":18" /> As a result of Goma's burgeoning urbanization, the city was officially designated as the provincial capital of the newly established North Kivu province under Ordinance Law No. 88-178, issued on 15 November 1988.<ref name=":18" />

===1994 Hutu refugee crisis===

The [[Rwandan genocide|1994 Rwandan genocide]] was executed by the interim Rwandan government against the [[Tutsi]] population and [[Hutu]] moderates. In response, the [[Rwandan Patriotic Front]] (RPF), formed by Tutsi refugees from Uganda, who already held control over significant portions of northern Rwanda after their invasion in 1990 and the ongoing [[Rwandan Civil War|Civil War]], overthrew the Hutu government in [[Kigali]], forcing them out.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Wrong |first=Michela |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=S7_pDwAAQBAJ |title=Do Not Disturb: The Story of a Political Murder and an African Regime Gone Bad |date=2021-03-30 |publisher=PublicAffairs |isbn=978-1-61039-843-5 |location=New York City, New York, United States}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Tilly |first=Charles |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=LbGtAQAAQBAJ&dq=hutus+were+killed+by+RPF+IN+1994&pg=PT104 |title=The Politics of Collective Violence |date=2003-03-17 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-1-107-49480-0 |location=Cambridge, England, United Kingdom}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bentrovato |first=Denise |date=2015-07-06 |title=Rwanda, Twenty Years On |url=https://journals.openedition.org/etudesafricaines/18095 |journal=Cahiers d'études africaines |language=fr |issue=218 |pages=231–254 |doi=10.4000/etudesafricaines.18095 |issn=0008-0055}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Dizolele |first=Mvemba Phezo |date=2024-02-22 |title=The Dark Side of Rwanda's Rebirth |url=https://foreignpolicy.com/2021/05/29/the-dark-side-of-rwandas-rebirth/ |access-date=2024-02-15 |website=Foreign Policy |publication-place=Washington, D.C., United States}}</ref> Over two million Hutus fled the country to Zaire and many Tutsis and Hutus were internally displaced within Rwanda.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Roper |first=Steven D. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=IfhADwAAQBAJ&dq=hutus+were+killed+by+RPF+IN+1994&pg=PT32 |title=Designing Criminal Tribunals: Sovereignty and International Concerns in the Protection of Human Rights |date=2017-11-30 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-351-16010-0 |location=Thames, Oxfordshire United Kingdom}}</ref> Although Hutu extremists were responsible for the mass killing of Tutsis, scholars like Judi Rever and [[Filip Reyntjens]] argue that the main perpetrators of the slaughter were the Tutsi-dominated RPF, led by [[Paul Kagame]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Rever |first=Judi |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=i9LMDwAAQBAJ&q=In+Praise+of+Blood:+The+Crimes+of+the+Rwandan+Patriotic+Front |title=In Praise of Blood: The Crimes of the Rwandan Patriotic Front |date=18 February 2020 |publisher=[[Random House of Canada]] |isbn=978-0-345-81210-0 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Epstein |first=Helen |date=7 June 2018 |title=The Mass Murder We Don't Talk About |url=https://www.nybooks.com/articles/2018/06/07/rwanda-mass-murder-we-dont-talk-about/ |access-date=24 October 2024 |work=[[The New York Review of Books]] |language=en |publication-place=New York, New York, United States |volume=65 |issue=10 |issn=0028-7504}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=6 June 2018 |title=Debate: Judi Rever will not let anything stand in the way of her quest to document a second Rwandan genocide |url=https://msf-crash.org/en/publications/war-and-humanitarianism/debate-judi-rever-will-not-let-anything-stand-way-her-quest |access-date=24 October 2024 |website=Msf-crash.org |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Reyntjens |first=Filip |date=2004 |title=Rwanda, Ten Years on: From Genocide to Dictatorship |journal=African Affairs |volume=103 |issue=411 |pages=177–210 |doi=10.1093/afraf/adh045 |jstor=3518608 |issn=0001-9909|doi-access=free }}</ref> According to Judi Rever, Kagame personally commanded massacres at places like [[Byumba]] soccer stadium in northern Rwanda and ordered the pursuit of Hutus in the Zairean forests.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Mass Murder at the Byumba Stadium – Hutu Genocide |url=https://www.hutugenocide.org/mass-murder-at-the-byumba-stadium/ |access-date=24 October 2024 |website=Hutugenocide.org |language=en-US}}</ref> They devised ways to dispose of large numbers of bodies by "dissolving them in acid, dumping them in rivers and swamps, or burning them, and established open air crematorium".<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kuzmarov |first=Jeremy |date=7 December 2018 |title=Exposing the Crimes of the CIAs Fair-Haired Boy, Paul Kagame, and the Rwandan Patriotic Front |url=https://www.counterpunch.org/2018/12/07/exposing-the-crimes-of-the-cias-fair-haired-boy-paul-kagame-and-the-rwandan-patriotic-front/ |access-date=24 October 2024 |website=CounterPunch.org |language=en-US}}</ref> Various UN missions attempted to establish safe zones and facilitate the movement of refugees. Between 13 June and 14 July 1994, an overwhelming number of refugees, ranging from 10,000 to 12,000 per day, fled across the border to Goma, resulting in a severe [[humanitarian crisis]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.radionetherlandsarchives.org/healers-without-borders/|title=Healers without borders|date=February 15, 1995|website=radionetherlandsarchives.org}}</ref> as there was an acute lack of shelter, food and water. However, the Zairean government took it upon itself to garner attention for the situation. Shortly after the arrival of nearly one million [[refugee]]s,<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.radionetherlandsarchives.org/the-long-wait-the-rwandan-refugees-in-zaire/|title=The long wait – the Rwandan refugees in Zaire|date=November 13, 1995|website=radionetherlandsarchives.org}}</ref> a deadly [[cholera]] outbreak swept through the Hutu refugee camps near Goma, claiming thousands of lives. RPF-aligned forces, which had fought in the conflict, crossed the border to Zaire and in acts of revenge also claimed several lives
[[File:Mihanda camp.jpg|thumb|Aerial photograph of the Mihanda refugee camp]]

=== First Congo War ===
{{Further information|First Congo War|Massacres of Hutus during the First Congo War}}

As early as mid-1996, infiltrated units from Rwanda began targeting [[Massacres of Hutus during the First Congo War|Hutu refugee camps]] along the [[Rutshuru]] road, even before formal hostilities began. On the evening of 27 June 1996, an infiltrated group allegedly carried out an attack on the Kibumba refugee camp, resulting in casualties among Hutu refugees, soldiers from the ''Contingent Zaïrois pour la sécurité des camps'' (CZSC), and [[International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement|Red Cross]] personnel.<ref name=":10">{{Cite web |date=15 June 2009 |title=Attacks against hutu refugees in camps on the Goma to Rutshuru road (North Kivu) |url=https://www.mapping-report.org/en/attacks-against-hutu-refugees-in-camps-on-the-goma-to-rutshuru-road-north-kivu/ |access-date=15 February 2024 |website=Mapping-report.org |publisher=[[DRC Mapping Exercise Report]] |publication-place=Geneva, Switzerland, New York City, United States}}</ref>

During the [[First Congo War]], from mid-October 1996, Rwandan infiltrations intensified, accompanied by sporadic attacks on refugee camps along the Goma to Rutshuru road by the newly formed [[AFDL|Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo]] (AFDL), a rebel movement led by [[Laurent-Désiré Kabila]], and [[Rwanda Defence Force|Rwandan Patriotic Army]] (RPA) led by [[Paul Kagame]], who aimed to overthrow [[Mobutu Sese Seko]]'s regime, accusing him of excluding Tutsis from governance and failing to stop the [[génocidaires]].<ref name=":10" /> However, the [[United Nations Security Council]] noted that both the RPA and AFDL pillaged Zaire's minerals for nearly two and a half decades and conducted massacres throughout the conflict.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Rever |first=Judi |date=25 September 2023 |title=Rwanda is the 'Wild West' and should be removed from the mineral supply chain |url=https://canadiandimension.com/articles/view/rwanda-is-the-wild-west-and-should-be-removed-from-the-mineral-supply-chain |access-date=24 October 2024 |website=[[Canadian Dimension]] |language=en |publication-place=Winnipeg, Manitoba, Canada}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=16 October 2002 |title=Letter dated 15 October 2002 from the Secretary-General addressed to the President of the Security Council |url=https://www.securitycouncilreport.org/atf/cf/%7B65BFCF9B-6D27-4E9C-8CD3-CF6E4FF96FF9%7D/DRC%20S%202002%201146.pdf |access-date=24 October 2024 |website=[[United Nations Security Council]] |publication-place=New York, New York, United States}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=April 2024 |title=Blood Minerals: The laundering of DRC's 3T minerals by Rwanda and private entities |url=https://amsterdamandpartners.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/2024.04.25-AP-DRC-Blood-Minerals.pdf |access-date=24 October 2024 |publisher=Amsterdam & Partners LLP |pages=25–51 |publication-place=London, England, United KIngdom}}</ref> The Kibumba camp, situated twenty-five kilometers north of Goma, was the first to fall under assault. On the night of 25–26 October 1996, AFDL and RPA soldiers bombarded the Kibumba camp, resulting in casualties among Hutu refugees and the destruction of the camp's hospital. Subsequently, approximately 194,000 refugees fled Kibumba towards the Mugunga camp.<ref name=":10" /> The Katale camp also faced attacks on the same night, but [[Forces Armées Zaïroises]] (FAZ)/CZSC soldiers and ex-FAR/[[Interahamwe]] units repelled the assailants initially.<ref name=":10" /> However, on 26 October 1996, AFDL and RPA forces attacked the Katale camp, resulting in numerous Hutu refugee casualties and the death of a Zairian soldier. They also allegedly killed several Hutu refugees using [[Edged and bladed weapons|bladed weapons]]. Following confrontations with FAZ soldiers and ex-FAR/Interahamwe units from the Katale camp, who offered reinforcement, AFDL and RPA forces seized control of the FAZ military camp at [[Rumangabo]].<ref name=":10" />

By 30 October, refugees from Katale and [[Katindo|Kahindo]] camps began to depart, with some heading towards [[Masisi]] via Tongo ''groupement'' of [[Bwito Chiefdom]], while others attempted to reach the Mugunga camp through the [[Virunga National Park]]. However, AFDL and RPA troops had blocked the road to Goma, complicating the refugees' escape routes. On 31 October 1996, AFDL and RPA soldiers allegedly massacred hundreds of Hutu refugees who remained in the Kahindo and Katale camps.<ref name=":10" /> [[:es:Roberto Garretón|Roberto Garretón]], the [[United Nations special rapporteur|Special Rapporteur]] on the violation of human rights in Zaire, estimated the casualties and highlighted the brutality inflicted on the refugees.<ref name=":10" />

In the aftermath of AFDL/RPA offensives in North Kivu, some refugees opted to return to Rwanda, though their numbers remained small. UNHCR reported approximately 900 Hutu refugees returning to Rwanda between 26 October and 31 October 1996. The reluctance of many refugees to return stemmed from both physical and psychological pressures, including fear of reprisals from AFDL/RPA soldiers.<ref name=":10" /> There were reports of AFDL/RPA soldiers killing refugees who expressed a desire to return to Rwanda.<ref name=":10" /> Determining the exact number of refugees killed by AFDL/RPA soldiers in attacks along the Goma to Rutshuru road was challenging. However, local NGOs involved in burial operations provided insights into the scale of the atrocities. The [[DRC Mapping Exercise Report|United Nations Mapping Report]] team documented numerous alleged incidents, including mass burials and killings in and around refugee camps between November 1996 and April 1997.<ref name=":10" /> The violence extended beyond the dismantling of refugee camps; Hutu survivors faced persecution while attempting to flee. In November 1996, AFDL/RPA soldiers reportedly targeted Hutu survivors from Kahindo and Katale camps, executing adult males.<ref name=":10" /> These survivors, along with others who resettled in makeshift camps, were subjected to further attacks in the Virunga National Park, resulting in additional casualties.<ref name=":10" /> The atrocities persisted for several months, with killings reported well into 1997. Witness testimonies highlighted the grim reality faced by refugees, with bodies discovered daily in former camp sites.<ref name=":10" /> On 11 April 1997, AFDL/RPA soldiers allegedly massacred hundreds of refugees near Kibumba village. These refugees, intercepted while attempting to return to Rwanda, were detained and subsequently killed by AFDL/RPA forces.<ref name=":10" />

By the end of 1997, AFDL rebels advanced to [[Kinshasa]], driving out Mobutu and leading to Laurent-Désiré Kabila proclaiming himself president on 17 May, renaming the country the [[Democratic Republic of the Congo]] (DRC).<ref name=":12">{{Cite book |last1=Usanov |first1=Artur |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=en5eBAAAQBAJ&dq=second+congo+war+Laurent+Kabila+refuse+to+share+power&pg=PA36 |title=Coltan, Congo and Conflict |last2=Ridder |first2=Marjolein de |last3=Auping |first3=Willem |last4=Lingemann |first4=Stephanie |last5=Espinoza |first5=Luis Tercero |last6=Ericsson |first6=Magnus |last7=Farooki |first7=Masuma |last8=Sievers |first8=Henrike |last9=Liedtke |first9=Maren |date=2013-06-05 |publisher=The Hague Centre for Strategic Studies |isbn=978-94-91040-81-8 |location=Hague, Netherlands |pages=36}}</ref>

=== Second Congo War ===
{{Further information|Second Congo War}}
Within a year of assuming power, [[Laurent-Désiré Kabila]] found himself in conflict with his former allies, and in 1998, the Rwandan government threw its support behind a Goma-based rebel movement known as the [[Rally for Congolese Democracy|Congolese Rally for Democracy]] (RCD), occasionally denoted as [[Rally for Congolese Democracy–Goma|RCD-Goma]].<ref name=":11">{{Cite book |last=Scherrer |first=Christian P. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RJLDEAAAQBAJ&dq=Rwanda+supports+RCD+against+Kabila&pg=PA266 |title=Genocide and Crisis in Central Africa: Conflict Roots, Mass Violence, and Regional War |date=2001-11-30 |publisher=Bloomsbury Publishing USA |isbn=978-0-313-01617-2 |pages=266}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Holmes |first=Georgina |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ShGMDwAAQBAJ |title=Women and War in Rwanda: Gender, Media and the Representation of Genocide |date=2013-10-25 |publisher=Bloomsbury Publishing |isbn=978-0-85772-317-8 |location=London, England, United Kingdom |pages=26}}</ref> The Goma refugee encampments, where Hutu refugees and Interahamwe militants had forged a militia known as the [[Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda|Democratic Force for the Liberation of Rwanda]] (FDLR), morphed into battlegrounds as Rwandan government forces and the RCD clashed with them to assert dominion.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Ciment |first=James |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BpGXBwAAQBAJ&dq=Rwanda+supports+RCD+against+Kabila&pg=PA144 |title=Encyclopedia of Conflicts Since World War II |date=2015-03-27 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-317-47186-8 |location=Thames, Oxfordshire, United Kingdom |pages=144–146}}</ref><ref name=":11" />

On 2 August 1998, General Sylvain Buki announced via ''[[Radio-Télévision nationale congolaise|Radio-Télévision Nationale Congolaise]]'' (RTNC) in Goma that a rebellion had erupted within the [[Air Force of the Democratic Republic of the Congo|Congolese Armed Forces]] (FAC).<ref name=":13">{{Cite web |date=15 June 2009 |title=Second Congo War – Attacks on other civilian populations – North Kivu |url=https://www.mapping-report.org/en/second-congo-war-attacks-on-other-civilian-populations-north-kivu/ |access-date=15 February 2024 |website=Mapping-report.org |publisher=[[United Nations]] |publication-place=Geneva, Switzerland, New York City, United States}}</ref> The 10th Brigade of the FAC mutinied, leading to the swift capture of Goma by the RCD and Rwandan Patriotic Army (RPA), with minimal resistance. Goma remained beyond the reach of the Kinshasa government's forces for nearly three years, save for [[Barrage (artillery)|sporadic barrage]].<ref name=":13" /> Amidst these conflicts, the RCD's bias towards the local Tutsi community, Rwandan interference in provincial affairs, and the brutality of RCD and RPA troops towards civilians in North Kivu prompted many locals to join [[Mai-Mai|Mayi–Mayi]] armed groups to defend their communities. The Mayi–Mayi militias utilized forested areas and national parks as bases for launching attacks against RCD and RPA forces.<ref name=":13" />

With support from Kinshasa, the Mayi–Mayi and [[Army for the Liberation of Rwanda|ALiR]] intensified ambushes and pillaging against RCD/RPA soldiers and civilian populations. Consequently, RCD/RPA control was limited to certain urban areas. In response, they increased search operations in various regions.<ref name=":13" /> The [[Second Congo War]] was unprecedented in Africa for the loss of civilian life in massacres and atrocities. By 2003, the Rwandan [[Banyamulenge]]-supported insurgent factions wearied of the conflict, and discord surfaced between them and Rwanda. In 2002 and 2003, a tenuous [[Pretoria Accord|negotiated peace]] ensued among the myriad factions embroiled in the conflict.<ref>{{Cite web |date=September 23, 2002 |title=Peace Agreements Digital Collection |url=https://www.usip.org/sites/default/files/file/resources/collections/peace_agreements/drc_rwanda_pa07302002.pdf |access-date=2024-02-16 |website=[[United States Institute of Peace]] |publisher=United States Institute of Peace |publication-place=Washington, D.C., United States}}{{dead link|date=April 2025|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last1=Aktas |first1=Tufan |last2=Kavak |first2=Gokhan |date=February 3, 2023 |title=Rwanda, Congo drifting toward war again as rebels surge anew |url=https://www.aa.com.tr/en/africa/rwanda-congo-drifting-toward-war-again-as-rebels-surge-anew/2805426 |access-date=2024-02-15 |website=www.aa.com.tr}}</ref>

===Ongoing conflict, 2002-present===
[[File:La città di Goma e il lago Kivu (RD Congo).JPG|thumb|right|Aerial view of Goma in October 2010]]
Since the conclusion of the Second Congo War, Goma has been plagued by conflict despite the peace agreements of 2002. In 2006, it became a focal point for the [[Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of the Congo]]'s 81st and 83rd Brigades, who remained faithful to Congolese Tutsi military defector [[Laurent Nkunda]], who accused the government of neglecting to assimilate his military faction into the national army and failing to safeguard their interests.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2007-01-05 |title=Goma: vers le mixage entre FARDC et éléments de Laurent Nkunda |trans-title=Goma: towards the mix between FARDC and elements of Laurent Nkunda |url=https://www.radiookapi.net/sans-categorie/2007/01/05/goma-vers-le-mixage-entre-fardc-et-elements-de-laurent-nkunda |access-date=2024-02-21 |website=Radio Okapi |language=fr}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2007-01-20 |title=Nord-Kivu : début de mixage des troupes de Nkunda et des FARDC |trans-title=North Kivu: start of mixing of Nkunda and FARDC troops |url=https://www.radiookapi.net/sans-categorie/2007/01/20/nord-kivu-debut-de-mixage-des-troupes-de-nkunda-et-des-fardc |access-date=2024-02-21 |website=Radio Okapi |language=fr |publication-place=Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of the Congo}}</ref> Numerous heinous crimes were committed by Nkunda during his reign of terror. In 2002, he sanctioned the massacre of over 150 people in [[Kisangani]].<ref name=":14">{{Cite web |date=2006-02-02 |title=Human Rights Watch demande l'arrestation de Laurent Nkunda |trans-title=Human Rights Watch calls for the arrest of Laurent Nkunda |url=https://www.radiookapi.net/sans-categorie/2006/02/02/human-rights-watch-demande-l%25e2%2580%2599arrestation-de-laurent-nkunda |access-date=2024-02-21 |website=Radio Okapi |language=fr |publication-place=Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of the Congo}}</ref> In [[Bukavu]] in 2004, his insurgent affiliates, in conjunction with Colonel [[Jules Mutebutsi]], executed widespread atrocities, including sexual violence and arbitrary detentions, predominantly targeting young girls.<ref name=":14" /><ref>{{Cite web |date=2007-02-28 |title=Sud-Kivu : 6 officiers FARDC refoulés de Bukavu |trans-title=South Kivu: 6 FARDC officers pushed back from Bukavu |url=https://www.radiookapi.net/sans-categorie/2007/02/28/sud-kivu-6-officiers-fardc-refoules-de-bukavu |access-date=2024-02-21 |website=Radio Okapi |language=fr |publication-place=Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of the Congo}}</ref> [[Human Rights Watch]] clamored for Nkunda's arrest in February 2006,<ref name=":14" /> but it wasn't until June of that year that his military faction made significant territorial gains, capturing localities like [[Bunagana, Democratic Republic of the Congo|Bunagana]], located 80&nbsp;km from Goma.<ref name=":15">{{Cite web |date=6 December 2006 |title=Nord-Kivu : les Fardc reprennent deux des trois localités occupées par Laurent Nkunda |trans-title=North Kivu: the Fardc retake two of the three localities occupied by Laurent Nkunda |url=https://www.radiookapi.net/sans-categorie/2006/12/06/nord-kivu-les-fardc-reprennent-deux-des-trois-localits-occupes-par-laurent-nkunda |access-date=21 February 2024 |website=[[Radio Okapi]] |language=fr |publication-place=Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of the Congo}}</ref>
[[File:15 novembre 2014. Goma, Nord-Kivu, RD Congo. Une vue aérienne de la ville de Goma. (16927160596).jpg|thumb|left|View of houses in Goma, 2014]]
Despite intermittent losses and counteroffensives by FARDC's 9th Integrated Brigade,<ref name=":15" /> Nkunda's forces maintained control over certain areas like Bunagana and Runyoni. By November 2006, reports cited three fatalities and 41 injuries, among them civilians,<ref>{{Cite web |date=26 November 2006 |title=Affrontements de Sake, près de Goma : 3 morts et plus de 40 blessés |trans-title=Clashes in Sake, near Goma: 3 dead and more than 40 injured |url=https://www.radiookapi.net/sans-categorie/2006/11/26/affrontements-de-sake-prs-de-goma-3-morts-et-plus-de-40-blesss |access-date=8 November 2024 |website=[[Radio Okapi]] |language=fr}}</ref> and by December, the violence had displaced over 80,000 people, many of whom sought refuge on the outskirts of Goma.<ref>{{Cite web |date=20 December 2006 |title=Nord-Kivu: plus de 80 000 déplacés de guerre |trans-title=North Kivu: more than 80,000 war displaced |url=https://www.radiookapi.net/sans-categorie/2006/12/20/nord-kivu-plus-de-80-000-dplacs-de-guerre |access-date=21 February 2024 |website=[[Radio Okapi]] |language=fr |publication-place=Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of the Congo}}</ref> The conflict escalated further in early 2007, with Goma's healthcare organization, Groupe d'Entraide et de Solidarité Médicale (GESOM), treating an average of three rape survivors daily from both urban and rural sectors.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2 February 2007 |title=Prise en charge des femmes victimes de viols à Goma |trans-title=Support for women victims of rape in Goma |url=https://www.radiookapi.net/emissions-2/2007/02/02/prise-en-charge-des-femmes-victimes-de-viols-a-goma |access-date=8 November 2024 |website=[[Radio Okapi]] |language=fr}}</ref> On 17 May, FARDC arrested 14 Rwandan nationals, including members of Nkunda's brigade, as [[MONUSCO]] noted that his militia in North Kivu was wearing distinctive Rwandan military uniforms.<ref>{{Cite web |date=3 June 2007 |title=Goma: 14 Rwandais aux arrêts |trans-title=Goma: 14 Rwandans arrested |url=https://www.radiookapi.net/sans-categorie/2007/06/03/goma-14-rwandais-aux-arrets |access-date=21 February 2024 |website=[[Radio Okapi]] |language=fr |publication-place=Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of the Congo}}</ref> Later in May, the French Ambassador to the Democratic Republic of Congo, Bernard Prévost, visited the Mugunga displacement camp near [[Sake, Democratic Republic of the Congo|Sake]] and announced that [[France]] would allocate over [[Euro sign|€]]2.6 million to the [[World Food Programme]] to support displaced persons in the eastern DRC.<ref>{{Cite web |date=31 May 2007 |title=Goma: la France promet 2 millions d'euros pour les déplacés de guerre |trans-title=Goma: France promises 2 million euros for war displaced persons |url=https://www.radiookapi.net/actualite/2007/05/31/goma-la-france-promet-2-millions-d%25e2%2580%2599euros-pour-les-deplaces-de-guerre |access-date=8 November 2024 |website=[[Radio Okapi]] |language=fr}}</ref> In June 2007, [[William L. Swing|William Lacy Swing]], Director General of the [[International Organization for Migration]], expressed profound concern about the escalating conflict, citing rising insecurity, ethnic discord, the swelling numbers of internally displaced persons, and an increase in human rights abuses in North Kivu.<ref>{{Cite web |date=28 June 2007 |title=De Goma, William Swing appelle les troupes mixées à aller au brassage |trans-title=From Goma, William Swing calls on the mixed troops to go to the brewing |url=https://www.radiookapi.net/sans-categorie/2007/06/28/de-goma-william-swing-appelle-les-troupes-mixees-a-aller-au-brassage |access-date=8 November 2024 |website=[[Radio Okapi]] |language=fr}}</ref> Toward the end of June, Rwandan combatants launched a deadly assault on Lake Kivu, resulting in the deaths of four people, including three fishermen and a [[Navy of the Democratic Republic of the Congo|Congolese naval]] officer.<ref name=":26">{{Cite web |date=19 July 2007 |title=Goma: un bandit rwandais tué sur le lac Kivu |trans-title=Goma: Rwandan bandit killed on Lake Kivu |url=https://www.radiookapi.net/sans-categorie/2007/07/19/goma-un-bandit-rwandais-tue-sur-le-lac-kivu |access-date=8 November 2024 |website=[[Radio Okapi]] |language=fr}}</ref> The attackers also looted valuable fishing equipment and an [[outboard motor]]. Initial negotiations with Rwandan officials regarding cross-border security on Lake Kivu ultimately facilitated the partial recovery of the stolen fishing assets in Rwanda.<ref name=":26" />
[[File:Displaced people set camp in Goma outskirts (7703457692).jpg|thumb|Displaced residents from the Kibumba-[[Rutshuru]] axis, fleeing clashes between Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and advancing [[March 23 Movement]] rebels, set up camp in Kanyaruchinya, 4 km north of Goma]]
On 6 September, MONUSCO brokered a ceasefire between the FARDC and forces loyal to Laurent Nkunda.<ref name=":27">{{Cite web |date=7 September 2007 |title=Sake: le cessez-le-feu respecté |trans-title=Sake: the ceasefire respected |url=https://www.radiookapi.net/sans-categorie/2007/09/07/sake-le-cessez-le-feu-respecte |access-date=8 November 2024 |website=[[Radio Okapi]] |language=fr}}</ref> However, the following day saw renewed clashes, with most of the population from Goma's surrounding regions seeking shelter in the Mugunga, Lac-Vert, and Ndosho neighborhoods, as well as Goma Centre, fearing further confrontations between the FARDC and Nkunda's forces.<ref name=":27" /> Fighting between Nkunda's forces and the [[Mai-Mai]] community-based militia, Congolese Patriotic Resistance (PARECO), which claimed to protect its community from Nkunda's forces, led to the deaths of 5 people in Bitonga in southern Masisi Territory.<ref>{{Cite web |date=13 September 2007 |title=Encore des affrontements à Masisi |trans-title=More clashes in Masisi |url=https://www.radiookapi.net/sans-categorie/2007/09/13/encore-des-affrontements-a-masisi |access-date=8 November 2024 |website=[[Radio Okapi]] |language=fr}}</ref> Nine deceased people were subsequently uncovered in three separate [[mass grave]]s within Rubare, approximately 12&nbsp;km from [[Rutshuru]], north of Goma.<ref>{{Cite web |date=18 September 2007 |title=Rubare: encore 9 corps découverts dans des fosses communes |trans-title=Rubare: 9 more bodies discovered in mass graves |url=https://www.radiookapi.net/sans-categorie/2007/09/18/rubare-encore-9-corps-decouverts-dans-des-fosses-communes |access-date=8 November 2024 |website=[[Radio Okapi]] |language=fr}}</ref> Two other bodies were discovered in the administrative support post of Kisharo's office, around 20 kilometers from Kiwanja, along the route to Nyamilima and Shasha, within Rutshuru Territory.<ref>{{Cite web |date=18 September 2007 |title=Kisharo: 2 corps retrouvés dans le bureau du chef de poste |trans-title=Kisharo: 2 bodies found in the station chief's office |url=https://www.radiookapi.net/sans-categorie/2007/09/18/kisharo-2-corps-retrouves-dans-le-bureau-du-chef-de-poste |access-date=8 November 2024 |website=[[Radio Okapi]] |language=fr}}</ref> On 27 October 2008, the [[2008 Nord-Kivu campaign|Battle of Goma]] broke out in the city between the Congolese army, supported by MONUSCO, and Nkunda's [[National Congress for the Defence of the People|CNDP]] rebels; 200,000 refugees fled the town.<ref name="CNNuproot">{{cite news |date=27 October 2008 |title=U.N. says recent Congo fighting uproots 200,000 |url=http://edition.cnn.com/2008/WORLD/africa/10/24/Congo.displaced.ap/index.html?iref=newssearch |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081029213801/http://edition.cnn.com/2008/WORLD/africa/10/24/Congo.displaced.ap/index.html?iref=newssearch |archive-date=October 29, 2008 |access-date=28 October 2008 |publisher=[[CNN]]}}</ref>

On 3 November 2012, there was a [[2012 Congolese–Rwandan border clash|clash between Congolese and Rwandan troops]] on the border just north of Goma. Goma was later seized by the [[M23 rebellion (2012–2013)|M23 Movement]] on 20 November 2012.<ref name="Callimachi">[https://web.archive.org/web/20121221033507/http://www.businessweek.com/ap/2012-11-20/congolese-rebels-penetrate-goma-take-airport "Congolese rebels seize Goma, take airport."] Melanie Goubyrukmini Callimachi, ''Bloomberg BusinessWeek'', November 20, 2012. Retrieved 20 November 2012.</ref> Later that year, the Rwandan-backed rebel group, the [[March 23 Movement]] (M23), made significant territorial gains in North Kivu. Fighting began with the FARDC in [[Nyiragongo Territory]], particularly in the [[Bukumu Chiefdom#Groupements|Kibumba ''groupement'']] of [[Bukumu Chiefdom]], resulting in the M23 taking direct control of the entire territory. The territorial administrator and most of his staff fled strategically.<ref name=":49">{{Cite web |last=Mussa |first=Kanambe Juakaly |date=2012 |title=L'émergence du M23 au Nord-Kivu et son impact sur la situation socio-économique des habitants de la ville de Goma |trans-title=The emergence of the M23 in North Kivu and its impact on the socio-economic situation of the inhabitants of the city of Goma |url=https://www.memoireonline.com/11/13/7719/L-emergence-du-M23-au-Nord-Kivu-et-son-impact-sur-la-situation-socio-economique-des-habitants-de-l.html |access-date=27 December 2025 |publisher=Institut Supérieur de Développement Rural des Grands Lacs (ISDR-GL) |language=fr |publication-place=Goma, North Kivu, Democratic Republic of the Congo}}</ref> As clashes spread to the southern part of the [[Bukumu Chiefdom#Groupements|Munigi ''groupement'']] and surrounding areas, Goma ultimately fell to M23 on 20 November 2012. Under M23 rule, the city's residents experienced terror due to the rebel presence, limited access to drinking water, lack of electricity, deteriorating hygiene and sanitation, sharply rising prices, higher unemployment, restrictions on freedom of expression, and increased social inequality. 13 people were killed, 23 women were sexually assaulted, 17 men were kidnapped, 109 motorcycles were confiscated, and 1,970 laptops were stolen.<ref name=":49" /><ref>{{Cite web |last1=Hendriks |first1=Maarten |last2=Büscher |first2=Karen |date=August 2019 |title=Insecurity in Goma: Experiences, actors and responses |url=https://riftvalley.net/wp-content/uploads/2020/02/Insecurity-in-Goma-by-Maarten-Hendriks-and-Karen-Buscher-RVI-Usalama-Project-2019.pdf |access-date=21 February 2024 |website=Riftvalley.net |publisher=Rift Valley Institute |page=17 |publication-place=Nairobi, Kenya}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Congo Violence: Tens of Thousands of Civilians Flee Goma |url=http://www.huffingtonpost.com/2012/11/23/congo-violence-goma_n_2177612.html|access-date=23 November 2012|newspaper=Huffington Post|date=2012 |author=Pete Jones |author2=Jerome Delay}}</ref>

On 22 February 2021, the [[List of ambassadors of Italy to the Democratic Republic of the Congo|Italian ambassador]], [[Luca Attanasio]], was killed in an apparent kidnapping attempt near [[Virunga National Park]]. He was part of the U.N.'s [[World Food Programme]] (WFP). Two others were also killed.

The [[M23 campaign (2022–present)|M23 campaign]], which pitted M23 against the FARDC and other armed groups, has displaced around 1.1 million people, including over 600,000 now confined to overcrowded, unsanitary displacement sites surrounding Goma.<ref name=":23">{{Cite web |date=21 June 2023 |title=RDC : MSF demande une augmentation rapide et concrète de l'aide humanitaire face à une crise d'ampleur historique au Nord-Kivu |trans-title=DRC: MSF calls for a rapid and concrete increase in humanitarian aid in the face of a crisis of historic proportions in North Kivu |url=https://www.msf.fr/communiques-presse/rdc-msf-demande-une-augmentation-rapide-et-concrete-de-l-aide-humanitaire-face-a-une-crise-d-ampleur-historique-au-nord-kivu |access-date=2 March 2024 |website=www.msf.fr |language=fr |publication-place=Paris, France}}</ref> Some regional efforts have sought to contain the crisis, including the deployment of [[Southern African Development Community]] (SADC) forces and high-level summits aimed at reviving the peace process and securing a ceasefire.<ref name=":24">{{Cite web |date=1 March 2024 |title=Évaluation Rapide de Crise M23: Rapport 15, Province du Nord Kivu, 1 mars 2024 – Democratic Republic of the Congo |trans-title=M23 Rapid Crisis Assessment: Report 15, North Kivu Province, March 1, 2024 |url=https://reliefweb.int/report/democratic-republic-congo/evaluation-rapide-de-crise-m23-rapport-15-province-du-nord-kivu-1-mars-2024 |access-date=2 March 2024 |website=[[ReliefWeb]] |publisher=[[International Organization for Migration]] |publication-place=Geneva, Switzerland}}</ref> On 12 February, South Africa announced the dispatch of 2,900 troops to support the [[SADC Mission in the Democratic Republic of Congo|SADC mission in eastern DRC]],<ref>{{Cite news |last=Felix |first=Bate |date=12 February 2024 |editor-last=Choy |editor-first=Marguerita |title=South Africa to deploy 2,900 troops to fight armed groups in eastern Congo |url=https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/south-africa-deploy-2900-troops-fight-armed-groups-eastern-congo-2024-02-12/ |access-date=2 March 2024 |work=[[Reuters]] |publication-place=London, England}}</ref> though the operation suffered losses when two South African soldiers were killed and three wounded by M23 [[Mortar (weapon)|mortar fire]] on 15 February.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Peyton |first=Nellie |date=15 February 2024 |editor-last=Russell |editor-first=Ros |others=(ed.). Oatis, Jonathan |title=South African military: 2 soldiers killed, 3 wounded on Congo mission |url=https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/south-african-military-2-soldiers-killed-3-wounded-congo-mission-2024-02-15/ |access-date=2 March 2024 |work=[[Reuters]] |location=London, England}}</ref> Despite these initiatives, prospects for lasting peace remain uncertain, particularly in the absence of [[Democratic Republic of the Congo–Rwanda conflict (2022–present)|direct dialogue between the Democratic Republic of Congo and Rwanda]].<ref name=":24" /> By [[M23 campaign (2022–present)#2025 Goma and Bukavu offensives|January 2025, Goma was again targeted in a renewed M23 offensive]], resulting in widespread casualties, looting, infrastructure damage, and mass displacement,<ref>{{cite news |date=26 January 2025 |title=Leader of Congo's rebel alliance says they have taken Goma |url=https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/un-peacekeeper-death-toll-eastern-congo-rises-six-2025-01-26/ |access-date=28 January 2025 |work=Reuters.com |publisher=[[Reuters]]}}</ref> with nearly 3,000 people reportedly killed.<ref>{{cite news |last=Jaime |first=Caroline |last2=Stambaugh |first2=Alex |last3=Elsamra |first3=Mounira |date=6 February 2025 |title=Nearly 3,000 people killed after rebels seize key city in DR Congo, UN says |url=https://edition.cnn.com/2025/02/06/africa/dr-congo-goma-violence-deaths-intl-hnk/index.html |work=Edition.cnn.com |publisher=[[CNN]]}}</ref> On 27 January, the city was captured by M23, and more than 4,000 detainees escaped from Muzenze prison amid the fighting,<ref>{{cite news |last=Princewill |first=Nimi |date=7 February 2025 |title=More than 150 female inmates raped and burned to death during Goma jailbreak in DRC, UN says |url=https://edition.cnn.com/2025/02/06/africa/female-inmates-raped-killed-goma-jailbreak-intl/index.html |work=Edition.cnn.com |publisher=[[CNN]]}}</ref> during which hundreds of female inmates were reportedly raped and burned alive.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Bastmeijer |first1=Joost |last2=Townsend |first2=Mark |last3=Houttuin |first3=Saskia |date=5 February 2025 |title=Hundreds of women raped and burned to death after Goma prison set on fire |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2025/feb/05/democratic-republic-congo-goma-women-raped-burned-death-prison-m23-rebels-rwanda |access-date=5 February 2025 |work=[[The Guardian]] |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref> A year later, on 27 January 2026, the Congolese government organized a national commemoration titled ''Résistance, Résilience et Unité du peuple congolais'' (meaning "Resistance, Resilience, and Unity of the Congolese People") at the [[Académie des Beaux-Arts (Kinshasa)|Académie des Beaux-Arts]] in Kinshasa to honor civilians killed or displaced by the conflict.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Mutuba |first=James |date=28 January 2026 |title=L'an 1 d'occupation de Goma par l’AFC/M23: à Kinshasa, le gouvernement organise "une journée de mémoire" en hommage aux victimes du conflit dans l'Est |trans-title=The first year of the AFC/M23 occupation of Goma: in Kinshasa, the government is organizing a "day of remembrance" in tribute to the victims of the conflict in the East |url=https://actualite.cd/2026/01/28/lan-1-doccupation-de-goma-par-lafcm23-kinshasa-le-gouvernement-organise-une-journee-de |access-date=9 February 2026 |website=[[Actualite.cd]] |language=fr |publication-place=Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of the Congo}}</ref>

=== Coltan conflict-driven crime ===
[[File:Quarry nearby Goma - North Kivu (21052488542).jpg|thumb|[[Quarry]] near Goma]]
The regional conflict surrounding [[coltan]] and other lucrative resources has compounded Goma's challenges with crime.<ref name=":132">{{Cite web |date=31 March 2003 |title=Democratic Republic of Congo: 'Our brothers who help kill us": Economic exploitation and human rights abuses in the east |url=https://www.amnesty.org/en/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/afr620102003en.pdf |access-date=14 November 2024 |website=Amnesty.org |publisher=[[Amnesty International]] |pages=35–39 |publication-place=London, England, United Kingdom}}</ref> Armed groups, including the Rwandan military, the RCD-Goma, and various opposition factions, have been implicated in the systemic targeting of civilians as they vied for dominion over resource-abundant zones.<ref name=":1322">{{Cite web |date=31 March 2003 |title=Democratic Republic of Congo: 'Our brothers who help kill us": Economic exploitation and human rights abuses in the east |url=https://www.amnesty.org/en/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/afr620102003en.pdf |access-date=14 November 2024 |website=Amnesty.org |publisher=[[Amnesty International]] |pages=35–39 |publication-place=London, England, United Kingdom}}</ref> During 2000 and 2001, RCD-Goma forces reportedly conducted a spate of violent incursions into residences, particularly targeting individuals engaged in the [[coltan]] trade. Notably, on 18 November 2000, armed men, including RCD-Goma combatants, attacked the residence of Edouard Kasereka Kahimba, a coltan buyer.<ref name=":1322" /> The assailants demanded [[business record]]s and coltan, injuring Kahimba and assaulting his family members.<ref name=":1322" /> On 29 December 2000, combatants reportedly targeted a coltan trader known as "Safro" Sanvura, ransacking his residence and shooting indiscriminately. Similar incidents persisted into 2001, such as the attack on Pierre Hakizimana on 9 April, in which he was robbed of $3,000 at gunpoint.<ref name=":1322" />

On 8 September 2001, unidentified men in uniform conducted an early-morning attack on Sengiyumva, a 41-year-old coltan trader residing in Katoyi.<ref name=":1322" /> He sustained three gunshot wounds to his leg after being beaten with sticks, with both cash and mineral resources being seized.<ref name=":1322" /> Subsequently, on 14 October 2001, another trader, Papy, aged 26, endured a violent assault in his home, resulting in two gunshot wounds to the abdomen, allegedly inflicted by RCD-Goma forces. Though Papy survived, he required prolonged hospitalization for recovery.<ref name=":1322" />

== Volcanic activity ==
Due to the [[Great Rift Valley]] being pulled apart, the area experiences frequent [[earthquake]]s and the formation of new [[volcano]]es. Over time, volcanic eruptions have directly impacted Goma, with significant [[lava]] flows destroying nearby villages, neighborhoods, and roads north of the city.<ref name=":19" /> The 1923 and 1997 eruptions caused significant damage and loss of life, with lava flows encroaching upon [[Lake Kivu]]'s shores and destroying sections of the city.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Szeglat |first=Marc |title=Volcano Nyiragongo in Congo |url=https://www.vulkane.net/en/volcanoes/nyiragongo/nyiragongo.html |access-date=28 February 2024 |website=Vulkane.net}}</ref><ref name=":19" /><ref>{{Cite web |last1=Nyandwi |first1=Blaise Mafuko |last2=Kervyn |first2=Matthieu |last3=François |first3=Habiyaremye Muhashy |last4=Kervyn |first4=François |date=30 April 2021 |title=Volcanic risk communication challenges in the Global South: the case of Goma, Eastern Democratic Republic of Congo |url=https://presentations.copernicus.org/EGU21/EGU21-15597_presentation-h815290.pdf |access-date=28 February 2024 |website=Copernicus.org |publication-place=Göttingen, Germany}}</ref>

=== 2002 Nyiragongo volcano eruption ===
[[File:Nyiragongo volcano - SRTM.jpg|thumb|right|Computer image of Nyiragongo volcano generated from satellite photographs, showing the Goma-Gisenyi conurbation on the lake shore in the foreground. In the background, left, is the [[Nyamuragira]] volcano. Note that the vertical scale has been exaggerated.|222x222px]]
In January 2002, [[Nyiragongo]] erupted, sending a stream of [[lava]] {{convert|200|m|yd|0}} to {{convert|1|km|yd|abbr=off|spell=in}} wide and up to two meters (6½&nbsp;ft) deep through the center of the city as far as the lake shore. Agencies monitoring the volcano were able to give a warning and most of the population of Goma evacuated to Gisenyi. The lava destroyed 40% of the city (more than 4,500 houses and buildings). There were some fatalities caused by the lava and by emissions of [[carbon dioxide]], which causes [[asphyxiation]]. The lava also covered over the northern 1&nbsp;km of the {{convert|3|km|ft|adj=on}} [[runway]] of [[Goma International Airport]], isolating the terminal and apron which were at that end.<ref>[http://www.eri.u-tokyo.ac.jp/KAZANKYO/n_report/72.pdf "Cooperative Observations at Nyiragongo Volcano in D.R. of Congo".] Earthquake Research Institute, University of Tokyo. Retrieved 3 September 2007.</ref> The lava can easily be seen in satellite photographs,<ref>[http://earth.google.com Google Earth] has high resolution photographs showing the affected part of the airport at coordinates −1.658, 29.237. Retrieved 3 September 2007.</ref> and aircraft can be seen using the 2-km (6,500-ft) southern section of the runway which is clear of lava.

In March 2004, emissions from Nyiragongo volcano polluted the surrounding areas of North Kivu, including Rusayo, Bishusha, Birambizo, Tongo, [[Kitchanga|Kitshanga]], and [[Sake, Democratic Republic of the Congo|Sake]] with [[water vapor]] ({{chem2|H2O}}) laden with [[fluorine]] and [[carbon dioxide]] ({{chem2|CO2}}).<ref>{{Cite web |date=17 March 2004 |title=Le gaz de Nyiragongo, un danger pour les villages environnants |trans-title=Nyiragongo gas, a danger for surrounding villages |url=https://www.radiookapi.net/sans-categorie/2004/03/17/le-gaz-de-nyiragongo-un-danger-pour-les-villages-rnrnrnrnenvironnants |access-date=28 February 2024 |website=[[Radio Okapi]] |language=fr |publication-place=Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of the Congo}}</ref>

=== 2021 Nyiragongo volcano eruption ===
{{further|2021 Mount Nyiragongo eruption}}
{{Multiple image
| image1      = The Nyirangongo volcano, one of the most active in the Great Lakes region, erupted on Saturday, May 22, causing the displacement of populations who feared for their safety (51229412299).jpg
| image2      = The Nyirangongo volcano, one of the most active in the Great Lakes region, erupted on Saturday, May 22, causing the displacement of populations who feared for their safety (51228861853).jpg
| image3      = The Nyirangongo volcano, one of the most active in the Great Lakes region, erupted on Saturday, May 22, causing the displacement of populations who feared for their safety (51229412829).jpg
| footer      = The 2021 Mount Nyiragongo eruption forced many residents to flee their homes in search of safety.
| total_width = 200
| direction   = vertical
}}

On 22 May 2021, Mount Nyiragongo erupted with lava flows closing a road and reaching the [[Goma International Airport|municipal airport]].<ref>{{cite news |last=Knowles |first=H. |date=May 2021 |title=Congo volcano erupts for first time in years, sending people fleeing from major city |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/2021/05/22/congo-volcano-eruption-nyiragongo/?outputType=amp |accessdate=May 22, 2021 |newspaper=[[Washington Post]]}}</ref> The Buhene ''quartier'', located on the edge of Goma, was engulfed in [[flame]]s, and more than 500 homes were covered in cooling [[lava]]. Parts of Virunga Energies's electricity facilities, which supplied electricity to nearly 15,000 homes in the city, were destroyed.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Katumwa |first=Justin Kabumba |title=Mount Nyiragongo: At least 15 dead, over 170 children feared missing after volcano erupts in eastern Congo, officials say |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/world/2021/05/23/mount-nyiragongo-congo-volcano-deaths-victims/5236294001/ |access-date=28 February 2024 |website=[[USA Today]]|publication-place=New York, New York, United States}}</ref> Thousands of people fled to nearby regions, with some boarding boats on [[Lake Kivu]], which lies on the border of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Rwanda. Around 5,000 people crossed the border into Rwanda, while another 25,000 went northwest towards [[Sake, Democratic Republic of the Congo|Sake]].<ref name=":20">{{Cite web |last=Brackett |first=Ron |date=23 May 2021 |title=At Least 15 Dead After Congo's Mount Nyiragongo Volcano Erupts; Lava Engulfs Neighborhood {{!}} Weather.com |url=https://weather.com/news/news/2021-05-23-congo-volcano-mount-nyiragongo-eruption-goma-evacuation |access-date=28 February 2024 |website=Weather.com/news |publication-place=Atlanta, Georgia, United States|publisher=[[The Weather Channel]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=25 May 2021 |title="Je n'ai pas pu sauver mon mari malade de la lave" |url=https://www.bbc.com/afrique/region-57240950 |access-date=28 February 2024 |website=BBC News Afrique |language=fr|trans-title=Nyiragongo volcano in Goma: "I couldn't save my sick husband from the lava"}}</ref> The lava stopped flowing around 3 a.m. on 30 May 2021, and the Congolese government ordered the city's evacuation plan to be set in motion.<ref name=":20" /> On the same day, residents returned to Goma to check on their homes. However, the [[UNICEF|United Nations Children's Fund]] reported that more than 170 children were still missing.<ref name=":20" /> The official report on the number of deaths is yet to be released, but the Minister of Communication and Media, [[Patrick Muyaya Katembwe]], said at least 15 people died. Nine people died in a [[traffic collision]], four died while trying to escape from the central prison of Munzenze, and two were calcined by lava.<ref>{{Cite web |date=23 May 2021 |title=Eruption du volcan Nyiragongo: 15 morts (Officiel) |trans-title=Eruption of the Nyiragongo volcano: 15 dead (Official) |url=https://www.radiookapi.net/2021/05/24/actualite/societe/eruption-du-volcan-nyiragongo-15-morts-officiel |access-date=28 February 2024 |website=[[Radio Okapi]] |language=fr |publication-place=Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of the Congo}}</ref>

=== 2023 Nyamulagira volcano eruption ===
On 9 May 2023, lava flows were seen inside the central [[crater]] of [[Nyamuragira|Nyamulagira volcano]]. By 17 May, a large glow above the volcano was visible, leading to lava flows in [[Virunga National Park]].<ref name=":21">{{Cite web |last=Blašković |first=Teo |date=22 May 2023 |title=Lava flows on the flanks of Nyamulagira volcano, large emissions of gas and fine particles, DR Congo |url=https://watchers.news/2023/05/22/lava-flows-on-the-flanks-of-nyamulagira-volcano-large-emissions-of-gas-and-fine-particles-dr-congo/ |access-date=28 February 2024 |website=Watchers.news}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Pulver |first=Dinah Voyles |date=22 May 2023 |title=Volcanoes are erupting, spewing ash on these three continents |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/nation/2023/05/22/popocatepetl-volcano-mexico-etna-eruption-italy-nyamulagira-africa/70245438007/ |access-date=28 February 2024 |website=[[USA Today]]|publication-place=New York, New York, United States}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Global Volcanism Program: Report on Nyamulagira (DR Congo) — 17–23 May 2023 |url=https://volcano.si.edu/ShowReport.cfm?wvar=GVP.WVAR20230517-223020 |access-date=28 February 2024 |website=volcano.si.edu|date=May 2023|publisher=[[Global Volcanism Program]]}}</ref> While the lava flows do not harm the population, the volcano emits large amounts of gas and fine particles. [[Thermal radiation]] over the crater increased sharply on 19 May, indicating an increase in the outpouring of lava, but the activity was still confined to the summit.<ref name=":21" /> [[Effusive eruption]] increased further on 20 May, forming two large lobes — one outside the [[caldera]] to the west and another to the south. Although not visible, [[Satellite imagery|satellite images]] on May 19 and 20 showed that the current eruption at the volcano was emitting enormous amounts of [[sulfur dioxide]] (SO<sub>2</sub>).<ref name=":21" />

===Threat posed by Lake Kivu===
{{Main|Limnic eruption}}

[[Lake Kivu]] is one of three lakes in Africa identified as having huge quantities of dissolved gas held at pressure in its depths. The other two, [[Cameroon]]'s [[Lake Monoun]] and [[Lake Nyos]], experienced [[limnic eruptions]] or "lake overturns", catastrophic releases of suffocating carbon dioxide probably triggered by landslides. Lake Nyos's overturn in 1986 was particularly lethal, killing nearly two thousand people in the area around the lake. Kivu is 2,000 times bigger than Lake Nyos and also contains dissolved methane as an additional hazard – though concentration of carbon dioxide is much lower than in Lake Nyos.<ref name="solidarites">{{cite web |author=Halbwachs |display-authors=etal |date=9 March 2002 |title=Investigations in Lake Kivu(East Central Africa) after the Nyiragongo Eruption of January 2002: Specific study of the impact of the sub-water lava inflow on the lake stability |url=http://www.eawag.ch/research_e/apec/Scripts/Lorke_publication_lake_kivu_2002.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080528121843/http://www.eawag.ch/research_e/apec/Scripts/Lorke_publication_lake_kivu_2002.pdf |archive-date=28 May 2008 |access-date=17 August 2008 |publisher=Solidarities}}</ref> Nearly two million people, including the population of Goma, live in the vicinity of Lake Kivu and could be in danger from a limnic eruption triggered by one of the nearby volcanoes and the earthquakes associated with them.<ref>[https://www.bbc.co.uk/science/horizon/2001/killerlakes.shtml "Killer Lakes"]. [[BBC Two]], 4 April 2002. Summarised at 
www.bbc.co.uk.</ref>

The [[Carbon dioxide|CO<sub>2</sub>]]-rich gas location, known locally as [[mazuku]], caused the deaths of people and animals in 2023.<ref>{{cite web |date=1 November 2005 |title=NOVA – Transcripts – Volcano Under the City – PBS |url=https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/nova/transcripts/3215_volcanoc.html |access-date=28 December 2024 |website=Pbs.org|publisher=[[PBS]]|publication-place=Arlington, Virginia, United States}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last1=Muhambya |first1=Katya |last2=Chaubey |first2=Nirbhay Kumar |last3=Kasereka |first3=Selain K. |last4=Mulondo |first4=Kayitoghera G. |date=16 October 2023 |title=GIS-based Modeling of Nyiragongo's Lava Flow Inundation Probability And Mazuku: A Spatial Environment for a Successful Evacuation Plan for Goma City |url=https://assets.researchsquare.com/files/rs-3431997/v1_covered_0e24e85a-4738-4991-b490-861fb2f6e603.pdf |access-date=28 February 2024 |page=2}}</ref>

== Demographics ==

=== Population ===
In 1984, Goma's population was estimated at 80,000.<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=DzhsDwAAQBAJ&dq=goma+population&pg=PT104 |title=Revue de l'urbanisation en République démocratique du Congo: Des villes productives et inclusives pour l'émergence de la République démocratique du Congo |date=2018 |publisher=World Bank Publications |isbn=978-1-4648-1206-4 |location=NW, Washington, D.C. |language=fr}}</ref> Its population has since grown through [[Rate of natural increase|natural increase]], [[internal migration]], and [[refugee]] arrivals.<ref name=":02">{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=DzhsDwAAQBAJ&dq=Goma,+en+particulier,+a+%C3%A9t%C3%A9+le+centre+des+mouvements+de+population.+Cette+ville+de+pr%C3%A8s+de+80+000+personnes+(recensement+de+1984)&pg=PT107 |title=Revue de l'urbanisation en République démocratique du Congo: Des villes productives et inclusives pour l'émergence de la République démocratique du Congo |date=2018 |publisher=World Bank Publications |isbn=978-1-4648-1206-4 |location=NW, Washington, D.C. |language=fr}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Ferris |first=Elizabeth G. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=DaEcl8QoawUC&q=Goma%20grew%20with%20population%20of |title=Uprooted!: Refugees and Forced Migrants |date=1998 |publisher=Friendship Press |isbn=978-0-377-00319-4 |pages=49 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=lNERAQAAMAAJ&q=Goma%20grew%20with%20population%20of |title=Bollettino di geofisica teorica ed applicata, Volume 50 |date=2009 |publisher=Osservatorio geofisico sperimentale. |location=Trieste, Friuli-Venezia Giulia, Italy |pages=119 |language=en}}</ref> The 1994 [[Rwandan genocide]] and the Congo wars of 1996–1997 and 1998–2003 contributed to displacement and migration to the city. Subsequent conflict in the region has continued to influence population movements and urban expansion.<ref name=":25" /><ref name=":25" />

A 2024 estimate put Goma's population at approximately 782,000,<ref name=":45" /> although other estimates place it above two million, partly due to migration that is not officially recorded.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Murhabazi |first=Glody |date=12 June 2020 |title=Goma: 60% de la population n'ont pas accès à l'eau potable |trans-title=Goma: 60% of the population do not have access to drinking water |url=https://7sur7.cd/2020/06/12/goma-60-de-la-population-nont-pas-acces-leau-potable |access-date=31 December 2024 |website=7sur7.cd |language=fr}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last1=Cyuzuzo |first1=Samba |last2=Jones |first2=Mayeni |date=12 February 2024 |title=Violences en RD Congo: Panique à Goma face à l'avancée des rebelles du M23 |trans-title=Violence in DR Congo: Panic in Goma as M23 rebels advance |url=https://www.bbc.com/afrique/region-68275585 |access-date=31 December 2024 |work=BBC News Afrique |language=fr}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=12 February 2024 |title=En RDC, la population de Goma craint l'avancée des rebelles du M23 |trans-title=In the DRC, the population of Goma fears the advance of the M23 rebels |url=https://www.radiofrance.fr/franceculture/podcasts/la-revue-de-presse-internationale/la-revue-de-presse-internationale-emission-du-lundi-12-fevrier-2024-7803306 |access-date=31 December 2024 |website=[[Radio France]] |language=fr |publication-place=Paris, France}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Rigaud |first=Christophe |date=5 February 2024 |title=Conflit en RDC: l'engrenage du pire au Nord-Kivu |trans-title=Conflict in the DRC: the spiral of the worst in North Kivu |url=https://afrikarabia.com/wordpress/conflit-en-rdc-lengrenage-du-pire-au-nord-kivu/ |access-date=31 December 2024 |website=Afrikarabia.com |language=fr-FR}}</ref> 

Goma is home to several [[Bantu languages|Bantu]]-speaking ethnic groups, including the [[Konjo people|Nande]], [[Nyanga people|Nyanga]], [[Hunde people|Hunde]], [[Hutu]], Tembo, [[Komo people (Democratic Republic of the Congo)|Kumu]], [[Bushi (region)|Shi]], Piri, Kano, Mbuba, [[Mbuti people|Mbuti]], and [[Tutsi]].<ref name=":25" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Karumba |first=Janvier Bagula |date=2011 |title=De l'opportunité du développement du tourisme au nord Kivu. Cas de la ville de Goma |trans-title=On the opportunity of developing tourism in North Kivu. Case of the city of Goma |url=https://www.memoireonline.com/01/14/8505/De-l-opportunite-du-developpement-du-tourisme-au-nord-Kivu-Cas-de-la-ville-de-Goma.html |access-date=31 December 2024 |publisher=Institut Supérieur de Tourisme (ISTou-Goma) |language=fr |publication-place=Goma, North Kivu, Democratic Republic of the Congo}}</ref> The Hunde speak [[Hunde language|Kihunde]], the Nande speak [[Nande language|Kinande (or Kiyira)]], the Piri speak Kipiri, the Talinga speak [[Talinga language|Kitalinga]], the Kano speak Kikano, the Kusu speak Kikusu, the Kumu speak [[Komo language (Bantu)|Kikumu]], the Mbuba speak Kimbuba, the Nyanga speak [[Nyanga language|Kinyanga]], and the Tembo speak [[Tembo (Kitembo) language|Kitembo]]. Meanwhile, the [[Hutu]] and [[Tutsi]] speak [[Kinyarwanda]], and the [[Mbuti people|Mbuti]] speak [[Asoa language|Kimbuti]].<ref name=":49" />

=== Education ===
{{Further|Education in the Democratic Republic of the Congo}}{{Multiple image
| image1      = ULPGL GOMA, Campus Moïse vue de couloir droit.jpg

Education has three levels: [[kindergarten]] (ages 3–5), [[primary school]] (ages 6–12), and [[secondary school]] (ages 12–18).<ref name=":43" /> The city also has several [[Tertiary education|higher-education]] institutions, including the [[Free University of the Great Lakes Countries]] (ULPGL) and the [[University of Goma]], which fall under the relevant national higher-education framework.<ref name=":42">{{Cite web |last=Mughole |first=Inès Kasoki |date=2012 |title=Etude sur les causes d'insuffisance ponderale des enfants a la naissance dans la zone de sante urbaine de Karisimbi ville de Goma |trans-title=Study on the causes of low birth weight in newborns in the Karisimbi Urban Health Zone, Goma city |url=https://www.africmemoire.com/part.3-chapitre-i-presentation-du-milieu-detude-1609.html |access-date=13 January 2025 |publisher=Institut Supérieur de Développement Rural de Bukavu (ISDR-Bukavu) |language=fr |publication-place=Bukavu, South Kivu, Democratic Republic of the Congo}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Kihimba |first=Trésor Mumbere |date=2012 |title=Problématique de gestion des latrines dans les institutions supérieures et universitaires |trans-title=Problems of latrine management in higher education and university institutions |url=https://www.memoireonline.com/01/13/6839/m_Problematique-de-gestion-des-latrines-dans-les-institutions-superieures-et-universitaires4.html |access-date=13 January 2025 |publisher=[[Free University of the Great Lakes Countries]] |language=fr |publication-place=Goma, North Kivu, Democratic Republic of the Congo}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=MAXIMUM |first=LE |date=18 May 2020 |title=Meilleures universités en RDC |trans-title=Best universities in DRC |url=https://lemaximum.cd/2020/05/18/societe/meilleures-universites-en-rdc/ |access-date=13 January 2025 |website=Le Maximum |language=fr-FR}}</ref>

In 2016, ULPGL ranked second nationally according to International Colleges and Universities and third nationally in the Webometrics ranking, in which it placed 19,099th globally.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Bakenga |first=Dieudonné |title=L'ULPGL classée 2è ou 3è université de la RDC |trans-title=ULPGL ranked 2nd or 3rd university in the DRC |url=https://ulpgl.net/lulpgl-classee-2e-ou-3e-universite-de-la-rdc/ |access-date=13 January 2025 |website=Ulpgl.net |publisher=[[Free University of the Great Lakes Countries]] |language=fr |publication-place=Goma, North Kivu, Democratic Republic of the Congo}}</ref>

Goma is also home to other operational higher education institutions:<ref>{{Cite web |last=Buchekabiri |first=Ephrem Chiruza |date=2015 |title=Apport de la communication dans la gestion d'une institution universitaire en concurrence, cas de l'unic Goma |trans-title=Contribution of communication in the management of a competitive university institution, case of UNIC Goma |url=https://www.memoireonline.com/01/17/9499/m_Apport-de-la-communication-dans-la-gestion-d-une-institution-universitaire-en-concurrence-cas-de-l19.html |access-date=13 January 2025 |publisher=Université du CEPROMAD (UNIC-Goma) |language=fr |publication-place=Goma, North Kivu, Democratic Republic of the Congo}}</ref>
