name="UNESCO-consequences">{{cite web|url=https://en.unesco.org/themes/education-emergencies/coronavirus-school-closures/consequences|title=Adverse consequences of school closures | date=10 March 2020|website=UNESCO|language=en|access-date=15 March 2020}}</ref><ref name="fastcompany-economic-impacts">{{cite web|url=https://www.fastcompany.com/90476445/school-closures-are-starting-and-theyll-have-far-reaching-economic-impacts|title=School closures are starting, and they'll have far-reaching economic impacts| vauthors = Lindzon J |date=12 March 2020|website=Fast Company|language=en-US|access-date=22 March 2020}}</ref><ref name="Aristovnik et al. 2020">{{cite journal | vauthors = Aristovnik A, Keržič D, Ravšelj D, Tomaževič N, Umek L|title = Impacts of the COVID-19 Pandemic on Life of Higher Education Students: A Global Perspective| journal = Sustainability | volume = 12 | issue = 20 | pages = 8438 | date = October 2020 | doi=10.3390/su12208438| doi-access = free| bibcode=2020Sust...12.8438A }}</ref>

School closures shed light on various [[Social impact of the COVID-19 pandemic|social]] and [[Economic impact of the COVID-19 pandemic|economic issues]], including [[student debt]],<ref>{{Cite news| vauthors = Jamerson J, Mitchell J |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/student-loan-debt-relief-offers-support-to-an-economy-battered-by-coronavirus-11584735842|title=Student-Loan Debt Relief Offers Support to an Economy Battered by Coronavirus|date=20 March 2020|work=[[The Wall Street Journal]]|access-date=23 March 2020|language=en-US|issn=0099-9660}}</ref> [[digital learning]],<ref name="Aristovnik et al. 2020" /><ref>{{cite web|url=https://en.unesco.org/themes/education-emergencies/coronavirus-school-closures/solutions|title=Distance learning solutions | date=5 March 2020|website=UNESCO|language=en|access-date=23 March 2020}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news | vauthors = Karp P, McGowan M |url=https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/2020/mar/24/clear-as-mud-schools-ask-for-online-learning-help-as-coronavirus-policy-confusion-persists|title='Clear as mud': schools ask for online learning help as coronavirus policy confusion persists|date=23 March 2020|work=[[The Guardian]]|access-date=23 March 2020 |language=en-GB|issn=0261-3077}}</ref> [[food security]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.npr.org/2020/03/20/818300504/schools-race-to-feed-students-amid-coronavirus-closures|title=Schools Race To Feed Students Amid Coronavirus Closures|website=NPR.org|date=20 March 2020 |language=en|access-date=23 March 2020 | vauthors = Turner C }}</ref> and [[homelessness]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.statesville.com/news/education/homeless-students-during-the-coronavirus-pandemic-we-have-to-make/article_4b41ed40-43f2-5215-97ce-6040b54de755.html|title=Homeless students during the coronavirus pandemic: 'We have to make sure they're not forgotten'| vauthors = Sessons B |website=Statesville.com|date=23 March 2020 |language=en|access-date=23 March 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/opinion/2020/03/17/coronavirus-closings-can-strand-poor-foreign-homeless-college-students-column/5054621002/|title=Coronavirus closings: Are colleges helping their foreign, homeless and poor students?| vauthors = Ngumbi E |website=[[USA Today]]|language=en-US|access-date=23 March 2020}}</ref> as well as access to [[Child care|childcare]],<ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://time.com/5804176/coronavirus-childcare-nannies/|title=Coronavirus Forces Families to Make Painful Childcare Decisions|magazine=Time|language=en|access-date=23 March 2020}}</ref> [[health care]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2020/03/20/coronavirus-who-says-health-systems-collapsing-this-isnt-just-a-bad-flu-season.html|title=WHO officials warn health systems are 'collapsing' under coronavirus: 'This isn't just a bad flu season'| vauthors = Feuer W |date=20 March 2020|website=[[CNBC]]|language=en|access-date=23 March 2020}}</ref> [[housing]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2020/03/23/coronavirus-on-campus-students-face-food-insecurity-housing-crunch.html|title=Coronavirus on campus: College students scramble to solve food insecurity and housing challenges| vauthors = Barrett S |date=23 March 2020|website=[[CNBC]]|language=en|access-date=23 March 2020}}</ref> [[internet]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://thehill.com/blogs/congress-blog/technology/488848-coronavirus-outbreak-shining-an-even-brighter-light-on|title=Coronavirus outbreak shining an even brighter light on internet disparities in rural America| vauthors = Jordan C |date=22 March 2020|website=[[The Hill (newspaper)|The Hill]]|language=en|access-date=23 March 2020}}</ref> and [[Disability rights movement|disability services]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.npr.org/sections/coronavirus-live-updates/2020/03/23/820138079/education-dept-says-disability-laws-shouldnt-get-in-the-way-of-online-learning|title=Education Dept. Says Disability Laws Shouldn't Get In The Way Of Online Learning|website=NPR.org|date=23 March 2020|language=en|access-date=23 March 2020|last1=Nadworny|first1=Elissa}}</ref> The impact was more severe for disadvantaged children and their families, causing interrupted learning, compromised nutrition, childcare problems, and consequent economic cost to families who could not work.<ref name="UNESCO2020">{{cite web |url=https://en.unesco.org/themes/education-emergencies/coronavirus-school-closures |title=COVID-19 Educational Disruption and Response |date=4 March 2020 |publisher=[[UNESCO]] |access-date=28 March 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |url=http://www.thetelegram.com/news/world/coronavirus-deprives-nearly-300-million-students-of-their-schooling-unesco-419714/ |title=Coronavirus deprives nearly 300 million students of their schooling: UNESCO |agency=[[Reuters]]|work=[[The Telegram]] |access-date=11 March 2020}}</ref>

In response to school closures, [[UNESCO]] recommended the use of [[distance learning]] programmes and [[Open educational resources|open educational applications]] and platforms that schools and teachers can use to reach learners remotely and limit the disruption of education. In 2020, UNESCO estimated that nearly 24 million will dropout, with [[South Asia]] and [[Western Asia]] being the most affected.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://en.unesco.org/news/290-million-students-out-school-due-covid-19-unesco-releases-first-global-numbers-and-mobilizes |title=290 million students out of school due to COVID-19: UNESCO releases first global numbers and mobilizes response |date=4 March 2020 |publisher=[[UNESCO]] |access-date=6 March 2020}}</ref></onlyinclude>
{{TOC limit}}

As of early 2025, academic recovery from pandemic-related disruptions remained slow and uneven across many regions.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.brookings.edu/articles/5-years-after-covid-19-hit-test-data-converge-on-math-gains-stalled-reading-recovery/ |title=5 years after COVID-19 hit: Test data converge on math gains, stalled reading recovery |website=Brookings |access-date=2025-04-24}}{{cite web |url=https://www.nwea.org/blog/2024/new-data-how-far-off-is-covid-academic-recovery/ |title=New data: How far off is COVID academic recovery? |website=NWEA |date=30 July 2024 |access-date=2025-04-24}}</ref> While some data indicated modest gains in mathematics proficiency since 2022, progress in reading often lagged significantly or showed continued decline in certain areas.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://educationrecoveryscorecard.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/Pivoting-from-Pandemic-Recovery-to-Long-Term-Reform-A-District-Level-Analysis.pdf |title=Pivoting from Pandemic Recovery to Long-Term Reform |website=Center for Education Policy Research at Harvard University |access-date=2025-04-24}}</ref> Experts noted that, at current rates, full academic recovery could take several more years, with average student achievement still behind pre-pandemic levels.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://communities.springernature.com/posts/the-lasting-impact-of-covid-19-on-education |title=The Lasting Impact of COVID-19 on Education |website=Research Communities by Springer Nature |date=17 January 2025 |access-date=2025-04-24}}</ref>

== Past school closures ==
{{Further|Impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on children}}

[[File:Online Classroom example.png|thumb|right|A staged example of an online classroom using [[Jitsi]], where the teacher is sharing their screen]]
Efforts to slow the spread of [[Coronavirus disease 2019|COVID-19]] through non-pharmaceutical interventions and preventive measures such as [[Social distancing|social-distancing]] and [[Isolation (health care)|self-isolation]] have prompted the widespread closure of [[Primary school|primary]], [[secondary school|secondary]], and [[Tertiary education|tertiary]] schooling in over 100 countries.<ref name="UNESCO">{{cite web|url=https://en.unesco.org/themes/education-emergencies/coronavirus-school-closures|title=COVID-19 Educational Disruption and Response|website=UNESCO|language=en|access-date=17 March 2020}}</ref>

Previous outbreaks of infectious diseases have prompted, widespread school closings around the world, with varying levels of effectiveness.<ref name=":9">{{cite news|url=https://www.cnn.com/2020/03/11/health/coronavirus-children-sick/index.html|title=Children's coronavirus cases are not as severe, but that doesn't make them less serious| vauthors = Simon M |website=[[CNN]]|access-date=15 March 2020}}</ref><ref name=":8">{{cite web|url=https://chalkbeat.org/posts/us/2020/03/09/coronavirus-school-closures-research/|title=Should schools close due to coronavirus? Here's what research says|vauthors=Barnum M|date=9 March 2020|website=[[Chalkbeat]]|access-date=15 March 2020|archive-date=16 March 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200316131133/https://chalkbeat.org/posts/us/2020/03/09/coronavirus-school-closures-research/|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name=":10">{{cite news|url=https://www.cnn.com/2020/03/11/health/coronavirus-lessons-from-ebola/index.html|title=Lessons from Ebola: The secret of successful epidemic response| vauthors = Frieden T | work = CNN |access-date=15 March 2020}}</ref> [[Mathematical model]]s have shown that transmission may be delayed by closing schools.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Jackson C, Mangtani P, Hawker J, Olowokure B, Vynnycky E | title = The effects of school closures on influenza outbreaks and pandemics: systematic review of simulation studies | journal = PLOS ONE | volume = 9 | issue = 5 | article-number = e97297 | date = 15 May 2014 | pmid = 24830407 | pmc = 4022492 | doi = 10.1371/journal.pone.0097297 | bibcode = 2014PLoSO...997297J | doi-access = free }}</ref> However, effectiveness depends on the contacts children maintain outside of school.<ref name="Zumla2010">{{Cite book | vauthors = Zumla A, Yew WW, Hui DS |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=c9CQn9C4JaQC&pg=PA614|title=Emerging Respiratory Infections in the 21st Century, An Issue of Infectious Disease Clinics|date=2010|publisher=Elsevier Health Sciences |volume=24 |number=3 |isbn=978-1-4557-0038-7 |page=614|language=en}}</ref><ref name="CauchemezFerguson2009">{{cite journal | vauthors = Cauchemez S, Ferguson NM, Wachtel C, Tegnell A, Saour G, Duncan B, Nicoll A | title = Closure of schools during an influenza pandemic | journal = The Lancet. Infectious Diseases | volume = 9 | issue = 8 | pages = 473–81 | date = August 2009 | pmid = 19628172 | pmc = 7106429 | doi = 10.1016/S1473-3099(09)70176-8 }}</ref> 

School closures appear effective in decreasing cases and deaths, particularly when enacted promptly.<ref name=":28">{{cite journal | vauthors = Auger KA, Shah SS, Richardson T, Hartley D, Hall M, Warniment A, Timmons K, Bosse D, Ferris SA, Brady PW, Schondelmeyer AC, Thomson JE | title = Association Between Statewide School Closure and COVID-19 Incidence and Mortality in the US | journal = JAMA | volume = 324 | issue = 9 | pages = 859–870 | date = September 2020 | pmid = 32745200 | pmc = 7391181 | doi = 10.1001/jama.2020.14348 }}</ref> If school closures occur late relative to an outbreak, they are less effective and may not have any impact at all.<ref name=":9" /><ref name=":8" /> Additionally, in some cases, the reopening of schools after a period of closure has resulted in increased [[infection]] rates.<ref name=":11">{{cite journal | vauthors = Jackson C, Vynnycky E, Hawker J, Olowokure B, Mangtani P | title = School closures and influenza: systematic review of epidemiological studies | journal = BMJ Open | volume = 3 | issue = 2 | article-number = e002149 | date = 2013 | pmid = 23447463 | pmc = 3586057 | doi = 10.1136/bmjopen-2012-002149  | doi-access = free}}</ref> As closures tend to occur concurrently with other interventions such as public gathering bans, it can be difficult to measure the specific impact of school closures.<ref name=":11" />

During the [[Spanish flu|1918–1919 influenza pandemic]] in the [[United States]], school closures and public gathering bans were associated with lower total mortality rates.<ref name=":8" /> Cities that implemented such interventions earlier had greater delays in reaching peak mortality rates.<ref name=":12">{{cite journal | vauthors = Markel H, Lipman HB, Navarro JA, Sloan A, Michalsen JR, Stern AM, Cetron MS | title = Nonpharmaceutical interventions implemented by US cities during the 1918-1919 influenza pandemic | journal = JAMA | volume = 298 | issue = 6 | pages = 644–54 | date = August 2007 | pmid = 17684187 | doi = 10.1001/jama.298.6.644 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref name=":11" /> Schools closed for a median duration of 4 weeks according to a study of 43 US cities' responses to the Spanish Flu.<ref name=":12" /> School closures were shown to reduce [[morbidity]] from the [[Influenza A virus subtype H2N2|Asian flu]] by 90% during the 1957–58 outbreak,<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Chin TD, Foley JF, Doto IL, Gravelle CR, Weston J | title = Morbidity and mortality characteristics of Asian strain influenza | journal = Public Health Reports | volume = 75 | issue = 2 | pages = 149–158 | date = February 1960 | pmid = 19316351 | pmc = 1929395 | doi = 10.2307/4590751 | jstor = 4590751 }}</ref> and up to 50% in controlling influenza in the US, 2004–2008.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Wheeler CC, Erhart LM, Jehn ML | title = Effect of school closure on the incidence of influenza among school-age children in Arizona | journal = Public Health Reports | volume = 125 | issue = 6 | pages = 851–9 | year = 2010 | pmid = 21121230 | pmc = 2966666 | doi = 10.1177/003335491012500612 }}</ref>

Multiple countries successfully slowed the spread of infection through school closures during the [[2009 flu pandemic|2009 H1N1 Flu pandemic]]. School closures in the city of [[Ōita (city)|Oita]], [[Japan]], were found to have successfully decreased the number of infected students at the peak of infection; however closing schools was not found to have significantly decreased the total number of infected students.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Kawano S, Kakehashi M | title = Substantial Impact of School Closure on the Transmission Dynamics during the Pandemic Flu H1N1-2009 in Oita, Japan | journal = PLOS ONE | volume = 10 | issue = 12 | article-number = e0144839 | date = 15 December 2015 | pmid = 26669757 | pmc = 4682869 | doi = 10.1371/journal.pone.0144839 | bibcode = 2015PLoSO..1044839K | doi-access = free }}</ref> Mandatory school closures and other social distancing measures were associated with a 29% to 37% reduction in influenza transmission rates.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.nih.gov/news-events/nih-research-matters/flu-pandemic-study-supports-social-distancing | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160106115017/http://www.nih.gov/news-events/nih-research-matters/flu-pandemic-study-supports-social-distancing | url-status = dead | archive-date = 6 January 2016 | title = Flu Pandemic Study Supports Social Distancing | work = NIH Research Matters | date = 6 June 2011 }}</ref> Early school closures in the United States delayed the peak of the 2009 [[Influenza A virus subtype H1N1|H1N1]] Flu pandemic.<ref name=":9" /> Despite the overall success of closing schools, a study of school closures in Michigan found that "district level reactive school closures were ineffective."<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Davis BM, Markel H, Navarro A, Wells E, Monto AS, Aiello AE | title = The effect of reactive school closure on community influenza-like illness counts in the state of Michigan during the 2009 H1N1 pandemic | journal = Clinical Infectious Diseases | volume = 60 | issue = 12 | pages = e90-7 | date = June 2015 | pmid = 25896795 | doi = 10.1093/cid/civ182 | doi-access = free | hdl = 2027.42/111817 | hdl-access = free }}</ref>

[[File:Children and youth out of school due to COVID-19 closures and Young people classified as NEET.png|thumb|right|Children and youth out of school due to COVID-19 closures and young people classified as [[NEET]]]]
During the [[2009 flu pandemic in the United Kingdom|swine flu outbreak in 2009 in the UK]], in an article titled "Closure of schools during an influenza pandemic" published in the ''[[The Lancet|Lancet Infectious Diseases]]'', a group of epidemiologists endorsed the closure of schools in order to interrupt the course of the infection, slow further spread and buy time to research and produce a vaccine.<ref name="Wardrop2009">{{Cite news| vauthors = Wardrop M |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/health/swine-flu/5874683/Swine-flu-schools-should-close-to-halt-spread-of-virus-ministers-told.html |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220112/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/health/swine-flu/5874683/Swine-flu-schools-should-close-to-halt-spread-of-virus-ministers-told.html |archive-date=12 January 2022 |url-status=live|title=Swine flu: schools should close to halt spread of virus, ministers told|date=21 July 2009|work=[[The Daily Telegraph|The Telegraph]]|access-date=17 March 2020|language=en-GB|issn=0307-1235|url-access=subscription}}{{cbignore}}</ref> 

Having studied previous influenza pandemics including the [[Spanish flu|1918 flu pandemic]], the [[Influenza A virus subtype H2N2|influenza pandemic of 1957]] and the [[1968 flu pandemic]], they reported on the economic and workforce effect school closure would have, particularly with a large percentage of doctors and nurses being women, of whom half had children under the age of 16. They also looked at the dynamics of the spread of influenza in [[France]] during French school holidays and noted that cases of flu dropped when schools closed and re-emerged when they re-opened. They noted that when teachers in [[Israel]] went on [[Social distancing|strike during the flu season of 1999–2000]], visits to doctors and the number of respiratory infections dropped by more than a fifth and more than two fifths respectively.<ref name="Reuters2009">{{Cite news | url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-flu-schools-idUSTRE56J4OO20090720|title=Closing schools won't stop pandemics: study|date=20 July 2009|publisher=[[Reuters]]|access-date=17 March 2020| veditors = Walsh E |language=en}}</ref>

== Hazard controls ==
{{Further|Workplace hazard controls for COVID-19}}
[[File:Student studies in classroom during face to face learning in Padang, Indonesia.webm|thumb|left|Students in Indonesia went back to schools located in low-risk areas on the first day of school in 2021 under tight health protocols after the closure of education facilities for months due to the [[COVID-19 pandemic in Indonesia|COVID-19 pandemic]].]]
For schools and childcare facilities, the [[United States|U.S]]. [[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]] recommends short-term closure to clean or disinfect if an infected person has been in a school building regardless of community spread. When there is minimal to moderate community transmission, [[social distancing]] strategies can be implemented such as postponing or cancelling [[field trip]]s, assemblies, and other large gatherings such as [[physical education]] or choir classes or meals in a cafeteria, increasing the space between desks, staggering arrival and dismissal times, limiting nonessential visitors, and using a separate health office location for children with flu-like symptoms. When there is substantial transmission in the local community, in addition to social distancing strategies, extended school dismissals may be considered.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cdc.gov/coronavirus/2019-ncov/community/schools-childcare/guidance-for-schools.html|title=Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) - Interim Guidance for Administrators of US Childcare Programs and K-12 Schools | date=12 March 2020|website=U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention|language=en-us|access-date=21 March 2020}} {{PD-notice}}</ref>

As the pandemic progresses, schools may continue with remote learning or decide to reopen. Strategies such as cohorting, rotating schedules, eating lunch in the classroom, and utilizing outdoor spaces are some ways to minimize close contact.<ref>{{Cite web|last=CDC|date=11 February 2020|title=Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) - FAQs for Administrators|url=https://www.cdc.gov/coronavirus/2019-ncov/community/schools-childcare/reopening-schools-faqs.html|access-date=3 August 2020|website=Centers for Disease Control and Prevention|language=en-us}}</ref> Additional precautions include face masks, [[hand sanitizer]] stations, rearranging classrooms to enable physical distancing, and frequent cleaning.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web|website=National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine|title=Reopening K-12 Schools During the COVID-19 Pandemic|url=https://www.nationalacademies.org/news/2020/07/schools-should-prioritize-reopening-in-fall-2020-especially-for-grades-k-5-while-weighing-risks-and-benefits|access-date=3 August 2020|archive-date=19 January 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210119162735/https://www.nationalacademies.org/news/2020/07/schools-should-prioritize-reopening-in-fall-2020-especially-for-grades-k-5-while-weighing-risks-and-benefits|url-status=dead}}</ref> The CDC made a School Decision Tree to aid administrators in the planning process for reopening.<ref>{{cite web | title = Transitioning from CDC's Indicators for Dynamic School Decision-Making (released September 15, 2020) to CDC's Operational Strategy for K-12 Schools through Phased Mitigation (released February 12, 2021) to Reduce COVID-19 | date = 18 February 2021 | url = https://www.cdc.gov/coronavirus/2019-ncov/community/schools-childcare/indicators.html | publisher = U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention }}</ref> The [[American Academy of Pediatrics]] urges re-entry policies need to be flexible and responsive as new information about the virus emerges.<ref>{{Cite web|title=COVID-19 Planning Considerations: Guidance for School Re-entry|url=http://services.aap.org/en/pages/2019-novel-coronavirus-covid-19-infections/clinical-guidance/covid-19-planning-considerations-return-to-in-person-education-in-schools/|access-date=3 August 2020|website=services.aap.org|language=en}}</ref>

The National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine states that in-person instruction for grades K-5 and students with special needs should be prioritized to prevent children from falling behind.<ref name=":4" /> Younger children are at higher risk of suffering from long-term academic consequences and developmental deficits without in-person learning.<ref name=":4" /><ref>{{Cite web|title=Return to School During COVID-19|url=https://www.healthychildren.org/English/health-issues/conditions/COVID-19/Pages/Return-to-School-During-COVID-19.aspx|access-date=3 August 2020|website=HealthyChildren.org}}</ref>

== Academic integrity ==
The impact on [[academic integrity]] has been observed around the world.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Eaton SE | title = Academic integrity during COVID-19: Reflections from the University of Calgary. | journal = International Studies in Educational Administration | date = 12 July 2020 | volume = 48 | issue = 1 | pages = 80–85 | url = https://prism.ucalgary.ca/handle/1880/112293 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | vauthors = Agrba L | date = 27 March 2020 | title = How Canadian universities are evaluating students during the coronavirus pandemic. | work = Maclean's | url = https://www.macleans.ca/education/how-canadian-universities-are-evaluating-students-during-the-coronavirus-pandemic/ }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | title = S. Korean Universities Seek to Ensure Both Academic Integrity and Anti-virus Measures. | work =  Korea Bizwire | date = 16 June 2020 | url = http://koreabizwire.com/s-korean-universities-seek-to-ensure-both-academic-integrity-and-anti-virus-measures/162320 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | work = Quality Assurance Agency for Higher Education (UK) (QAA). | date = 2020 | title = Canada COVID-19 Resources | url = https://www.qaa.ac.uk/en/news-events/support-and-guidance-covid-19/international-policy-practice/canada }}</ref> A rise in [[contract cheating]], academic [[File sharing|file-sharing]], and exam cheating<ref>{{cite web | vauthors = Appiah KA | date = 7 April 2020 | title = If My Classmates Are Going to Cheat on an Online Exam, Why Can't I? | work = [[The New York Times]] | url = https://www.nytimes.com/2020/04/07/magazine/if-my-classmates-are-going-to-cheat-on-an-online-exam-why-cant-i.html }}</ref> were identified as particularly problematic.<ref>{{Cite journal| vauthors = Lancaster T, Cotarlan C |date= December 2021 |title=Contract cheating by STEM students through a file sharing website: a Covid-19 pandemic perspective|url= |journal=International Journal for Educational Integrity|language=en|volume=17|issue=1|article-number= 3 |doi=10.1007/s40979-021-00070-0|issn=1833-2595|pmc=7857863}}</ref> With remote learning, cheating has become far easier for students.<ref>{{Cite web| vauthors = Newton D |date=7 August 2020|title=Another problem with shifting education online: cheating|url=https://hechingerreport.org/another-problem-with-shifting-education-online-cheating/|access-date=8 December 2020|website=The Hechinger Report|language=en-US}}</ref> There is no remorse from students who would rather succeed in class than learn.<ref>{{Cite news| vauthors = DeWitt P |title=6 Reasons Students Aren't Showing Up for Virtual Learning|url=http://blogs.edweek.org/edweek/finding_common_ground/2020/04/6_reasons_students_arent_showing_up_for_virtual_learning.html?cmp=SOC-SHR-FB|access-date=8 December 2020|newspaper=Education Week|date=26 April 2020}}</ref> Online education has also exposed various as yet unresolved legal issues, including copyright and unapproved misuse of lectures.<ref>{{Cite journal|doi = 10.1007/s12115-021-00584-w|issn=0147-2011 |title = The Right to Teach in a Hyper-Digital Age: Legal Protections for (Post-)Pandemic Concerns|year = 2021|last1 = Deflem|first1 = Mathieu|journal = Society|volume = 58|issue = 3|pages = 204–212|pmid = 34075264|pmc = 8161721}}</ref>

Many institutions turned to commercial services to take over [[exam proctoring]],<ref>{{cite web | vauthors = Grabish A | date = 2020 | title = University of Manitoba uses anti-cheating software to monitor remote exams. | work = CBC News | url = https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/manitoba/anti-cheating-software-university-of-manitoba-1.4223737 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | vauthors = Eaton SE | date = 2020 | title = E-Proctoring: Understanding the debate about invigilating remote exams. | url = https://drsaraheaton.wordpress.com/2020/05/12/e-proctoring-understanding-the-debate-about-invigilating-remote-exams/ }}</ref> but almost immediately concerns were raised<ref>{{cite news | vauthors = Strauss V | date = 22 April 2020 | title = An open letter to the College Board about online, at-home AP tests. | newspaper = [[The Washington Post]] | url = https://www.washingtonpost.com/education/2020/04/22/an-open-letter-college-board-about-online-at-home-ap-tests/ }}</ref> about student privacy,<ref>{{cite web | vauthors = Scott B | date = 23 June 2020 | title = Remote proctoring services at odds with MU student privacy concerns. | work = Missourian | url = https://www.columbiamissourian.com/news/covid19/remote-proctoring-services-at-odds-with-mu-student-privacy-concerns/article_6107b0a8-b0bf-11ea-9ac2-ab3eee4f79a4.html }}</ref> surveillance,<ref>{{cite web | vauthors = Hubler S | date = 2020 | title = Keeping Online Testing Honest? Or an Orwellian Overreach? | work = [[The New York Times]] | url =  https://www.nytimes.com/2020/05/10/us/online-testing-cheating-universities-coronavirus.html }}</ref> and the impact on student mental health.<ref name="Aristovnik et al. 2020"/><ref>{{cite news | vauthors = Harwell D | date = 1 April 2020 | title = Mass school closures in the wake of the coronavirus are driving a new wave of student surveillance. | newspaper = [[The Washington Post]] | url = https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/2020/04/01/online-proctoring-college-exams-coronavirus/ }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | vauthors = Chin M | date = 29 April 2020 | title = Exam anxiety: How remote test-proctoring is creeping students out. | work = The Verge | url = https://www.theverge.com/2020/4/29/21232777/examity-remote-test-proctoring-online-class-education }}</ref>

The lack of student to teacher interaction also led some students to feel less passionate about the integrity of their work. Some students turned in half-completed assignments, got the answers from friends in class, or turned in nothing at all simply because education became less important due to COVID-19.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Is online learning shrinking your attention span?|url=https://www.upbeacon.com/article/2020/09/tips-for-studing-at-home|access-date=10 December 2020|website=The Beacon}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=COVID-19 and student performance, equity, and U.S. education policy: Lessons from pre-pandemic research to inform relief, recovery, and rebuilding|url=https://www.epi.org/publication/the-consequences-of-the-covid-19-pandemic-for-education-performance-and-equity-in-the-united-states-what-can-we-learn-from-pre-pandemic-research-to-inform-relief-recovery-and-rebuilding/|access-date=10 December 2020|website=Economic Policy Institute|language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Covid-19's Impact on Students' Academic and Mental Well-Being|url=https://www.edutopia.org/article/covid-19s-impact-students-academic-and-mental-well-being|access-date=10 December 2020|website=Edutopia|language=en}}</ref>

Due to COVID-19, many students had problems with staying focused and lost their sense of routine. Many researchers believe this is not due to the school closures, but to "brain fog" caused by the disease itself.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Students struggle with the long-term effects of COVID-19 |url=https://www.miamistudent.net/article/2022/12/students-struggle-with-the-long-term-effects-of-covid-19 |access-date=2024-12-30 |website=Students struggle with the long-term effects of COVID-19 - The Miami Student |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=MD |first=Andrew E. Budson |date=2021-03-08 |title=What is COVID-19 brain fog — and how can you clear it? |url=https://www.health.harvard.edu/blog/what-is-covid-19-brain-fog-and-how-can-you-clear-it-2021030822076 |access-date=2024-12-30 |website=Harvard Health |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Long COVID Brain Fog: What It Is and How to Manage It |url=https://www.yalemedicine.org/news/how-to-manage-long-covid-brain-fog |access-date=2024-12-30 |website=Yale Medicine |language=en}}</ref>

Engagement and focus are vital to the learning process, and some students feel they focus better in in-person classes.<ref name=7-missing-pieces>{{Cite web |title=7 missing pieces: why students prefer in-person over online classes |url=https://www.universityaffairs.ca/features/feature-article/7-missing-pieces-why-students-prefer-in-person-over-online-classes/ |access-date=2023-12-11 |website=University Affairs |date=2 December 2020 |language=en-US}}</ref>

Students may interpret that lack of structure to mean that they do not have to do anything, or they may find themselves overwhelmed with too much to do and an inability to determine what order to do it in.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Common Online Learning Distractions You Can Fix |url=https://www.iconschool.org/blog/why-cant-i-focus-on-my-school-work-when-it-is-online |access-date=2023-12-11 |website=www.iconschool.org |language=en-us}}</ref> However, some students thrived in this new environment with test scores that went up during online learning.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Some Students Do Better in Online School |url=https://www.chicagobooth.edu/review/some-students-do-better-in-online-school |access-date=2024-12-30 |website=The University of Chicago Booth School of Business |language=en}}</ref>

== Gender disparities ==
{{main|Impacts of the COVID-19 crisis on female education}}
The COVID-19 lockdowns has widened the gender gap in education between females and males. The rapid spread of COVID-19 lockdowns forced many females into the traditional roles as caretakers. Common gender disparities that impact a female's education during the pandemic are finances enabling higher dropout rates, domestic violence, child marriage, early pregnancy, and exploitation of child labour.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Krywult-Albanska |first1=Malgorzata |last2=Albanksi |first2=Lukas |date=2021 |title=Gender and Educational Inequalities during the COVID-19 Pandemic: Preliminary Insights from Poland|journal=Sustainability|volume=13 |issue=22 |article-number=12403 |doi=10.3390/su132212403 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2021Sust...1312403K }}</ref> 

Female caretakers drop out of schools to provide care for sick family members or become a source of income for their families. In settings with gender disparities in rates of school completion, girls are at increased risk of not returning to school after lockdown if tasked with income-generating activities or caretaking or they become pregnant.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Ryan|first1=Nessa E.|last2=El Ayadi|first2=Alison M.|date=1 September 2020|title=A call for a gender-responsive, intersectional approach to address COVID-19|url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/17441692.2020.1791214 |journal=Global Public Health |language=en |volume=15 |issue=9 |pages=1404–1412 |doi=10.1080/17441692.2020.1791214 |pmid=32633628|s2cid=220385717|issn=1744-1692|url-access=subscription}}</ref> There is a correlation between increased unemployment rates with higher female school dropout rates. Malala Fund research estimates that as a result of the pandemic, 20 million girls in developing countries may never return to the classroom.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Witter|first=Arielle|date=5 March 2021|title=How COVID-19 is threatening girls' education|url=https://www.one.org/international/blog/girls-education-crisis-covid-19/|access-date=24 January 2022|website=ONE|language=en-US|archive-date=24 January 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220124205357/https://www.one.org/international/blog/girls-education-crisis-covid-19/|url-status=dead}}</ref> Consequently, there is a decreased level of women returning to school, particularly in nations with poverty. 

Out of the total population of students enrolled in education globally, UNESCO reported as of 31 March 2020 that over 89% were out of school because of COVID-19 closures. This represented 1.54 billion children, and youth enrolled in school or university, including nearly 743 million girls.<ref name="ReferenceA">{{Cite web|date=31 March 2020|title=Covid-19 school closures around the world will hit girls hardest|url=https://en.unesco.org/news/covid-19-school-closures-around-world-will-hit-girls-hardest|access-date=24 January 2022|website=UNESCO|language=en}}</ref> During the pandemic, females attending school reported encountering technical challenges with remote learning. Using data from the National Study STEM faculty and students (NSSFS) collected 2020, the report describes gender disparities in experiences of transitioning to remote teaching/learning among US STEM faculty and students.<ref>Saw, G. K., Chang, C.-N., Lomelí, U., & Zhi, M. (2020). Gender disparities in remote learning during the COVID-19 pandemic: A national survey of STEM faculty and students (NREED Data Brief. No 2). Claremont, CA: Network for Research and Evaluation in Education.</ref> According to the survey, females reported higher technical challenges in remote learning against their male counterparts. The two main areas that females found challenging in remote learning were adaptability to the course design and transitioning from face-to-face school to remote online learning curriculums. 

Countries with poverty reported increased gender disparities as families could not afford internet usage in low-income households to pay for female education. Additionally, there was a preference in male over female education as they were seen as sole providers. Over 111 million of these girls are living in the world's least developed countries where getting an education is already a struggle. These are contexts of extreme poverty, economic vulnerability, and crisis where gender disparities in education are highest. In Mali, Niger, and South Sudan — 3 countries with some of the lowest enrolment and completion rates for girls — closures have forced over 4 million girls out of school.<ref name="ReferenceA" /> 

The broadened gap in gender disparities impacts female education that will exceed beyond the pandemic and seep into their futures. There have been several efforts by UNESCO and other organizations to raise funds for female education, but due to the financial hardships of the pandemic, those efforts have fallen short. Lack of government involvement in the issue and inability to address the increasing concerns of gender disparities in education during the pandemic has limited educational opportunities for females globally.
{{Excerpt|only=paragraph|hat=no|Impacts of the COVID-19 crisis on female education}}

== Racial disparities ==
The impact of COVID-19 lockdowns on racial disparities in online learning during the pandemic has received research attention.<ref name=":33">{{Cite journal|last1=Spievack |first1=Natalie |last2=Gallagher |first2=Meghan |date=23 June 2020|title=Urban Wire|url=https://www.urban.org/urban-wire/students-color-remote-learning-environments-pose-multiple-challenges|access-date=13 December 2021|journal=Urban Institute|language=en}}</ref> A recent study from the Urban Institute covers some of these findings. Urban's study points to issues in access to a computer and internet. A 2018 survey of households showed that 48% of surveyed households of Alaskan Natives did not have access to computers compared to 35% of Black households, 35% Latino, and 19% White.<ref name=":33" /> Minimal access to computers and the internet was found in 1.3 to 1.4 times as many Black and Hispanic households with school-aged children as it was in white households, with more than two out of five low-income households having just limited access.<ref>{{Cite web|last=McDonald|first=John|date=8 December 2020|title=Despite improved access, digital divide persists for minority, low-income students|url=https://newsroom.ucla.edu/releases/digital-divide-persists-for-minority-low-income-students|access-date=13 December 2021|website=UCLA Newsroom}}</ref>

A 2021 report from the Black Education Research Collective analyses the impact of COVID-19 lockdowns on Black education. It evaluates how Black students, parents, educators and community members experience systemic racism during COVID.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Horsford|first=Sonya Douglass|date=July 2021|title=Black Education in the Wake of COVID-19 & Systemic Racism: Toward a Theory of Change & Action|url=https://www.tc.columbia.edu/media/centers/berc/Final-BERC-COVID-Report-20July2021.pdf|journal=Black Education Research Collective at the Teachers College of Columbia|page=4|access-date=13 December 2021|archive-date=7 April 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220407085315/https://www.tc.columbia.edu/media/centers/berc/Final-BERC-COVID-Report-20July2021.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref> The study seeks to show how the pandemic has interrupted education across the country, highlighting existing racial and economic inequities. The study also argues that even before the outbreak, students in vulnerable neighborhoods, primarily Black, Indigenous, and other majority-minority areas, faced disparities in everything from resources (ranging from books to counselors) to student-teacher ratios and extracurricular activities.<ref>{{Cite web|last1=García|first1=Emma |last2=Weiss|first2=Elaine |title=COVID-19 and student performance, equity, and U.S. education policy: Lessons from pre-pandemic research to inform relief, recovery, and rebuilding|url=https://www.epi.org/publication/the-consequences-of-the-covid-19-pandemic-for-education-performance-and-equity-in-the-united-states-what-can-we-learn-from-pre-pandemic-research-to-inform-relief-recovery-and-rebuilding/|access-date=13 December 2021|website=Economic Policy Institute|language=en-US}}</ref>

== Timeline ==
* '''26 January:''' [[COVID-19 pandemic in mainland China|China]] was the first country which instituted measures to contain the COVID-19 outbreak including extending the [[Chinese New Year|Spring Festival]] [[Golden Week (China)|holiday]] and became the first to close all universities and schools around the country.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.chinadaily.com.cn/a/202001/27/WS5e2e0f0ea31012821727356b.html|title=China's State Council extends Spring Festival holiday - Chinadaily.com.cn|last=李雪晴|website=chinadaily.com.cn|access-date=15 March 2020}}</ref>

[[File:امتحانات نهایی در شرایط کرونا 3470479.jpg|thumb|Students take end-of-year exams in [[Tabriz]], Iran, 6 June 2020.]]
* '''4 March:''' [[UNESCO]] released the first global numbers on school closures and affected students on 3 March. It reported that 22 countries on three continents had enacted preventive measures including the temporary closure of schools and universities, impacting 290.5 million students around the world. In reaction, UNESCO called on countries to support affected students and families and facilitate large-scale inclusive distance learning programmes.<ref name=":14">{{cite web|url=https://en.unesco.org/news/290-million-students-out-school-due-covid-19-unesco-releases-first-global-numbers-and-mobilizes|title=290 million students out of school due to COVID-19: UNESCO releases first global numbers and mobilizes response|date=12 March 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200312190142/https://en.unesco.org/news/290-million-students-out-school-due-covid-19-unesco-releases-first-global-numbers-and-mobilizes|access-date=16 March 2020|archive-date=12 March 2020}}</ref>

* '''5 March:''' The majority of learners affected by COVID-19 emergency measures were located in China, with 233 million learners affected, followed by [[COVID-19 pandemic in Japan|Japan]] at 16.5 million and Iran at 14.5 million.<ref name=":3">{{cite web|url=https://news.un.org/en/story/2020/03/1058791|title=Coronavirus update: 290 million students now stuck at home|date=5 March 2020|website=UN News|language=en|access-date=15 March 2020}}</ref> 

* '''10 March:''' One in five students worldwide was "staying away from school due to the COVID-19 crisis" while another one in four was barred from higher education institutions, according to UNESCO.<ref name=":13">{{cite web|url=https://en.unesco.org/news/one-five-learners-kept-out-school-unesco-mobilizes-education-ministers-face-covid-19-crisis|title=With one in five learners kept out of school, UNESCO mobilizes education ministers to face the COVID-19 crisis|date=12 March 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200312172700/https://en.unesco.org/news/one-five-learners-kept-out-school-unesco-mobilizes-education-ministers-face-covid-19-crisis|access-date=16 March 2020|archive-date=12 March 2020}}</ref>

* '''13–16 March:''' National governments in 49 countries announced or implemented school closures on 13 March, including 39 countries which closed schools nationwide and 22 countries with localised school closures.<ref name="UNESCO" /> By 16 March, this figure increased to 73 countries according to UNESCO.<ref name="UNESCO" /> 

* '''19 March:''' A total of 50% of the students worldwide were affected by school closures, corresponding to nationwide closures in 102 countries and local closures in 11 countries affecting 1 billion people.

* '''20 March:''' Over 70% of the world's learners were impacted by closures, with 124 country-wide school closures.<ref name="UNESCO" />

* '''27 March:''' Nearly 90% of the world's student population was out of class.<ref name="BloombergSchoolsClose">{{cite news|vauthors=Mokhtar F, Gross S|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2020-03-27/should-schools-close-to-fight-virus-these-countries-say-no|title=Should Schools Close to Fight Virus? These Places Say No|date=27 March 2020|work=[[Bloomberg News|Bloomberg]]|access-date=31 March 2020}}</ref>

* '''29 March:''' More than 1.5 billion children and other students were affected by nationwide school closures. Others were disrupted by localized closures.<ref name="UNESCO2020" />

* '''Mid-April:''' A total of 1.58 billion students globally had been affected by the closure of schools and higher education institutions in response to the [[COVID-19 pandemic]].<ref name="Srivastava"/><ref name="UNPB"/> Based on UNESCO Monitoring Reports, 200 countries implemented national closures, affecting about 94% of the world's student population. The percentage of students affected was as high as 99% for low and lower-middle income countries.<ref name="UNPB"/><ref name="Lennox"/>
* '''30 June:''' The [[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention|CDC]] revised its guidelines for institutes of [[K–12|primary, secondary]], and [[Higher education in the United States|tertiary]] education, in which it expressly did not recommend the universal testing of students and staff. Rather, the CDC only recommended testing people who are exhibiting [[Coronavirus disease 2019#Symptoms and signs|COVID-19 symptoms]] or who have come into contact with a known COVID-19 case.<ref>{{Cite web|last=CDC|date=30 April 2020|title=Communities, Schools, Workplaces, & Events|url=https://www.cdc.gov/coronavirus/2019-ncov/community/colleges-universities/ihe-testing.html|access-date=20 August 2020|website=Centers for Disease Control and Prevention|language=en-us}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=CDC|date=30 April 2020|title=Communities, Schools, Workplaces, & Events|url=https://www.cdc.gov/coronavirus/2019-ncov/community/schools-childcare/k-12-testing.html|access-date=20 August 2020|website=Centers for Disease Control and Prevention|language=en-us}}</ref>

== Consequences of school closures ==
{{See also|Social impact of the COVID-19 pandemic|Impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on children}}

School closures in response to the [[Coronavirus disease 2019|COVID-19]] pandemic have shed a light on numerous issues affecting access to education, as well as broader [[Social issue|socio-economic issues]].<ref name="UNESCO" /> As of 12 March, more than 370 million [[child]]ren and [[youth]] are not attending [[school]] because of temporary or indefinite country wide school closures mandated by [[government]]s in an attempt to slow the spread of COVID-19.<ref name="UNESCO" /><ref>{{cite web|url=https://news.un.org/en/story/2020/03/1058791|title=Coronavirus update: 290 million students now stuck at home|date=5 March 2020|website=UN News|language=en|access-date=7 March 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.businessinsider.com/coronavirus-school-closures-have-left-kids-feeling-scared-confused-2020-3|title=Parents are struggling to cope as coronavirus worries shut down schools, leaving kids scared and confused| vauthors = Goldberg E |website=[[Business Insider]]|date=8 March 2020|access-date=9 March 2020}}</ref> As of 29 March, nearly 90% of the world's learners were impacted by closures.<ref name="UNESCO" />

According to the [[UNICEF|United Nations International Children's Fund (UNICEF)]], the COVID-19 pandemic has affected more than 91% of students worldwide, with approximately 1.6 billion children and youngsters unable to attend physical schools due to temporary closures and lockdowns.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Keeping the world's children learning through COVID-19|url=https://www.unicef.org/coronavirus/keeping-worlds-children-learning-through-covid-19|access-date=22 July 2020|website=UNICEF|language=en}}</ref> 

Even when school closures are temporary, it carries high social and economic costs. The disruptions they cause affect people across [[Community|communities]], but their impact is more severe for disadvantaged children and their families including interrupted learning, compromised nutrition, childcare problems and consequent economic cost to families who cannot work.<ref name="UNESCO" /><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.thetelegram.com/news/world/coronavirus-deprives-nearly-300-million-students-of-their-schooling-unesco-419714/|title=Coronavirus deprives nearly 300 million students of their schooling: UNESCO |work=The Telegram|agency=[[Reuters]]|last=Lough|first=Richard|language=en|access-date=11 March 2020}}</ref> According to Studi Economici Dell'Ocse (OECD) studies, school performance hinges critically on maintaining close relationships with teachers.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Learning remotely when schools close: How well are students and schools prepared? Insights from PISA|url=http://www.oecd.org/coronavirus/policy-responses/learning-remotely-when-schools-close-how-well-are-students-and-schools-prepared-insights-from-pisa-3bfda1f7/|access-date=10 June 2020|website=OECD|language=en}}</ref> This is particularly true for students from disadvantaged backgrounds, who may not have the parental support needed to learn on their own.<ref name="OECD">{{Cite web|title=OECD|url=https://read.oecd-ilibrary.org/view/?ref=127_127063-iiwm328658&title=Learning-remotely-when-schools-close|website=read.ecd-ilibrary.org|access-date=7 May 2020}}</ref> Working parents are more likely to miss work when schools close in order to take care of their children, incurring wage loss in many instances and negatively impacting productivity.<ref name="UNESCO-consequences" /> Localised school closures place burdens on schools as parents and officials redirect children to schools that are open.<ref name="UNESCO-consequences" />

=== Strain on healthcare workforce ===
Women make up almost 70% of the healthcare workforce, exposing them to a greater risk of infection.<ref>{{Cite web|title=OECD|url=https://read.oecd-ilibrary.org/view/?ref=127_127000-awfnqj80me&title=Women-at-the-core-of-the-fight-against-COVID-19-crisis|website=read.oecd-ilibrary.org|access-date=7 May 2020}}</ref> They often cannot attend work because of childcare obligations that result from school closures. In fact, in the U.S., the healthcare sector has one of the highest rates of childcare obligations in the broader economy, with approximately 28.8% of the workforce responsible for providing care to children aged 3–12.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Bayham|first=Jude|date=1 May 2020|title=Impact of school closures for COVID-19 on the US health-care workforce and net mortality: a modelling study|journal=The Lancet|volume=5|issue=5|pages=E271–E278|doi=10.1016/S2468-2667(20)30082-7|pmid=32251626|pmc=7270508}}</ref> At best, this means that school closures put pressure on health workers in systems already strained by COVID-19 caseloads. At worst, this means that some medical professionals may miss work at health facilities altogether.<ref name="UNESCO-consequences" />

=== Online learning ===
[[File:Урок математики во время пандемии COVID-19.png|thumb|upright|A math distance lesson over a video conference during the COVID-19 pandemic in Russia]]
Online learning has become a critical lifeline for education, as institutions seek to minimize the potential for community transmission.<ref name=":30">{{cite journal|vauthors=Skulmowski A, Rey GD|title=COVID-19 as an accelerator for digitalization at a German university: Establishing hybrid campuses in times of crisis|journal=Human Behavior and Emerging Technologies|volume=2|issue=3|pages=212–216|date=May 2020|pmid=32838228|pmc=7283701|doi=10.1002/hbe2.201}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal| vauthors = Murphy MP |date=30 April 2020|title=COVID-19 and emergency eLearning: Consequences of the securitization of higher education for post-pandemic pedagogy|journal=Contemporary Security Policy|volume=41|issue=3|pages=492–505|doi=10.1080/13523260.2020.1761749|issn=1352-3260|doi-access=free}}</ref> Technology can enable teachers and students to access specialized materials well beyond textbooks, in multiple formats and in ways that can bridge time and space.<ref name="OECD"/> [[Digital media in education]] can take many forms, including high-tech solutions such as tablet-based adaptive learning software or low-tech solutions such as radio, [[SMS|sms]], and [[instructional television]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Mindspark|url=https://mindspark.in/maths|access-date=1 July 2021|website=mindspark.in}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=TV and Radio for distance learning|url=https://edtechhub.org/tv-and-radio-for-distance-learning/|access-date=1 July 2021|website=EdTech Hub|language=en-US}}</ref> Teachers may operate in dual mode, teaching local and remote learners simultaneously.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2021 |title=TEACHING ON-CAMPUS AND ONLINE SIMULTANEOUSLY |url=https://lta.hw.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/10_RBL-Teaching-online-and-on-campus-simultaneously.pdf |website=Heriot Watt University}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Williams |first=Hunter |date=2021-10-09 |title=Dual Teaching: Simultaneous Remote and In-Person Learning During COVID |url=https://digitalcommons.usmalibrary.org/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1563&context=usma_research_papers |website=USMA Digital Commons |access-date=29 April 2022 |archive-date=24 October 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221024050051/https://digitalcommons.usmalibrary.org/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1563&context=usma_research_papers |url-status=dead}}</ref>

Due to the [[COVID-19 pandemic]], many schools across the world began conducting classes via [[videotelephony]] software such as [[Zoom (software)|Zoom]], [[Google Classroom]] and/or [[Google Meet]]. The [[OECD|Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development]] has created a framework to guide an education response to the COVID-19 pandemic for [[Distance education|distance learning]].<ref>{{Cite web| vauthors = Reimers RM, Schleicher A |date=2020|title=A framework to guide an education response to the COVID-19 Pandemic of 2020|url=https://read.oecd-ilibrary.org/view/?ref=126_126988-t63lxosohs&title=A-framework-to-guide-an-education-response-to-the-Covid-19-Pandemic-of-2020|access-date=5 July 2020|website=OECD}}</ref> Whenever this was possible, the ability to teach in real time significantly helped educators handle the transition, in comparison with their colleagues who had to rely on asynchronous instruction. In addition, studies have shown that online learning led to more proactive learning strategies for students, rather than passive learning at the urging of a teacher. By examining students' online learning behaviors, including student practices, students' perceptions of social belonging, and perceptions of the online learning learning climate, the results suggest that successful online learning can be achieved through a positive learning climate and strategies, as positive learning strategies create communication between students and between students and teachers.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lemay |first1=David John |last2=Bazelais |first2=Paul |last3=Doleck |first3=Tenzin |date=2021-08-01 |title=Transition to online learning during the COVID-19 pandemic |journal=Computers in Human Behavior Reports |volume=4 |article-number=100130 |doi=10.1016/j.chbr.2021.100130 |issn=2451-9588 |pmc=8452462 |pmid=34568640}}</ref>

Some [[Digital media in education|online learning solutions]] like [[Coursera]] expanded their accessibility by offering more free online courses during the pandemic.

==== Unequal access to technology ====
Lack of access to technology or fast, reliable internet access can prevent students in rural areas and from disadvantaged families. Lack of access to technology or good internet connectivity is an obstacle to continued learning, especially for students from disadvantaged families.<ref name="UNESCO-consequences" /> Teachers have reported that students are more likely to complete assignments if they have access to internet at home.<ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=Stelitano L, Doan S, Woo A, Diliberti M, Kaufman JH, Henry D|title=The digital divide and COVID-19: Teachers' perceptions of inequities in students' Internet access and participation in remote learning.|journal=RAND|date=2020|url=https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RRA134-3.html}}</ref> In response to school closures caused by COVID-19, [[UNESCO]] recommends the use of [[distance learning]] programmes and [[Open educational resources|open educational applications]] and platforms that schools and teachers can use to reach learners remotely and limit the disruption of [[education]].<ref name="290million">{{cite web|url=https://en.unesco.org/news/290-million-students-out-school-due-covid-19-unesco-releases-first-global-numbers-and-mobilizes|title=290 million students out of school due to COVID-19: UNESCO releases first global numbers and mobilizes response|author=UNESCO|date=4 March 2020|website=UNESCO|language=en|access-date=6 March 2020}}</ref> However, in regions where online learning is not feasible, due to a lack of access to distance learning tools such as smart phones and internet connectivity, some parents have resorted to child labour or early marriage as a means to cope with the financial stress placed on them by the pandemic.<ref name="Masih">{{Cite news|last=Masih|first=Niha|date=30 December 2020|title=Schools in India have been closed since March. The costs to children are mounting|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/asia_pacific/india-coronavirus-school-closures/2020/12/23/7e80f628-3efc-11eb-b58b-1623f6267960_story.html|access-date=1 July 2021}}</ref>

To aid in slowing the transmission of COVID-19, hundreds of libraries have temporarily closed. In the United States, numerous major cities announced public library closures, including Los Angeles, San Francisco, Seattle, and New York City, affecting 221 libraries.<ref name=":2">{{cite web | vauthors = Hauck G, Stanglin D |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/health/2020/03/13/coronavirus-updates-us-testing-death-toll-stocks-school-closures/5032550002/|title=Coronavirus updates: Trump declares national emergency; schools in 12 states shut down; cruise lines halted |website=[[USA Today]]|language=en-US|access-date=15 March 2020}}</ref> For students without internet at home, this increases the difficulty of keeping up with distance learning.<ref>{{Cite web|title=The COVID-19 pandemic has changed education forever. This is how|url=https://www.weforum.org/agenda/2020/04/coronavirus-education-global-covid19-online-digital-learning/|access-date=10 June 2020|website=World Economic Forum|date=29 April 2020 |language=en}}</ref>

[[Yale]] economist [[Fabrizio Zilibotti]] co-authored a January 2022 study with professors from the [[University of Pennsylvania]], [[Northwestern University]] and the [[University of Amsterdam]], showing that unequal access to technology during "the pandemic is widening educational inequality and that the learning gaps created by the crisis will persist."<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Agostinelli |first1=Francesco |last2=Doepke |first2=Matthias |last3=Sorrenti |first3=Giuseppe |last4=Zilibotti |first4=Fabrizio |title=When the Great Equalizer Shuts Down: Schools, Peers, and Parents in Pandemic Times |date=December 2020 |volume=206 |issue=104574 |doi=10.3386/w28264 |url=https://www.nber.org/papers/w28264 |access-date=27 July 2022 |journal=Journal of Public Economics |issn=0047-2727 |id=28264 |quote=Online education is an imperfect substitute for in-person learning, particularly for children from low-income families. Peer effects also change: schools allow children from different socio-economic backgrounds to mix together, and this effect is lost when schools are closed.|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Cummings |first1=Mike |title=COVID school closures most harm students from poorest neighborhood |url=https://news.yale.edu/2021/01/05/covid-school-closures-most-harm-students-poorest-neighborhoods |website=news.yale.edu |publisher=Yale News |access-date=27 July 2022 |date=5 January 2022}}</ref>

==== Copyright ====
Lack of [[limitations and exceptions to copyright]] can also have an impact on the ability of students to access the textbooks and materials they need to study.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://creativecommons.org/2020/03/31/education-in-times-of-crisis-and-beyond-maximizing-copyright-flexibilities/|title=Education in Times of Crisis and Beyond: Maximizing Copyright Flexibilities|date=31 March 2020|website=Creative Commons|language=en-US|access-date=16 April 2020}}</ref> Several initiatives were taken to grant that students and teachers can have access to open educational resources, or understand copyright limitations. The [[International Council for Open and Distance Education]] issued a special website to provide webinars, tips for online teaching and resources for teachers.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.icde.org/corona|title=Coronavirus and Online and Distance Teaching|website=ICDE|language=en-GB|access-date=16 April 2020|archive-date=3 June 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210603033936/https://www.icde.org/corona|url-status=dead}}</ref>

In [[New Zealand]], a group of publishers agreed to allow for virtual public readings of their materials from libraries and classrooms.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://lianza.org.nz/covid-19/virtual-storytimes/|title=Virtual Storytimes – LIANZA|language=en-US|access-date=16 April 2020|archive-date=3 June 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210603033929/https://lianza.org.nz/covid-19/virtual-storytimes/|url-status=dead}}</ref> A similar agreement took place in [[Australia]], where the Australian Publishers Association, the [[Australian Library and Information Association]] and the [[Australian Society of Authors]] agreed on a set of exceptional measures to allow libraries to provide educational content.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://bookscreate.com.au/book-industry-partners-come-to-agreement-on-copyright/|title=Book industry partners come to agreement on copyright|date=19 March 2020|website=Books Create Australia|language=en-AU|access-date=16 April 2020}}</ref> The Australian organization [[APRA AMCOS|AMCOS]] agreed to give a gratis license for all their music sheets to all schools across Australia.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.smartcopying.edu.au/educational-resources/covid-19-copyright-issues/increased-digital-rights-in-print-music-for-schools-due-to-covid-19-crisis|title=Increased digital rights in print music for schools due to COVID-19 crisis|website=www.smartcopying.edu.au|access-date=16 April 2020|archive-date=2 January 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210102051336/https://www.smartcopying.edu.au/educational-resources/covid-19-copyright-issues/increased-digital-rights-in-print-music-for-schools-due-to-covid-19-crisis|url-status=dead}}</ref>

An advocacy organization in [[Netherlands]] launched a website to allow teachers use free-licensed music and video for their classes.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.opennederland.nl/algemeen/online-lesstof-muziek-en-fotos-voor-in-je-videos/|title=Online lesstof {{!}} Muziek en foto's voor in je video's|date=2 April 2020|website=Open Nederland|language=nl|access-date=16 April 2020|archive-date=4 May 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210504041639/https://www.opennederland.nl/algemeen/online-lesstof-muziek-en-fotos-voor-in-je-videos/|url-status=dead}}</ref>

A coalition of over 500 civil society organizations and individuals issued a letter to [[Francis Gurry]], Director of the [[World Intellectual Property Organization]], asking, among other things, a special set of limitations and exceptions to copyright for the duration of the pandemic.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://infojustice.org/archives/42220|title=CIVIL SOCIETY LETTER TO WIPO DIRECTOR GENERAL FRANCIS GURRY ON COVID-19 AND INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY |website=infojustice.org|access-date=16 April 2020}}</ref>

Several organizations are also working to explain to teachers how to navigate complex copyright scenarios. The National Copyright Unit of Australia, a specialist copyright team responsible for copyright policy and administration for Australian schools and [[Technical and further education|TAFE]], issued a set of recommendations to follow on copyright issues while doing remote learning<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.smartcopying.edu.au/information-sheets/schools/remote-online-learning-during-the-covid-19-outbreak|title=Remote & Online Learning During the COVID-19 Outbreak|website=www.smartcopying.edu.au|access-date=16 April 2020|archive-date=14 April 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200414175052/https://www.smartcopying.edu.au/information-sheets/schools/remote-online-learning-during-the-covid-19-outbreak|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.smartcopying.edu.au/educational-resources/covid-19-copyright-issues|title=COVID-19 Copyright Issues|website=www.smartcopying.edu.au|access-date=16 April 2020}}</ref> and a set of recommendations for using openly licensed content, specially aimed to parents supporting students.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.smartcopying.edu.au/information-sheets/schools/useful-creative-commons-and-other-free-educational-resources-for-parents-supporting-students|title=Useful Creative Commons and Other Free Educational Resources for Parents Supporting Students|website=www.smartcopying.edu.au|access-date=16 April 2020|archive-date=28 October 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201028113913/https://www.smartcopying.edu.au/information-sheets/schools/useful-creative-commons-and-other-free-educational-resources-for-parents-supporting-students|url-status=dead}}</ref> Centrum Cyfrowe in Poland is holding open calls to support the work of teachers and educators leading in the open education sector.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://oerpolicy.eu/open-education-links-17/|title=Open Education Links #17 – Open Educational Resources Policy in Europe|website=oerpolicy.eu|date=7 April 2020 |language=en-GB|access-date=16 April 2020}}</ref> The Program on Information Justice and Intellectual Property at the [[American University]] is holding a set of webinars for different educators to guide them through copyright issues when delivering online teaching<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.wcl.american.edu/impact/initiatives-programs/pijip/impact/best-practices-in-fair-use/best-practices-in-fair-use-for-open-educational-resources/|title=Best Practices in Fair Use for Open Educational Resources|website=American University Washington College of Law|language=en|access-date=16 April 2020}}</ref> and how to address best practices for fair use.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Best Practices in Fair Use for Open Educational Resources|url=https://www.wcl.american.edu/impact/initiatives-programs/pijip/impact/best-practices-in-fair-use/best-practices-in-fair-use-for-open-educational-resources/|website=American University Washington College of Law|language=en|access-date=25 May 2020}}</ref>

=== Childcare ===
{{Main|Impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on children}}
[[ File:8938Filipino_homeschooling_students_01.jpg|thumb|200px|right| Filipino homeschooling students - blended (printed-digital modular) distance learning with self-learning materials during the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic in [[San Miguel, Bulacan]]]]
Closures of early childhood education and care as well as schools increases work-family conflicts particularly for parents with younger children who are in more need of care and supervision of distance learning. School closures puts a strain on parents and guardians to provide childcare and manage distance learning while children are out of school.<ref name=":3" /> In the absence of alternative options, working parents often leave children alone when schools close and this can lead to risky behaviours, including increased influence of peer pressure and substance abuse.<ref name="UNESCO-consequences"/> Alternatively, in some emerging economies, parents may resort to bringing their children to work and engaging them in menial labour, as has been the case in Maharashtra, India, where some out-of-school teenagers have been working in sugar cane fields alongside their day labourer parents.<ref name="Masih"/>

In the United States, as of early April, more than half of existing childcare programs had shut down at least temporarily and were not serving any children.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Nationwide Survey: Child Care in the Time of Coronavirus {{!}} Bipartisan Policy Center|url=https://bipartisanpolicy.org/blog/nationwide-survey-child-care-in-the-time-of-coronavirus/|date=10 April 2020|website=bipartisanpolicy.org|language=en|access-date=15 May 2020}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=The Child Care Industry Is About To Collapse. There's No Bailout Coming.|url=https://www.huffpost.com/entry/child-care-industry-coronavirus-no-bailout-congress_n_5ebe9ea0c5b6ae86c2fd2c00| vauthors = Peck E  |date=15 May 2020|website=[[HuffPost]]|language=en|access-date=15 May 2020}}</ref>

=== Women in the workforce ===
Many working mothers dropped out of the labour force to take care of their children during school closures and online learning. In places where part-time school attendance or fully virtual learning is implemented, working parents are typically left with a choice of either arranging childcare or to stop working during days when their children are not at school. However, childcare is often difficult to find or unaffordable, due to its increased demand and closures of daycare centres during the pandemic, making it not a viable option for many parents.<ref name=":31">{{Cite web |title='Clusterbomb,' 'Catastrophe,' 'Disaster': Experts Predict a Dire Fall for Working Moms |url=https://www.workingmother.com/clusterbomb-catastrophe-disaster-experts-predict-fall-with-grim-consequences-for-working-moms |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210406143920/https://www.workingmother.com/clusterbomb-catastrophe-disaster-experts-predict-fall-with-grim-consequences-for-working-moms |archive-date=6 April 2021 |access-date=7 April 2021 |website=Working Mother |language=en}}</ref>

Due to the difficulty of securing accommodations and flexibility from their employers to allow them to take care of their children, [[women in the United States]], particularly Black and [[Hispanic and Latino Americans|Latina]] women, have lost a disproportionate share of jobs since the beginning of the pandemic. These include forced attritions from women being unable to meet their productivity goals, and voluntary resignations from women who face too much pressure from managing both their paid and unpaid responsibilities. In many cases, women in the workforce were unable to afford private childcare, hence necessitating them to take a leave of absence from work or resigning from their job.<ref name=":31" /> A spring 2021 academic study suggested that a much larger proportion of mothers left the workforce in US states where schools offered primarily remote education. Between February 2020 and 2021, more than 2.3 million women in the US have left the labour force. In January 2021, only 57% of American women participated in the labour force, the lowest rate in 33 years.<ref name=":32">{{Cite web |date=18 February 2021 |title=Study: Moms Are More Likely to Quit Work in States With Remote-Only School |url=https://www.workingmother.com/study-moms-more-likely-to-quit-remote-only-school-reopening |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210504041707/https://www.workingmother.com/study-moms-more-likely-to-quit-remote-only-school-reopening |archive-date=4 May 2021 |access-date=7 April 2021 |website=Working Mother |language=en}}</ref>

A study from [[Washington University in St. Louis]] found that mothers have reduced their paid working hours four to five times more than fathers from February to April 2020, which widened the gender gap in working hours by a maximum of 50%. According to authors of the study, the disparity may lead to droves of women leaving the workforce and massive layoffs for women.<ref>{{Cite news| author=Kitchener C |title=Moms are working dramatically fewer hours than dads during coronavirus. It's a 'red flag' for what's ahead.|newspaper=Washington Post |date=16 July 2020 |url=https://www.thelily.com/moms-are-working-dramatically-fewer-hours-than-dads-during-coronavirus-its-a-red-flag-for-whats-ahead/|access-date=7 April 2021|language=en-US}}</ref> [[Betsey Stevenson]], an economist at the [[University of Michigan]], warned that the exodus of women from the workforce during the pandemic may lead to long-term impacts in women's labour market outcomes.<ref name=":31" /> Because working hours are a major cause of the [[gender pay gap]], and periods of non-employment has adverse impacts on future earnings and job mobility, experts warn that the pandemic-induced reduction can set women's advancement back for decades.<ref name=":32" />

=== Nutrition and food insecurity ===
Nutrition plays a critical role in cognitive development and academic performance for children.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = McCary JM | title = Improving access to school-based nutrition services for children with special health care needs | journal = Journal of the American Dietetic Association | volume = 106 | issue = 9 | pages = 1333–4, 1336 | date = September 2006 | pmid = 16963333 | doi = 10.1016/j.jada.2006.07.022 }}</ref> Many children worldwide rely on free or discounted meals at schools.<ref name=":3" /> When schools close, nutrition is especially compromised for children in schools where food is provided.<ref name="UNESCO" /> 

In the United States, [[National School Lunch Act|school lunch programmes]] are the second-biggest anti-hunger initiative after [[Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program|food stamps]]. Every year, nearly 30 million children rely on schools to provide free or low-cost meals including breakfast, lunch, snacks, and even dinner.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.npr.org/2020/03/20/818300504/schools-race-to-feed-students-amid-coronavirus-closures|title=Schools Race To Feed Students Amid Coronavirus Closures|website=NPR.org|date=20 March 2020 |language=en|access-date=21 March 2020 | vauthors = Turner C }}</ref> In [[Washington (state)|Washington State]], around 45% of the states 1.1 million students enrolled in traditional public and charter schools qualify for subsidised school meals. At least 520,000 students and their families may be affected by food insecurity as a result of school closures.<ref name=":1">{{cite web|url=https://www.seattletimes.com/education-lab/inslee-announces-all-washington-k-12-schools-to-close-in-an-effort-to-slow-the-spread-of-coronavirus/|title=Inslee expands coronavirus K-12 school closure, 250-person gathering ban, across Washington | vauthors = Furfaro H, O'Sullivan J, Morton N, Bazzaz D |date=13 March 2020|website=[[The Seattle Times]]|language=en-US|access-date=15 March 2020}}</ref> In [[Alabama]], where state-wide school closures as of 18 March have affected over 720,000 students, the state Superintendent announced that staff in schools disproportionately affected by poverty would create meal distribution networks to provide food for students who rely on school lunches.<ref name=":5">{{cite web|url=https://www.al.com/news/2020/03/alabama-closes-all-k-12-schools.html|title=Alabama closes all K-12 schools, first COVID-19 case confirmed in Jefferson County| vauthors = Powell Crain T |date=13 March 2020|website=al|language=en|access-date=15 March 2020}}</ref>

Many families with low income qualified for school lunch programs funded by the federal government and subsidized at the state level. Schools were required to stay open amid the COVID-19 crisis to provide meals to children who qualified for free or reduced rate meals. School sent out a weekly survey to reach every student who might have qualified for the programme.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Goldschmidt K | title = The COVID-19 Pandemic: Technology use to Support the Wellbeing of Children | journal = Journal of Pediatric Nursing | volume = 53 | pages = 88–90 | date = July–August 2020 | pmid = 32317129 | pmc = 7161478 | doi = 10.1016/j.pedn.2020.04.013 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

In the UK, footballer [[Marcus Rashford]] pushed the government to extend free school meals over the summer holidays in August. It was voted out at first, by 61 votes. However, in a U-turn, [[58th parliament of the United Kingdom|Boris Johnson's government]] changed it and agreed to carry on paying.<ref>{{Cite web|date=8 November 2020|title=Marcus Rashford forces Boris Johnson into second U-turn on child food poverty|url=http://www.theguardian.com/education/2020/nov/08/marcus-rashford-forces-boris-johnson-into-second-u-turn-on-child-food-poverty|access-date=23 December 2020|website=[[The Guardian]]|language=en}}</ref> Rashford was given an [[Order of the British Empire|MBE]] for his efforts.<ref>{{Cite web|date=9 October 2020|title=Manchester United striker Marcus Rashford humbled after receiving MBE|url=https://metro.co.uk/2020/10/09/manchester-united-marcus-rashford-humbled-after-receiving-mbe-13398267/|access-date=23 December 2020|website=Metro|language=en}}</ref>

=== Student learning outcomes ===
[[File:Chloe hard at work in class today at Tigard High School (51240557632).jpg|thumb|upright|Student taking an online class in the US]]
School closures negatively impact student learning outcomes.<ref name="UNESCO-consequences"/><ref name="Aristovnik et al. 2020"/> Schooling provides essential learning and when schools close, children and youth are deprived opportunities for growth and development. The disadvantages are disproportionate for under-privileged learners who tend to have fewer educational opportunities beyond school.<ref name="290million" /> When schools close, parents are often asked to facilitate the learning of children at home and can struggle to perform this task. This is especially true for parents with limited education and resources.<ref name="UNESCO-consequences" />

Students gain literacy slower during school closures than in a business-as-usual academic year. It has been estimated that the rate of reading ability gain in kindergarten children in the U.S. slows down by 66% during school closures compared to active schooling.<ref name="Bao 2020"/> A recent study of the effect of the [[2005 Kashmir earthquake|2005 Kashmir Earthquake]] found that school closures of an average of 14 weeks has resulted in affected children being 1.5 to 2 years behind their peers who were unaffected by the disaster and its resulting school closures.<ref name="riseprogramme.org">{{Cite web|title=COVID-19 is Poised to Exacerbate the Learning Crisis, Evidence from Long-term School Closures in Pakistan|url=https://riseprogramme.org/blog/COVID-19-Exacerbate_Learning_Crisis|access-date=1 July 2021|website=RISE Programme|date=10 June 2020 |language=en}}</ref> In practical terms, this learning loss could result in affected children earning 15% less in every adult year of their lives.<ref name="riseprogramme.org"/>
