Student drop-out rates tend to increase as an effect of school closures due to the challenge of ensuring all students return to school once school closures ends. This is especially true of protracted closures.<ref name=":3" /><ref name="UNESCO-consequences"/> Disadvantaged, at-risk, or homeless children are more likely not to return to school after the closures are ended, and the effect will often be a life-long disadvantage from lost opportunities.<ref>{{Cite news| vauthors = Baker J |url=https://www.smh.com.au/national/the-kids-who-will-never-return-to-school-after-covid-19-20200411-p54j0e.html#comments|title=The kids who will never return to school after COVID-19|date=12 April 2020|work=The Sydney Morning Herald|access-date=13 April 2020}}</ref>

Schools are also hubs of social activity and human interaction. When schools are closed, many children and youth miss out on social contact that is essential to learning and development.<ref name="UNESCO-consequences"/> Accordingly, teachers' perception of student coping significantly decreased with each education level handled, with university instructors finding their students to handle the situation much better than elementary school teachers did.

=== Inaccessibility to mitigation strategies ===
[[File:Ijerph-17-06371-g002.png|alt=|thumb|upright|The predicted reading ability gain before, during, and after COVID-19 related school closures<ref name="Bao 2020" />|330x330px]]
The effect of school closure on academic achievement has been studied in the summer months.<ref>{{Cite journal| vauthors = Cooper H, Nye B, Charlton K, Lindsay J, Greathouse S |date=September 1996|title=The Effects of Summer Vacation on Achievement Test Scores: A Narrative and Meta-Analytic Review|journal=Review of Educational Research|volume=66|issue=3|pages=227–268|doi=10.3102/00346543066003227|s2cid=145635039|issn=0034-6543}}</ref> Many of the strategies used to prevent academic slump, such as attending summer school, visiting libraries, and/or participating in literacy-rich summer-based activities are not available during the pandemic. Reading every day to a child, an option available while staying at home, reduced the rate of loss by 42%.<ref name="Bao 2020" />

=== Special education services ===
Potential impacts of school closures and reliance on distance learning are not addressed in US federal acts of legislation in the early months of the pandemic.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{cite web|url=https://ies.ed.gov/ncser/pdf/pl108-446.pdf|title=Public Law 108-446|website=uscode.house.gov|access-date=18 March 2020|archive-date=11 February 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200211222805/https://ies.ed.gov/ncser/pdf/pl108-446.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref> Special education students are potentially one of the most impacted groups of COVID-19. Educators continue to focus on implementing strategies to deliver services and accommodations in virtual, hybrid, and in person settings.<ref>{{Cite web |title=코로나 이후 1년, 교육은 어떻게 변했을까 – Sciencetimes |url=https://www.sciencetimes.co.kr/news/%ec%bd%94%eb%a1%9c%eb%82%98-%ec%9d%b4%ed%9b%84-1%eb%85%84-%ea%b5%90%ec%9c%a1%ec%9d%80-%ec%96%b4%eb%96%bb%ea%b2%8c-%eb%b3%80%ed%96%88%ec%9d%84%ea%b9%8c/ |access-date=2022-09-25 |language=ko-KR}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=한국교육학술정보원 - 지식정보 - KERIS 보고서 - 연구보고서 |url=https://www.keris.or.kr/main/ad/pblcte/selectPblcteRRInfo.do?mi=1138&pblcteSeq=13445 |access-date=2022-09-25 |website=www.keris.or.kr}}</ref> Studies show that children with special needs felt more socially isolated during the pandemic which had a significant impact on their mental health.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Dickinson |first=Helen |last2=Smith |first2=Catherine |last3=Yates |first3=Sophie |last4=Tani |first4=Massimiliano |date=2023-09-14 |title=The importance of social supports in education: survey findings from students with disability and their families during COVID-19 |url=https://doi.org/10.1080/09687599.2021.1994371 |journal=Disability & Society |volume=38 |issue=8 |pages=1304–1326 |doi=10.1080/09687599.2021.1994371 |issn=0968-7599|hdl=1959.4/unsworks_77852 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> However, information of how severe they have been affected, and how and if their grades will be affected due to their status and how this would affect their future are not specified.

=== Effect on COVID-19 cases and mortality ===
The effect of school closure on COVID-19 cases and mortality has been examined in multiple studies. 

A mathematical modelling study investigated the impact of school closures on COVID-19 dynamics in 74 countries.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ragonnet |first1=Romain |last2=Hughes |first2=Angus E. |last3=Shipman |first3=David S. |last4=Meehan |first4=Michael T. |last5=Henderson |first5=Alec S. |last6=Briffoteaux |first6=Guillaume |last7=Melab |first7=Nouredine |last8=Tuyttens |first8=Daniel |last9=McBryde |first9=Emma S. |last10=Trauer |first10=James M. |date=2025-01-21 |title=Estimating the impact of school closures on the COVID-19 dynamics in 74 countries: A modelling analysis |journal=PLOS Medicine |language=en |volume=22 |issue=1 |article-number=e1004512 |doi=10.1371/journal.pmed.1004512 |doi-access=free |pmid=39836691 |pmc=11793732 |issn=1549-1676}}</ref> It highlighted that the effect on infections, hospitalisations and deaths varied significantly by country. School closures were estimated to reduce SARS-CoV-2 infections, peak hospital occupancy, and deaths in most countries. However, the study also found that, in a few cases, school closures may have inadvertently increased cumulative COVID-19 mortality. 

In a study that looked specifically at school closure in the United States, closure of schools was associated with 1.37 million fewer cases and 40,600 fewer deaths from COVID-19 in a six-week study period.<ref name=":28" /> However, two international studies examining the impact of reopening schools from [[kindergarten]] to grade 12 found no consistent relationship between the reopening of these schools and the spread of COVID-19, with another study from the United States showing no increased risk to childcare workers who continued to work.<ref>{{Cite web| vauthors = Kamenetz A |date=27 October 2020|title=Are The Risks Of Reopening Schools Exaggerated?|url=https://www.npr.org/2020/10/21/925794511/were-the-risks-of-reopening-schools-exaggerated|access-date=22 February 2021|website=NPR.org|language=en}}</ref> Other studies that looked at multiple policy changes have shown more modest changes associated with school closure.<ref name=":29">{{cite journal |vauthors = Courtemanche C, Garuccio J, Le A, Pinkston J, Yelowitz A |title = Strong Social Distancing Measures In The United States Reduced The COVID-19 Growth Rate |journal = Health Affairs |volume = 39 |issue = 7 |pages = 1237–1246 |date = July 2020 |pmid = 32407171 |doi = 10.1377/hlthaff.2020.00608 |s2cid = 218648003 |doi-access = free}}</ref>

== Impact on formal education ==
[[File:COVID-19 School closure sign in Williamsport, PA, USA.jpg|thumb|upright|An electronic sign announces public school closures due to COVID-19 in [[Williamsport, Pennsylvania]], United States.]]
Formal education — as opposed to ''[[informal education]]'' or ''[[Nonformal learning|non-formal education]]'' — tends to refer to schools, colleges, universities and training institutions.<ref name=":21">{{Cite book| vauthors = Coombs PH, Manzoor A, Israel BB |title=Attacking rural poverty; how nonformal education can help|date=1974|publisher=Johns Hopkins University Press |isbn=0-8018-1600-9|location=Baltimore|oclc=897554}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://infed.org/mobi/informal-non-formal-and-formal-education-a-brief-overview-of-some-different-approaches/|title=informal non-formal and formal education – a brief overview of some different approaches {{!}} infed.org|language=en-GB|access-date=22 March 2020|archive-date=3 June 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210603034157/https://infed.org/mobi/informal-non-formal-and-formal-education-a-brief-overview-of-some-different-approaches/|url-status=dead}}</ref> A 1974 report by the [[World Bank]] defined formal education as the following:<blockquote>''Formal education'': the hierarchically structured, chronologically graded "education system", running from primary school through the university and including, in addition to general academic studies, a variety of specialised programmes and institutions for full-time technical and professional training.<ref name=":21" /></blockquote>The majority of data collected on the number of students and learners impacted by COVID-19 has been calculated based on the closure of formal education systems.<ref name="en.unesco.org">{{cite web|url=https://en.unesco.org/themes/education-emergencies/coronavirus-school-closures|title=COVID-19 Educational Disruption and Response | date=4 March 2020|website=UNESCO|language=en|access-date=22 March 2020}}</ref> The [[UNESCO Institute for Statistics]] provides figures on students impacted by COVID-19 corresponding to the number of learners enrolled at pre-primary, primary, lower-secondary, and upper-secondary levels of education ([[International Standard Classification of Education|ISCED]] levels 0 to 3), as well as at tertiary education levels (ISCED levels 5 to 8).<ref name="en.unesco.org"/>

=== Early childhood education ===
{{See also|Early childhood education}}
[[File:Stevens Elementary School during COVID epidemic 05.jpg|thumb|left|upright|Playground at a Seattle elementary school is closed due to the epidemic on 25 March 2020.]]
Early childhood educational programmes are usually designed for children below the age of 3 and may refer to [[preschool]]s, nursery schools, [[kindergarten]]s, and some [[Child care|day care programmes]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.naeyc.org/about-us|title=About Us {{!}} NAEYC|website=www.naeyc.org|access-date=21 March 2020}}</ref> While many primary and secondary schools have closed around the world due to COVID-19, measures impacting early childhood educational programmes have varied. In some countries and territories for instance in Australia preschools and day cares are considered necessary services and have not closed in tandem with broader school closure measures.<ref>{{Cite web| vauthors = Collignon P  |title=Other countries are shutting schools – why does the Australian government say it's safe to keep them open?|url=http://theconversation.com/other-countries-are-shutting-schools-why-does-the-australian-government-say-its-safe-to-keep-them-open-134538|access-date=16 June 2020|website=The Conversation|date=25 March 2020 |language=en}}</ref>

In the United States, the Washington State Department of Children, Youth, and Families encouraged child care and early learning centres to stay open. Some school districts may offer alternative child care options, prioritising the children of first responders and healthcare workers.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.seattletimes.com/education-lab/social-distancing-is-impossible-in-a-preschool-child-care-during-coronavirus/|title='Social distancing is impossible in a preschool': Child care during coronavirus|date=16 March 2020|website=[[The Seattle Times]]|language=en-US|access-date=21 March 2020}}</ref> The governor of Maryland mandated that specific child care services remain open for the children of emergency personnel while Washington State and California have left it to the discretion of care providers.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.baltimoresun.com/2020/03/21/i-dont-understand-petition-calls-on-maryland-gov-hogan-to-close-child-cares-amid-coronavirus-pandemic/|title='I don't understand': Petition calls on Maryland Gov. Hogan to close child cares amid coronavirus pandemic| vauthors = Oyefusi D |website=baltimoresun.com|date=21 March 2020 |access-date=22 March 2020}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{cite news|url=https://calmatters.org/health/coronavirus/2020/03/coronavirus-california-child-care-providers-parents-kids/|title=Coronavirus has Californians asking: Who'll watch the kids?|date=21 March 2020|website=CalMatters|language=en-US|access-date=22 March 2020 |last1=Aguilera |first1=Elizabeth }}</ref> California Governor [[Gavin Newsom]] explained his state's position, saying "We need our child care facilities, our daycare centers, to operate to absorb the impact of these school closures."<ref name=":0" /> Colorado has encouraged the development of "tool kits" for parents to use at home to emulate the lessons children would have received in their early learning programmes.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://denverite.com/2020/03/13/what-denver-daycares-and-preschools-are-doing-about-coronavirus/|title=What Denver daycares and preschools are doing about coronavirus|date=13 March 2020|website=Denverite|language=en-US|access-date=22 March 2020}}</ref> Over a million eligible American children were not enrolled in kindergarten for the 2021–2022 school year.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Goldstein |first1=Dana |title=The Kindergarten Exodus|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/08/07/us/covid-kindergarten-enrollment.html |access-date=27 July 2022 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=7 August 2021}}</ref> The 2022 annual ''Report on the Condition of Education''<ref>{{cite web |last1=Kena |first1=Grace |title=Where can I find information about the condition of education in the United States? |url=https://nces.ed.gov/blogs/nces/post/where-can-i-find-information-about-the-condition-of-education-in-the-united-states |website=nces.ed.gov |publisher=[[National Center for Education Statistics]] |access-date=8 August 2022 |date=26 May 2016}}</ref> conducted by the [[National Center for Education Statistics]] (NCES) for the [[United States Department of Education|U.S. Department of Education]]<ref>{{cite news |last1=Kuykendall |first1=Kristal |title=Report: Historic Decline in U.S. Public School Enrollment From Fall 2019 to Fall 2020; Dropout Rates Fell Since 2010 Among Hispanic, Black Students |url=https://thejournal.com/articles/2022/05/31/report-shows-historic-decline-in-us-public-school-enrollment-from-fall-2019-to-fall-2020.aspx |access-date=7 August 2022 |work=thejournal.com |publisher=The Journal |date=31 May 2022}}</ref> indicates that, during 2019 to 2020, there was a 13% decrease in enrollment for eligible students aged three and four, from 54% to 40%.<ref name=NCES>{{cite web |author1=Véronique Irwin and Josue De La Rosa |title=Report on the Condition of Education 2022 |url=https://nces.ed.gov/pubs2022/2022144.pdf |website=nces.ed.gov |publisher=National Center for Education Statistics, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education |access-date=8 August 2022 |date=May 2022}}</ref>

In Japan, Prime Minister Shinzo Abe closed all schools throughout the country until 8 April, however, children's daycare facilities were excluded.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ft.com/content/957bf9f6-594f-11ea-a528-dd0f971febbc|title=Japan shuts all schools to combat coronavirus | vauthors = Harding R, Inagaki K |date=27 February 2020|website=[[Financial Times]]|access-date=22 March 2020}}</ref> In early March, five adults associated with a nursing facility for preschool children in [[Kobe]] tested positive for coronavirus. After testing over one hundred children at the facility, a preschool student was found to be carrying the virus.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nippon.com/en/news/yjj2020031200144/coronavirus-cluster-suspected-at-child-facility-in-kobe.html|title=Coronavirus Cluster Suspected at Child Facility in Kobe|date=12 March 2020|website=nippon.com|language=en|access-date=22 March 2020|archive-date=22 March 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200322002227/https://www.nippon.com/en/news/yjj2020031200144/coronavirus-cluster-suspected-at-child-facility-in-kobe.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>

=== Primary (or Elementary) Education ===
[[File:Empty classroom 2020.jpg|thumb|upright|An empty classroom in closed elementary school due to COVID-19 in [[Kikinda]], [[Serbia]]]]
Primary or elementary education typically consists of the first four to seven years of formal education. Kindergarten is the first time children participate in formal education. Based on a comparison of longitudinal literacy data in kindergarten-aged students during a spring semester of schooling versus during summer vacation, one study predicted that [[Coronavirus disease 2019|COVID-19]] school closures would slow the rate of literacy ability gain by 66% in kindergarten children in the absence of mitigating alternative educational strategies.<ref name="Bao 2020" /> The study estimates that over an 8-month period from 1 January to 1 September 2020, assuming school closures from 16 March to 1 September 2020 (and taking into account the summer vacation that would have still normally taken place during that time), that these kindergarten children would have gained 31% less literacy ability on average than if school closures had not occurred.<ref name="Bao 2020" /> In the United States, there was a 6% decrease in kindergarten enrollment rates for the 2019 - 2020 school year for those aged five, dropping from 91% to 84%.<ref name=NCES/>

==Inequalities in Education==

=== Pre-Tertiary Education Inequality===

The COVID-19 pandemic significantly increased existing inequalities in pre-tertiary education. Between March 2020 and February 2021, schools worldwide faced closures for an average of 95 days, severely disrupting traditional learning environments.<ref name="doi.org">Haelermans, C., Korthals, R., Jacobs, M., de Leeuw, S., Vermeulen, S., van Vugt, L., Aarts, B., Prokic-Breuer, T., van der Velden, R., van Wetten, S., & de Wolf, I. (2022). Sharp increase in inequality in education in times of the COVID-19-pandemic. PloS one, 17(2), e0261114. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0261114</ref> In many Western countries, schools relied on remote learning, yet this shift revealed massive disparities in technology access and interpersonal interaction.<ref name="doi.org"/> Many studies report negative consequences on children's development due to these school closures.<ref name="doi.org"/> Moreover, research highlights that children from lower socio-economic backgrounds experienced more developmental setbacks, as they often lacked access to necessary technology and a productive learning environment.<ref name="doi.org"/> For instance, lower-class parents in the United Kingdom spent less time helping their children with schoolwork than middle-class parents – further widening the educational inequality gap.<ref name="doi.org"/> This intersection between socio-economic status and educational outcomes can create long-term problems of absolute mobility, as children from disadvantaged backgrounds may face challenges in exceeding their parents’ achievements, thereby restricting their opportunities to move up to a higher socio-economic class.<ref>Chetty, R., Hendren, N., Kline, P., Saez, E., & Turner, N. (2014). Is the United States still a land of opportunity? recent trends in intergenerational mobility. American Economic Review, 104(5), 141–147. https://doi.org/10.3386/w19844 
</ref>

===Early Education Inequality===

A study conducted in Israel aimed to examine how the shift to distance learning during the  COVID-19 pandemic affected the language abilities in early childhood, specifically children from low socioeconomic status families.<ref name="Nevo, E. 2023">Nevo, E. (2023). The effect of the COVID-19 pandemic on low SES kindergarteners' language abilities. Early Childhood Education Journal. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10643-023-01444-4</ref> Researchers compared the linguistic skills – vocabulary and morphological awareness– of children who attended early education before the pandemic with those who experienced the interruption in learning during it.<ref name="Nevo, E. 2023"/> The results revealed that mid-COVID-19 children scored significantly lower in morphological awareness (between 20% and 61%)  particularly in verb derivation, compared to their pre-pandemic peers.<ref name="Nevo, E. 2023"/> These gaps were attributed to less learning hours, reduced social interaction and additional challenges related to distance learning. Earlier studies have shown that early education is crucial for children's academic and social-emotional development, especially for those from low SES backgrounds who struggled to compensate for missed school hours at home.<ref>Yoshikawa, H. (1995). Long-term effects of early childhood programs on social outcomes and delinquency. The Future of Children, 5(3), 51-75. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8835514/</ref> Parents of these children lacked time and resources to effectively assist their children with remote learning.<ref name="Yildiz, S. 2023">Yildiz, S., Kilic, G. N., & Acar, I. H. (2023). Early childhood education during the COVID-19 outbreak: The perceived changing roles of preschool administrators, teachers, and parents. Early Childhood Education Journal, 51(4), 743-753. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10643-022-01339-w</ref> As a result, this study concluded that children from lower socioeconomic status families were disproportionately affected, due to less access to learning resources as well as parental support during distance learning.<ref name="Yildiz, S. 2023"/> The findings of this study highlight the critical need for targeted educational support –  specifically for low SES children – involving both parents and teachers to support language development.

===Primary Education Inequality===

A study done in the Netherlands analysed the differences in learning gains from children in primary education from lower-educated and poorer parents as compared to high educated parents and wealthier families.<ref name="Yildiz, S. 2023"/> The study looked at gains in education in reading, spelling, and math, using standardized test scores for approximately 300,000 students.<ref name="Yildiz, S. 2023"/> The results demonstrate that children with less educated parents faltered in their learning gains, particularly in math and spelling, as compared to their higher income peers.<ref name="Yildiz, S. 2023"/> Students were more dependent on their parents’ help during online learning, so those with less educated parents were at an unfair disadvantage. Additionally, children's learning was impacted by household income where those children whose families were in the middle to upper class experienced greater gains in spelling and math while lower income children did not.<ref name="Yildiz, S. 2023"/> The disparity in educational gains based on family income can be attributed to wealthier families’ ability to pay for additional help and materials for their children while schooling from home.  

===Inequality in Secondary Education===

An additional study done in Colombia looked at inequality during COVID-19 on students at the secondary-level. The study used standardized exams to examine educational inequality and found an increase of inequality between 48% to 372% depending on the independent variable.<ref name="Marín Llanes 2023">Marín Llanes, L., Rodríguez Pico, M., Maldonado, D., & García, S. (2023). Learning inequality during covid-19: Evidence from secondary schools in Colombia. International Journal of Educational Development, 100, 102788. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijedudev.2023.102788</ref> Results find that the change in educational inequality increased by 48% during the pandemic between low-income and high-income households.<ref name="Marín Llanes 2023"/> Another result of the study was the inequality between private and public school's. Prior to COVID-19 it was found that the educational differences between the school's were statistically insignificant while after 2020, there was a significant increase in the inequality divide –– by roughly 372%.<ref name="Marín Llanes 2023"/> This study has implications for how to increase the levelling of schooling in public schools and for lower income children, potentially hiring better teachers or increasing educational infrastructure to help the vulnerable students.<ref name="Marín Llanes 2023"/> Additionally, the study has implications for how there is a rationing of sufficient education in private institutions that contributes to inequality.<ref>Grusky, D., & Weeden, K. (2011). Is Market Failure Behind the Takeoff in Inequality? In The Inequality Reader: Contemporary and Foundational Readings in Race, Class, and Gender (Second, pp. 90–99). essay, Westview Press.</ref>{{not in source|reason=Source is from 2011; no relevance to COVID-19.|date=June 2026}}

=== Grade deflation ===
However, the IBO came under heavy criticism worldwide for their methods in calculating the students' final grades and their "Enquiry upon results" (EUR) strategy after results were released on 6 July 2020. Consequently, many students not only received much lower grades than what they were predicted to by their teachers but also missed the entrance requirements to every university they applied to, affecting approximately 170,000 students in 153 countries. As a result, petitions that garnered dozens of thousands of signatures were created online with the hashtag "IBSCANDAL" becoming viral, schools and people have lost confidence with the education company and are considering other alternatives for secondary education, and educational reforms are being suggested where students will deviate away from taking significant examinations in the future.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.tes.com/news/coronavirus-ib-results-scandal-pupils-demand-new-grades|title=IB results 'scandal': Students demand new grades|website=Tes}}</ref>

== <span class="anchor" id="Tertiary"></span>Higher education ==
{{See also|Online learning in higher education}}
Tertiary education, also known as higher education, refers to the non-compulsory educational levels that follow completion of secondary school or high school. Tertiary education is normally taken to include [[undergraduate]] and [[postgraduate education]], as well as [[Vocational education|vocational education and training]]. Individuals who complete tertiary education generally receive [[Academic certificate|certificates]], [[diploma]]s, or [[academic degree]]s.<ref name=":22">{{cite web|url=http://www.unesco.org/education/information/nfsunesco/doc/isced_1997.htm|title=International Standard Classification of EducationI S C E D 1997|date=19 March 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170319192113/http://www.unesco.org/education/information/nfsunesco/doc/isced_1997.htm|access-date=22 March 2020|archive-date=19 March 2017}}</ref>

For higher education, the preparation of the future workforce is a key priority. Many occupations rely on education that has been supported through campus-focused activities such as face-to-face interactions with other students, work-integrated learning, and further hands-on exercises.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kumar |first1=Arunaz |title=Impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on teaching and learning in health professional education: a mixed methods study protocol |journal=BMC Medical Education |year=2021 |volume=21 |issue=1 |article-number=439 |doi=10.1186/s12909-021-02871-w |pmid=34412603 |pmc=8374410 |doi-access=free }}</ref> For example, the healthcare workforce of doctors, nurses, and allied health professionals have been trained by in-person observations - similar to the apprenticeship model. In-person education has been shown to create stronger student-tutor and student-student interactions and relationships, which can promote better engagement. With COVID-19 and the pivot to distance learning, a similar level of depth is highly difficult to achieve. More evidence on feasibility, benefits, and obstacles is needed to analyse the drivers of economic impact for the various types of initiatives introduced in online education. 

=== Undergraduate education ===
[[File:TRACE OSU COVID-19 testing sign and students- 50624665398.jpg|thumb|left|upright|Sign at [[Oregon State University]] directing students to testing site]]
Undergraduate education is education conducted after [[secondary education]] and prior to [[post-graduate education]], for which the learner is typically awarded a [[bachelor's degree]].<ref name=":22" />

The closure of colleges and universities has widespread individual, organizational, and learning and teaching implications for students, faculty, administrators, and the institutions themselves.<ref name="Aristovnik et al. 2020"/><ref name="Crawford et al. 2020b">{{cite journal |vauthors=Crawford J, Percy A |date=2020 |title=JUTLP Editorial 17.3: Connection, digital education, and student-centric teaching practice before COVID-19 |url=https://ro.uow.edu.au/jutlp/vol17/iss3/1/ |journal=Journal of University Teaching and Learning Practice |volume=17 |issue=3 |access-date=24 August 2020 |doi=10.53761/1.17.3 |doi-broken-date=1 July 2025 |doi-access=free |archive-date=1 May 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210501101743/https://ro.uow.edu.au/jutlp/vol17/iss3/1/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> The initial period of rapid adaption during 2020 contained three primary responses to COVID-19: minimal legal response, delayed commencement of study periods, and rapid digitalization of curriculum.<ref name="Crawford et al. 2020a">{{cite journal | vauthors = Crawford J, Butler-Henderson K  |date=2020 |title=COVID-19: 20 countries' higher education intra-period digital pedagogy responses |url=https://journals.sfu.ca/jalt/index.php/jalt/article/view/191 |journal=Journal of Applied Learning & Teaching |volume=3 |issue=1 |pages=9–28 |doi=10.37074/jalt.2020.3.1.7 |access-date=24 August 2020|doi-access=free|hdl=10197/11344 |hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Panjehfouladgaran |first1=Hamidreza |last2=Stavropoulou |first2=Foteini |last3=Teimouri |first3=Misha |date=2024-02-13 |title=How Has the COVID-19 Pandemic Affected Students' Online Social Presence? |url=https://pubsonline.informs.org/doi/10.1287/ited.2022.0054 |journal=INFORMS Transactions on Education |volume=25 |issue=2 |pages=106–121 |language=en |doi=10.1287/ited.2022.0054 |issn=1532-0545|doi-access=free }}</ref> Thoughts about what to make of this situation resulted in optional learning online or in person depending on what the university declared as being mandatory.<ref>{{Cite web|title=6 Ways Universities Are Responding To Coronavirus|url=https://www.npr.org/2020/03/06/812462913/6-ways-universities-are-responding-to-coronavirus|access-date=8 December 2020|website=NPR.org|date=6 March 2020 |language=en | vauthors = Kamenetz A }}</ref>

Millions of students are expected to defer the start of their studies for their undergraduate degree to a later year due to the pandemic. This not only will negatively affect the future university intake process due to [[Shortage|shortages in places available]] but universities worldwide are expected to lose billions of USD in equivalent due to the number of students expected to study at university in the 2020–2021 academic year.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.theguardian.com/education/2020/may/20/uk-universities-facing-760m-hit-one-in-five-students-plan-defer|title=UK universities facing £760m hit as one in five students plan to defer|date=20 May 2020|website=[[The Guardian]]}}</ref>

Colleges and universities across the United States have been called upon to issue refunds to students for the cost of [[Tuition payments|tuition]] and [[room and board]].<ref name=":23">{{cite web|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/education/2020/03/21/coronavirus-college-students-online-closing-private-liberal-arts/2889546001/|title=Small colleges were already on the brink. Now, coronavirus threatens their existence| vauthors = Jesse D  |website=[[USA Today]]|language=en-US|access-date=22 March 2020}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news| vauthors = Korn M, Belkin D |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/to-fight-coronavirus-colleges-sent-students-home-now-will-they-refund-tuition-11584625536|title=To Fight Coronavirus, Colleges Sent Students Home. Now Will They Refund Tuition?|date=19 March 2020|work=[[The Wall Street Journal]]|access-date=22 March 2020|language=en-US|issn=0099-9660}}</ref>

While $6 billion in emergency relief is to be made available to students during the pandemic, Education Secretary [[Betsy DeVos]] decided on 21 April 2020 that it will only be made available to those students who are also already eligible for federal financial aid. This rule will exclude tens of thousands of undocumented students who participate in the government's [[Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals]] (DACA, or "Dreamers") program from being able to receive emergency relief funds.<ref>{{Cite news| vauthors = Green EL |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/04/22/us/politics/coronavirus-funds-colleges-dreamers.html|title=DeVos Excludes 'Dreamers' From Coronavirus College Relief|date=22 April 2020|work=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=23 April 2020|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

Apart from colleges losing vast amounts of income<ref>{{Cite web|title=Coronavirus pandemic brings staggering losses to colleges and universities|url=https://abcnews.go.com/Business/coronavirus-pandemic-brings-staggering-losses-colleges-universities/story?id=70359686|access-date=8 December 2020|website=[[ABC News (United States)|ABC News]]|language=en}}</ref> undergraduate students themselves have lost vast amounts of imperative education due to COVID-19.<ref>{{Cite news| vauthors = Goldstein D |date=5 June 2020|title=Research Shows Students Falling Months Behind During Virus Disruptions|language=en-US|work=[[The New York Times]]|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/06/05/us/coronavirus-education-lost-learning.html|access-date=8 December 2020|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> With the lack of regular education amongst all students, learning seems harder to manage. Before the COVID-19 pandemic, college students would have in-person classes, in-person office hours, and in-person extracurricular activities. However, the pandemic has created an atmosphere where students who have an idea about their future occupation, are learning essential information behind a screen. These changes have made focusing on classes built around a students selected major very difficult, as they are not experiencing what they are passionate about to the fullest extent.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Is online learning shrinking your attention span?|url=https://www.upbeacon.com/article/2020/09/tips-for-studing-at-home|access-date=8 December 2020|website=The Beacon}}</ref> The result of this is lost passion for specific subjects, the inability to focus on crucial information, and tainted academic integrity all over.

== Education in different countries==

=== Private schools in the United States ===
One effect of the COVID-19 outbreak in the United States was in the form of increases in private school enrollment. Many parents who sought out private school instruction needed a place to send their child due to the parents need to work outside of the home.<ref>{{Cite web| vauthors = Dickler J |date=8 November 2020 |title=Families jump to private schools as coronavirus drags on|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2020/11/08/coronavirus-why-families-are-jumping-to-private-schools.html |access-date=8 February 2021 |website=[[CNBC]]|language=en}}</ref>

An unintended consequence of this migration to private schooling is the widening inequality gap between families that can afford private school tuition and those who cannot.<ref>{{Cite magazine|title=What Happens When Private Schools Reopen and Public Schools Don't?|url=https://time.com/5885106/school-reopening-coronavirus/ |access-date=8 February 2021 |magazine=Time}}</ref> These families often had their children at home in virtual learning environments. Issues like poor broadband connection and the inability for parents to properly support their children's learning due to lack of English language skills or work conflicts saw certain students fall behind academically.<ref>{{Cite web |title=가난한 가정에겐 잔인한 여름방학 |url=https://h21.hani.co.kr/arti/world/world_general/41887.html |access-date=2022-09-25 |website=한겨레21 |language=ko}}</ref>

=== Primary and secondary schools in Kenya ===
A study on "teachers' and parents' preparedness to support virtual [[Impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on education in the United States|learning]] during the COVID-19 pandemic in Kenya" shows that most parents and teachers were not prepared to support virtual learning.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Ireri M | date = 2021 | title = Teachers' and parents' preparedness to support virtual learning during the COVID-19 pandemic in Kenya. | journal = African Journal of Empirical Research | volume = 2 | issue = 1 | pages = 95–102 <!-- | doi = 10.51867/ajer.v2i1.17 not working --> | doi = 10.51867/ajer.v2i1.17 | url = https://zenodo.org/record/4604609 | doi-access = free }}</ref> This issue affected all schools: public 8-4-4 schools, private 8-4-4 schools, international schools, and private schools in the country. This points to a weak support system for virtual education in Kenyan schools during COVID-19 outbreak affecting virtual learning delivery.

== Impact on local economies ==
In the United States of America, colleges and universities operate as "mini-cities" which generate significant revenue for cities, states, and regions.<ref name=":24">{{Cite news|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2020-03-10/college-towns-to-clear-out-with-virus-upending-local-businesses|title=College Towns to Clear Out as Virus Upends Local Businesses|date=10 March 2020|work=[[Bloomberg News|Bloomberg]]|access-date=22 March 2020|language=en}}</ref> For example, [[Princeton University]] estimated in 2017 that it contributed $1.58 billion [[United States dollar|USD]] per year to the [[New Jersey]] economy, and that students spent about $60 million in off-campus spending.<ref name=":24" /> College and university closures had a [[domino effect]] on economies with far-reaching implications.<ref name="fastcompany-economic-impacts" />

In March, [[Linda Bilmes]] of the [[John F. Kennedy School of Government|Harvard Kennedy School]] noted that "local hotels, restaurants, cafes, shops, car rental agencies and other local businesses obtain a significant share of annual revenue from graduation week and college reunions... these communities will suffer a lot of economic damage if the colleges remain closed at that time."<ref name=":24" />

Small towns which rely on college students to support the local economy and provide labour to local businesses were especially impacted by school closures and the exodus of students from campus.<ref name=":23" /> In [[Ithaca, New York]], [[Cornell University]] students spent at least $4 million a week in [[Tompkins County, New York|Tompkins County]]. In the wake of Cornell's decision to keep students home following spring break and transition to virtual instruction, the Mayor of Ithaca called for "immediate and forceful federal action — we will see a horrific economic impact as a result of Cornell University closing."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ithacajournal.com/story/news/local/2020/03/11/economic-impact-ithaca-cornells-closing-coronavirus/5022867002/|title=Loss of Cornell students during coronavirus pandemic could cost Ithaca, Tompkins $4M a week | vauthors = Platsky J |website=Ithaca Journal|language=en|access-date=22 March 2020}}</ref>

== Responses to the crisis ==

=== UNESCO recommendations ===
[[File:At home assignments during COVID-19 pandemic.png|thumb|upright|Digital assignment during COVID-19 pandemic in a Texas public school]]
UNESCO made ten recommendations for engaging in online learning:
# '''Examine the readiness and choose the most relevant tools:''' Decide on the use high-technology and low-technology solutions based on the reliability of local power supplies, internet connectivity, and digital skills of teachers and students. This could range through integrated digital learning platforms, video lessons, MOOCs, to broadcasting through radios and TVs.
# '''Ensure inclusion of the distance learning programmes:''' Implement measures to ensure that students including those with disabilities or from low-income backgrounds have access to distance learning programmes, if only a limited number of them have access to digital devices. Consider temporarily decentralising such devices from computer labs to families and support them with internet connectivity.
# '''Protect data privacy and data security:''' Assess data security when uploading data or educational resources to web spaces, as well as when sharing them with other organisations or individuals. Ensure that the use of applications and platforms does not violate students' data privacy.
# '''Prioritize solutions to address psychosocial challenges before teaching:''' Mobilize available tools to connect schools, parents, teachers, and students with each other. Create communities to ensure regular human interactions, enable social caring measures, and address possible psychosocial challenges that students may face when they are isolated.
# '''Plan the study schedule of the distance learning programmes:''' Organise discussions with stakeholders to examine the possible duration of school closures and decide whether the distance learning programme should focus on teaching new knowledge or enhance students' knowledge of prior lessons. Plan the schedule depending on the situation of the affected zones, level of studies, needs of students needs, and availability of parents. Choose the appropriate learning methodologies based on the status of school closures and home-based quarantines. Avoid learning methodologies that require face-to-face communication.
# '''Provide support to teachers and parents on the use of digital tools:''' Organise brief training or orientation sessions for teachers and parents as well, if monitoring and facilitation are needed. Help teachers to prepare the basic settings such as solutions to the use of internet data if they are required to provide live streaming of lessons.
# '''Blend appropriate approaches and limit the number of applications and platforms:''' Blend tools or media that are available for most students, both for synchronous communication and lessons, and for asynchronous learning. Avoid overloading students and parents by asking them to download and test too many applications or platforms.
# '''Develop distance learning rules and monitor students' learning process:''' Define the rules with parents and students on distance learning. Design formative questions, tests, or exercises to monitor closely students' learning process. Try to use tools to support submission of students' feedback and avoid overloading parents by requesting them to scan and send students' feedback
# '''Define the duration of distance learning units based on students' self-regulation skills:''' Keep a coherent timing according to the level of the students' self-regulation and metacognitive abilities especially for livestreaming classes. Preferably, the unit for primary school students should not be more than 20 minutes, and no longer than 40 minutes for secondary school students. 
# '''Create communities and enhance connection:''' Create communities of teachers, parents, and school managers to address sense of loneliness or helplessness, facilitate sharing of experience and discussion on coping strategies when facing learning difficulties.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://en.unesco.org/news/how-plan-distance-learning-solutions-during-temporary-schools-closures|title=How to plan distance learning solutions during temporary schools closures|date=6 March 2020|website=UNESCO|language=en|access-date=16 March 2020}}</ref>

=== Open Education Community response ===
Open Education community members have shared [[Open educational resources|open educational resources (OER)]] in response to COVID-19, including:

* Commonwealth of Learning created the resource "Keeping the doors of learning open".<ref>{{Cite web|title=Keeping the doors of learning open COVID-19 {{!}} COL|url=https://www.col.org/resources/keeping-doors-learning-open-covid-19|website=www.col.org|access-date=26 May 2020|archive-date=3 June 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210603034657/https://www.col.org/resources/keeping-doors-learning-open-covid-19|url-status=dead}}</ref> The project brings together a curated list of resources for policymakers, school and college administrators, teachers, parents and learners that will assist with student learning during the closure of educational institutions. Most of these are available as OER.
*Community Contributed Open Educational Resources for Teaching and Learning in the COVID-19 Era is a co-created spreadsheet of resources. There are multiple tabs on the spreadsheet providing links to: K-12 (primary / secondary) resources, OER repositories, OER toolkits, student support, online teaching, and more.<ref>{{Cite web|title=COVID-19 Open Education Community Contributed Resources|url=https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1iQtZoDphA5XYKHR32zUYJ9imjCh4c1DOfg14MRB7G_I/edit?usp=embed_facebook|website=Google Docs|language=en-US|access-date=26 May 2020}}</ref>
*OERu online courses<ref>{{Cite web|title=Capacity development – OER response to Covid-19|url=https://oer4covid.oeru.org/initiatives/capacity-development/|language=en-NZ|access-date=26 May 2020|archive-date=3 June 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210603034724/https://oer4covid.oeru.org/initiatives/capacity-development/|url-status=dead}}</ref> is a resource to build capacity in the design and development of OER-enabled online learning. The OERu offers two facilitated online courses including free access to a competency certification in copyright and [[Creative Commons license|Creative Commons licensing]]. These courses will provide skills for participants wanting to design and publish their own online courses using the OERu's open source, component-based digital learning environment.
*Teaching and Learning Online is a website by SkillsCommons and [[MERLOT]] that offers a free online resource page in response to COVID-19. This page helps teachers and students prepare to start teaching and learning online.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Teaching and Learning Online|url=https://www.merlot.org/merlot/viewSite.htm?id=9160704|website=www.merlot.org|access-date=26 May 2020}}</ref>
* The University of Arizona University Libraries created a "Library Support for Shifting to Online Teaching" page<ref>{{Cite web|title=LibGuides: Library Support for Shifting to Online Teaching: For Your K-12 Kids|url=https://libguides.library.arizona.edu/disruption/kids|vauthors=Church-Duran J|website=libguides.library.arizona.edu|language=en|access-date=26 May 2020|archive-date=26 May 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210526065004/https://libguides.library.arizona.edu/disruption/kids|url-status=dead}}</ref> and a Free-to-Use Course Materials webinar.<ref>{{Citation|title=Being efficient: What are sources of free-to-use course materials? Tuesday 1pm Session|url=https://arizona.hosted.panopto.com/Panopto/Pages/Viewer.aspx?id=2121eba3-cc86-4241-a0fd-ab840008bc88|language=en|access-date=26 May 2020}}</ref>
*WirLernenOnline is a German online platform to find learning material for digital lessons in primary school, secondary school, upper secondary and vocational education.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Homepage|url=https://wirlernenonline.de/|website=Wir lernen online|language=de-DE|access-date=26 May 2020}}</ref>

== Online learning platforms ==

Many educational institutions adopted online platforms and tools to continue teaching during the pandemic. Governments and private organizations also provided initiatives to bridge the digital divide and ensure students could access education.

=== Coursera ===
With schools closed, demand for online education platforms has increased.<ref name="EconTimes-IPO">{{Cite news|title=Coursera files for US IPO as edtech booms amid the pandemic | vauthors = Nishant N |date=6 May 2021 |work=The Economic Times |url=https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/tech/startups/coursera-files-for-us-ipo-as-edtech-booms-amid-the-pandemic/articleshow/81358853.cms |access-date=18 March 2021}}</ref> [[Coursera]], which can be taught online, also grew significantly during the pandemic.<ref name="EconTimes-IPO" />
* Coursera saw 59% revenue growth year over year, largely due to a pandemic-induced boom in digital learning.<ref name="CNBC-IPO">{{Cite web| vauthors = de León R |date=5 March 2021 |title=Coursera files for IPO amid online learning boom |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2021/03/05/coursera-files-for-ipo-amid-online-learning-boom-.html|access-date=18 March 2021 |website=[[CNBC]]|language=en}}</ref> 
* Total registered users in 2020 grew 65% over 2019.<ref name="CNBC-IPO" />
* During the pandemic, Coursera also partnered with more than 330 government agencies across 70 countries and 30 US states and cities as part of the Coursera Workforce Recovery Initiative.<ref name="CNBC-IPO" />

=== Zoom ===
The need for a platform for video conferences and facilitating online classrooms was created by the pandemic. [[Zoom (software)|Zoom]] had significantly grown from a lesser-known work software to one of the most popular video conferencing applications.<ref name="Zoom Vox">{{cite web |last1=Molla |first1=Rani |title=The pandemic was great for Zoom. What happens when there's a vaccine? |url=https://www.vox.com/recode/21726260/zoom-microsoft-teams-video-conferencing-post-pandemic-coronavirus |website=[[Vox (website)|Vox]]|date=4 December 2020 |access-date=29 March 2022}}</ref>
*In December in 2019, Zoom had just 10 million daily meeting participants. This number increased significantly due to the pandemic moving classrooms and workspaces online to 350 million.<ref name="Zoom Vox" />
*At the peak of online learning within the pandemic, there were more than 90,000 schools using Zoom.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Iqbal |first1=Mansoor |title=Zoom Revenue and Usage Statistics (2022) |url=https://www.businessofapps.com/data/zoom-statistics/ |website=Business of Apps |access-date=29 March 2022}}</ref>

=== Google Classroom ===
The closure of schools created a need for a virtual classroom portal, and [[Google Classroom]] served that purpose for many schools. It offered teachers features such as the integration of the [[Google Suite]] along with learning management tools for uploading and submitting assignments.<ref name="GoogleClass">{{cite web |last1=De Vynck |first1=Gerrit |last2=Bergin |first2=Marc |title=Google Classroom Users Doubled as Quarantines Spread |url=https://www.bloombergquint.com/business/google-widens-lead-in-education-market-as-students-rush-online |website=Bloomberg Quint |date=9 April 2020 |access-date=29 March 2022}}</ref> Another factor that helped Google Classroom become a large option for schools is the integration with [[Chromebooks]] that many schools had already utilized before the pandemic.<ref name="GoogleClass" />
*From 2020 to 2021, Google Classroom saw an increase from 40 million to over 150 million users <ref name="TechCrunch">{{cite web |last1=Perez |first1=Sarah |title=Google to roll out slate of over 50 updates for Classroom, Meet and other online education tools |url=https://techcrunch.com/2021/02/17/google-to-roll-out-slate-of-over-50-updates-for-classroom-meet-and-other-online-education-tools/ |website=Tech Crunch |date=17 February 2021 |access-date=29 March 2022}}</ref>

In India, initiatives like the [[National Level Common Entrance Examination]] (NLCEE) provided free online coaching to students during the pandemic. By offering scholarships and virtual career guidance, NLCEE supported underprivileged students in continuing their education and preparing for competitive exams despite the disruptions caused by COVID-19.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.thehindu.com/news/national/other-states/start-up-offers-free-coaching-to-100-needy-students-via-competitive-exam/article65490830.ece|title=Start-up offers free coaching to 100 needy students via competitive exam|newspaper=The Hindu|access-date=8 January 2025}}</ref>

== Vaccination ==
[[File:Unvaxxed Parents NYC 20-Feb-2022.png|thumb|Divergent after-school pickup instructions for vaccinated and unvaccinated parents at an elementary school in New York City]]
Over 1000 colleges in the United States required on-campus students to be fully-vaccinated against COVID-19 for the 2021–2022 academic year.<ref>{{Cite web |date=11 October 2021 |title=What Colleges Require the COVID-19 Vaccine? {{!}} BestColleges |url=https://www.bestcolleges.com/news/2021/10/11/list-of-colleges-that-require-covid-19-vaccine/ |access-date=23 March 2022 |website=www.bestcolleges.com |language=en-US |archive-date=24 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220324003605/https://www.bestcolleges.com/news/2021/10/11/list-of-colleges-that-require-covid-19-vaccine/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> Of those 1000 schools, over 300 also require that students receive a booster shot.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Teague |first=Katie |title=Big Cities Drop Vaccine Requirements as COVID Cases Fall |url=https://www.cnet.com/health/vaccine-mandates-cities-lift-requirements-as-covid-cases-drop/ |access-date=23 March 2022 |website=CNET |language=en}}</ref> These mandates came after over 700,000 COVID cases were linked to U.S. colleges from the start of the pandemic to the end of May 2021.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wolf |first1=Susan M |last2=Hodge |first2=James G |date=15 January 2022 |title=Designing COVID-19 vaccine mandates in colleges and universities: a roadmap to the 10 key questions |journal=Journal of Law and the Biosciences |volume=9 |issue=1 |article-number=lsab035 |doi=10.1093/jlb/lsab035 |issn=2053-9711 |pmc=8761499 |pmid=35047186}}</ref> Many of these colleges also required staff and faculty to be fully vaccinated as well, especially after federal vaccine mandates were announced in November 2021.<ref>{{cite web |title=New federal COVID-19 vaccination rule affects colleges |url=https://www.insidehighered.com/news/2021/11/05/new-federal-covid-19-vaccination-rule-affects-colleges |access-date=23 March 2022 |website=www.insidehighered.com }}</ref> 

All states have laws that require that universities offer medical exemptions to the vaccine mandate and most also require that Universities offer religious exemptions to the mandate. Universities took varied approaches to disciplining students who did provide proof of vaccination or have an approved medical or religious exemption. The University of Virginia disenrolled students who did not follow the mandate including 49 students who had already been enrolled in classes for the Fall 2021 semester.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Reilly|first=Liam|date=21 August 2021|title=University of Virginia disenrolls 238 students for not complying with university's vaccine mandate|url=https://www.cnn.com/2021/08/20/us/uva-disenrolling-students-vaccine/index.html|access-date=21 August 2021|website=[[CNN]]}}</ref>

=== Localised closures ===
As of {{Education statistics on the COVID-19 pandemic|date}}, {{Education statistics on the COVID-19 pandemic|local}} countries have localised school closures. [[UNESCO]] estimates 473,933,356&nbsp;learners are potentially at risk (pre-primary to upper-secondary education) and 77,938,904 learners are potentially at risk in tertiary education.<ref name="UNESCO" />

!scope="row"| [[Australia]]
|Australia did not unilaterally close schools or universities in line with advice from the [[Australian Health Protection Principal Committee]]. 
Some private and independent schools have chosen to close.<ref name=":25">{{Cite news| vauthors = Karp P |url= https://www.theguardian.com/world/2020/mar/16/why-australia-is-not-shutting-schools-to-help-control-the-spread-of-coronavirus |title=Why Australia is not shutting schools to help control the spread of coronavirus|date=16 March 2020|work=[[The Guardian]]|access-date=16 March 2020|language=en-GB|issn=0261-3077}}</ref>

On 22–23 March, the state governments of [[Victoria (Australia)|Victoria]] and the [[Australian Capital Territory]] contradicted federal government advice by enacting school closures, while the [[New South Wales]] state government encouraged students to stay home from school if possible.<ref name=":26">{{cite web|url=https://www.canberratimes.com.au/story/6691357/confusion-over-coronavirus-school-closures/|title=Confusion over coronavirus school closures | vauthors = McCulloch D |date=23 March 2020|website=The Canberra Times|access-date=26 March 2020}}</ref> Many universities closed temporarily and transitioned to [[Online learning in higher education|online learning]].<ref name=":27">{{cite web|url=https://www.itnews.com.au/news/online-mass-exodus-how-australian-unis-are-coping-with-covid-19-539630|title=Online mass exodus: How Australian unis are coping with COVID-19|website=iTnews|access-date=26 March 2020}}</ref>
|[[COVID-19 pandemic in Australia]]
|<ref name=":25" /><ref name=":26" /><ref name=":27" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Edwards |first1=Ben |last2=Moschion |first2=Julie |last3=Zhu |first3=Anna |date=2023 |title=Children and youth in the age of COVID -19 |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ajs4.262 |journal=Australian Journal of Social Issues |language=en |volume=58 |issue=1 |pages=4–12 |doi=10.1002/ajs4.262 |s2cid=257642712 |issn=0157-6321|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

!scope="row"| [[Brazil]]
|As of 16 March, Brazil has more confirmed cases of coronavirus than any other Latin American country, however President [[Jair Bolsonaro]] has issued few country-wide measures to slow the spread of the virus.<ref name=":17" /><ref name=":18" /> Because the president and federal government failed to act regarding the pandemic and had, as of 18 March, not decided to cancel classes in the whole country, lower instances of government acted autonomously. State schools, municipal schools, private institutions and universities acted differently regarding suspending classes at once, gradually or not at all, and between replacing classes with [[distance education]] or simply postponing them. Because of that, there are only "localised" (as opposed to "national") school closures, as of 20 March, according to UNESCO.<ref name="UNESCO" />

States such as São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro and Pernambuco have cancelled classes in state schools, but some municipal schools continue having classes normally even in those states.<ref name="g1rj13">{{cite web|url=https://g1.globo.com/rj/rio-de-janeiro/blog/edimilson-avila/noticia/2020/03/13/municipio-do-rio-vai-suspender-aulas-na-rede-publica-semana-que-vem.ghtml|title=Escolas públicas e particulares do RJ não terão aulas a partir de segunda-feira | vauthors = Ávila E |date=13 March 2020|publisher=G1 Rio de Janeiro|language=pt}}</ref><ref name="g1sp17">{{cite web|url=https://g1.globo.com/sp/sao-paulo/noticia/2020/03/17/coronavirus-escolas-estaduais-tem-menos-de-5percent-de-presenca-e-municipais-30percent-nesta-terca.ghtml|title=Coronavírus: escolas estaduais de SP têm menos de 5% de presença e municipais, 30% nesta terça|date=17 March 2020|publisher=G1 São Paulo|language=pt}}</ref><ref name="g1pb17">{{cite web|url=https://g1.globo.com/pb/paraiba/noticia/2020/03/17/governo-da-pb-suspende-aulas-na-rede-estadual-e-recomenda-cancelamento-de-eventos-por-90-dias.ghtml|title=Governo da PB suspende aulas na rede estadual e recomenda cancelamento de eventos por 90 dias|date=17 March 2020|publisher=G1 Pernambuco|language=pt}}</ref> [[Minas Gerais]] state initially cancelled classes for public schools between for only three days<ref name="em15">{{cite web|url=https://www.em.com.br/app/noticia/gerais/2020/03/15/interna_gerais,1129119/coronavirus-governo-de-minas-suspende-aulas-na-rede-estadual.shtml|title=Coronavírus: governo de Minas suspende aulas na rede estadual | vauthors = Ronan G |date=15 March 2020|publisher=Estado de Minas Gerais|language=pt}}</ref> and on 18 March, the state governor announced that classes in the region of the state capital [[Belo Horizonte]] were cancelled indefinitely, because there was confirmed [[community transmission]] in the region, but the rest of the state would continue having classes normally until further notice.<ref name="am18">{{cite web|url=http://www.agenciaminas.mg.gov.br/noticia/rede-estadual-tem-calendario-de-aulas-alterado-como-medida-preventiva-contra-o-coronavirus|title=Rede estadual tem calendário de aulas alterado como medida preventiva contra o coronavírus|date=18 March 2020|publisher=Agência Minas|language=pt}}</ref>

In São Paulo, classes are being cancelled gradually, so that parents had time to come up with solutions that didn't involve letting the kids be with their grandparents. Between 16 and 20 March, students could go to class, but absentees would not be penalised. Classes were indefinitely cancelled starting on 23 March.<ref name="g1sp17" />

Regarding the food safety of students, some municipal and state schools announced "food kits" for weekly pickup such as in [[Recife]]<ref name="jc15">{{cite web|url=https://g1.globo.com/pe/pernambuco/noticia/2020/03/15/universidades-e-instituicoes-de-ensino-tecnico-suspendem-aulas-em-pernambuco.ghtml |title=Universidades e instituições de ensino técnico suspendem aulas em Pernambuco | trans-title = Universities and technical education institutions suspend classes in Pernambuco | vauthors = Alves P |date=15 March 2020|publisher= State of Pernambuco | language=pt}}</ref> or that some selected schools would remain open for students to have lunch, such as in [[Espírito Santo]].<ref name="g1es16">{{cite web|url=https://g1.globo.com/es/espirito-santo/noticia/2020/03/16/aulas-da-rede-estadual-no-es-sao-suspensas-para-evitar-contagio-por-novo-coronavirus.ghtml|title=Coronavírus: Governo do ES suspende aulas e antecipa férias|date=16 March 2020|publisher=G1 Espírito Santo|language=pt}}</ref>

In higher education, [[Unicamp]] was the first university of the country to cancel all classes, stating on 13 March. Initially, classes were cancelled until 31 March, but later the university extended the suspension until 12 April.<ref name="unicamp16">{{cite web|url=https://www.unicamp.br/unicamp/noticias/2020/03/16/coronavirus-resolucao-gr-242020-suspende-atividades-ate-12-de-abril|title=Coronavírus: Novo Comunicado. Reitor destaca regras para funcionamento da Universidade|date=16 March 2020|publisher=Unicamp|language=pt}}</ref> On 11 March, one student of [[University of São Paulo|USP]] was confirmed with the disease, leading one department to cancel classes for a single day,<ref name="carta11">{{cite web|url=https://www.cartacapital.com.br/saude/usp-confirma-primeiro-caso-de-coronavirus-e-cancela-aulas-em-departamento|title=USP confirma primeiro caso de coronavírus e cancela aulas em departamento | vauthors = Galvani G |date=11 March 2020|publisher=Carta Capital|language=pt}}</ref> and it wasn't until 17 March that the whole university cancelled classes.<ref name="uol13">{{cite web|url=https://noticias.uol.com.br/saude/ultimas-noticias/redacao/2020/03/13/usp-e-unesp-vao-suspender-as-aulas-a-partir-do-dia-17-de-marco.htm|title=Coronavírus: USP e Unesp suspenderão as aulas a partir do dia 17 de março|date=13 March 2020|publisher=UOL|language=pt}}</ref> Many universities across the country cancelled classes, such as [[Universidade Federal de Viçosa|UFV]] (since 16 March)<ref name="ufv14">{{cite web|url=https://www2.dti.ufv.br/noticias/scripts/exibeNoticiaMulti.php?codNot=32257|title=UFV decide suspender atividades acadêmicas por tempo indeterminado|date=14 March 2020|publisher=Universidade Federal de Viçosa|language=pt}}</ref> and [[UNILA]] (since 17 March),<ref name="unila16">{{cite web|url=https://portal.unila.edu.br/noticias/coronavirus-unila-suspende-aulas-e-implementa-expediente-administrativo-especial|title=Coronavírus: UNILA suspende aulas e implementa expediente administrativo especial|date=16 March 2020|publisher=Universidade Federal da Integração Latino-Americana|language=pt}}</ref> but others remain open.

In the city of [[São Paulo]], which is home to half of [[History of the Jews in Brazil|Brazil's 120,000 Jews]], Jewish schools have closed and some are providing class remotely over video. In Rio de Janeiro, Jewish day schools also closed in the absence of a state-wide decision regarding the closure of Rio's public and private schools.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.timesofisrael.com/brazilian-jewish-schools-close-to-prevent-coronavirus-infections/|title=Brazilian Jewish schools close to prevent coronavirus infections| vauthors = Gilban MM |website=timesofisrael.com|language=en-US|access-date=16 March 2020}}</ref>

!scope="row"| [[Finland]]{{Ref|NoteB|b}}
|Pre-primary education and grades 1–3 will continue for the children of parents working in sectors critical to the functioning of society, as well as for children with special needs from pre-primary to upper secondary education. Early Childhood Education and Care will be provided for all children, whose parents are unable to arrange their care at home. In other levels of education, contact teaching can continue, if considered necessary for the completion of studies.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Education services and the coronavirus|url=https://www.oph.fi/en/news/2020/education-services-and-coronavirus|access-date=16 June 2020|website=[[Finnish National Agency for Education]]|language=en}}</ref>

!scope="row"| [[Sweden]]{{Ref|NoteB|b}}
||Schools have mainly remained open during the pandemic. However, on March 17, 2020, the Swedish government declared that high schools, vocational schools and Universities should close, and instead recommended continuing lectures by distance education. Already after the summer breaks, however, Swedish high schools reopened, as the negative impact of school closures were assessed as outweighing the potential benefits. Universities and other adult educational forms were referred to the general recommendations that applied for the society.

!scope="row"| [[United States]]
|{{Anchor|United States}}{{As of|2020|04|10}}, most American public and private elementary and secondary schools—at least 124,000—had stopped in-person instruction nationwide, affecting at least 55.1 million students.<ref name="EdWeekMap">{{cite news|url=https://www.edweek.org/ew/section/multimedia/map-coronavirus-and-school-closures.html|title=Map: Coronavirus and School Closures|website=Education Week|date=7 March 2020 |publisher=Editorial Projects in Education|access-date=23 April 2020}}</ref> By 2 May, school buildings had been ordered or recommended to be closed for the remainder of the academic year in 47 states, four territories, and the District of Columbia.<ref name="EdWeekMap" /> Most schools shifted to online learning; however, there are concerns about student access to necessary technology, absenteeism, and accommodations for special needs students.<ref>{{cite news|title=As School Moves Online, Many Students Stay Logged Out| vauthors = Goldstein D, Popescu A, Hannah-Jones N  |date=6 April 2020|work=[[The New York Times]]|location=New York City, New York|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/04/06/us/coronavirus-schools-attendance-absent.html|access-date=11 April 2020}}</ref> School systems also looked to adjust grading scales and graduation requirements to mitigate the disruption caused by the unprecedented closures.<ref>{{cite news|title=Grading Students During the Coronavirus Crisis: What's the Right Call?| vauthors = Sawchuk S  |date=1 April 2020|work=Education Week|location=Bethesda, Maryland|url=https://www.edweek.org/ew/articles/2020/04/01/grading-students-during-the-coronavirus-crisis-whats.html |access-date=11 April 2020}}</ref>

A large number of higher educational institutions cancelled classes and closed dormitories in response to the outbreak, including all members of the [[Ivy League]],<ref>{{cite web | vauthors = Murray C |title=Online classes, travel bans: How the Ivy League is responding to the coronavirus outbreak |url=https://www.thedp.com/article/2020/03/penn-coronavirus-ivy-league-online-classes-travel |website=thedp.com |access-date=29 March 2020}}</ref> and many other public and private universities across the country.<ref>{{cite web |title=Columbia, Harvard, NYU, and other major US colleges and universities that have switched to remote classes and are telling students to move out of dorms to prevent the spread of the coronavirus |url=https://www.businessinsider.com/major-colleges-and-universities-going-remote-over-coronavirus-fears |website=[[Business Insider]] |access-date=29 March 2020}}</ref> Many universities also expanded the use of pass/fail [[Academic grading in the United States|grading]] for the Spring 2020 semester.<ref>{{cite news|title=#Pass/Fail Nation| vauthors = Burke L |date=19 March 2020|work=Inside Higher Education|location=Washington, D.C.|url=http://www.insidehighered.com/news/2020/03/19/colleges-go-passfail-address-coronavirus|access-date=11 April 2020}}</ref> On 27 March, President Donald Trump signed the CARES Act, which includes economic relief for student loan borrowers. The Act placed all federally held student loans into forbearance with no interest to be added through 30 September 2020.<ref>{{cite web |title=Coronavirus and Forbearance Info for Students, Borrowers, and Parents |url=https://studentaid.gov/announcements-events/coronavirus |website=Federal Student Aid |access-date=28 April 2020}}</ref>

'''Kenya''',{{efn|{{IPAc-en|ˈ|k|ɛ|n|j|ə}},<ref>{{Cite Collins Dictionary|Kenya}}</ref> {{IPA|sw|ˈkɛɲɑ|lang|small=no}}}} officially the '''Republic of Kenya''',{{efn|{{langx|sw|Jamhuri ya Kenya}}}} is a country located in East Africa. With an estimated population of more than 54.2&nbsp;million as of mid-2026,<ref>{{cite web |date=23 December 2021 |title=Kenya National Bureau of Statistics – Kenya's Top Data Site |url=https://www.knbs.or.ke/ |access-date=11 January 2025 |language=en-US}}</ref>{{update after|2030}} it is the [[List of countries and dependencies by population|26th-most populous country]] in the world<ref name="KNBS2019"/> and the [[List of African countries by population|seventh-most populous]] in Africa. Kenya's capital and largest city is [[Nairobi]]. The second-largest and oldest city is [[Mombasa]], a port city located on [[Mombasa Island]]. Other major cities within the country include [[Kisumu]], [[Nakuru]] and [[Eldoret]]. Going clockwise, Kenya is bordered by South Sudan to the northwest, Ethiopia to the north, Somalia to the east, the Indian Ocean to the southeast, Tanzania to the southwest, and [[Lake Victoria]] and Uganda to the west. [[Geography of Kenya|Its geography]], [[Climate change in Kenya|climate]] and [[Demographics of Kenya|population]] vary. In western Rift Valley counties, the landscape includes cold, snow-capped mountaintops (such as Batian, Nelion, and Point Lenana on [[Mount Kenya]]) with surrounding forests, wildlife, and fertile agricultural regions in temperate climates. In other areas there are dry, [[arid]], and [[Semi-arid climate|semi-arid]] climates, as well as absolute deserts (such as the [[Chalbi Desert]] and [[Nyiri Desert]]).

Kenya's earliest inhabitants included some of the first humans to evolve from ancestral members of the genus [[Homo]]. Ample fossil evidence for this evolutionary history has been found at [[Koobi Fora]]. Later, Kenya was inhabited by [[hunter-gatherer]]s similar to the present-day [[Hadza people]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=African Hunter-Gatherers: Survival, History and Politics of Identity |url=https://repository.kulib.kyoto-u.ac.jp/dspace/bitstream/2433/68396/1/ASM_S_26_257.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181104052710/https://repository.kulib.kyoto-u.ac.jp/dspace/bitstream/2433/68396/1/ASM_S_26_257.pdf |archive-date=4 November 2018 |access-date=18 October 2021 |website=repository.kulib.kyoto-u.ac.jp}}</ref><ref name=researchgate_271694891>{{cite web |title=The East African Bushmen |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/271694891 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220109200619/https://www.researchgate.net/publication/271694891_The_Myth_of_the_East_African_%27Bushmen%27 |archive-date=9 January 2022 |access-date=18 October 2021 |website=researchgate.net}}</ref> According to archaeological dating of associated artefacts and skeletal material, [[South Cushitic languages|Cushitic speakers]] first settled in the region's lowlands between 3,200 and 1,300 BC, a phase known as the Lowland [[Savanna Pastoral Neolithic]]. [[Nilo-Saharan languages|Nilotic]]-speaking [[Pastoralism|pastoralists]] (ancestral to Kenya's Nilotic speakers) began migrating from present-day South Sudan into Kenya around 500 BC.<ref name="EhretCHS" /> [[Bantu languages|Bantu people]] settled at the coast and the interior between 250 BC and 500 AD.<ref>{{cite web |title=Wonders Of The African World |url=http://www.pbs.org/wonders/Episodes/Epi2/swahi_2.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191019091759/http://www.pbs.org/wonders/Episodes/Epi2/swahi_2.htm |archive-date=19 October 2019 |access-date=18 October 2021 |publisher=PBS}}</ref> European contact began in 1500 AD with the [[Portuguese Empire]], and effective colonisation of Kenya began in the 19th century during the [[European exploration of Africa]]. Modern-day Kenya emerged from [[East Africa Protectorate|a protectorate]], established by the [[British Empire]] in 1895, and the subsequent [[Kenya Colony]], which began in 1920. Mombasa was the capital of the [[British East Africa Protectorate]],<ref name=britannica_20250110>{{cite web |date=10 January 2025 |title=Mombasa {{!}} History, Map, Location, Population, & Facts {{!}} Britannica |url=https://www.britannica.com/place/Mombasa |access-date=11 January 2025 |website=www.britannica.com}}</ref> which included most of what is now Kenya and southwestern Somalia, from 1889 to 1907. Disputes between the UK and the colony led to the [[Mau Mau revolution]], which began in 1952, and the declaration of Kenya's independence in 1963. After independence, Kenya remained a member of the [[Commonwealth of Nations]].

Kenya is a [[Presidential system|presidential]] [[representative democratic]] republic, in which elected officials represent the people and the president is the head of state and government.<ref name=vic_20071213>{{Cite web |date=13 December 2007 |title=Victorian Electronic Democracy – Final Report – Table of ContentsVictorian Electronic Democracy – Final Report – Glossary |url=http://www.parliament.vic.gov.au/SARC/E-Democracy/Final_Report/Glossary.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071213045132/http://www.parliament.vic.gov.au/SARC/E-Democracy/Final_Report/Glossary.htm |archive-date=13 December 2007 |access-date=29 January 2019}}</ref> The country is a member of the United Nations, [[Commonwealth of Nations|the Commonwealth]], [[World Bank]], [[International Monetary Fund]], [[World Trade Organization]], [[COMESA]], [[International Criminal Court]], as well as several other international organisations. It is also a [[major non-NATO ally]] of the United States. [[Kenya's economy]] is the largest in East and Central Africa, with Nairobi serving as a major regional commercial hub.<ref name="largest-economy">{{cite news | url= https://www.express.co.uk/news/world/2045350/africa-richest-country-kenya-overtake-ethiopia | title= One of Africa's 'richest' countries set to be overtaken by neighbour – £12bn more | work=Express | date=27 April 2025 | access-date=29 April 2025 | author=Robinson, Rebecca }}</ref> With a per-capita [[Gross National Income]] of $2,110,<ref>{{Cite web |title=GNI per capita, Atlas method (current US$) – Kenya |url= https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/NY.GNP.PCAP.CD?locations=KE&year_high_desc=true |access-date=29 April 2025 |website=worldbank.org |publisher=World Bank }}</ref> the country is a [[Developing country|lower-middle-income]] economy. Agriculture is the country's largest economic sector; tea and coffee are the sector's traditional cash crops, while fresh flowers are a fast-growing export. The [[service industry]], particularly tourism, is also one of the country's major economic drivers. Kenya is a member of the [[East African Community]] trade bloc,<ref>{{cite web |title=East African Community |url=https://www.eala.org/uploads/The_Treaty_for_the_Establishment_of_the_East_Africa_Community_2006_1999.pdf |access-date=19 December 2023 |website=eala.org |archive-date=24 December 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231224100426/https://www.eala.org/uploads/The_Treaty_for_the_Establishment_of_the_East_Africa_Community_2006_1999.pdf |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=East African Federation |url=https://www.eac.int/political-federation |access-date=19 December 2023 |website=eac.int |archive-date=15 December 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231215003829/https://www.eac.int/political-federation |url-status=live}}</ref> though some international trade organisations categorise it as part of the [[Greater Horn of Africa]].<ref>Maxwell, Daniel, and Ben Watkins. "Humanitarian information systems and emergencies in the Greater Horn of Africa: logical components and logical linkages." Disasters 27.1 (2003): 72–90.</ref> Africa is Kenya's largest export market, followed by the European Union.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Mwangi S. Kimenyi |last2=Francis M. Mwega |last3=Njuguna S. Ndung'u |date=May 2016 |title=The African Lions: Kenya country case study |url=http://www.brookings.edu/~/media/research/files/papers/2016/05/16-kenya-country-case-study/kenya-country-case.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160527210738/http://www.brookings.edu/~/media/research/files/papers/2016/05/16-kenya-country-case-study/kenya-country-case.pdf |archive-date=27 May 2016 |access-date=23 May 2016 |publisher=The Brookings Institution}}</ref>

== Etymology ==
The Republic of Kenya is named after [[Mount Kenya]]. The earliest recorded version of the modern name was written by German explorer [[Johann Ludwig Krapf]] in the 19th century. While travelling with a Kamba caravan led by the long-distance trader [[Chief Kivoi Mwendwa|Chief Kivoi]], Krapf spotted the mountain peak and asked what it was called. Kivoi told him "''Kĩ-Nyaa''" or "''Kĩlĩma- Kĩinyaa''", probably because the pattern of black rock and white snow on its peaks reminded him of the feathers of the male ostrich.<ref name="sullivan">{{cite book |last=Sullivan |first=Paul |title=Kikuyu Districts |publisher=Mkuki na Nyota Publishers |year=2006 |location=Dar es Salaam, Tanzania}}</ref> In archaic [[Gikuyu language|Kikuyu]], the word 'nyaga' or more commonly 'manyaganyaga' is used to describe an extremely bright object. The Agikuyu, who inhabit the slopes of Mt. Kenya, call it Kĩrĩma Kĩrĩnyaga (literally 'the mountain with brightness') in [[Kikuyu language|Kikuyu]], while the [[Embu people|Embu]] call it "''Ki-nyaga''" or Kirima Kinyaga. All three names have the same meaning.<ref>{{cite web |title=History |url=http://www.kenyaembassy.com/aboutkenyahistory.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160526191351/http://www.kenyaembassy.com/aboutkenyahistory.html |archive-date=26 May 2016 |access-date=13 May 2016}}</ref>

Ludwig Krapf recorded the name as both ''Kenia'' and ''Kegnia''.<ref name="Krapf">{{cite book |last=Krapf |first=Johann Ludwig |title=Travels, Researches, and Missionary Labours in Eastern Africa |publisher=Frank Cass & Co.
